Low calcium, low phosphate, low PTH

question: Which of the following biochemical patterns is most characteristic of primary hyperparathyroidism?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most common cause of primary hyperparathyroidism is a solitary parathyroid adenoma, which autonomously secretes parathyroid hormone (PTH), leading to hypercalcemia.

  • Primary hyperparathyroidism results from autonomous overproduction of parathyroid hormone (PTH), leading to hypercalcemia

  • The distribution of causes is:

    • Solitary parathyroid adenoma → ~80-85% (most common)

    • Parathyroid hyperplasia (all four glands) → ~10-15%

    • Parathyroid carcinoma → <1%

  • Solitary adenoma:

    • Usually, a benign neoplasm of chief cells

    • Produces unregulated PTH secretion

    • Leads to classic biochemical findings: hypercalcemia, hypophosphatemia, increased bone resorption

Parathyroid carcinoma (Option A): Hypercalcemia due to excess calcium intake + absorbable alkali, not bone turnover.

Diffuse hyperplasia of all four parathyroid glands (Option B): Less common; classically associated with MEN 1.

Multiple parathyroid adenomas (Option D): Occur, but are far less frequent than a single adenoma.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3275, 3276.
lessonTitle: Disorders of Parathyroid Gland and MEN Syndromes

options.text: Diffuse hyperplasia of all four parathyroid glands

question: Which of the following findings represents the most common underlying cause of primary hyperparathyroidism?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Hypercalcemia results from increased calcium entry into the extracellular fluid, which can occur via:
    • Increased bone resorption
    • Increased intestinal calcium absorption
    • Increased renal calcium reabsorption
  • Hyperthyroidism causes hypercalcemia through:
    • Thyroid hormone-mediated high bone turnover
    • Bone resorption exceeds bone formation
    • Occurs in up to 20% of hyperthyroid patients
  • Resulting hypercalcemia is usually mild to moderate but reflects a bone-driven mechanism
  • Common features of hypercalcemia across causes include:
    • Neurologic: fatigue, lethargy, confusion
    • Renal: polyuria, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
    • GI: constipation, nausea
    • Musculoskeletal: proximal muscle weakness
    • Cardiac: shortened QT interval

Milk-alkali syndrome (Option A): Hypercalcemia due to excess calcium intake + absorbable alkali, not bone turnover.

Vitamin D intoxication (Option B): Predominantly causes hypercalcemia via increased intestinal calcium absorption.

Sarcoidosis (Option D): Caused by unregulated extrarenal 1,25-(OH)₂D production, increasing gut absorption.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3274, 3275.
lessonTitle: Disorders of Parathyroid Gland and MEN Syndromes
question: Which of the following conditions causes hypercalcemia primarily due to increased bone turnover, in which bone resorption exceeds bone formation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The gastrointestinal symptom most commonly associated with hypercalcemia is constipation.

  • Hypercalcemia causes depression of neuromuscular excitability by increasing the threshold for action potentials.
  • This results in smooth muscle relaxation, particularly affecting the gastrointestinal tract

System-wise clinical manifestations of hypercalcemia:

System

Clinical manifestation

Gastrointestinal
  • Constipation (most common)
  • Anorexia
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Abdominal pain
  • Ileus in severe hypercalcemia

Renal
  • Polyuria and polydipsia
  • Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
  • Dehydration → prerenal azotemia
  • Nephrolithiasis
  • Nephrocalcinosis (chronic cases)

Neurologic / Psychiatric
  • Fatigue
  • Impaired concentration
  • Confusion and lethargy
  • Stupor and coma in severe hypercalcemia
  • Depression, apathy (“psychiatric overtones ”)

Musculoskeletal
  • Proximal muscle weakness
  • Bone pain (if due to malignancy or hyperparathyroidism)

Cardiovascular
  • Shortened QT interval
  • Arrhythmias in severe cases
  • These findings are classically remembered as “stones, bones, groans, thrones, and psychiatric overtones.”

Diarrhoea (Option A) and Hyperactive bowel sounds (Option B): Hypercalcemia causes decreased GI motility, not diarrhoea or hyperactive bowel sounds

Hematochezia (Option D): Hematochezia is unrelated to calcium homeostasis



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3274, 3275.
lessonTitle: Disorders of Parathyroid Gland and MEN Syndromes
question: Which of the following gastrointestinal symptoms is most commonly associated with hypercalcemia?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The parathyroid glands, located behind the thyroid, consist of four small glands that produce parathyroid hormone (PTH), an 84-amino acid peptide.
  • The calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) regulates PTH secretion, which responds to changes in serum calcium levels.

FGF-23 (Fibroblast growth factor 23) (Option B) is a phosphaturic hormone that suppresses parathyroid hormone (PTH). It regulates calcium and phosphate metabolism by reducing phosphate levels and increasing calcium levels in the blood, which can lead to nephrolithiasis.

Vitamin D3 (Option C) promotes calcium absorption, bone mineralisation and tissue differentiation. Deficiency of this vitamin leads to hypocalcemia, rickets, and osteomalacia, while its excess can result in hypercalcemia.

Calcitonin (Option D) is a peptide hormone secreted by the parafollicular C cells of the thyroid gland. It is a tumour marker in medullary thyroid carcinoma and can be used therapeutically for conditions such as osteoporosis and Paget’s disease of bone.



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Volume I, Page 3169, 3170.
  2. Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 661.
lessonTitle: Disorders of Parathyroid Gland and MEN Syndromes
question: A 65-year-old patient presents with constipation, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, confusion, and bone pain. Laboratory tests reveal elevated calcium levels. Considering the role of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) in calcium homeostasis, which of the following is regulated by CaSR?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) is a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) expressed predominantly on the chief cells of the parathyroid glands and in the kidneys.

  • It continuously monitors extracellular ionized calcium concentration and plays a central role in calcium homeostasis.
    • High serum calcium activates the CaSR, which suppresses PTH secretion and decreases PTH synthesis.
    • Low serum calcium reduces CaSR activation, leading to increased PTH secretion.
  • Thus, PTH secretion is directly regulated by CaSR, making it the principal physiological target of this receptor.

FGF-23 (Option B) is produced by osteocytes and osteoblasts and primarily regulates phosphate homeostasis by reducing renal phosphate reabsorption and suppressing 1α-hydroxylase activity. It is not directly regulated by CaSR.

Vitamin D3 (Option C): Active vitamin D (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is synthesised in the kidney under the influence of PTH. Although CaSR indirectly influences vitamin D metabolism through its effects on PTH, it does not directly regulate vitamin D synthesis.

Calcitonin (Option D) is secreted by the parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid gland in response to elevated serum calcium. While calcium stimulates its release, CaSR-mediated regulation of calcitonin is not the primary mechanism.



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Volume I, Pages 3169, 3170.
  2. Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 661.

question: A 65-year-old man presents with constipation, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, confusion, and bone pain. Laboratory investigations reveal hypercalcemia. Considering the role of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) in calcium homeostasis, which of the following is directly regulated by CaSR?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is Cowden Syndrome, characterized by a family history of breast and thyroid cancers and pituitary tumors. The patient's symptoms of irregular menstrual cycles, infertility, and the pituitary tumor on MRI are consistent with this syndrome.

Cowden Syndrome:

  • Cause: PTEN mutation (chr 10q23.31)
  • Features: Multiple hamartomas (skin, mucosa, organs), ↑ risk of thyroid, breast, pituitary tumors
  • Endocrine: Prolactin-secreting pituitary adenomas → irregular menses, infertility; requires monitoring

McCune-Albright Syndrome (MAS) (Option A): GNAS1 mutation; polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait spots, precocious puberty

Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) Disease (Option B): VHL mutation (chr 3); hemangioblastomas, organ cysts, RCC, pheochromocytoma, possible pituitary tumors

Carney Complex (CNC) (Option D): PRKAR1A mutation (chr 17q); myxomas, spotty pigmentation, endocrine tumors including GH-secreting pituitary adenomas → acromegaly



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2990, 2991, 2992

question: A 28-year-old woman presents with complaints of irregular menstrual cycles and infertility & reports increased headaches and visual changes over the past few months. An MRI reveals a large pituitary tumor. Family history is significant for several relatives with breast and thyroid cancers. Which syndrome is most likely associated with her condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Presentation of diabetes mellitus and autoimmunity in a 40-year-old man is suggestive of Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome type 2.
  • Hypoparathyroidism is a part of APS type 1.
  • APS is a group of disorders characterized by the simultaneous occurrence of multiple autoimmune conditions affecting the endocrine system, which are also associated with non-endocrine conditions.

Addison's disease (Option A), Autoimmune thyroiditis (Option B), and Celiac disease (Option C) are all associated with APS type 2



Reference:

Harrison’s principle of internal medicine, 22nd edition, Page 3089
lessonTitle: Disorders of Parathyroid Gland and MEN Syndromes
question: 40-year-old man presents with salt wasting, salt craving and postural hypotension. He has a family history of autoimmune disorders. Laboratory tests reveal elevated blood glucose levels and positive autoantibodies. Autoimmune Polyendocrine Syndrome is suspected. Which of the following statements regarding the diagnosis is not true?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient features points toward multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (MEN2A).

  • Primary hyperparathyroidism → causes kidney stones and elevated calcium.
  • Pheochromocytoma → explains hypertension.
  • Medullary thyroid carcinoma → suggested by family history of thyroid cancer.

MEN Type 1 (Option A) involves the “3 Ps”: parathyroid, pancreatic endocrine tumors, and pituitary tumors, typically not associated with medullary thyroid carcinoma.

MEN Type 4 (Option B) is rare, caused by CDKN1B mutations, and resembles MEN1 but usually without thyroid carcinoma.

MEN Type 2B (Option C) Features medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, and Marfanoid habitus. Kidney stones and parathyroid hyperplasia are uncommon.



Reference:

Harrison’s principle of internal medicine, 21st edition, Page 2983 - 2990

Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 868, 869

question: A 35-year-old man presents with recurrent kidney stones, abdominal pain, and peptic ulcers. His blood pressure is elevated, and he has a family history of thyroid carcinoma. Laboratory tests reveal high serum calcium and parathyroid hormone levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The gene mutation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D 1α-hydroxylase (CYP27B1) enzyme, which helps in the conversion of inactive metabolites of Vitamin D to the active form (1,25 (OH) Vit D3), is called Type 1 Vitamin D dependent Rickets, and it is treated with supplementing the active form, Calcitriol.
  • If rickets is resistant to treatment with vitamin D supplementation, it is most likely due to either type 1 or type 2 vitamin D-dependent rickets or hypophosphatemic rickets.

An increase in vitamin D dosage (Option A) wouldn't help due to a defect in the enzyme needed to convert vitamin D into its active form in this type of rickets; therefore, it is managed by administering the active form directly.

Initiate phosphate supplementation (Option B) alone does not correct the underlying defect.

Administer Calcium (Option C) may help transiently but will not address the vitamin D activation deficiency.



Reference:

Harrison’s principle of internal medicine, 21st edition, Page 3168

Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 1052, 1053

question: A 3-year-old boy with growth delays and leg bowing has not improved after six months of vitamin D treatment. Labs show low calcium, low phosphate, and elevated alkaline phosphatase. Genetic testing indicates a Vitamin D gene mutation. What is the best management option?

correctAnswer: D. High Parathyroid hormone, Low Calcium
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The child appears to have nutritional rickets, which commonly results from vitamin D deficiency. This leads to secondary hyperparathyroidism (high PTH).
  • This condition is associated with low calcium and low phosphate levels (due to increased renal excretion), causing defective mineralisation of the bone matrix at the growth plate in children before the fusion of epiphysis.

Low Parathyroid hormone, High Calcium (Option A) is not consistent, as PTH would rise in low calcium states.

Low Calcium, High Phosphate (Option B) is seen in hypoparathyroidism, not nutritional rickets.

High Calcium, Low Phosphate (Option C) occurs in primary hyperparathyroidism, not in dietary deficiency-induced rickets.



Reference:

Harrison’s principle of internal medicine, 21st edition, Page 3168

Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 1051, 1052

question: A 6-year-old boy presents with a history of recurrent fractures and pain in his lower limbs.He has a history of poor dietary intake, particularly low dairy consumption. Clinical examination leads to the findings similar to the images given below. Based on these observations, which of the following lab findings would be most consistent with his condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Tertiary hyperparathyroidism occurs in chronic kidney disease after prolonged secondary hyperparathyroidism, leading to autonomous PTH secretion and hypercalcemia despite persistent kidney disease.

[[figure-1]]


Primary Hyperparathyroidism (Option A) usually presents with elevated calcium and PTH but without underlying CKD.

Secondary Hyperparathyroidism (Option B) presents with low or normal calcium and high PTH due to CKD, not hypercalcemia.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism (Option C) presents with hypocalcemia and elevated PTH due to target organ resistance, not hypercalcemia.



Reference:

Harrison’s principle of internal medicine, 21st edition, Page 3188.

lessonTitle: Disorders of Parathyroid Gland and MEN Syndromes
question:
A 65-year-old woman with a history of chronic kidney disease secondary to hypertension presents with symptoms of nausea, vomiting, and confusion. On Investigating her Lab values are

  1. Serum calcium: 12.0 mg/dL (normal range: 8.5-10.5 mg/dL)
  2. Serum phosphate: 4.9 mg/dL (normal range: 2.5-4.5 mg/dL)
  3. Serum PTH: 200 pg/mL (normal range: 10-65 pg/mL)

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

PHP1A :

  • Albright hereditary osteodystrophy (AHO): short stature, shortened 4th/5th metacarpals
  • Biochemistry: ↑ PTH, ↓ calcium, ↑ phosphate
  • Mechanism: Renal resistance to PTH due to defective Gsα subunit
  • This combination is classic for PHP1A.



Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism (PPHP) (Option A) shows skeletal features but normal calcium, phosphate, and PTH levels.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1b (PHP1B) (Option C) lacks skeletal deformities but has renal PTH resistance.

Hypoparathyroidism (Option D) presents with low PTH, hypocalcemia, and hyperphosphatemia but no skeletal defects.



Reference:

Harrison’s principle of internal medicine, 21st edition, Page 3188

question: An 8-year-old boy presents with characteristic skeletal and developmental defects, such as short stature and shortened 4th and 5th metacarpals. Laboratory findings show elevated PTH levels, hypocalcemia, and hyperphosphatemia. Genetic testing reveals a deficiency in the Gsα subunit. Based on these findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Chronic hypocalcemia, especially due to hypoparathyroidism, leads to basal ganglia calcification causing extrapyramidal symptoms, soft tissue calcium deposition due to hyperphosphatemia, and chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis due to immune dysfunction.

Chronic Hypocalcemia

  • In chronic hypocalcemia, often associated with conditions like chronic kidney disease, hyperphosphatemia (Option B) can lead to ectopic calcifications in tissues.
  • Extrapyramidal symptoms like dystonia (Option A) occurs due to basal ganglia calcifications
  • Ocular cataract
  • Abnormal dentition
  • Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome
    • Cutaneous candidiasis (Option C)
    • Salt wasting
    • Postural hypotension


Reference:

Harrison’s principle of internal medicine, 21st edition, Page 3186-3187

options.text: Tissue deposition of calcium due to hyperphosphatemia

question: A 45-year-old adult patient presents with symptoms of chronic hypocalcemia. Which of the following features is associated with this condition?

correctAnswer: B. Aggressive hydration with normal saline
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The first-line treatment for severe hypercalcemia in primary hyperparathyroidism is aggressive intravenous hydration with normal saline to correct hypovolemia and promote renal calcium excretion.

Intravenous bisphosphonates (Option A) are used after hydration to inhibit bone resorption.

Peritoneal dialysis (Option C) is reserved for refractory hypercalcemia with renal failure.

Calcitonin nasal spray (Option D) has a rapid but short-lived effect and is not first-line therapy.



Reference:

Harrison’s principle of internal medicine, 21st edition, Page 3182-3183

question: A 65-year-old woman with primary hyperparathyroidism presents with nausea, vomiting, confusion, and dehydration. She shows signs of hypovolemia and altered mental status. Labs reveal high serum calcium, low phosphate, and elevated PTH. What is the first line of treatment?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Teriparatide, a recombinant PTH analog, is the most appropriate treatment for chronic hypoparathyroidism when calcium and Vitamin D supplements fail to maintain normal calcium levels. It helps restore calcium-phosphate balance and mimics natural PTH action.

Initiate intravenous calcium gluconate (Option A) is used for acute, symptomatic hypocalcemia.

Administration of Alendronate (Option B) is used for osteoporosis, not hypoparathyroidism.

Start oral calcium and Vitamin D supplement (Option D) is the initial therapy but may not suffice in refractory cases.



Reference:

Harrison’s principle of internal medicine, 21st edition, Page 3187

options.text: Start oral calcium and Vitamin D supplement

question: A 52-year-old man diagnosed with hypoparathyroidism six months ago after neck surgery presents with tingling in his hands and feet, muscle cramps, and fatigue. His lab results indicate low serum calcium, elevated phosphate, and severely low parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels. What is the most appropriate treatment for his condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Chvostek's sign is a clinical sign of hypocalcemia, where tapping over the facial nerve (at the parotid gland) causes twitching of the facial muscles. This occurs due to the increased neuromuscular excitability caused by low calcium levels, commonly seen in hypoparathyroidism.

Trousseau sign (Option A) is carpopedal spasm induced by inflating a BP cuff in hypocalcemia.

Hoffman’s sign (Option C) indicates corticospinal tract lesion, not hypocalcemia.

Brudzinski’s sign (Option D) is seen in meningitis, not in postoperative hypocalcemia.



Reference:

Harrison’s principle of internal medicine, 21st edition, Page 358, 3185-3186
lessonTitle: Disorders of Parathyroid Gland and MEN Syndromes
question: A 45-year-old woman undergoes total thyroidectomy for a large goiter. Two days post-surgery, investigations reveal low serum calcium and low parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels. During clinical examination, the following observation is made. What is this sign known as ?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The condition described, characterized by neuromuscular excitability, low calcium, low PTH, and elevated phosphate levels, is diagnosed as Hypoparathyroidism, which can be associated with DiGeorge syndrome.

DiGeorge Syndrome: Failure of development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches

  • Features - CATTCH-22
    • Deletion of chromosome 22q11
    • Congenital heart disease
    • Abnormal facial features - Low set ears and hypertelorism
    • Thymus gland abnormalities or absence and Tracheo-esopahgeal fistulas
    • Cleft platelet/lip
    • Hypoparathyroidism and Hypocalcemia

Cushing’s syndrome (Option A) is characterised by excess cortisol, which leads to symptoms such as weight gain (moon facies), tiredness, muscle weakness, hypertension, mood swings, hirsutism, osteoporosis, and elevated blood sugar. It is not associated with hypocalcemia, low PTH, or neuromuscular excitability.

McCune-Albright Syndrome (Option B) is a genetic disorder caused by an active mutation in a G protein (mosaic pattern). It involves bone abnormalities (fibrous dysplasia), skin pigmentation, and endocrine issues (e.g., precocious puberty). It does not typically affect the parathyroid glands or cause hypocalcemia.

Turner syndrome (Option C) is a genetic disorder affecting females, characterised by a 45XO karyotype. It presents with short stature, a fish-like mouth, a high-arched palate, a webbed neck, a broad chest, and underdeveloped ovaries, leading to primary amenorrhea and infertility. It is not associated with parathyroid dysfunction or abnormal calcium and phosphate levels.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Volume I, Page 358, 3187,

Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 664.

question: A 45-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with muscle cramps, tingling in her fingers, and a tight sensation around her mouth. She has a history of thyroid surgery for papillary carcinoma. Examination revealed increased neuromuscular excitability. Lab results show low PTH, low calcium, and elevated phosphate levels. Which syndrome is most likely associated with this presentation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has secondary hyperparathyroidism due to CKD. In CKD, the kidneys fail to excrete phosphate and cannot activate vitamin D adequately. This leads to:

  • Hyperphosphatemia → phosphate binds calcium → ↓ serum calcium
  • Reduced 1,25-(OH)₂ vitamin D → ↓ intestinal calcium absorption
  • Hypocalcemia → stimulates ↑ PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism)
  • High PTH → increased bone turnover → bone pain, tenderness, ↑ alkaline phosphatase

Therefore, Serum calcium is low, not high.


Raised serum alkaline phosphatase (Option B): Seen due to high bone turnover from elevated PTH → typical in secondary hyperparathyroidism.


Elevated serum phosphate (Option C): CKD reduces phosphate excretion → hyperphosphatemia is expected.


Raised urinary albumin creatinine ratio (Option D): Reflects ongoing kidney damage and is commonly elevated in CKD.



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Volume I, Page 2313, 2314,
  2. Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 663.

question: A 58-year-old man with chronic kidney disease (CKD) returns for a follow-up, reporting fatigue, bone pain, and muscle weakness. Examination reveals bone tenderness, and lab tests show elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels. Which of the following findings is not typically associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given scenario indicates Primary Hyperparathyroidism, where the treatment of choice is surgical excision of the tumor. Age <50 years is an indication for surgery.

The treatment of choice for parathyroid adenoma is surgical excision.

  • Indications for surgery:
    • Age <50 years
    • Nephrolithiasis (Option A) confirmed by imaging
    • Elevated serum calcium level (documented)
    • Osteoporosis (Option D) confirmed by DEXA scan (T-score < -2.5 S.D.)
    • Renal impairment (Option B) (creatinine clearance <60 ml/min)
    • Elevated urinary calcium levels (24 hours)
    • Vertebral fracture confirmed by imaging


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Volume I, Page 31776-3178.

Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 663, 664.

question: A 39-year-old woman presents with persistent constipation, abdominal pain, and intermittent lower back pain. She has a history of recurrent kidney stones and reports fatigue. Lab tests reveal elevated calcium and decreased phosphate levels. She has been advised to undergo a sestamibi Tc-99 scan. Which of the following is not an indication for surgery in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The scenario of constipation, abdominal pain, elevated calcium levels, increased bone turnover (indicated by elevated alkaline phosphatase), and decreased phosphate levels suggests Primary Hyperparathyroidism, where tetany is not observed; instead, it is typically seen in hypoparathyroidism.
  • Tetany is characterized by muscle spasms resulting from increased excitability of peripheral nerves due to serum calcium levels falling below 7 mg/dl, as seen in hypoparathyroidism.

Recurrent nephrolithiasis (Option A) is common due to hypercalciuria.

Osteitis fibrosa cystica (Option B) is a classic skeletal manifestation of hyperparathyroidism.

Urinary tract infection (Option D) can occur secondary to nephrolithiasis and urinary stasis.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Volume I, Page 3175, 3176.

Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 663.

question: A 60-year-old female presents with complaints of abdominal pain, constipation, and recent episodes of confusion and depression. Laboratory tests reveal elevated serum calcium and alkaline phosphatase (SAP) levels and decreased phosphate levels. Which of the following clinical features is not typically associated with this condition?

correctAnswer: B. Inactivating mutation of the growth hormone receptor
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Laron syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder characterised by growth hormone receptor anomalies, resulting in failure of GH signalling despite elevated circulating GH levels.
  • Because GH cannot act on its receptor, hepatic synthesis of IGF-1 is markedly reduced, leading to severe proportionate short stature, characteristic facies, and recurrent hypoglycemia (due to loss of GH’s counter-regulatory effect on insulin).
  • Treatment is by subcutaneous administration of recombinant IGF-1, not growth hormone, as GH therapy is ineffective in receptor-level resistance.

[[figure-1]]

GHRH deficiency (Option A): Causes secondary GH deficiency with low GH and low IGF-1, not elevated GH.

Somatotroph hypoplasia (Option C): Produces primary pituitary GH deficiency, again associated with low GH levels, not GH resistance.

Primary IGF-1 deficiency (Option D): Extremely rare; GH levels are not typically markedly elevated and the defect is post-receptor synthetic failure, not receptor insensitivity.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2984, 2296.

options.text: Inactivating mutation of the growth hormone receptor

question: A 4-year-old boy is brought in with proportionate short stature, frontal bossing and recurrent episodes of fasting hypoglycemia. His serum growth hormone levels are markedly elevated, but IGF-1 levels are very low. Which of the following is the most likely underlying abnormality?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical features of progressive enlargement of hands and feet, coarse facial features, loud snoring (due to soft-tissue overgrowth), and tingling in fingers from median nerve compression, along with MRI showing a pituitary macroadenoma, are characteristic of acromegaly due to a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma. Excess growth hormone leads to increased IGF-1, causing soft-tissue and bony overgrowth and systemic complications.

  • Chronic GH-IGF-1 excess causes widespread multisystem involvement:
    • Musculoskeletal: Prognathism, carpal tunnel syndrome (Option B), paresthesia, proximal myopathy
    • Skin/soft tissue: Acral enlargement, hyperhidrosis, acanthosis nigricans, skin tags
    • Visceral: Enlargement of the tongue, thyroid, liver, spleen, kidney, prostate
    • Metabolic: Diabetes mellitus, hyperphosphatemia (Option A), hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, hypertriglyceridemia
    • Cardiopulmonary: Left ventricular hypertrophy (Option D), hypertension, obstructive sleep apnea
    • Reproductive: Loss of libido, impotence, galactorrhea
    • Ophthalmic: Headache, visual field defects, cranial nerve palsies
  • Diabetes insipidus is not a feature of acromegaly itself and occurs only as a post-transsphenoidal surgery complication.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3008.
question: A 48-year-old man presents with progressive enlargement of hands and feet, coarse facial features, loud snoring during sleep and tingling sensations in his fingers. MRI findings are shown below.. Which of the following is least likely to be a manifestation of his underlying disorder?

correctAnswer: B. Failure of GH suppression after oral glucose load
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Growth hormone is a counter-regulatory hormone against hypoglycemia and is physiologically suppressed by hyperglycemia.
  • In acromegaly, GH secretion becomes autonomous; therefore, GH fails to suppress following an oral glucose load, which is the confirmatory biochemical test.
  • Patients also develop:
    • Impaired glucose tolerance/diabetes mellitus due to insulin antagonism
    • Galactorrhea due to associated hyperprolactinemia
    • Hypertension due to increased aldosterone secretion
    • Hyperphosphatemia due to increased vitamin D activation and renal phosphate retention

Rise in GH after TRH (Option A): Seen in acromegaly, but it is not the diagnostic confirmatory test.

Low serum phosphate (Option C): GH causes phosphate retention which causes hyperphosphatemia.

Reduced aldosterone (Option D): Aldosterone is increased, causing hypertension.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3008.

options.text: Rise in GH after TRH stimulation
Failure of GH suppression after oral glucose load

question: A 44-year-old man presents with enlargement of hands and feet, excessive sweating, new-onset diabetes mellitus, milky nipple discharge and persistent hypertension. MRI sella reveals a pituitary macroadenoma. Which of the following findings would be most appropriate to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical scenario of a middle-aged woman with an acute onset of symptoms, along with her imaging, points towards the diagnosis of pituitary apoplexy and Graves’ disease (hyperthyroidism) is not associated with it.
  • Pituitary apoplexy is a life-threatening endocrine emergency caused by acute haemorrhage or infarction of the pituitary gland, most commonly occurring in patients with pituitary adenomas.

[[figure-1]]

  • It is precipitated by conditions that cause vascular instability, infarction, or haemorrhage, including:
    • Pituitary adenoma (spontaneous)
    • Acute shock
    • Diabetes mellitus
    • Hypertension
    • Sickle cell anaemia
    • Sheehan syndrome


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2993.
question: A 38-year-old woman with a known pituitary adenoma presents with a sudden onset of severe headache, vomiting and rapidly progressive visual loss. MRI brain suggests an acute haemorrhage within the pituitary gland. Which of the following conditions is not associated with increased risk of developing this emergency?

correctAnswer: D. Biopsy shows cholesterol crystals within the cyst
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Craniopharyngiomas are benign epithelial suprasellar tumors derived from Rathke’s pouch remnants.
  • They characteristically contain cholesterol-rich machine oil fluid, so a biopsy reveals cholesterol crystals within the cyst (Option D).
  • Causes central diabetes insipidus, hypopituitarism, and bitemporal hemianopia.
  • Bimodal age distribution (children & 50-65 yrs).
  • They are locally adherent to surrounding hypothalamic and optic structures, so complete surgical excision is not curative in most patients and must be followed by post-operative radiotherapy to prevent recurrence. (Option C)
  • Two pathological variants exist:
    • Adamantinomatous (children) (Option B): cystic, calcifications common, keratin nodules

[[figure-1]]

  • Papillary (adults) (Option A): solid, calcifications rare

[[figure-2]]



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3002.

options.text: In the papillary variant, calcifications are commonly seen
In the adamantinomatous variant, calcifications are rare
Complete surgical excision is usually curative
Biopsy shows cholesterol crystals within the cyst

question: A 14-year-old boy presents with progressive headache, vomiting, declining school performance and polyuria. MRI brain reveals the following finding. Which of the following statements about this lesion is most accurate?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Craniopharyngiomas are benign suprasellar cystic tumors derived from Rathke’s pouch remnants.
  • They commonly cause early obstruction of CSF pathways and raised intracranial pressure, making headache the most common presenting symptom across both pediatric and adult age groups.
  • Raised intracranial pressure also produces:
    • Early-morning vomiting
    • Papilledema
    • Lethargy
    • Hydrocephalus

Craniopharyngiomas can present with:

  • Headache - most common symptom
  • Hypopituitarism - due to pituitary destruction
  • Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Option B) - Results from pituitary stalk involvement and hypothalamic damage
  • Central diabetes insipidus (Option D) - due to posterior pituitary involvement
  • Bitemporal hemianopia (Option A) - due to optic chiasmal compression


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3002.
question: A 49-year-old man presents with gradually progressive lethargy, loss of appetite and intermittent vomiting for several months. He also reports excessive thirst and passing large volumes of urine. MRI brain shows a suprasellar mass with mixed cystic-solid components and areas of calcification. Which of the following is the most common initial clinical presentation of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • MEN 2 is characterised by medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, and hyperparathyroidism, but does not involve pituitary adenomas.
  • Therefore, routine pituitary imaging and hormonal screening are not indicated in MEN 2.
  • MEN 2 includes MEN-2A, MEN-2B (MEN-3), and familial medullary thyroid carcinoma variants - none of which involve pituitary tumours.

The genetic syndromes associated with pituitary tumours include:

  • MEN 1 (Option A): Caused by menin gene mutation; classically causes pituitary adenomas, pancreatic NETs, and parathyroid hyperplasia (“3 Ps”).
  • MEN 4 (Option B): CDKN1B mutation syndrome; MEN-1-like disorder that includes pituitary adenomas.
  • Carney complex (Option C): Associated with GH-secreting pituitary adenomas, leading to acromegaly, along with cardiac myxomas and skin pigmentation.
  • McCune-Albright syndrome is another important genetic disorder associated with GH-secreting pituitary adenomas.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3004, 3080.
question: A 28-year-old man is diagnosed with a hereditary endocrine tumour syndrome and is being planned for surveillance imaging. In which of the following conditions is routine pituitary tumour screening not required?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This patient has a pituitary macroprolactinoma causing early optic chiasmal compression.
  • Pituitary macroadenomas (>10 mm) initially compress the ventral portion of the optic chiasm, which contains the inferior nasal retinal fibres.
  • These fibres carry information from the superior temporal visual fields.
  • Therefore, the earliest visual field defect is bitemporal (heteronymous) superior quadrantanopia.
  • With further tumour growth, complete bitemporal hemianopia develops.

Homonymous superior quadrantanopia (Option B): Occurs due to temporal lobe optic radiation lesions (“pie in the sky”), not chiasmal compression.

Central scotoma (Option C): Seen in optic neuritis and macular disease.

Monocular temporal hemianopia (Option D): Indicates pre-chiasmal optic nerve compression, not chiasmal involvement.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 222, 223.
question: A 34-year-old woman presents with secondary amenorrhea and spontaneous galactorrhea for 6 months. She also complains of gradually worsening peripheral vision. MRI brain reveals a 16-mm pituitary lesion. Which of the following visual field defects is most likely in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient has a pituitary macroadenoma causing panhypopituitarism.
  • Large pituitary macroadenomas destroy normal pituitary tissue, leading to panhypopituitarism:
    • ↓ ACTH → Secondary adrenal insufficiency
    • ↓ TSH → Secondary hypothyroidism (Option C)
    • ↓ LH/FSH → Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (Option B)
    • ↓ GH → Growth failure and adult hyposomatotropism
    • ↓ PRL→ Lactation failure
  • Because ACTH levels are low, melanocyte-stimulating activity is reduced; therefore, mucocutaneous hyperpigmentation does not occur.
    • Hyperpigmentation is seen only when ACTH is in excess (primary adrenal failure, ectopic ACTH).
  • Cortisol deficiency also causes increased adiponectin → increased insulin sensitivity. (Option A)


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3055.
question: A 55-year-old man presents with progressive fatigue and recent visual field defects. MRI shows a large sellar mass compressing the pituitary gland. Which of the following findings would be least likely to be present in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient has a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma (prolactinoma) with biochemical hyperprolactinemia.
  • Pituitary adenomas are classified based on size:
    • Microadenoma: < 10 mm
    • Macroadenoma: ≥ 10 mm
  • Pituitary adenomas may be detected incidentally on imaging or suspected in patients with features of hormone hypersecretion (e.g., galactorrhea, amenorrhea) or mass effect.
  • MRI with contrast is the best investigation to detect pituitary tumours and assess suprasellar extension and optic chiasm involvement.
  • In all patients with suspected pituitary adenoma, measurement of pituitary hormone levels is mandatory to evaluate both hypersecretion and hyposecretion syndromes.
  • Microadenomas commonly cause endocrine symptoms, while macroadenomas commonly present with visual field defects and hypopituitarism.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3003.
question: A 28-year-old woman presents with oligomenorrhea and spontaneous galactorrhea. Serum prolactin is 78 ng/mL. MRI of the sellar region is planned. Which of the following lesion sizes would classify the pituitary tumour as a microadenoma?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient has a non-functioning pituitary adenoma producing mass-effect manifestations and evolving hypopituitarism.
  • Non-functioning pituitary adenomas do not produce clinically active hormone excess and therefore typically present with mass-effect symptoms rather than endocrine syndromes.
  • Nearly 80% of non-functioning pituitary adenomas arise from gonadotroph cells, making them the most common cell of origin.
  • As these tumours enlarge, they produce:
    • Headache and bitemporal hemianopia from optic chiasm compression
    • Cranial nerve palsies causing diplopia and ptosis
    • Mild hyperprolactinemia (stalk effect) due to loss of dopaminergic inhibition
    • Progressive hypopituitarism in later stages from compression of normal pituitary tissue

Lactotroph cells (Option A): Cause prolactinomas, which produce marked hyperprolactinemia with galactorrhea and amenorrhea.

Corticotroph cells (Option B): Produce ACTH-secreting adenomas causing Cushing's disease.

Thyrotroph cells (Option D): Produce TSH-secreting adenomas causing hyperthyroidism.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3013.
question: A 46-year-old man presents with progressively worsening headache and difficulty seeing objects in the peripheral field of vision. MRI reveals a large sellar mass compressing the optic chiasm. Hormonal evaluation shows mildly elevated serum prolactin with low cortisol and low TSH levels. Which of the following cell types is the most likely origin of this tumour?

correctAnswer: B. Serum free T4 and TSH levels
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient has hyperprolactinemia, causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
  • Primary hypothyroidism is a frequent, reversible cause of hyperprolactinemia.
  • Primary hypothyroidism causes low circulating thyroid hormone, leading to elevated TRH.
  • TRH directly stimulates pituitary lactotrophs, producing hyperprolactinemia, which suppresses GnRH → ↓ LH/FSH → amenorrhea, galactorrhea and infertility.
  • Therefore, thyroid function testing must be done before pituitary imaging or dopamine-agonist therapy.
  • Correction of hypothyroidism alone can normalise prolactin levels.

[[figure-1]]

Diagnostic algorithm of hyperprolactinemia. CKD = Chronic kidney disease; PRL = Prolactin; MPRL = Macroprolactin; mPRL = Monomeric prolactin; HR: Hormonal replacement; DA = Dopamine agonists; RPCS = Progressive chiasmatic syndrome; PA = Pituitary apoplexy; NFPA = Non-functioning pituitary adenoma; TSS = Transphenoidal surgery.

MRI pituitary (Option A): Should be performed only after excluding reversible causes of hyperprolactinemia.

LH & FSH (Option C): Will be suppressed, but do not identify the aetiology.

Start cabergoline (Option D): May mask a reversible endocrine cause if started prematurely.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3005.

options.text: Serum free T4 and TSH levels

question: A 27-year-old woman presents with 6 months of amenorrhea, spontaneous galactorrhea and infertility. Serum prolactin is 120 ng/mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C) Diminished libido

Explanation:

  • The patient is suffering from hyperprolactinemia, causing hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
  • Hyperprolactinemia suppresses pulsatile GnRH secretion, leading to decreased LH and FSH, producing:
    • Amenorrhea (secondary > primary)
    • Galactorrhea (Option A): Due to prolactin-mediated milk secretion
    • Infertility (Option B): Occurs due to suppression of gonadotropins and anovulation
    • Visual field defects (Option D) due to optic chiasmal compression (in macroadenomas)
  • Always rule out hypothyroidism (↑TRH → ↑PRL) and pregnancy before labelling idiopathic hyperprolactinemia.
  • Diminished libido is not a typical presenting feature in women and is classically described in men with hyperprolactinemia.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3004.
question: A 29-year-old woman presents with secondary amenorrhea and milky nipple discharge for 6 months. She also reports an inability to conceive despite regular unprotected intercourse. Which of the following clinical features would be least likely to be part of her underlying disorder?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Acromegaly is caused by chronic excess growth hormone secretion after epiphyseal fusion, leading to elevated IGF-1 levels and progressive acral enlargement, arthropathy, hyperhidrosis and metabolic complications.
  • In more than 95% of cases, acromegaly is pituitary in origin, and the most common cause is a pure somatotroph pituitary adenoma, making it the predominant etiology.
  • Oral glucose suppression failure is diagnostic of acromegaly.
  • Most patients present with macroadenomas.
  • First-line treatment is transsphenoidal surgery.

Causes of acromegaly are classified as:

1. Pituitary causes (~98%)

  • Pure somatotroph adenoma - ~60% (most common)
  • Mixed somatotroph-lactotroph adenoma
  • Other plurihormonal pituitary tumours
  • These are responsible for autonomous GH secretion and account for the vast majority of cases.

2. Extrapituitary causes (Rare)

A. Ectopic GH-GH-secreting tumours

  • Very rare
  • Can be seen in neuroendocrine tumours

B. Excess GHRH secretion

  • Central: Hypothalamic hamartoma
  • Peripheral:
    • Bronchial carcinoid
    • Pancreatic neuroendocrine (islet cell) tumours
  • These cause secondary pituitary somatotroph hyperplasia rather than a discrete adenoma.

Ectopic GHRH secretion (Option A): Causes secondary pituitary somatotroph hyperplasia; rare compared to pituitary adenoma.

Lactotroph adenoma with stalk effect (Option C): May cause hyperprolactinemia but does not produce GH excess.

Hypothalamic hamartoma (Option D): Can secrete GHRH, but is a very uncommon cause of acromegaly.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3008.

options.text: Ectopic GHRH secretion from bronchial carcinoid

question: A 40-year-old man presents with progressive increase in ring and shoe size, coarse facial features, excessive sweating, arthralgia and new-onset diabetes mellitus. Serum IGF-1 is elevated, and growth hormone fails to suppress following an oral glucose tolerance test. MRI sella reveals a pituitary mass. What is the most common underlying aetiology of his condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has acromegaly, caused by chronic growth hormone (GH) excess after epiphyseal fusion.

  • The diagnosis is supported by elevated serum IGF-1, failure of GH suppression following an oral glucose tolerance test, and the presence of a pituitary mass on MRI.
  • More than 95% of cases of acromegaly are caused by a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma, with pure somatotroph adenoma being the most common subtype.
  • These tumours secrete GH autonomously, resulting in increased hepatic production of IGF-1, which mediates the characteristic somatic overgrowth and metabolic abnormalities.

Causes of acromegaly:

  • Pituitary causes (>95%)
    • Pure somatotroph adenoma (most common)
    • Mixed somatotroph-lactotroph adenoma
    • Other plurihormonal pituitary adenomas
  • Extrapituitary causes (rare)
    • Ectopic GHRH secretion
      • Bronchial carcinoid
      • Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors
      • Hypothalamic gangliocytoma/hamartoma (rare)
    • Ectopic GH-secreting tumours (extremely rare)
  • Most patients have pituitary macroadenomas at diagnosis.
  • Transsphenoidal surgical resection is the first-line treatment for most GH-secreting pituitary adenomas.

Ectopic GHRH secretion from a bronchial carcinoid (Option A): A rare cause of acromegaly that produces secondary pituitary somatotroph hyperplasia rather than a primary pituitary adenoma.

Lactotroph adenoma with stalk effect (Option C): Lactotroph adenomas cause hyperprolactinemia and may produce pituitary stalk compression, but they do not cause autonomous GH excess or acromegaly.

Hypothalamic hamartoma (Option D): A very uncommon cause of acromegaly that may secrete GHRH, leading to secondary pituitary somatotroph hyperplasia rather than a discrete GH-secreting adenoma.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3008.

question: A 40-year-old man presents with progressive enlargement of his hands and feet, increasing ring and shoe size, coarse facial features, excessive sweating, arthralgia, and newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus. Serum IGF-1 is elevated, and growth hormone fails to suppress following an oral glucose tolerance test. MRI of the sella demonstrates a pituitary mass. What is the most common underlying etiology of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • TRH physiologically stimulates TSH and prolactin secretion and does not stimulate GH.
  • A rise in GH after TRH is abnormal and indicates pituitary or hypothalamic pathology with aberrant TRH receptor expression or dysregulated somatotroph control.
  • In acromegaly, the somatotroph adenoma:
    • Expresses ectopic TRH receptors
    • Shows autonomous GH secretion
    • Demonstrates abnormal pituitary receptor cross-reactivity
  • This produces a classical paradoxical GH rise following TRH administration.

Other conditions known to show paradoxical GH Rise after TRH:

  • Prolactinoma/mixed GH-PRL adenoma: Aberrant lactotroph-somatotroph cross-talk
  • Anorexia nervosa / chronic starvation: Central hypothalamic dysregulation
  • Liver failure: ↓ IGF-1 feedback → ↑ GH with abnormal TRH sensitivity

Simple protein-energy malnutrition (Option B): Peripheral nutritional deficiency without hypothalamic reprogramming does not cause paradoxical TRH-GH response.

Cushing syndrome (Option C): Excess cortisol suppresses GH secretion.

Chronic kidney disease (Option D): CKD produces GH resistance and altered clearance, but does not produce TRH-induced GH rise.



Reference:

https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/2110409/
question: A 23-year-old woman undergoes dynamic pituitary testing. Following TRH administration, her serum growth hormone (GH) levels show a paradoxical rise. Which of the following clinical conditions is most likely to show this response?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Growth hormone is a potent counter-regulatory hormone to insulin and antagonises insulin action, leading to impaired glucose tolerance and hyperglycemia; hence, it is contraindicated in uncontrolled diabetes mellitus.
  • GH also causes dose-related sodium, potassium and water retention, producing weight gain, oedema and hypertension.
  • It stimulates linear bone growth and epiphyseal cartilage widening, predisposing to slipped capital femoral epiphysis (Option A), and increases intracranial pressure, causing headache and pseudotumor cerebri (Option C).
  • Other recognised adverse effects include:
    • Tinnitus (Option B),
    • Carpal tunnel syndrome,
    • Joint pains,
    • Gynecomastia,
    • Pituitary tumour regrowth,
    • Progression of skin lesions,
    • Acromegaloid changes.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2997.
question: A 15-year-old boy receiving recombinant growth hormone therapy for constitutional short stature presents with progressive weight gain, facial puffiness and new-onset impaired fasting glucose. Which of the following adverse effects is he least likely to develop due to growth hormone therapy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Lanreotide, a long-acting somatostatin analog, is the preferred preoperative medical therapy for GH-secreting pituitary adenomas.
  • It effectively reduces tumor size and controls GH/IGF-1 levels, improving acromegaly symptoms and metabolic complications like impaired glucose tolerance.


Cabergoline (Option A) and Bromocriptine (Option C) are dopamine agonists. They are less effective in shrinking GH-secreting tumors and are usually reserved for mild cases or patients intolerant to somatostatin analogs.


Pegvisomant (Option D) is a GH receptor antagonist that normalizes IGF-1 and improves metabolic complications but does not reduce tumor size, so it is not preferred preoperatively.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3009
question: A patient with acromegaly presents with large spade-like hands and impaired glucose tolerance. The pituitary MRI shows a somatotrope adenoma. Which of the following is the preferred medical therapy to shrink the tumor preoperatively?

correctAnswer: B. Glucocorticoid → thyroid hormone → Sex hormones → Growth hormone
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

For panhypopituitarism, the sequence of hormone replacement therapy is Glucocorticoid → thyroid hormone → Sex hormones → Growth hormone

Hormonal therapy for Panhypopituitarism

Hormone deficient

Hormone replacement

Corticosteroid replacement should be started first to reduce the risk of triggering an adrenal crisis.

  • Cortisone acetate 15-25 mg/day in divided doses
  • Prednisolone 5 mg/day

TSH

Thyroid hormone replacement is then added for hypothyroidism

  • L-thyroxine 0.0075 - 0.15 mg/day

FSH/LH

After thyroid hormone replacement - sex hormone replacement is initiated

  • Males - testosterone
  • Females - estrogen / progesterone / gonadotropins

GH
  • Adults - Somatotropin (0.1 - 1.25 mg SC QID)
  • Children - Somatotropin (0.02 - 0.05 mg/kg/day)

Vasopressin

  • Intranasal desmopressin (5–20 g BID/day)

question: Which of the following diseases is mismatched with its hormonal profile and management

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Considering this patient’s history of pituitary adenoma and his current clinical presentation, he has most likely developed pituitary apoplexy.
  • High-dose IV glucocorticoids are the first-line treatment that addresses adrenal insufficiency, stabilizes blood pressure, and corrects hypoglycemia.

Pituitary apoplexy

Management

  • High-dose glucocorticoids is the first line of treatment to correct adrenal insufficiency, stabilize blood pressure, and correct hypoglycemia.
  • Patients without evident visual loss or impaired consciousness can be managed conservatively with high-dose glucocorticoids.
  • Urgent surgical decompression (Option A): Required for patients with significant or progressive visual loss, cranial nerve palsy, or loss of consciousness.
  • Monitoring: Visual recovery is inversely correlated with the duration of time after the acute event, so timely intervention is crucial.

IV dextrose administration (Option C) can temporarily address hypoglycemia but it does not address the underlying adrenal insufficiency which is a medical emergency.

Oral hydrocortisone (Option D) is not preferred as this is an acute endocrine emergency, and oral corticosteroids are not fast acting thus only IV forms of corticosteroid are preferred.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2897 and 2898
question: A 60-year-old male with a history of pituitary adenoma presents with sudden-onset severe headache, palpitations, excessive sweating, and hypotension. Lab results show severe hypoglycemia, and imaging reveals hemorrhage within the pituitary and deviation of the pituitary stalk. What is the initial management for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Pituitary hormone levels in different pituitary gland disorders

Hypopituitarism

It occurs due to damage in the pituitary gland caused by tumors, surgery, trauma, or genetic conditions.

GH, ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH, prolactin, ADH ↓ (deficiency varies based on which cells are affected).

Sheehan syndrome

Postpartum hypopituitarism caused by ischemic necrosis of the pituitary gland following severe blood loss during childbirth.

GH, ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH, prolactin ↓ and ADH normal

Pituitary apoplexy

A medical emergency involving sudden hemorrhage or infarction in the pituitary gland.

Severe ↓ ACTH and GH, other hormones may be ↓ or normal

Stalk effect

Compression or disruption of the pituitary stalk causing a reduction in hypothalamic inhibition of prolactin, resulting in elevated prolactin levels without other pituitary hormone abnormalities.

GH, ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH normal or ↓, prolactin ↑




Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2898, 2906

question:
Match the following pituitary gland disorders with their respective serum hormone levels.

Pituitary gland disorder

Serum hormone levels

1. Hypopituitarism

a) Severe ↓ ACTH and GH, other hormones maybe ↓ or normal

2. Sheehan syndrome

b) GH, ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH, prolactin, ADH ↓

3. Pituitary apoplexy

c) GH, ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH normal or ↓; prolactin ↑

4. Stalk effect

d) GH, ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH, prolactin ↓ and ADH normal

correctAnswer: A. Hyperprolactinemia occurs due to a hypersecreting macroadenoma
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Hyperprolactinemia in the stalk effect occurs due to compression of the pituitary stalk by a non-secreting pituitary macroadenoma and not due to a hypersecreting macroadenoma.
  • Compression of the pituitary stalk results in reduced hypothalamic dopamine delivery to the pituitary due to stalk compression, which leads to unopposed prolactin secretion (Option B ruled out)
  • A serum prolactin level below 200 ng/mL can be observed in cases with a "stalk effect". Serum prolactin level above 200 ng/mL typically indicates a prolactin-secreting macroadenoma. (Option D ruled out)
  • Other pituitary hormones are usually normal initially, but large tumors may eventually cause hypopituitarism (Option C ruled out)
  • Thus, the hormonal profile in the stalk effect
    • GH, ACTH, TSH, LH, FSH normal or ↓
    • Prolactin ↑ but less than 200 ng/mL

[[figure-1]]



Reference:
  1. Pituitary Adenoma - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
  2. Factors Influencing Disconnection Hyperprolactinemia and Reversal of Serum Prolactin after Pituitary Surgery in a Non-Functioning Pituitary Macroadenoma - PMC

correctAnswer: B. Bromocriptine therapy till pregnancy is confirmed
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In order to restore fertility in this patient, Bromocriptine therapy can be used until pregnancy is confirmed

Treatment of prolactinoma in pregnancy

Desire for fertility

DOC - Bromocriptine

  • Bromocriptine therapy is initiated to restore fertility
  • It is short-acting and has low teratogenic effects
  • After pregnancy is confirmed - the drug is discontinued, and serial monitoring of prolactin levels
  • Drug may be reintroduced if tumor growth is apparent

Visual field defect

If the tumor is very large and threatens the vision, surgical decompression may be done

Cabergoline therapy (Option A), although it is the first line therapy for prolactinoma, is not preferred in those patients desiring fertility because it is long acting as it has a high affinity for D2-receptors.

Radiotherapy for mass reduction of tumor (Option C) is reserved for aggressive tumors that do not respond to dopamine agonists or surgery; thus, it is not recommended for this patient.

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Pages 2911 and 2912

question: A 32 year old nulliparous woman comes to the OB-GYN department for investigation of infertility. She also complains of occasional headaches and galactorrhoea. Lab tests and imaging lead to a diagnosis of prolactinoma. If we want to restore fertility in this patient, which of the following is the treatment of choice in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • For patients with macroadenomas and significant symptoms, initiation of dopamine agonist therapy (such as cabergoline or bromocriptine) is the first-line treatment to reduce prolactin levels and shrink the tumor.
  • Lanreotide is used to shrink GH producing adenoma in case of acromegaly.

Diagnosis of Prolactinoma:

  • PRL levels > 200 μg/L most likely indicates prolactinoma
  • PRL levels below 100 μg/L may indicate microadenomas
  • MRI Head is recommended for all patients with hyperprolactinemia
    • Shows suprasellar mass.

Management:

  • Asymptomatic microadenomas: No treatment if fertility is not desired. Regular monitoring and imaging are recommended.
  • Symptomatic microadenomas: Use dopamine agonists, titrated for optimal PRL suppression. Normal PRL levels do not guarantee tumor shrinkage.
  • Macroadenomas: Perform visual field testing before starting dopamine agonists. Follow-up with MRI and visual field assessments every 6-12 months.



Reference:

Page 3004, Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22 nd Edition,
question: A 40-year-old man presents with erectile dysfunction and galactorrhea. Blood tests confirm elevated prolactin levels and an MRI reveals a macroadenoma. Which of the following management strategies is most appropriate for this patient?

correctAnswer: B. Men generally present with symptoms earlier than women
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical scenario with elevated prolactin levels & MRI showing a mass in the sellar region suggests Prolactinoma, where men often present later with larger tumours due to less obvious signs of hormonal imbalance.
  • Prolactin levels correlate with the size of the tumour (Option D ruled out)

Classification of Tumors:

  • Microadenomas: Tumors < 1 cm in diameter.
  • Macroadenomas: Tumors greater than 1 cm in diameter & can be locally invasive and compress adjacent structures such as Optic Chaisma, resulting inBitemporal Hemianopia) (Option C ruled out)
    • Female-to-male ratio for micro prolactinomas is approximately 20:1 (Option A ruled out)
    • For macroadenomas, the ratio is close to 1:1.



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2908, 2909
  2. Stress-Induced Hyperprolactinemia: Pathophysiology and Clinical Approach - PMC.

question: A 28-year-old woman presents to her primary care physician with complaints of irregular menstrual cycles, galactorrhea, and difficulty conceiving. Laboratory tests reveal elevated serum prolactin levels. MRI of the patient is given below. Which of the following statements about the given condition is not true?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation, along with a history of PPH during delivery & low cortisol & thyroid hormone levels, suggests Sheehan Syndrome.
  • The initial management for a patient with suspected Sheehan syndrome, particularly with evidence of adrenal insufficiency, is to start hydrocortisone to replace cortisol.

Sheehan syndrome

Management

Hormone Replacement Therapies:

  • Cortisol Replacement:
    • Administer hydrocortisone (Initial treatment) if there is ACTH deficiency.
    • Mineralocorticoid is not typically recommended. (Option C)
  • Thyroid Hormone Replacement:
    • Indication: Levothyroxine (50–150 μg) should be given once daily.
    • Aim to maintain serum T4 in the upper range of normal.
    • Thyroid hormone (Option A) should not be administered without glucocorticoid therapy in cases of adrenal insufficiency, as this can lead to an adrenal crisis.
  • Sex Hormone Replacement: Recommended for women under 50 years with gonadotropin deficiency and for men to restore sexual function and prevent osteoporosis.
  • Growth Hormone Replacement:
    • Growth hormone (GH) is given via daily subcutaneous injections for children and adolescents with GH deficiency (Option D)
    • Side Effects: The primary side effect is sodium retention, which may present as peripheral oedema or carpal tunnel syndrome
    • GH replacement should start at a low dose, with regular monitoring of serum IGF-1 to assess response.



Reference:

Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 682

Speroff’s Clinical Gynecologic Endocrinology And Infertility, 9th Edition, Page 904
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for a patient with Sheehan syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation, along with a history of PPH during delivery, suggests sheehan syndrome.
  • It refers to acute infarction and ischemic necrosis of the pituitary gland due to postpartum hemorrhage and subsequent hypovolemic hypotension.
  • Melatonin is released from pineal gland and regulates circadian rhythm /sleep–wake cycle and does not need replacement in sheehan syndrome

Lifelong hormone replacement is of

1. Glucocorticoids (Hydrocortisone / Prednisone) → always replace first to avoid adrenal crisis.

2. Levothyroxine (for secondary hypothyroidism)

3. Estrogen ± Progesterone (for women not desiring fertility) Or GnRH/gonadotropins if fertility desired.

4. Growth Hormone/ Somatotropin replacement may be considered in selected adults with hypopituitarism to improve metabolic function and quality of life, but is not required in all cases.



Reference:

Page 2996: Harrison 22nd edition
question: A 32-year-old woman experiences severe postpartum hemorrhage during delivery, requiring a blood transfusion. Two weeks later, she reports fatigue, weight loss and failure of lactation. Which of the following hormone replacement will not be required in this case?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical signs of enlargement of feet, visual field defects likely from optic chiasma compression and biochemical evidence of excess of GH points to acromegaly.
  • MRI head shows somatotroph pituitary macroadenoma with mass effect.
  • Transsphenoidal surgical resection is the preferred treatment.

Management of Acromegaly

Surgical Treatment

Transsphenoidal surgical resection is the preferred treatment, especially for those with GH-secreting adenomas.

Post-Surgery:

  • Improvement in soft tissue swelling and normalization of GH levels typically occur shortly after surgery
  • IGF-1 levels normalize within 3-4 days.
  • There is a 10% recurrence rate of acromegaly years later, and up to 15% of patients may develop hypopituitarism.

Medical therapy

Preferred in medical therapy if curative surgery is not feasible or if GH fails to decrease post resection

  • Somatostatin Receptor Ligands (SRLs): (Option B ruled out)
    • Long-acting injectable forms (octreotide, lanreotide).
    • Normalizes GH and IGF-1 levels in about 50% of patients.
    • Side Effects: GI disturbances, transient nausea, and gallbladder issues.
  • GH receptor antagonist:
    • Pegvisomant blocks peripheral GH receptors, normalizing IGF-1 levels in about 70% of patients, though GH levels remain elevated. It is administered through daily subcutaneous injections and is used for recurrences or poor responses to SRLs.
  • Dopamine Agonists: (Option A ruled out)
    • High doses of cabergoline can provide modest GH suppression.

Radiation Therapy (Option D ruled out)

External beam radiation therapy or stereotactic techniques are considered for patients not achieving biochemical control through surgery or medical therapy.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd edition, Page 3010
question: 45-year-old man presents with headaches, frequent change in shoe size and visual field defects. MRI head is shown below. IGF-1 is elevated and GH levels remain elevated on glucose challenge. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?

explanationHtml:
• GH is counter regulatory hormone causing increase of blood glucose and impaired glucose tolerance in patients with acromegaly.
  • Presence of Mammosomatotrope cell adenoma can explain galactorrhea
  • Pituitary adenoma > 10 mm can press on optic chiasma leading to bitemporal hemianopia
  • Acromegaly is associated with increased risk of colonic polyps and mortality from colonic malignancy


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3008
question: 50-year-old woman presents with increase in size of hand and feet with voice changes and carpal tunnel syndrome. IGF -1 levels are increased. Which of the following findings will likely not be seen in this case?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient has classic features of acromegaly (spade-like hands, coarse facial features, increased interdental spacing).

  • IGF-1 is the best screening test because:

    • It reflects integrated GH secretion over the day

    • It is elevated consistently in acromegaly

    • It is not affected by pulsatile GH release

IGF-2 levels (Option B):
IGF-2 is not used in acromegaly screening.


GH levels (Option C):
GH secretion is pulsatile, making random GH levels unreliable.


GH levels after 2-hour OGTT (Option D):
This is the confirmatory (diagnostic) test. Failure of GH suppression after glucose load confirms acromegaly.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2912
