question: A girl experiences prolonged menstrual bleeding and has normal platelet count, PT, and aPTT, but an increased bleeding time, which was determined to be due to a deficiency of GpIIb-IIIa after further analysis. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • HPLC (High-Performance Liquid Chromatography) showing elevated HbS indicates Sickle Cell Disease (SCD).
  • SCD is due to a mutation in the β-globin gene, which causes HbS to polymerize under low oxygen, leading to sickling of RBCs, in turn causing chronic hemolysis and vaso-occlusive crises.
  • Hydroxyurea is the standard of care for all patients with sickle cell anemia and HbS-β0 thalassemia regardless of symptoms. Although in some symptomatic patients with HbSC disease, its benefits in this genotype are understudied.
  • The major mechanism of action of hydroxyurea is to induce high levels of HbF. Hydroxyurea increases HbF unevenly among red cells (heterocellularly), so some cells have greater protection from HbS polymerization than others.
  • Hydroxyurea should be given to all infants with sickle cell anemia and HbS-β0 thalassemia starting at 9 months of age at a dose of ~20 mg/kg and titrated to the maximal tolerated dose based on neutrophil and platelet counts.

Other treatments for sickle cell anemia:

  1. Voxelator (Option C): Voxelotor increases the affinity of the hemoglobin molecule for O2, but it is not the 1st line of treatment in sickle cell anemia. At a dose of 1500 mg daily, hemoglobin concentration increased ~1 g/dL in 59% of patients with a reduction in the biomarkers of hemolysis.
  2. Crizanlizumab: A P-selectin-blocking monoclonal antibody, given intravenously every month, reduced acute painful episodes by ~45%. Hemolysis was unaffected.
  3. l-Glutamine: It causes a reduction of oxidative stress in sickle erythrocytes, and was associated with a 25% reduction in painful episodes and 33% reduction in
    hospitalization.
  4. Transfusion: Major indications for transfusion include-
    • Severe symptomatic anemia
    • Treatment and prevention of stroke
    • Increasing hemoglobin level to ~10 g/dL before surgery requiring general anesthesia
    • Severe acute chest syndrome
  5. Stem Cell Transplantation
  6. Gene Therapy:

Azacytidine (Option B): DNA methyltransferase inhibitor used in myelodysplastic syndromes/AML, not for SCD.

Bortezomib (Option D): Proteasome inhibitor used in multiple myeloma, unrelated to SCD.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 775-776
question: A child with progressive pallor and bone has an elevated HbS based on the HPLC report. Which is the best treatment to manage hemolysis in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most appropriate course of action for managing a patient presenting with fatigue, a hemoglobin level below 9 g/dL, and sickle-shaped red blood cells on peripheral smear examination is blood transfusion.
  • In patients with sickle cell disease (SCD), a hemoglobin (Hb) level below 9 g/dL accompanied by symptoms such as fatigue indicates significant anemia. Blood transfusion is the primary treatment to increase the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood, alleviate symptoms, and prevent complications associated with severe anemia.
  • According to the 2014 evidence-based report by expert panel members, transfusion therapy is recommended in SCD patients with symptomatic anemia to improve oxygen delivery and reduce the risk of stroke and other complications.

[[figure-1]]

Administer IV antibiotics (Option A): While antibiotics are essential in managing infections in SCD patients, they do not address anemia directly.

Administer desferoxamine (Option C): Desferoxamine is an iron-chelating agent used to treat iron overload from chronic transfusions. It is not suitable for acute management of anemia.

Wait and watch (Option D): Delaying treatment in symptomatic anemia can lead to worsening hypoxia and increased risk of complications.



Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482164/

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10195315/
question: What would be the most appropriate course of action for managing a patient presenting with fatigue, a haemoglobin level below 9 g/dl, and sickle-shaped red blood cells on peripheral smear examination?

explanationHtml:
• Gaisböck syndrome, primarily associated with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), is characterized by polycythemia secondary to chronic hypoxemia. The condition develops when the body responds to chronic hypoxemia by increasing erythropoietin production, leading to erythrocytosis.
  • The patients with this syndrome typically present with elevated blood pressure rather than hypotension, due to the underlying respiratory disease and increased blood viscosity.

Gaisböck syndrome

Key Clinical Features
  • High hematocrit levels
  • Erythrocytosis (Option B Ruled Out)
  • Normal leukocyte counts (Option C Ruled Out)
  • No splenomegaly
  • Hypertension
  • Facial rubor

Patient Characteristics
  • Predominantly affects males
  • Obese and anxious personality (Option D Ruled Out)
  • Often cigarette smokers

Risk Factors
  • Alcoholism
  • Diuretic therapy
  • Physical & Emotional stress
  • Obesity
  • Smoking

Pathophysiological Mechanisms
  • Psychiatric disorders causing chronic stress
  • Volume contraction (diuresis)
  • Hypertension
  • Nocturnal hypoxemia
  • Increased erythropoietin production

Complications
  • Formation of microthrombi
  • Cerebral infarction
  • Vascular disease

Treatment Approach
  • Management of hypertension
  • Weight reduction
  • Smoking cessation
  • Alcohol reduction/cessation
  • Stress management


Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8865286/
question: Which of the following is not a feature of Gaisböck syndrome?

explanationHtml:
• Hereditary spherocytosis is an inherited disorder characterized by abnormal red blood cells that are spherical in shape instead of the normal biconcave disc shape. Elective splenectomy is the primary treatment for Hereditary spherocytosis.
  • In HS, splenectomy is particularly effective because the spleen is the primary site of spherocyte destruction. The timing of splenectomy varies with disease severity: severe HS requires elective splenectomy at 4-6 years of age, moderate HS can be delayed until puberty, while mild cases may be managed with folic acid supplementation alone.

Management of Hereditary Spherocytosis (HS)

Splenectomy as Primary Treatment
  • Splenectomy significantly improves anemia by prolonging red cell survival, reducing the need for transfusions, and preventing iron overload and related organ damage.
  • Post splenectomy: Spherocytosis and altered osmotic fragility persist, but reticulocyte counts and erythrocyte lifespan normalize.

Blood Film Changes Post-Splenectomy
  • Features like Howell-Jolly bodies, acanthocytes, target cells, cabot ring and Pappenheimer bodies appear after splenectomy.

[[figure-1]]

Indications for Splenectomy
  • Recommended for patients with severe, transfusion-dependent anemia, growth failure, skeletal changes, leg ulcers, or extramedullary hematopoietic tumors.

Timing of Splenectomy:

  • Should be delayed until age 5–9 if possible or at least age 3, to reduce the risk of post-splenectomy sepsis while balancing the increased risk of gallstones in older children.

Laparoscopic Splenectomy
  • Preferred method, with benefits like less discomfort, quicker recovery, and shorter hospital stays. Combined laparoscopic splenectomy and cholecystectomy is an option for patients with symptomatic gallstones.

Partial Splenectomy
  • Used in infants or young children to alleviate anemia while preserving some splenic immune function. It reduces transfusion needs but may eventually require total splenectomy in about half of patients.

Pre- and Post-Splenectomy Care

  • Vaccination: Patients should receive vaccines against pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae type B, and meningococcus before surgery.
  • Antibiotic Prophylaxis: Use of prophylactic antibiotics post-splenectomy is controversial but recommended by some for at least 5 years or even lifelong.
  • Folic Acid: Continued supplementation (1 mg/day) is recommended to prevent folate deficiency.

G6PD deficiency (Option A): In G6PD deficiency, splenectomy may actually worsen the anemia because the spleen filters and removes damaged red blood cells from the circulation. The primary management involves avoiding oxidative stressors and managing acute hemolytic episodes.

Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (Option B): In PNH, there is an abnormality in the complement system, and stem cell transplant is the best curative treatment. Splenectomy is not indicated as the hemolysis is complement-mediated and occurs throughout the circulation.

Hairy cell leukemia (Option D): In hairy cell leukemia, chemotherapy is the standard treatment. Splenectomy may be considered only in cases with massively enlarged spleen or if there is resistance to other treatments, but it is not the preferred initial treatment option.



Reference:
  • Williams Hematology, 10th Edition, Page 736
question: Elective splenectomy is preferred in which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Citrate, which is commonly used to anticoagulate BCs, chelates calcium and causes hypocalcemia, manifested by circumoral paresthesia, and changes in cardiac function may result from multiple rapid transfusions.
  • Hence, the most immediate complication seen after massive blood transfusion is hypocalcemia.
  • Although citrate is quickly metabolized to bicarbonate, calcium infusion (through a separate line) may be required.

Complications after Massive Blood Transfusion:

  • Reactions related to massive transfusion, i.e., transfusion of 50% of the patient’s total blood volume over 3 h or >5–10 units of RBCs (plus associated BCs), include:
    • Citrate toxicity
    • Hypothermia
    • Hyperkalemia
    • Dilutional coagulopathy

Rationale of other complications and treatment:

  • Rapid transfusion of BCs still at 4°C can result in hypothermia and cardiac dysrhythmias.
    • Use of an inline warmer will prevent this complication.
  • RBC leakage during storage, longer storage, and irradiation increase the concentration of potassium in the unit.
  • Neonates and patients with renal failure or other comorbidities (e.g., hyperglycemia or hypocalcemia) are at risk of hyperkalemia and resulting acute cardiac toxicity.
    • Treatment includes insulin, glucose, calcium gluconate, and furosemide
    • Prevention includes the use of washed or plasma-reduced RBCCs or a storage age of <7–10 days and the avoidance of RBCs stored for >24 h after irradiation


Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 912

question: A 26-year-old female presents with menorrhagia and excessive bleeding after a minor surgery. She gave the history of her father and sister having the same bleeding issues and the pattern of inheritance was determined to be autosomal dominant. What is the most likely disorder?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA) is characterized by selective failure of red blood cell production, while other cell lines (WBCs and platelets) remain normal. The hallmark laboratory finding is:

  • Low hemoglobin + severe reticulocytopenia (very low reticulocyte count)

  • This reflects the underlying marrow problem: Erythroid precursors are absent or extremely reduced, causing minimal or no reticulocyte release.

  • Common causes include thymoma, autoimmune disease, parvovirus B19 infection, medications, and lymphoid malignancies.

Aplastic Anemia (Option A): Produces pancytopenia (↓RBCs, ↓WBCs, ↓platelets). Not consistent with the normal WBC and platelet counts in this case.


Iron Deficiency Anemia (Option C): Usually shows increased reticulocyte count after treatment, but even before treatment, reticulocytes are not severely suppressed as in PRCA. Also presents with microcytic hypochromic RBCs, not mentioned here.


Hemolytic Anemia (Option D): Characterized by elevated reticulocyte count due to increased marrow response. A low reticulocyte count rules out hemolysis.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 798
question: A patient presents with fatigue, pallor, and weakness. Laboratory tests reveal low hemoglobin and a markedly low reticulocyte count, while white blood cell and platelet counts remain normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical manifestations indicate Essential Thrombocytosis, a myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by an isolated elevation in platelet count. The patient presents with classic symptoms including headaches, easy bruising, and visual disturbances, along with the key diagnostic finding of elevated platelets with normal RBC and WBC counts.
  • This condition results from abnormal proliferation of megakaryocytes in the bone marrow, leading to excessive platelet production.

Essential Thrombocytosis

Definition
  • Clonal myeloproliferative disorder
  • Characterized by increased platelet production
  • Abnormal megakaryocyte proliferation

Genetics
  • JAK2 V617F mutation (50-60% of cases)
  • CALR mutations (type 1 and 2)
  • MPL mutations

Lab Findings
  • Platelet count >450,000/μL
  • Increased bone marrow megakaryocytes
  • Normal RBC and WBC Count

Clinical Features
  • Often asymptomatic
  • Thrombotic events (arterial > venous)
  • Erythromelalgia
  • Ocular migraines & visual disturbances
  • TIAs
  • Spontaneous bleeding & easy bruising

Diagnostic Criteria
  • Platelet count >450,000/μL
  • Bone marrow showing megakaryocyte proliferation
  • Not meeting WHO criteria for other myeloid neoplasms
  • Presence of JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation

Complications
  • Thrombosis (major cause of morbidity)
  • Hemorrhage (especially with counts >1 million/μL)
  • Progression to myelofibrosis
  • Small risk of leukemic transformation

Treatment
  • Low-dose aspirin for thrombosis prevention
  • Hydroxyurea for high-risk patients
  • Anagrelide for cytoreduction
  • Plateletpheresis for severe cases

Polycythemia Vera (Option B) presents with elevated levels of all three blood cell lines—RBCs, WBCs, and platelets. The normal RBC count in this case makes this diagnosis unlikely. Patients typically present with ruddy complexion, pruritus, and thrombotic complications.

Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (Option C) typically shows elevation in granulocytes and often an increase in platelets as well. The presence of normal WBC count makes CML an unlikely diagnosis, as it characteristically presents with marked leukocytosis.

Acute Myeloid Leukemia (Option D) typically presents with abnormal levels of blood cells and can show varying counts of WBCs, RBCs, and platelets. The normal blood counts except for platelets make AML less likely, as it usually presents with cytopenias and blast cells in the peripheral blood.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 807-808
question: A young woman presents with recurrent headaches, easy bruising, and episodes of visual blurring. Her platelet count is elevated, while her red blood cell (RBC) and white blood cell (WBC) counts are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Bence Jones protein in urine
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Clinical features of CRAB (hypercalcemia, renal dysfunction, anemia, and bone lesions), along with the presence of an Gamma region M spike in serum electrophoresis, point towards the diagnosis of Multiple myeloma.

Investigations of Multiple myeloma:

  • Hematological Analysis:
    • It may reveal anemia; ESR is usually elevated.
    • Rare cases of plasma cell leukemia with high plasma cell counts >2000 plasma cells/μL.
    • Serum calcium and urea nitrogen may be elevated.
    • Serum alkaline phosphatase is usually normal.
    • Peripheral smear: Rouleaux formation
  • A/G ratio: Decreased
    • Increased level of β2 microglobulin.
    • Decreased albumin
  • Renal function test: Increased serum creatinine and uric acid.
  • Imaging:
    • Chest and bone radiographs: Lytic lesions/diffuse osteopenia
    • MRI: Extent of bone marrow infiltration and cord or root compression in patients with pain syndrome
    • PET/CT: Assess bone damage, extramedullary sites of the disease
  • Anion gap: (Na+ + K+) – (Cl- + HCO3-): Decreased
  • Serum or urine electrophoresis: M spike
  • Serum light chain assay: Increased
  • Immunofixation: Detects subtypes of light chain.
  • 24-hour urine specimen: Bence Jones protein (serum-free light chains) excretion
  • Fat pad biopsy: To detect amyloid deposits
  • Flow cytometry: CD 138+ (bone marrow plasma cells)
  • FISH:
    • Done to detect chromosomal abnormalities
    • Chromosome 17 deletion and translocation leads to poor prognosis.
  • Bone marrow biopsy: Plasmacytosis >10%

Liver function test (Option A): While liver function tests may be abnormal in some patients with multiple myeloma, they are not specific or diagnostic for the condition. LFTs are more useful in assessing liver involvement or complications.

Urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio (Option C): This test assesses kidney function and proteinuria but is not specific for multiple myeloma. While renal function may be affected in myeloma, UACR doesn't detect the characteristic Bence Jones proteins.

Heat and acetic acid test (Option D): This is an outdated test that is not used in modern diagnosis of multiple myeloma. Current diagnostic methods are more sensitive and specific.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Pages 867-875
question: A 46-year-old male presents to the outpatient department with a history of lower back pain and painful urination. Upon investigation, he is found to have normocytic normochromic anemia and hypercalcemia. Serum protein electrophoresis reveals an M-spike in the gamma region. Which of the following tests is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis of multiple myeloma?

correctAnswer: A. More commonly seen in females
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • MDS is actually more commonly seen in males than in females.

Myelodysplastic Syndrome:

  • The MDS are a heterogeneous group of hematologic disorders characterized by both
    • (1) cytopenias due to bone marrow failure and
    • (2) a high risk of development of AML
  • Anemia due to ineffective erythropoiesis, often with thrombocytopenia and neutropenia, occurs with dysmorphic (abnormal appearing) and usually a cellular bone marrow, or with specific chromosome abnormalities or acquired mutations.
  • MDS is a disease of the elderly; the mean age at onset is older than 70 years (Option C ruled out).
    • There is a slight male predominance (Option A).
  • Secondary or therapy-related MDS, usually related to previous iatrogenic exposure to alkylating agents and other chemotherapy or radiation, is not age-related (Option B ruled out).
  • Etiology:
    • Environmental exposures such as radiation, benzene, and smoking
    • Secondary, therapy-related MDS occurs as a late toxicity of cancer treatment;
      • Radiation (Option D ruled out) and the radiomimetic alkylating agents:
        • Busulfan,
        • nitrosourea, or
        • procarbazine (with a latent period of 5–7 years)
      • DNA topoisomerase inhibitors (2-year latency)
    • Acquired aplastic anemia, Fanconi anemia, and other constitutional marrow failure diseases can evolve into MDS


Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 815-817

question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding myelodysplastic syndrome?

correctAnswer: C. Type 1 von Willebrand disease presents with severe bleeding since childhood
explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - Type 1 von Willebrand disease presents with severe bleeding since childhood

Explanation:

  • Type 1 VWD is the most common form (≈70–80% of cases).

  • It involves a partial quantitative deficiency of von Willebrand factor (vWF).

  • Bleeding tendency is usually mild to moderate, not severe.

  • Symptoms may include easy bruising, epistaxis, menorrhagia, or bleeding after surgery/dental extraction.

  • Severe bleeding since childhood is more characteristic of Type 3 VWD.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Type 2 von Willebrand disease is associated with a moderate bleeding tendency: This statement is correct. Type 2 von Willebrand disease is characterized by a qualitative defect in von Willebrand factor, which leads to a moderate bleeding tendency. This type includes several subtypes with different defects in the von Willebrand factor.

Option B -Type 3 von Willebrand disease causes almost complete absence of von Willebrand factor, resulting in very low factor VIII levels: This statement is correct. Type 3 VWD is the most severe form.There is virtually no vWF, leading to markedly reduced factor VIII. Clinical features: severe mucocutaneous bleeding, hemarthroses, and spontaneous hemorrhage, similar to hemophilia.

Option D - Type 2 von Willebrand disease includes subtypes with varying defects in von Willebrand factor: This statement is correct. Type 2 von Willebrand disease includes several subtypes (e.g., 2A, 2B, 2M, 2N), each with different defects affecting the function of von Willebrand factor.

question: Which of the following statements regarding von Willebrand disease is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In hemolytic anemia, excessive destruction of red blood cells leads to the following changes

  • Indirect Van den Bergh test is positive (1): Hemolysis causes increased levels of unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin.
    • The indirect Van den Bergh test measures this rise, making it a hallmark of hemolytic anemia.
  • Urobilinogen is high (4): Increased hemoglobin breakdown leads to more bilirubin being converted into urobilinogen in the intestines, resulting in elevated urinary urobilinogen.
  • Serum conjugated bilirubin is raised (2): Hemolysis results in an increase in unconjugated bilirubin, not conjugated bilirubin, which is associated with liver or biliary tract conditions.
  • Serum transaminases are raised (3): Raised transaminases (ALT, AST) are markers of liver damage, not hemolysis.
  • GGT is elevated (5): Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) elevation is specific to liver and biliary tract pathology and is unrelated to hemolysis.

Feature

Prehepatic Jaundice

Hepatic Jaundice

Etiology

  • Sickle cell disease
  • G6PD deficiency
  • Liver diseases (e.g., viral hepatitis, cirrhosis, alcoholic liver disease)
  • Liver tumors
  • Drug-induced liver injury
  • Bile duct obstruction (e.g., gallstones, pancreatic cancer, cholangiocarcinoma, strictures, tumors)

Mechanism
  • Increased breakdown of red blood cells
  • Excessive bilirubin production
  • Impaired bilirubin conjugation and excretion due to liver dysfunction
  • Blocked bile flow
  • Accumulation of conjugated bilirubin in bloodstream

Prolonged PT

Dark urine (due to increased conjugated bilirubin)
  • Dark urine (due to conjugated bilirubin)
  • Pale stools (due to reduced bile excretion)

Van den Bergh test:

Purpose: Differentiates between conjugated and unconjugated bilirubin in serum.

Principle: Based on diazotization reaction: Bilirubin reacts with diazotized sulfanilic acid to form a colored complex.

Reagents Used: Diazotized sulfanilic acid, methanol (for indirect reaction)

Types of Reactions:

Reaction Type

Findings

Bilirubin Type

Clinical Significance

Direct (Positive within seconds)

Immediate pink-red color in aqueous solution

Conjugated (Water-soluble)

Seen in obstructive jaundice, hepatocellular jaundice

Indirect (Delayed or requires methanol)

Pink-red color appears only after adding methanol

Unconjugated (Water-insoluble)

Seen in hemolytic jaundice, Gilbert syndrome, Crigler-Najjar syndrome

Color change seen both in aqueous and after methanol addition

Mixed (Conjugated + Unconjugated)

Seen in hepatic jaundice (e.g., viral hepatitis, cirrhosis)

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Sickle cell anemia is caused by a missense point mutation in the β-globin (HBB) gene on chromosome 11.
  • This mutation changes - Glutamic acid (Glu) → Valine (Val) at position 6 of the β-globin chain.
  • This single amino-acid substitution produces Hemoglobin S (HbS).
  • When HbS becomes deoxygenated, it polymerizes, distorting red blood cells into a sickle shape, leading to hemolysis, vaso-occlusion, and recurrent painful crises.

question: Which of the following is not a feature of thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Deficiency of GpIb receptors:

Explanation:

  • Bernard–Soulier syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive platelet disorder characterized by a defect in platelet adhesion due to deficiency or dysfunction of the platelet membrane glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) complex, which is the receptor for von Willebrand factor (vWF).
  • This defect prevents platelets from binding to exposed subendothelial vWF during vascular injury, leading to defective primary hemostasis.
  • Clinically, it presents with mucocutaneous bleeding, prolonged bleeding time, and thrombocytopenia with giant platelets on peripheral smear.

Incorrect Options:

Deficiency of GpIIb/IIIa receptor (Option A): Seen in Glanzmann thrombasthenia — causes defective platelet aggregation, not adhesion.

Deficiency of von Willebrand factor (Option C): Seen in von Willebrand disease — results in both defective platelet adhesion and secondary coagulation defect due to reduced factor VIII stability.

Deficiency of ADP receptors (Option D): Seen in rare platelet function disorders like P2Y12 receptor defects — affects aggregation via ADP pathway, not adhesion.
question: What defect is seen in Bernard Soulier syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option D - Albumin and β₂-microglobulin

Explanation:
The International Staging System (ISS) for multiple myeloma — a widely accepted prognostic model — uses two lab values: serum β₂-microglobulin and serum albumin.

  • β₂-Microglobulin is a marker of tumor burden and renal function; elevated levels indicate more advanced disease and poorer prognosis.
  • Albumin reflects the patient’s general health and disease activity; lower levels are associated with more aggressive disease and worse outcomes.

Incorrect Options:

IgG and albumin (Option A): While IgG is commonly the paraprotein in multiple myeloma, it is not part of the ISS prognostic criteria.

IgM and albumin (Option B): Elevated IgM is characteristic of Waldenström macroglobulinemia, which differs from multiple myeloma in pathology and prognosis.

Albumin and LDH (Option C): Elevated LDH may suggest high tumor turnover or aggressive disease but is not part of standard ISS staging (though it may appear in the Revised-ISS combined with cytogenetics).

question: A 60-year-old female presents with weakness, back pain and repeated infections. Work up shows M spike on serum electrophoresis. Prognosis is determined by which of the following factors?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The diagnosis is a Large Patent Ductus Arteriosus, which manifests as differential cyanosis.
  • In this condition, chronic left-to-right shunting leads to severe pulmonary hypertension, eventually causing the shunt to reverse (right-to-left).
  • Deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary artery enters the aorta through the ductus, which is located distal to the origin of the brachiocephalic and left common carotid arteries.
  • Consequently, the deoxygenated blood is directed to the lower body, making the toes cyanotic, while the head, neck, and right arm (supplied by pre-ductal vessels) remain pink and well-oxygenated.

Pulmonary AV fistula (Option A) involves a bypass within the pulmonary circulation, causing generalised arterial desaturation that results in uniform cyanosis of both upper and lower limbs.

Partial anomalous pulmonary venous connection (Option B) is an acyanotic condition where some pulmonary veins drain into the right atrium; it does not lead to differential limb cyanosis.

Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome (Option D), also known as Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia, may cause cyanosis via pulmonary AV malformations, but this cyanosis is typically generalized rather than differential.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1859.
question: A patient develops cyanosis of the lower limbs on standing, while the upper limbs remain normal in color. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This patient has chronic aortic regurgitation.
  • The clinical features point toward wide pulse pressure, which is characteristic of aortic regurgitation.
  • The prominent, bounding carotid upstroke represents Corrigan’s pulse, while rhythmic nail bed blanching corresponds to Quincke’s pulse, both classic peripheral signs of significant AR.
  • In chronic aortic regurgitation, there is backflow of blood from the aorta into the left ventricle during diastole, producing a high-pitched, blowing, early diastolic decrescendo murmur, best heard along the left sternal border with the patient leaning forward in end-expiration.

Late diastolic murmur (Option A): Typically seen in mitral stenosis due to turbulent flow across a narrowed mitral valve, not associated with wide pulse pressure.

Systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur (Option C): Characteristic of aortic stenosis (ejection systolic murmur), not consistent with bounding pulses of AR.

Mid systolic murmur (Option D): Commonly associated with mitral valve prolapse or innocent flow murmurs and does not explain the peripheral signs seen here.

  • When performing a lumbar puncture (LP) or any neuraxial procedure, it is critical to avoid complications such as a spinal epidural haematoma, which can lead to permanent neurological deficits.

question: A 55-year-old patient with suspected meningitis requires an urgent diagnostic lumbar puncture. The patient is currently on multiple antithrombotic medications for ischemic heart disease. explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image demonstrates xanthochromia, a distinct yellowish discolouration of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) supernatant following centrifugation. This finding confirms the presence of blood breakdown products (such as bilirubin) or other pigments within the CSF space that occurred in vivo before the puncture.

The differential diagnoses for xanthochromia include:

  • Aneurysmal leaks
  • Severe hyperbilirubinaemia
  • SAH (Subarachnoid haemorrhage) (Statement 1)
  • Sentinel haemorrhage (Statement 3)
  • Excess carotenoid intake (carrots and spinach)
  • Conditions that cause elevated protein levels in the CSF (e.g., carcinomatosis, intracranial neoplasms, Froin's syndrome, tuberculosis, cryptococcal meningitis, and radicular demyelination). (Statement 2)

Clean traumatic lumbar puncture (Statement 4): In a traumatic tap, fresh red blood cells are artificially introduced into the sample during the procedure. When the sample is promptly centrifuged, these intact red blood cells precipitate to the bottom, leaving a classically clear and colourless supernatant.

question: A 65-year-old poorly compliant hypertensive male is brought to the emergency department after suddenly developing a staggering, broad-based gait and slurred speech. On examination, he exhibits a prominent tremor when attempting to touch the examiner's finger. Where is the acute lesion most likely located?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The acute onset of bilateral lower limb weakness combined with a distinct sensory level (umbilicus corresponds to T10) and sphincter dysfunction (urinary retention) is a neurological emergency indicating an acute spinal cord syndrome.
  • The most critical step is to quickly identify or exclude a compressive lesion (such as a spinal epidural abscess, haematoma, or metastatic cord compression) or transverse myelitis. Therefore, an urgent Spinal MRI is the modality of choice.

CT (Option A) is good for detecting bone fractures or acute intracranial haemorrhage, but it does not adequately visualise the spinal cord, discs, epidural abscess, or soft tissue compression. In suspected cord compression, MRI is superior.

question: A 55-year-old man is brought to the emergency department complaining of an acute inability to move both of his legs, accompanied by sensory loss below the umbilicus and urinary retention. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In the evaluation of any patient presenting with altered sensorium or coma, the immediate priority after stabilising the Airway, Breathing, and Circulation (ABCs) is to rule out reversible metabolic causes.
  • Hypoglycaemia is the most common, rapidly reversible, and potentially fatal metabolic cause of coma, particularly in a patient with a history of diabetes.
  • Hypoglycaemia specifically can mimic structural brain injury, presenting with focal neurological signs such as bilateral extensor plantar responses and autonomic instability (tachycardia and hypertension due to a sympathetic surge).
  • Metabolic encephalopathies (e.g., hypoglycaemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, or hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state) are far more common than structural lesions.

Amlodipine (Option B): The elevated blood pressure is likely a compensatory response to the acute stress or metabolic derangement. Rapidly lowering blood pressure in a comatose patient is contraindicated as it may critically reduce cerebral perfusion pressure, especially if the cause is an ischaemic stroke.

IV Mannitol (Option C): The patient presents with tachycardia (105/min). Signs of raised intracranial pressure typically include the Cushing's reflex (bradycardia, hypertension, and irregular respiration).

CT Brain (Option D): While neuroimaging is essential to rule out haemorrhage or infarction, it is a time-consuming process. Checking blood glucose takes seconds and must always precede transport to the CT scanner.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 189, 191-193.
question: An unconscious 70-year-old male with a known history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypertension is brought to the emergency room. explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • An autonomic storm, currently and more accurately termed Paroxysmal Sympathetic Hyperactivity (PSH), is a syndrome characterised by episodic surges in sympathetic tone. Clinical manifestations include tachycardia, hypertension, tachypnoea, diaphoresis, hyperthermia, and abnormal dystonic motor posturing.
  • Severe acquired brain injury is the most common cause, with Traumatic Brain Injury (TBI) accounting for nearly 80% of all reported cases.

Other causes include:

  • Spinal cord injury (Option D ruled out)
  • Drugs and toxins (phenylpropanolamine, cocaine, amphetamines, TCAs, tetanus, botulinum toxin) (Option A ruled out)
  • Guillain-Barré syndrome. (Option C ruled out)
  • Autonomic neuropathy
  • Chemodectomas (e.g., pheochromocytoma).

  • The GCS-P score combines the traditional Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) with the Pupil Reactivity Score (PRS) to provide a more accurate prognostic indicator for patients with traumatic brain injury.

The score is calculated by subtracting the PRS from the standard GCS score: GCS-P = GCS - PRS.

  • The minimum possible score on the standard GCS is 3 (E1, V1, M1).
  • The PRS reflects the number of unreactive pupils and ranges from 0 to 2:
    • 0 = both pupils react to light
    • 1 = one pupil is unreactive
    • 2 = both pupils are unreactive.
  • Therefore, the lowest possible GCS-P score is calculated as 3 (lowest GCS) minus 2 (highest PRS, meaning both pupils are unreactive), which equals 1.

The apnoea test is the final and most critical step in the clinical determination of brain death, designed to assess the functional integrity of the medullary respiratory centre. The test relies on the accumulation of carbon dioxide to maximally stimulate the respiratory drive.

According to standard clinical guidelines (such as those from the American Academy of Neurology), the test is considered positive, confirming the absence of brainstem function, if

  • The patient makes no respiratory effort and
  • Arterial PCO2 rises to ≥ 60 mmHg (or ≥ 20 mmHg above the pre-test baseline).

  • Most common seizure seen in children is febrile seizures and leading childhood epilepsy syndrome is Benign rolandic epilepsy (bening because of self limiting nature).
  • Note that question is not asking most type of seizures in children but the most common type of epilepsy syndrome.


Benign Rolandic Epilepsy

  • Occurs in children aged 4–10 years
  • Seizures often occur during sleep and involve face and cause drooling of saliva. Episodes during awake stage might lead to speech arrest
  • Self-limiting, resolves by adolescence

Janz Syndrome (Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy - JME) (Option A): This is the most common idiopathic generalized epilepsy syndrome, but its onset is typically in adolescence (mean age 12-18 years), making it less common than Rolandic epilepsy in the general "childhood" population.


Lennox-Gastaut Syndrome (LGS) (Option B): This is a severe and rare form of childhood epilepsy (an epileptic encephalopathy). It accounts for only about 1-2% of childhood epilepsies.


Febrile seizures (Option D): This is a key distinction. While febrile seizures are the most common type of seizure in childhood (affecting 2-5% of young children), they are generally not considered an epilepsy syndrome. Epilepsy is defined as a tendency toward recurrent, unprovoked seizures. Febrile seizures are provoked by fever and typically do not require chronic anti-seizure medication.

question: Which of the following manifestations is earliest to be seen in this neurocutaneous disorder

correctAnswer: A. Delayed neurological complication of measles vaccine
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • SSPE is caused by persistent defective measles virus in the brain (usually wild-type virus). It appears an average of ~6–8 years after natural measles infection.
  • It is not caused by MMR vaccine (measles-mumps-rubella).
  • The risk is highest if measles infection occurred before age 2 of years.
  • Inosine pranobex (Inoprinosine) is an antiviral and immunomodulatory agent that has been used to improve survival along with intraventricular interferon.

SSPE can be diagnosed if three out of five criteria are met:

  1. Typical clinical presentation (progressive neurologic deterioration)
  2. EEG showing stereotyped periodic complexes/ Periodic generalized high-voltage slow-wave complexes
  3. Brain biopsy or autopsy with characteristic histopathological findings
  4. CSF globulin levels greater than 20% of total CSF protein
  5. Elevated CSF measles antibody titers (≥1/4 by hemagglutination inhibition or ≥1/20 by ELISA)

correctAnswer: C. CSF shows Anti measles antibody
explanationHtml:
The child has features of Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE):

  • Unvaccinated child
  • Progressive behavioral and cognitive decline
  • Irritability and poor school performance
  • Myoclonic jerks
  • Motor dysfunction
  • EEG showing periodic high-voltage slow-wave complexes every 4-10 seconds

SSPE is a progressive neurodegenerative disease caused by persistent mutant measles virus infection of the CNS, occurring years after measles infection.

The most important diagnostic test is demonstration of elevated anti-measles antibodies in CSF (and serum).

Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis (SSPE)

About
  • SSPE is a rare, severe complication of the measles virus.
  • It typically presents in early adolescence and has a progressive course with high mortality.
  • Vaccination has reduced measles cases, but SSPE remains a concern due to measles re-emergence.

Pathophysiology
  • Caused by the measles virus, which is highly contagious and transmitted via aerosols.
  • The latency period ranges from 6-8 years post-infection, with shorter periods in younger children.
  • The virus targets lymphocytes and epithelial cells, causing significant immunosuppression.
  • SSPE is associated with a poor cellular immune response and persistent viral presence in the CNS.
  • Neuronal entry and infection mechanisms are not fully understood; mutations in the virus may facilitate evasion of the immune response.

Clinical Features
  • Symptoms typically arise 6-8 years after measles infection, starting with cognitive decline.
  • Early signs include personality changes, poor school performance, and lethargy.
  • Stage I: Personality and behavioural changes, including irritability, dementia, lethargy, social withdrawal, and speech regression.
  • Stage II: Progressive decline in motor function characterized by myoclonus, dyskinesia, and dystonia.
  • Stage III: Development of extrapyramidal symptoms, posturing, and spasticity.
  • Stage IV: Akinetic mutism, autonomic failure, or transition to a vegetative state.
  • Progressive motor function decline occurs, with myoclonus and focal paralysis.
  • Patients may develop seizures, leading to vegetative states or akinetic mutism.
  • Visual symptoms may precede other signs, including retinal lesions and vision loss.
  • Atypical presentations can involve psychiatric symptoms and rapid decline, especially in younger patients.

CSF electrophoresis showing oligoclonal bands (Option A):

  • Characteristic of Multiple Sclerosis.
  • Not diagnostic of SSPE.

CSF showing albuminocytological dissociation (Option B):

  • Characteristic of Guillain-Barré Syndrome.
  • Elevated protein with normal cell count.

CSF IgG index (Option D):

  • Increased IgG index may occur in several CNS inflammatory disorders.
  • Less specific than demonstrating anti-measles antibodies.

question: A 10 year boy unvaccinated child is brought to hospital with increased irritability, social withdrawal, and difficulty in school. On examination he has myoclonic jerks and motor difficulties. EEG shows periodic spikes of slow-wave discharges occurring every 4–10 seconds. Select the best investigation to be performed in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Focal seizure

  • EEG shows localized spikes or sharp waves in the region of the brain corresponding to the seizure onset.

Absence seizure

  • EEG exhibits 3 Hz spike-and-slow wave discharges, typically generalized and symmetric.

Hypsarrythmia

  • EEG presents chaotic, bursts of bilateral asynchronous high-amplitude slow waves interspersed with spikes followed by generalized voltage attenuation.

Periodic sharp wave complexes

  • EEG reveals generalized synchronized high-voltage sharp waves occurring at 1–2 Hz.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3409, 3410, 3417, 3418.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The progression from localized frontal intermittent rhythmical delta activity (FIRDA) to PSWC is characteristic of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD), along with the patient's rapid cognitive decline and myoclonus.


Periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWC)

  • The first EEG finding in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) is often localized frontal intermittent rhythmical delta activity (FIRDA).
  • FIRDA evolves to typical periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWC) after a few weeks.
  • PSWC is characterized by generalized synchronized high-voltage sharp waves with frequencies of 1–2 Hz.
  • While PSWC usually appear generalized, they may exhibit lateralized or localized distributions in the early stages of CJD.
  • PSWC is one of the criteria for the clinical diagnosis of CJD.
  • Hence, Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) presents with PSWC and myoclonic jerks.

[[figure-1]]

Periodic sharp wave complexes are seen on the EEG


Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis in CJD shows:

  • 14-3-3 protein (SA 14-3-3): Positive
  • Tau protein: Increased
  • Usually no pleocytosis


Hepatic and renal encephalopathy (Options A & C) may cause altered mental status, but not the rapid cognitive decline, myoclonus, and specific EEG findings seen in CJD.


Alzheimer’s disease (Option D) typically has a much slower progression and lacks these EEG patterns and associated myoclonus.

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3530, 3531
question: A 62 y/o man presents with rapid cognitive decline, visual disturbances, and myoclonus. An EEG shows localized frontal intermittent rhythmical delta activity (FIRDA) that evolves to periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWC) after a few weeks. Based on this presentation and EEG findings, which of the following conditions is most likely associated with his symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Subtle seizures are the most common seizure type in newborns, often presenting with changes in tone or subtle movements called jitteriness that often go unnoticed.
  • Types of Movements:
    • Ocular Movements: Includes random eye movements, sustained conjugate tonic deviation, eyelid blinking or fluttering, eye-rolling, and nystagmus.
    • Oral-Buccal-Lingual Movements: Such as sucking, smacking, chewing, and tongue protrusions.
    • Progressive Movements: Including rowing, swimming, pedalling, thrashing, or struggling movements.
    • Complex Purposeless Movements: Characterized by sudden arousal, episodic limb hyperactivity, and crying.

Benign rolandic epilepsy (Option A) is the most common type of epilepsy in children. It's also known as benign epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (BECTS).

Febrile seizures (Option C) are the most common type of epilepsy in infants and young children aged 6 months to 5 years, with a peak incidence between 12 and 18 months.


Myoclonic seizures (Option D) are less common than subtle seizures. They are rapid, single, or rhythmic repetitive jerks that involve a finger, limb, or the entire body. They are more common in pre-term infants than term infants. I

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK2599/
question: A 2-day-old neonate born at 39 weeks gestation by venthouse is having jitteriness. Which of the following is correct about this presentation?

correctAnswer: C. Consider alternative contraception methods due to carbamazepine's effect on oral contraceptives.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Carbamazepine can significantly reduce the effectiveness of oral contraceptives, so alternative methods (like IUDs) are recommended for women not planning to conceive.

Catamenial Epilepsy
  • Increased seizure frequency around menses due to estrogen/progesterone effects or antiseizure drug level changes.
  • Some women may require increased antiseizure drug dosages during menses.
  • Natural progestins or intramuscular medroxyprogesterone may benefit certain women.

Pregnancy
  • ~50% of women experience unchanged seizure frequency; ~30% may increase, and ~20% decrease.
  • Monitoring of serum antiseizure drug levels is essential during pregnancy.
  • Lamotrigine and levetiracetam are recommended as first-line monotherapy for generalized and focal onset seizures.
  • The higher teratogenic risk with multiple antiseizure drugs is noted.
  • Valproic acid is strongly associated with adverse fetal outcomes and is thus contraindicated in pregnancy.
  • Folate supplementation (1–4 mg/d) is recommended due to antifolate effects of anticonvulsants.
  • Enzyme-inducing drugs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, topiramate, phenobarbital, primidone) may cause vitamin K deficiency in newborns. Hence mothers should take oral vitamin K, and infants should receive intramuscular vitamin K at birth.

Contraception
  • Certain antiseizure medications (carbamazepine, phenytoin, phenobarbital, topiramate) reduce oral contraceptive efficacy via enzyme induction.
  • Alternative contraception methods (IUDs, long-acting reversible contraceptives) should be considered.

Breast-Feeding
  • Antiseizure medications are excreted in breast milk at varying levels (5% for valproic acid to 300% for levetiracetam).
  • Encouraged to breastfeed unless infant shows signs of drug effects (e.g., lethargy, poor feeding).



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3427.

question: A 25 y/o woman with a history of catamenial epilepsy reports an increase in seizure frequency just before her menstrual period. She is currently taking carbamazepine and is newly started on OCPs by her GP for contraception. What is the most appropriate advice for her regarding her current situation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Carbamazepine is a sodium channel blocker that is effective for focal seizures

  • But in idiopathic generalized epilepsies including absence, myoclonic, and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy, carbamazepine can exacerbate seizures.

  • This occurs because carbamazepine enhances thalamocortical oscillations and interferes with inhibitory circuits, promoting generalized epileptiform discharges.


Valproate, lamotrigine, and topiramate are broad-spectrum antiepileptics effective in generalized tonic–clonic, myoclonic, and absence seizures, and do not exacerbate them.

question: Which of the following antiepileptic drugs can worsen generalized seizures, particularly absence or myoclonic types, and should be avoided in idiopathic generalized epilepsy?

correctAnswer: B. MRI typically reveals an enlarged hippocampus with trilaminar architecture.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

MRI findings in Mesial Temporal Lobe Epilepsy (MTLE) Syndrome show a smaller hippocampus with a loss of the normal trilaminar architecture, reflecting the structural changes associated with the syndrome.

  • It is the most common focal epilepsy associated with impaired awareness and is characterized by distinctive clinical, EEG, MRI, and pathological features. It is strongly associated with hippocampal sclerosis, which plays a key role in its pathophysiology.
  • Pathological Findings:
    • Hippocampal sclerosis with selective neuronal loss.
    • Gliosis.
    • Granule cell layer dispersion.
  • Clinical Features (Option D ruled out):
    • Auras are common (e.g., epigastric rising sensation, déjà vu, fear, olfactory hallucinations).
    • Focal seizures with impaired awareness and behavioral arrest.
    • Complex automatisms are frequently present.
    • Postictal disorientation and confusion are common.
    • Memory impairment may occur.
    • Dysphasia may occur if the epileptic focus is in the dominant temporal lobe.
    • Contralateral dystonic (unilateral) posturing may be seen.
  • EEG Findings (Option A ruled out):
    • Unilateral or bilateral anterior temporal spikes may be seen on interictal EEG.
    • Interictal PET demonstrates temporal hypometabolism.
    • Ictal SPECT demonstrates temporal hyperperfusion.
    • The Wada (intracarotid amobarbital) test may reveal material-specific memory deficits in selected surgical candidates.
  • MRI Findings (Option B): Characteristic MRI findings of hippocampal sclerosis include:
    • Hippocampal atrophy (smaller hippocampus).
    • Loss of normal internal (trilaminar) architecture.
    • Increased T2/FLAIR signal intensity.
    • Enlargement of the ipsilateral temporal horn.
    • Ipsilateral temporal lobe volume loss.
  • Treatment (Option C ruled out):
    • MTLE is frequently refractory to antiseizure medications.
    • It responds well to surgical intervention (e.g., anterior temporal lobectomy or selective amygdalohippocampectomy) in appropriately selected patients, making recognition of this syndrome particularly important.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3411.

Her parents report that she has experienced GTCS, atonic seizures where she suddenly drops to the ground, and atypical absence seizures. The child has also shown signs of cognitive impairment. correctAnswer: B. During the tonic phase, the EEG typically shows a progressive increase in generalized low-voltage fast activity.

Explanation:

Hack to Rememeber

Focal Seizure- EEG

GTCS- EEG
  • The routine interictal EEG in patients with focal seizures is often normal. (Option A ruled out)
  • It may show brief discharges, such as epileptiform spikes or sharp waves.
  • Focal seizures can arise from areas like the medial temporal lobe or inferior frontal lobe, which may be distant from the scalp.
  • As a result, the EEG recorded during the seizure may be nonlocalizing.
  • The region of seizure onset can be identified using surgically placed intracranial electrodes.

question: A 25-year-old patient with a recently diagnosed PNET experiences recurrent episodes of fainting, often preceded by sweating, tremors and confusion. What is the most likely cause?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This is a classic case of epileptic spasms .

A 6-month-old infant presenting with brief episodes of sudden flexion of the trunk and limbs, each lasting a few seconds, is highly suggestive of epileptic spasms (infantile spasms/West syndrome). These events typically occur in clusters, especially after waking. The EEG finding of hypsarrhythmia is characteristic. It shows:

  • Chaotic, disorganized background
  • High-amplitude slow waves
  • Multifocal spikes and sharp waves

During the actual spasm, there is often electrodecremental response (background suppression), which is a key diagnostic feature. Clinically, these spasms involve:

  • Sudden flexion (more common) or extension
  • Predominantly proximal muscles (neck, trunk, limbs)
  • Also called “salaam attacks”

Absence seizures (Option A) occur in older children (4–14 years) with staring spells and 3 Hz spike-and-wave EEG, without motor flexion spasms.

Atonic seizures (Option B) cause sudden loss of muscle tone (drop attacks), not flexor spasms. EEG typically shows slow spike-wave (<3 Hz).

Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (Option D) presents later (1–8 years) with multiple seizure types and slow spike-wave EEG (<3 Hz), not hypsarrhythmia.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3410
question: A 6-month-old infant presents with brief episodes of sudden flexion of the trunk and limbs, lasting a few seconds. EEG shows hypsarrhythmia, and during the episodes, there's marked background suppression on the EEG. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The diagnosis is most likely to be variant creutzfeldt-jakob disease, due to the combination of dementia and myoclonic jerks (startle myoclonus).
  • Hyperintensity in the pulvinar nucleus of the thalamus on T2/FLAIR MRI is considered highly specific for vCJD.
  • It is also called the "hockey stick sign" when it extends to the dorsomedial thalamus.

Epileptic spasms (Option A) typically occur in infants and present with different EEG findings (hypsarrhythmia) rather than spike-and-slow-wave discharges.


Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (Option B): Although JME can cause myoclonic seizures and spike-and-slow-wave discharges, the history of beef consumption strongly suggests prion disease.


Anoxic brain injury (Option D): There's no evidence of hypoxia or brain injury, and the patient’s symptoms are better explained by prion-related vCJD.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3530
question: A 23 year patient presents with sudden, brief muscle jerks on loud auditory stimuli and dementia. T2/FLAIR MRI shows hyperintensity in the pulvinar nucleus of the thalamus. What is the first differential diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Episodes are triggered by photic stimulation
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This is a case of Absence seizures.
  • They occur due to T-type calcium channel dysfunction in the thalamus, which causes rhythmic 3 Hz spike-and-wave discharges on EEG.
  • They are often triggered by hyperventilation, stress, or flashing lights in mainly children aged 4–14 years.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3410, 3414

question: A 7 year child is brought to the clinic due to frequent episodes of "daydreaming" during school, which last for a few seconds and are accompanied by subtle eyelid blinking. Which of the following is correct about this condition?

correctAnswer: C. Focal Seizure with Impaired Awareness
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's unresponsiveness, automatisms, and post-seizure confusion are characteristics of focal seizure with impaired awareness.

[[figure-1]]

Image showing abnormal high voltage in right temporal leads. Since the abnormal electrical activity is seen only in some leads, it is a focal seizure.

Absence Seizure (Option A): Typically involves brief episodes of staring without postictal confusion or automatisms, which is more common in children.


Panic Attack (Option B): Presents with intense fear and physical symptoms, but does not include automatisms or loss of awareness.


Focal Seizure with Intact Awareness (Option D): Involves preserved awareness throughout the event, which is not seen in this case.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3409.
question: A 35 y/o woman experiences sudden unresponsiveness during conversations, followed by repetitive hand movements and lip-smacking. Afterwards, she seems confused and does not remember the event. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient has focal seizure activity without loss of awareness, consistent with a Jacksonian March.
  • This refers to a focal motor seizure in which abnormal clonic movements begin in one area (e.g., hand) and gradually spread to adjacent regions (e.g., arm and face).
  • The seizure progresses in a “marching” pattern, following the motor cortex's representation of the body.

[[figure-1]]

Absence seizure (Option A): This seizure typically involves a brief loss of awareness, where the person appears to “zone out” and is unresponsive. It is predominantly seen in children. Motor symptoms are usually absent, and the person does not experience the spreading involuntary movements seen in this patient.


Todd’s paralysis (Option B): Todd’s paralysis is a temporary weakness (paresis) affecting the same area involved in a seizure. It usually occurs after the seizure has ended (postictally), which is not the case in this patient. It is also a feature of focal motor seizures with intact awareness.


Epilepsia partialis continua (Option C): This refers to prolonged, continuous focal motor seizures, often restricted to one part of the body, lasting hours or even days. While awareness is usually intact, the condition is characterised by ongoing motor activity rather than the brief spreading movements described here.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3409.
question: A 32 y/o woman experiences involuntary movements that begin in her right hand and progressively spread to her right arm and face. She remains fully aware throughout the episode. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Post-ictal confusion further supports a seizure origin rather than a cardiovascular syncope.
  • Orthostatic hypotension (Option A) usually occurs upon standing, is gradual in onset, and typically does not cause post-event confusion.
  • In contrast, atonic seizures present with sudden loss of muscle tone, leading to abrupt falls (drop attacks) and brief loss of consciousness.

It is not GTCS (Option C), as there is no tonic-clonic movement or prolonged post-ictal phase—only a sudden loss of tone.


It is not myoclonic seizure (Option D), because those involve brief jerks without loss of consciousness or post-ictal confusion.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3410.
question: A 20-year-old student experiences episodes of sudden drop attacks with brief loss of consciousness and confusion after the episode. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This is a focal seizure with impaired awareness, as indicated by the automatisms (lip-smacking), duration of 1–2 minutes, and post-ictal confusion with amnesia.
  • In contrast, absence seizures are brief (typically <20 seconds), occur mostly in young children, and lack post-ictal confusion or automatisms. (Option B)
  • The presence of prolonged altered awareness and automatisms strongly points to temporal lobe epilepsy.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3409.
question: A 15-year-old boy is brought to the OPD with complaints of repeated episodes of blank staring, and lip-smacking movements lasting around 1–2 minutes. He is confused afterward and has no memory of the episode. Diagnosis is?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Vasovagal syncope can sometimes include brief convulsive movements, especially if there's cerebral hypoperfusion.
  • The event could have been triggered by prolonged standing.
  • GTCS (Option B) presents with post-ictal confusion , delayed recovery, incontinence, and often tongue biting

  • Features against GTCS:

    1. Autonomic features like sweating

    2. No tongue biting or incontinence

    3. Perioral pallor ( GTCS epidose has perioral pallor)

    4. Quick recovery within 1 minute



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3418.
question: A 19-year-old medical student collapses in the anatomy dissection hall. His friends report a brief period of limb jerking lasting about 10–15 seconds during the episode. He regained consciousness in a minute, he appeared pale around the lips with sweating on forehead. Diagnosis is?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient is showing left-sided hemineglect—ignoring the left half of her face and plate—as well as constructional apraxia (inability to copy simple shapes).

  • These features are classic for a lesion in the right (non-dominant) parietal lobe, which is responsible for spatial attention and visuospatial integration.

Left parietal lobe (Option A):The dominant (usually left) parietal lobe is responsible for language functions such as reading, writing, naming, and calculation. Damage here causes Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left–right disorientation), not hemispatial neglect.


Left temporal lobe (Option C): Dominant temporal lobe lesions typically cause Wernicke’s aphasia (fluent but nonsensical speech, poor comprehension).


Right temporal lobe (Option D): The temporal lobe is mainly involved in memory, emotion, and auditory processing.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 204.

question: A 50-year-old woman with T2DM is brought in by her family due to strange behaviour. Her daughter says that she noticed that her mother at her wedding was applying makeup only to the left side of her face and eating food from only the left half of her plate. When asked to copy simple shapes such as a triangle, square, and circle her drawings are incomplete and poorly organized. Which of the following brain regions is most likely affected?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient’s features are classic for conduction aphasia, which occurs due to damage to the arcuate fasciculus—the fiber tract connecting Broca’s and Wernicke’s areas.

  • Fluent speech → Broca’s area intact
  • Intact comprehension → Wernicke’s area intact
  • Impaired repetition → hallmark of arcuate fasciculus lesion
  • Naming and reading preserved

Broca’s area (Option A): Non-fluent, effortful speech → NOT seen here


Wernicke’s area (Option B): Fluent but nonsensical speech with poor comprehension → NOT seen here


Angular gyrus(Option D): Causes Gerstmann syndrome

  • Agraphia

  • Acalculia

  • Finger agnosia

  • Left–right disorientation

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 202.

question: A 60 -year-old retired banker and right-handed man is brought with complaints of speech difficulties. He speaks fluently and with normal grammar, and appears to understand both verbal and written commands. However, when asked to repeat phrases, he is unable to do so. His naming and reading comprehension are intact. Which of the following regions is most likely affected?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Weber syndrome is a midbrain ventral (basilar) lesion involving the oculomotor nerve fascicles and corticospinal/corticobulbar tracts. This produces ipsilateral CN III palsy (eye down and out) and contralateral hemiplegia + contralateral lower face weakness. Vertical gaze palsy is not a feature; it occurs in dorsal midbrain (Parinaud) syndrome, not Weber.

[[figure-1]]


It presents with:

  • Ipsilateral CN III palsy (ptosis, mydriasis, "down and out" eye)

  • Contralateral hemiplegia due to pyramidal tract involvement

  • Contralateral lower facial weakness may occur due to corticobulbar tract involvement

[[figure-2]]



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 234, 3431

question: Which of the following is not a feature of Weber syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This pattern of crossed sensory deficits (ipsilateral face + contralateral body), ataxia, and bulbar symptoms (dysphagia) is hallmark for lateral medullary infarction called Wallenberg syndrome.
  • Key features supporting the diagnosis:
    • Ipsilateral signs

      • Facial numbness (trigeminal spinal nucleus/tract involvement)

      • Limb ataxia & nystagmus (inferior cerebellar peduncle/vestibular nuclei)

      • Dysphagia, hoarseness, diminished gag reflex (nucleus ambiguus → CN IX, X)

    • Contralateral signs:

      • Loss of pain and temperature sensation on the body (spinothalamic tract involvement)

Brown-Séquard syndrome (Option A) causes ipsilateral motor loss + proprioception loss with contralateral pain/temp loss below lesion, but no cranial nerve involvement .


Locked-in syndrome (Option C) occurs due to ventral pons lesion, causing quadriplegia and loss of speech with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements.


Medial medullary syndrome (Option D) causes contralateral hemiparesis + proprioception loss with ipsilateral tongue paralysis,

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3433.

question: A 65-year-old woman presents to ER with history of suddenly falling down with difficulty in swallowing. On examination patient can stick out her tongue without any deviation, and gag reflex is diminished. Ipsilateral nystagmus is noted with ataxia of limbs, ipsilateral face numbness with a contralateral pain and temperature loss. Diagnosis is?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This syndrome is caused by infarction of the anterior spinal artery affecting the medial medulla. It presents with contralateral hemiparesis, contralateral loss of proprioception and vibration (medial lemniscus), and ipsilateral tongue deviation (hypoglossal nerve).
  • Facial sensation remains intact because the trigeminal nucleus lies more laterally.

Lateral Medullary Syndrome (Option A) involves the posterior inferior cerebellar artery and presents with dysphagia, hoarseness, ipsilateral facial sensory loss, and contralateral body pain/temp loss.


Central Pontine Myelinolysis (Option C) typically occurs in rapid correction of hyponatremia, leading to quadriplegia and pseudobulbar palsy.


Anterior Cerebral Artery Stroke (Option D) causes leg-predominant weakness and abulia.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3433

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560590/

question: A 70-year-old diabetic man presents with sudden right-sided weakness. On examination, there is loss of proprioception and vibration on the right side of the body, and his tongue deviates to the left on protrusion. Facial sensation is intact. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Due to high speed crash patient has developed damage to bilateral pons causing locked-in syndrome. It is characterized by quadriplegia and anarthria with preserved consciousness, and patients communicate using vertical eye movements or blinking.
  • Patients are fully conscious but “locked in” - they can hear conversations (including discussions about their prognosis) but cannot respond except via blinking or vertical eye movement, often using eye-tracking or blink-coded communication systems.

Brainstem death (Option A) presents with loss of all brainstem reflexes including pupillary, corneal, and oculocephalic reflexes, and there is no spontaneous breathing or eye movement, making vertical eye movements impossible.


Vegetative state (Option C) involves preserved sleep-wake cycles and autonomic functions, but no awareness of self or environment, and patients do not follow commands with eye movements.


Decerebrate posturing (Option D) occurs due to midbrain or upper pontine damage, leading to extension of arms and legs, often seen in comatose patients - not associated with preserved consciousness or vertical eye movement.



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3434.
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK559026/

question: A 38-year-old Formula 1 driver suffers a high-speed crash. At the hospital, he is unable to move his limbs, talk, or drink from a straw. Examination reveals quadriplegia with bilateral long tract signs, with absent gag reflex, but a nurse notices that he can move his eyes vertically on command. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Patient has crossed features implying brain stem stroke.
  • Left sided weakness with right sided 6th and 7th nerve palsy
  • Foville’s syndrome is involvement of nucleus of 6th nerve.
  • It communicates with opposite side 3rd nerve via medial longitudinal fasciculus.
  • Damage to 6th nerve nucleus means that gaze palsy will occur with lateral rectus of involved and medial rectus of non-involved side being involved.

Benedikt syndrome (Option B) has 3rd nerve palsy.


Millard Gubler (Option C) will have only lateral rectus weakness as only the nerve fascicle is involved.


Wallenberg syndrome (Option D) has 5,8,9,10,11 cranial nerve palsy.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 235.

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK544268/

question: A 62-year-old patient presents with left-sided arm and leg weakness, right-sided facial paralysis with lateral rectus gaze palsy and nystagmus. Which of the following syndromes is consistent with these symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This case is presenting with the classic triad of features that define Dejerine Roussy syndrome:

  1. Timing: Pain develops after stroke (in this case, few weeks post-stroke)
  2. Location: Lesion in ventroposterolateral thalamus confirmed by MRI
  3. Pain characteristics like Constant burning pain or hyperalgesia and allodynia especially to warm water which may be percieved as boiling water or acid.

Complex regional pain syndrome (Option A and D) is seen due to peripheral neuropathy.

Internal capsule infarct (Option C) will cause motor deficit like pure motor stroke or pure sensory stroke.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 176, 3432.

question: A 60-year-old male presents to neurology follow-up OPD four weeks after a stroke with persistent allodynia, especially while taking a bath with warm water. Which of the following is correct about this case?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient has Parinaud syndrome /dorsal midbrain syndrome which is typically caused by a pineal gland tumor as seen on neuroimaging in this case.
  • It affects the vertical gaze center / rostral interstitial nucleus of the medial longitudinal fasciculus.
  • The classic triad includes
    • Paralysis of upward gaze
    • Convergence-retraction nystagmus (jerky eye movements on attempted up gaze)
    • Pupillary light-near dissociation (pupils poorly reactive to light but responsive to near stimuli)
  • This results from compression of structures like the superior colliculi and pretectal area, which are involved in vertical gaze and pupillary light reflexes.
  • The chin-up posture is a compensatory mechanism for the vertical gaze palsy

M. Gravis (Option A) will present with diurnal variation in muscle weakness.


Neurosyphilis (Option B)will have Argyl robertson pupul with light near disssociation as described in this patient but is ruled out due to CT head showing pineal mass.


INO (Option C) will present with impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye on lateral gaze and abducting eye nystagmus on the contralateral side



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 236.

question: A 25-year-old woman presents with double vision. On examination, she has paralysis of vertical gaze and pupils that constrict during accommodation but not in response to light (light-near dissociation). CT head shows mass arising in pineal region. Diagnosis is?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient has crossed features implying brain stem involvement.
  • He has ipsilateral 3rd nerve palsy with contralateral ataxia implying lesion in the midbrain tegmentum affecting superior cerebellar peduncle, leading to contralateral ataxia.

[[figure-1]]

Weber syndrome (Option A): It involves the cerebral peduncle and oculomotor nerve, causing ipsilateral third nerve palsy with contralateral hemiparesis (not ataxia)


Benedikt syndrome (Option C): It has red nucleus involvement causing basal ganglia features like chorea and tremors with 3rd nerve palsy


Millard Gubler syndrome (Option D) : It has ispsilateral 6,7 th nerve palsy with contralateral hemiplegia



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 234.
  2. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11668228/

question: A 60-year-old man presents with a sudden onset drooping of left eye and balance issues. On examination, he has left-sided ptosis, dilated left pupil, and the left eye is "down and out." He demonstrates significant right-sided ataxia. He is unable to move his eyes vertically . Diagnosis is?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient is having atrial fibrillation and has presented with cardiovascular symptoms.
  • So using RACE algorithm:
    • First, Rate control and then oral anticoagulation will be started.
    • C is for Chemical cardioversion, and E is for Electrical cardioversion if the patient develops hemodynamic instability.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1949, 3677.

question: A 35-year-old alcoholic patient presents with palpitations for the last 2 hours. On examination, he has an irregularly irregular pulse, BP 130/100 mm Hg, and a GCS of 15/15. Higher mental functions and cranial nerve examination are normal. There is no focal neurological deficit. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • An irregularly irregular pulse is a classic clinical sign of atrial fibrillation.
  • In AF, chaotic atrial contractions lead to blood stasis, particularly in the left atrial appendage, which predisposes to clot formation.
  • These clots can embolize and cause ischemic strokes, often affecting the left middle cerebral artery territory.
  • This results in symptoms such as aphasia (due to dominant hemisphere involvement) and right-sided weakness (including the right arm), as the left MCA supplies the corresponding brain regions.
  • Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is the preferred imaging modality to evaluate the left atrial appendage for thrombus presence.
  • Detecting clots with TEE is critical to determine the indication for oral anticoagulation to prevent stroke recurrence. This assessment guides timely anticoagulant therapy, which is essential in managing patients with AF and stroke risk.

Transthoracic Echocardiography (TTE): TTE is usually the first-line screening tool for heart structure because it is non-invasive.

  • However, it has very low sensitivity for detecting clots in the Left Atrial Appendage.
  • In a patient with a high suspicion of a cardioembolic source (like this one), a "negative" TTE is not enough to rule out a clot.

Carotid Doppler (Option B): This is used to look for Carotid Artery Stenosis, which causes "artery-to-artery" embolic strokes.

  • While this is a common cause of stroke in older patients, the "irregularly irregular pulse" in this patient points directly to a cardiac source rather than a carotid one. Carotid Doppler would not explain the pulse finding.

MRI Brain (Option D): MRI (specifically Diffusion-Weighted Imaging) is the most sensitive test to confirm the diagnosis of an acute ischemic stroke and visualize the extent of brain tissue damage.

  • However, MRI tells us where the stroke is, not why it happened. The question asks for the investigation to determine the etiology, which is the cardiac embolus.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3444.
