question: A patient presents with sudden onset aphasia and right sided arm weakness for the past 4 hours. On examination he has irregularly irregular pulse. Which of the following investigations will be done to determine etiology of this case presentation?

correctAnswer: B. Oculomotor nerve and crus cerebri
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient presents with:

  • Right-sided ptosis, dilated pupil, eye deviated outward → Right oculomotor nerve (CN III) palsy
  • Left-sided spastic weakness, hyperreflexia → Contralateral corticospinal tract involvement
  • MRI: midbrain ischemic lesion
  • These features are classic for Weber syndrome (medial midbrain syndrome).

Arteries involved are paramedian branches of the posterior cerebral artery.

Structures Involved in a Midbrain Stroke:

  1. Oculomotor Nerve Nucleus (Cranial Nerve III):
    • Function: Controls most of the eye movements, pupillary constriction, and eyelid elevation (levator palpebrae superioris).
    • Clinical Findings: Damage to the oculomotor nerve leads to ptosis, a dilated pupil (mydriasis), and an eye that is deviated outward and downward (due to unopposed action of the lateral rectus and superior oblique muscles).
  2. Trochlear Nerve (Cranial Nerve IV):
    • Function: Innervates the superior oblique muscle, which helps in depression and intorsion of the eye.
    • Clinical Findings: A lesion of the trochlear nerve causes vertical diplopia - difficulty looking downwards and inwards, noticed while reading or descending stairs.
    • Trochlear nerve damage would not explain the ptosis or mydriasis seen in this patient
  3. Substantia Nigra:
    • Function: Part of the basal ganglia, it plays a crucial role in motor control and coordination, with loss of dopamine-producing neurons here leading to Parkinsonism.
    • Clinical Findings: Midbrain strokes affecting the substantia nigra can result in motor deficits, tremors, and bradykinesia, similar to Parkinson's disease.
    • The patient's main issues involve cranial nerve III and motor weakness, not Parkinsonism features
  4. Crus Cerebri (Corticospinal Tracts):
    • Function: Contains descending fibers of the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts, responsible for voluntary motor control.
    • Clinical Findings: Damage here leads to contralateral hemiparesis due to involvement of the corticospinal tract. In Weber syndrome, the lesion commonly affects both the oculomotor nerve and the crus cerebri.
    • While the crus cerebri is affected in this case, it alone does not account for the cranial nerve signs



Oculomotor motor and red nucleus (Option A): Lesion here → Claude syndrome

  • Features: Ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral ataxia / tremor (from red nucleus)

Oculomotor nerve and superior cerebellar peduncle (Option C): Lesion → Benedikt syndrome

  • Features: Ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral involuntary movements / tremor

Oculomotor nucleus and substantia nigra (Option D): Nuclear lesion → may cause conjugate gaze palsy

  • Substantia nigra → parkinsonism features



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 234.

question: A 54-year-old male presents with a sudden onset of double vision and left-sided weakness. On examination he has a right-sided ptosis, a dilated pupil that does not react to light, and an outward deviation of the right eye. The left side of his body shows spastic weakness with hyperreflexia. MRI reveals an ischemic lesion in the midbrain. Which of the following structures is most likely involved in this patient’s condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient cannot perform learned motor actions on command (e.g., waving goodbye, brushing teeth) despite intact comprehension and no weakness - this is ideomotor apraxia, which localizes to the dominant (left) parietal lobe, especially the supramarginal gyrus.
  • The patient also has impaired repetition with fluent speech and intact comprehension, which is characteristic of conduction aphasia.
    • This occurs due to damage to the arcuate fasciculus, which passes through the left parietal region connecting Wernicke’s and Broca’s areas.
  • Both findings strongly point to left parietal lobe involvement.

[[figure-1]]


Right Parietal (Option A): Lesions in the non-dominant (usually right) parietal lobe typically cause Hemispatial Neglect (ignoring the left side of the world) and Constructional Apraxia (inability to draw or build simple objects like a clock or a house). It does not typically cause aphasia or the inability to follow verbal motor commands.


Right Temporal (Option B): The right temporal lobe is involved in processing non-verbal sounds, music, and social cues. A lesion here might lead to Amusia (loss of musical ability) or difficulty interpreting the emotional tone of speech (Aprosadia).


Left Temporal (Option D): A lesion in the posterior left temporal lobe (Wernicke’s area) results in Sensory Aphasia. While the patient would be fluent, they would have poor comprehension (they wouldn't understand the command to "brush teeth" in the first place) and their speech would be "word salad" - fluent but meaningless. This patient understands the command, so the temporal lobe is largely intact.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 203.

When spoken a phrase “Repeat after me: ‘The sky is blue’”, the patient struggles to repeat it but speaks fluently and understands spoken language. Which lobe is most likely affected?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Note the patient is outside the 4.5-hour thrombolysis window (option D), but he is within the 6–24 hour extended window for thrombectomy for proven large vessel occlusion (LVO).

Rapid lowering of BP with nicardipine to achieve target BP 140/100 mm Hg (Option A): It would be perfect for hemorrhagic stroke presentation

Secure airway (Option C): No mention of airway compromise in the question

question: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden onset of right-sided face and arm weakness at the breakfast table at 8 am. He arrives at the ER at 4 pm in the evening. His pulse is 100/min, BP 180/100 mm Hg, NIHSS is 6, and GCS is 13/15. NCCT head shows hypodensity in the left MCA territory and CTA reveals a M1 left MCA occlusion. . Which of the following is the best intervention for management of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Sudden onset slurred speech and difficulty in understanding language (receptive aphasia) strongly suggest involvement of the left MCA (assuming left hemisphere dominance), which supplies Broca’s and Wernicke’s areas.
  • Thus, the MCA is the vessel most likely involved in this patient’s presentation.
  • Slurring of speech/ dysarthria can also be explained by weakness, paralysis, or incoordination of the muscles used for speech (face, tongue, lips, palate).

Left anterior cerebral artery (Option A):
Supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes—stroke causes contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss, not aphasia.


Right middle cerebral artery (Option C):
Affects the right hemisphere, leading to left-sided hemiplegia and hemispatial neglect, not language deficits.


Right anterior cerebral artery (Option D):
Causes contralateral leg weakness and abulia (lack of willpower), with no speech involvement.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3429.

question: A 60-year-old hypertensive man presents with sudden onset slurred speech and difficulty comprehending language. NCCT head scan reveals an ischemic stroke. The stroke likely involves which of the following vessels?

correctAnswer: A. Right anterior horn cells in spinal cord
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The presence of muscle atrophy and fasciculations indicates a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion.
  • Involvement of the right hand with corresponding muscle wasting and fasciculations localizes the lesion to the right anterior horn cells of the spinal cord — the site of LMNs that directly innervate skeletal muscle.

Left anterior horn cells (Option B): Would produce LMN signs on the left side, not the right.


Right parietal lobe (Option C): Involvement would cause contralateral sensory deficits or neglect, not LMN signs like fasciculations or atrophy.


Left parietal lobe (Option D): Would affect contralateral (right-sided) sensory and motor integration, but not cause LMN findings.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 168, 169.

Left anterior horn cells in spinal cord

question: A 40-year old lady complains of difficulty in kneading the dough for past 6 months. On examination she has atrophy of right hand muscles and fasiculations are noted in thenar muscles. Select the site of lesion?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Gait apraxia/ magnetic gait and urinary incontinence are hallmark features of frontal lobe dysfunction, particularly involving the medial aspect of the frontal lobes where the motor cortex and the bladder control centers reside.
  • Conditions like NPH/normal pressure hydrocephalus cause stretching or compression of the periventricular frontal white matter, disrupting these areas.

Temporal lobe (Option A): Associated with memory, emotion, and auditory processing.

  • Symptoms: Wernicke’s aphasia (fluent but nonsensical speech), memory loss (hippocampal involvement), and upper quadrantanopia (vision loss in the upper outer corner).
  • It does not control the lower limb motor planning (gait) or the autonomic signals for the bladder.

Parietal lobe (Option B): Involved in sensory integration and spatial awareness, not motor planning or continence.

  • Symptoms: Hemispatial neglect (ignoring one side of the body/world), agnosia (inability to recognize objects), and cortical sensory loss (inability to identify an object by touch).
  • While it deals with "where" things are in space, the actual "how-to" motor program for walking and the reflex inhibition for the bladder are frontal functions.

Occipital lobe (Option C): Responsible for visual processing.

  • Symptoms: Cortical blindness, homonymous hemianopia (losing half the visual field in both eyes), and visual hallucinations.
  • It has no direct role in motor coordination or urinary sphincters.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 178.

question: Gait apraxia and urinary incontinence are clinical features associated with damage to which lobe of the brain?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient’s selective inability to recognize familiar faces despite recognizing voices indicates prosopagnosia, caused by a lesion in the right fusiform gyrus (also called the fusiform face area).
  • This region, located in the inferior temporo-occipital area, is responsible for facial perception and recognition.
  • Auditory recognition pathways remain intact, explaining preserved voice identification.

Frontal lobe (Option A): Involved in executive functions, decision-making, and motor control.

  • Damage here affects behavior or movement, not recognition. A patient might act inappropriately toward a family member, but they would still know who they are looking at.

Parietal lobe (Option C): Handles spatial orientation and sensory integration.

  • Damage here causes spatial neglect or difficulty reaching for objects. The patient can't figure out where the person is in the room, but they don't lose the ability to identify the face once they see it.

Occipital lobe (Option D): Processes basic visual input (color, shape, motion) but not complex identification such as faces.

  • Pure occipital lesions cause blindness (scotomas) or field cuts.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 206.

question: A 65 year man can recognise voices of family members while talking over mobile phone. But when he meets them in person he is not able to recognise them. Lesion is present in which part of brain?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The left parietal lobe is responsible for writing, calculations, left-right orientation, and finger recognition—disruption causes the classic Gerstmann syndrome given in this case.

Left Temporal Lobe (Option A): Lesions here often cause receptive aphasia or memory impairment.


Right Parietal Lobe (Option B): Right parietal lesions can lead to left-sided neglect, constructional apraxia, and visuospatial deficits


Right Temporal Lobe (Option C): Lesions cause deficits in memory, facial recognition, or emotional processing



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 203.

question: A 60-year-old right-handed woman is brought by her husband after he notices she has trouble doing dishes and confuses her left and right sides since last evening. On examination, she cannot perform simple calculations, but her speech is fluent. The lesion is most likely in which structure?

correctAnswer: B. Posterior limb of internal capsule
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The posterior limb of the internal capsule contains corticospinal and corticobulbar motor fibers; infarcts here cause contralateral pure motor weakness affecting face, arm, and leg without sensory or cortical deficits.

Anterior limb of internal capsule (Option A): The anterior limb contains frontopontine and thalamocortical fibers. Its involvement causes cognitive and behavioral changes like confusion, impaired attention, agitation, and memory disturbances.


Genu of internal capsule (Option C): The genu contains corticobulbar fibers mainly affecting face muscles; isolated lesions here cause mostly facial weakness.


Thalamus (Option D): Thalamic lesions typically produce sensory disturbances rather than isolated motor weakness.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3446.

question: A patient presents with sudden onset weakness affecting the face, arm, and leg on one side of the body without sensory loss or cortical signs. Which is the most likely site of lesion?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The diagnosis of ischemic stroke is indicated by the patient's sudden-onset right-sided weakness and difficulty speaking coupled with CT scan ruling out hemorrhagic stroke further confirms the diagnosis.
  • Administering intravenous Alteplase immediately is appropriate as the patient presents with signs of an ischemic stroke and is within the treatment window for intravenous thrombolysis (within 3-4.5 hours).
  • Since the CT scan has ruled out hemorrhagic stroke, administering rtPA is crucial for improving outcomes by restoring blood flow to the affected area of the brain.
  • This patient is much below the threshod for contraindication for thrombolysis which is < 185/110 mm Hg.
  • Hence lowering of BP is not required.

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3440.

question: A 70-year-old male presents to ER with sudden-onset right-sided arm weakness and difficulty speaking which started 2 hours ago. His medical history includes hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and a prior TIA. His BP is 160/100 mm Hg. A CT scan of the head rules out hemorrhagic stroke. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management for this patient?

correctAnswer: B. Combination of ticagrelor plus aspirin
explanationHtml:
• Explanation:
  • Short-term dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) with ticagrelor/ clopidogrel-aspirin for 21-90 days is superior to aspirin alone in preventing recurrent stroke after TIA.
  • This regimen reduces 90-day stroke risk from 11.7% to 8.2% without significant increase in major hemorrhage

ABCD2 score helps stratify TIA patients' risk of stroke:

  1. Age ≥60 years (1 point)
  2. BP ≥140/90 (1 point)
  3. Clinical features (weakness=2, speech disturbance=1)
  4. Duration (≥60 min=2, 10-59 min=1)
  5. Diabetes (1 point)
  • High ABCD2 score (≥4) indicates high risk of early recurrent stroke:
  • Early aggressive antiplatelet therapy with DAPT (first 21-90 days) followed by monotherapy is the current standard of care for high-risk TIA patient



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3449.

question: A 65-year-old diabetic male presents to the emergency department with a sudden onset of right-sided weakness and slurred speech that resolved completely within 2 hours. His blood pressure is 160/90 mmHg. Based on his ABCD2 score of 6, what is the most appropriate immediate management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In ABCD2 score we consider current neurological symptoms in the patient and not the patient's past medical history of stroke. In fact, past medical history is considered in the CHADS2-VASc score used in atrial fibrillation.

ABCD2 score:

  • Age ≥60 years (1 point)
  • BP ≥140/90 (1 point)
  • Clinical features (weakness=2, speech disturbance=1)
  • Duration (≥60 min=2, 10-59 min=1)
  • Diabetes (1 point)

Risk of Stroke (2-Day Risk): The primary purpose of the score is to determine how likely a patient is to have a massive stroke within 48 hours of the TIA.

Score Risk Category 2-Day Stroke Risk Management Recommendation
0–3 Low 1.0% Outpatient evaluation
4–5 Moderate 4.1% Usually observation/hospitalization
6–7 High 8.1% Urgent hospitalization


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3448.

question: Which of the following is not correct about ABCD2 score for diagnosis of Transient ischemic attack?

correctAnswer: B. Mechanical thrombectomy after confirming salvageable tissue with CT perfusion
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • INR = 2.0 → IV thrombolysis is contraindicated (cutoff for Alteplase is INR ≤ 1.7).

  • The patient has a large vessel occlusion (LVO) in the left MCA, the most appropriate therapy is mechanical thrombectomy, provided CT perfusion (CTP) demonstrates a salvageable penumbra.

  • Thrombectomy is indicated both in the early window (0–6 h) and the extended window (up to 24 h) when CTP shows favorable perfusion.

Intravenous Alteplase (Option A): is contraindicated with INR >1.7 due to high bleeding risk.


Cardiology consult for chemical cardioversion (Option C): is a distraction option and focus should be on stroke management.


Mannitol and dual antiplatelet therapy (Option D): There is no evidence of raised ICP requiring mannitol; dual antiplatelets are not first-line for acute LVO stroke.



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3451.
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557411/

question: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden onset right arm weakness and slurred speech for 1 hour. His blood pressure is 170/100 mm Hg. He has a history of atrial fibrillation and is on warfarin; current INR is 2.0. NCCT head shows no intracranial hemorrhage. CT angiography reveals a left MCA occlusion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

correctAnswer: B. Inferior division of left middle cerebral artery
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The inferior division of the left MCA supplies Wernicke’s area in the posterior superior temporal gyrus, and its infarction leads to fluent aphasia with impaired comprehension, without motor deficits.

The superior division of the left MCA supplies Broca’s area (Option A) in the frontal lobe, so its infarct causes non-fluent aphasia with right face and arm weakness, not fluent speech with comprehension deficits.


The left anterior cerebral artery (Option C) supplies the medial frontal lobes, leading to contralateral leg weakness and abulia rather than language problems.


The left posterior cerebral artery (Option D) supplies the occipital lobe and inferomedial temporal regions, where infarction causes visual field defects or visual agnosia, not aphasia.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3429.

Inferior division of left middle cerebral artery

question: A 58-year-old right-handed man is brought to the ER for speaking fluently but producing nonsensical words and sentences. He has difficulty understanding spoken commands. Neurological exam shows no significant motor weakness. Which of the following vessels is most likely involved?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome) is caused by occlusion of the vertebral artery or PICA , leading to crossed findings: ipsilateral facial sensory loss and Horner’s, contralateral body pain/temp loss, and cerebellar signs.

[[figure-1]]

Parinaud syndrome (Option A): Vertical gaze palsy from dorsal midbrain lesion

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]


Dejerine syndrome (Option B): Medial medullary infarction causes contralateral hemiparesis and tongue weakness

[[figure-4]]

[[figure-5]]


Weber syndrome (Option D): Midbrain base infarct causes ipsilateral oculomotor palsy + contralateral hemiparesis, not cerebellar or sensory signs

[[figure-6]]

[[figure-7]]

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3433.

question: A 65-year-old male presents with sudden onset of vertigo, dysphagia, hoarseness, and left-sided facial numbness. On examination, he has left-sided Horner's syndrome, right-sided loss of pain and temperature sensation in the body, and left-sided cerebellar signs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Penentrating branches of lenticulostriate arteries
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The penetrating branches of lenticulostriate arteries arise from M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery.
  • They supply important deep structures, including the internal capsule, putamen, and caudate nucleus.
  • The described pure motor hemiparesis is a classic lacunar syndrome resulting from occlusion of a lenticulostriate artery affecting the posterior limb of the internal capsule.
  • Lacunar strokes result from occlusion of small penetrating arteries and typically cause distinct clinical syndromes like pure motor stroke described in stem of this question.




Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3429.

question: A 65-year-old hypertensive man presents with a sudden onset of right-sided weakness affecting his face, arm, and leg. The NCCT head shows an intraparenchymal bleed in left side basal ganglia. Which of the following vessels is most likely involved in this pathology?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Chronic burning pain not relieved by usual NSAIDs following a stroke is due to lacunar infarct of Ventroposterolateral Thalamus, known as Dejerine-Roussy syndrome (aka) Thalamic pain syndrome.

Small vessel stroke:

Sites & manifestations
  • Posterior limb of internal capsule (Option B)
  • Pure motor hemiparesis
  • Genu of internal capsule (Option C)
  • Clumsy hand dysarthria lacunar syndrome (facial weakness)
  • Cortical pontocerebellar tract (Option D)
  • I/L ataxia + C/L hemiparesis
  • Ventroposterolateral thalamus (Option A)
  • Dejerine-Roussy syndrome

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 176, 3432.

question: A 62-year-old woman presents with chronic burning pain, numbness, and tingling on the right side of her body not relieved with NSAIDs. The symptoms began 2 months after she suffered a stroke. On examination, she has hyperesthesia and allodynia on the right side. The clinician suspected it to be due to lacunar infarct. What could be the likely site of infarct causing her present symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • MRI shows Hummingbird sign - suggestive of Progressive supranuclear palsy [PSP] (a Parkinson-plus disorder).
  • Tremors are not a feature of PSP.

Progressive supranuclear palsy [PSP]
  • Early onset postural instability - H/O frequent falls + Dementia
  • Tremors - absent (Option B)
  • Defective downward gaze (Option A) + extended posture of body
  • Dystonia: Procerus sign (forehead) + Gunslinger’s gait (flexion at elbow & adduction at upper limb) (Option D)
  • Poor response to levodopa (Option C)
  • MRI: Hummingbird sign

question: An elderly patient presented with a history of slowing of movements, frequent falls and forgetfulness. MRI done is as shown below. Which among the following is not a feature of this condition?

correctAnswer: C. Oppenheim’s sign - Apply pressure along the medial aspect of tibia causing an extensor plantar response
explanationHtml:
• Oppenheim’s sign is elicited by applying pressure along the medial aspect of tibia to cause an extensor plantar response i.e. dorsiflexion of the great toe and fanning of the other toes.
  • Babinski’s sign is elicited by stroking the lateral aspect of the sole from the heel towards the little toe and then continuing up to the great toe. This results in an extensor plantar response as described above in a case of upper motor neuron lesion. Flexion of all toes indicates a normal person or the presence of a lower motor neuron lesion.
  • Gordon’s sign is elicited by squeezing the calf muscles to produce an extensor plantar response.
  • Chaddock’s sign is elicited by stimulating the dorsolateral aspect of the foot from the posterior portion of the skin just beneath the lateral malleolus anteriorly and along the external edge of the foot.

[[figure-1]]

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/medgen/735510

Gordon’s sign - A stroke beneath and in front of the lateral malleolus causing an extensor plantar response.

question: Which of the following clinical signs of upper motor neuron lesion is described correctly ?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical scenario of a 5 year old female child with complaints of recurrent seizures, left sided hemiplegia with a description of port-wine stain in the right ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve and a CT image showing the classical tram-track or rail-road sign suggests a diagnosis of Sturge Weber syndrome.

[[figure-1]]

Von-Hippel Lindau syndrome (Option A):

  • Mutations (3p deletion) lead to numerous vascular tumours in the body such as clear cell carcinoma of the kidneys, cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas and spinal cord angiomas.
  • Cerebellar signs and raised intracranial tension are the usual manifestations.

Neurofibromatosis (Option C):

  • This is the most common type of neurocutaneous syndrome.
  • They also present with recurrent seizures but instead of port-wine stain, they show neurofibromas with nervous system abnormalities of optic glioma, intraspinal neurofibroma, aqueductal stenosis and dural ectasia.

Ataxia telangiectasia (Option D):

  • It usually presents with slowly progressive truncal ataxia starting in infancy.
  • Skin manifestations start after the age of 2-3 years with cutaneous (at flexures) and ocular (bulbar conjunctiva) telangiectasia.
  • In addition, there is an immunodeficiency component leading to frequent sino-pulmonary infections and risk of lymphoreticular malignancies.


Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK459163/

question: A 5 year old female child presented to the casualty with recurrent seizures and left sided hemiplegia. On physical examination, a reddish skin lesion was found since birth over the right side of her forehead involving the right eye, nose and cheek. On CT imaging of the brain, the following picture was seen. What is the probable diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. Defect in P type ATP ase ATP7B protein
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical scenario of an adolescent male with neuropsychiatric symptoms, hepatomegaly and ophthalmological finding of Kayser-Fleischer ring is suggestive of Wilson’s disease.
  • The gene involved is ATP7B gene on chromosome 13. (ATP 7A In menke kinky hair disease).
  • The protein whose functioning is defective in Wilson disease is P type ATP ase ATP7B protein in liver that is responsible for hepatobiliary excretion of copper and incorporation into ceruloplasmin.
  • Due to this defect copper will accumulate in liver and other body tissue.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3339.

question: A 15 year old adolescent male patient came with his parents with complaints of neuropsychiatric symptoms such as tremors and an irritable mood. On physical examination, stigmata of liver disease and the following ophthalmological finding is seen. Which of the following is correct about this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • CT brain shows hyperdensities in bilateral sylvian cisterns and the basal cisterns producing star of death appearance.
  • The combination of CT findings and headache with nuchal rigidity implies subarachnoid hemorrhage.
  • Most common cause of SAH is trauma.

Intracerebral hemorrhage (Option A): Appears as a localized hyperdensity within brain parenchyma, not in the cisterns.

[[figure-1]]


Subdural hemorrhage (Option B): Presents as a crescent-shaped collection between dura and arachnoid, not involving basal cisterns.

[[figure-2]]

Extradural hemorrhage (Option D): Seen as a biconvex/lentiform hyperdensity between skull and dura, typically with lucid interval.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3458, 3459.
lessonTitle: Stroke, TIA and Image Based Questions
question: A 30 year old male patient was brought to the ER with a history of RTA and sustained multiple injuries. On primary assessment, he was disoriented and complained of severe headache. Meningeal signs are noted. On neuroimaging the following image was seen. What is the most probable diagnosis in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The non-contrast CT brain demonstrates hyperdense blood within the basal cisterns and bilateral Sylvian fissures, producing the characteristic "star sign" (star of death appearance), which is highly suggestive of acute subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH).

  • The patient's sudden, severe headache, altered sensorium, and meningeal signs (neck stiffness) are classic clinical features of SAH.
  • In this case, the haemorrhage is most likely traumatic, given the history of a road traffic accident.
  • Overall, trauma is the most common cause of subarachnoid haemorrhage, whereas the most common cause of spontaneous (atraumatic) SAH is rupture of a berry (saccular) aneurysm.

CT findings of SAH

  • Hyperdense blood in the basal cisterns
  • Blood within the Sylvian fissures
  • Blood in the interhemispheric fissure or cortical sulci
  • Classic "star sign" (star of death appearance) on axial CT

[[figure-1]]

Intracerebral haemorrhage (Option A): Appears as a localised hyperdense intraparenchymal hematoma with surrounding edema and mass effect rather than blood filling the basal cisterns.

[[figure-2]]

Subdural haemorrhage (Option B): Appears as a crescent-shaped extra-axial hyperdensity between the dura and arachnoid that can cross suture lines but does not involve the basal cisterns.

[[figure-3]]

Extradural haemorrhage (Option D): Appears as a biconvex (lentiform) extra-axial hyperdensity between the skull and dura, usually associated with a skull fracture and a lucid interval, and does not produce the characteristic basal cisternal "star sign."

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3458, 3459.
lessonTitle: Stroke, TIA and Image Based Questions
question: A 30-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. During primary assessment, he is disoriented and complains of a severe headache. Examination reveals neck stiffness and other meningeal signs. A non-contrast CT scan of the brain is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given clinical scenario of an elderly male patient with complaints of recent onset stooping,
  • Broad based abnormal gait (gait apraxia/ gait instability), short term memory loss (dementia) and urge incontinence and on radiological investigation the image shows bilateral lateral ventriculomegaly which is suggestive of normal pressure hydrocephalus.

Parkinson’s disease (Option A):
Characterized by resting tremor, rigidity, and bradykinesia, not broad-based gait or incontinence.


Alzheimer’s disease (Option B):
Presents with progressive memory loss and cognitive decline but no gait disturbance or urinary symptoms.


Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (Option D):
Occurs mainly in young obese females with headache, papilledema, and visual symptoms, not ventriculomegaly or gait apraxia.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3483.

question: A 75 year old male patient came to the OPD with complaints of recent onset stooping, broad based abnormal gait, short-term memory loss and urge incontinence. On radiological investigation, the following image is obtained. What is the probable diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Shagreen patch and Tuberous sclerosis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario of an adolescent male patient with complaints of poor scholastic performance (low IQ), history ofrecurrent seizures since infancy and clinical image showing shagreen patch suggests a probable diagnosis of tuberous sclerosis.

Tuberous sclerosis (BOURNEVILLE DISEASE)

Pathophysiology
  • It is an autosomal dominant disorder.
  • Genes involved are TSC1 in chromosome 9 producing hamartin protein and TSC2 is on chromosome 16 producing tuberin protein.
  • Both these proteins play a role in cell growth and cell division. Mutations lead to aberrant activation of mTOR pathway signalling giving rise to various tumours.

Clinical features
  • Classical triad of seizures (epilepsy), low IQ, facial angiofibromas (adenoma sebaceum)- EPILOIA
  • Other skin manifestations include shagreen patches, hypomelanotic macules (Ash leaf macules), periungual fibromas (Koenen tumours)
  • Associated with renal angiomyolipomas, cardiac rhabdomyomas (in children)
  • Increased risk of subependymal nodules, cortical tubers and subependymal giant cell astrocytomas (SEGAs)

Treatment
  • Anticonvulsants for seizures
  • mTOR inhibitors (sirolimus or everolimus) for SEGAs and seizure reduction

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

[[figure-3]]

Adenoma sebaceum and Tuberous sclerosis (Option B): It is incorrect since the image shows a shagreen patch and not adenoma sebaceum.

Neurofibroma and Neurofibromatosis (Options A) and Cafe-au-lait spots and Neurofibromatosis (Option D):

  • Neurofibromas and cafe-au-lait spots are associated with neurofibromatosis.
  • They are also associated with seizures but do not show shagreen patches.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:
  1. Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Pages 388, 707, 708
  2. Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 1264
  3. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6531247/

question: A 13 year old male patient presented with complaints of poor scholastic performance, history of recurrent seizures since infancy and the following incidental finding on his back. What does the incidental finding denote and probable diagnosis of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • MRI Brain shows Vestibular schwannoma with ice cream cone appearance at the cerebellopontine angle.
  • The trigeminal nerve (CN V) emerges from the lateral pons, superior and anterior to the entry of CN VIII.
  • So in case of tumor originating from 8th nerve, the fifth nerve is compressed and causes absent corneal reflex.

Cerebellar astrocytoma (Option B) is ruled out based on location and absence of features suggesting raised intracranial pressure.


Craniopharyngioma (Option C): MRI reveals a suprasellar cystic and solid mass, often with calcifications.


Prion Disease (Option D): MRI typically shows hyperintensity in the basal ganglia, thalamus (including the "hockey stick sign" in variant CJD), and cortical ribboning on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and FLAIR sequences, reflecting spongiform changes.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 164.

question: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive hearing loss in the right ear, occasional imbalance while walking, and a sensation of fullness in the ear. On examination, she has decreased corneal reflex on the right side. MRI of the brain is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Child is having parkinson like features and MRI shows bilateral hypointensity of the globus pallidus with a central area of hyperintensity.
  • This is called eye of tiger sign and is seen in Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration (PKAN) (aka Halloverdan spatz disease).
  • It is rare autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder marked by the accumulation of iron in the brain's nuclei.

[[figure-1]]

Huntington disease (Option B) is seen with chorea.

[[figure-2]]

Craniopharyngioma (Option C) is seen in children and presents with raised ICP.

[[figure-3]]

Prion disease (Option D) will present dementia and myoclonic jerks.

[[figure-4]]



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3518.

question: A 9-year-old child presents with progressive dystonia, difficulty walking, and slurred speech. On examination, he has oromandibular dystonia and choreoathetosis. MRI brain shows bilateral hypointensity of the globus pallidus with a central area of hyperintensity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pneumocephalus/pneumatocele/intracranial aerocele: The presence of air in the epidural, subdural, or subarachnoid space or within the brain parenchyma or ventricular cavities.

CT findings:

Sign

Observation

Mount Fuji Sign

Seen in Tension pneumocephalus and has accumulation of air in the frontal region, Frontal lobes are separated and compressed by air under pressure, forming a shape like Mount Fuji

[[figure-1]]

Air Bubble Sign

Small, round areas of low attenuation (dark regions) representing air pockets within cerebrospinal fluid spaces.

[[figure-2]]

Peaking Sign

Frontal lobes are compressed toward each other, but not separated, seen in non tension pneumocephalus.

[[figure-3]]


Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK535412/

question: Which of the following is a CT finding of Pneumocephalus?

correctAnswer: D. Leading infratentorial brain tumor in children
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The MRI findings are typical of a craniopharyngioma, a benign, supratentorial tumor seen primarily in children.

  • It commonly causes optic chiasm compression, leading to bitemporal hemianopia.

  • Craniopharyngiomas arise from Rathke pouch remnants and are often cystic with calcified walls, giving a heterogeneous appearance on imaging.

  • Pediatric tumors are usually of the adamantinomatous type; adults get the papillary type.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3002.

question: A 5-year-old is having daily headaches and difficulty copying from the board. He was found to have bitemporal hemianopia, and an MRI of the head was done. Which of the following is not correct about this condition?

correctAnswer: D. JEV-specific IgM in CSF by MAC‑ELISA
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • JEV-specific IgM in CSF by MAC‑ELISA is seen in Japanese encephalitis.
  • vCJD is a prion disease that causes progressive neurodegeneration.
  • Usual case presentation is a young person with dementia and myoclonic jerks.

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD) findings:

Electroencephalography (EEG)
  • Periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWC) (Option A ruled out)
  • These can be either lateralized in earlier stages or generalized in later stages.

    [[figure-1]]

MRI findings
  • Increased intensity in the basal ganglia (Option C ruled out)
  • Cortical ribboning (Option B ruled out)

    [[figure-2]]

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3529.

question: Which of the following is incorrect about variant creutzfeldt-jakob disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Given CT shows biconvex mass which is present in epidural hematoma.

CT findings:

Epidural hematoma

Subdural hematoma (Option C ruled out)
  • Biconvex or lens-shaped mass due to the limited ability of blood to expand within the fixed attachment of the dura to the cranial sutures
  • Does not cross suture lines.

    [[figure-1]]
  • Typically crescentic in configuration, extending over the cerebral convexity due to the lack of anatomical constraints in the subdural space.

    [[figure-2]]

Extradural Hematoma (Option B): This is synonym for epidural hematoma. While not incorrect in meaning, it is less commonly used in clinical practice, and "epidural" is the more standard term, making A the best answer.

Intracerebral Hematoma (Option D): Bleeding within the brain parenchyma itself, often due to hypertension or trauma. On CT, it appears as a hyperdense area within the brain tissue and is not typically associated with a lucid interval or a lens-shaped bleed.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3572.
lessonTitle: Stroke, TIA and Image Based Questions
question: A 35-year-old male presents to the ER after a fall, initially conscious but rapidly deteriorates following a brief lucid interval. The CT image is given below. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • MRI shows Dawson’s fingers, characteristic finding in Multiple Sclerosis (MS).
  • Criteria used is McDonald’s criteria and IV Methylprednisolone (Steroid) is the treatment of choice in MS.
  • Brighton criteria (Option B): Used for Gullaine barre syndrome (GBS) and treatment of choice is IVIg (Immunoglobulin).



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3583.
lessonTitle: Stroke, TIA and Image Based Questions
question: Based on the MRI finding (shown below) , Which of the following criteria and corresponding treatment used in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • MRI shows Dawson's fingers, multiple ovoid periventricular T2/FLAIR hyperintense lesions oriented perpendicular to the lateral ventricles, characteristic of Multiple Sclerosis (MS).
  • McDonald's criteria are used to diagnose MS by demonstrating dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT) using clinical and MRI findings (with CSF oligoclonal bands when required).
  • Acute MS relapses are treated with high-dose IV methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 3-5 days).

Multiple Sclerosis (MS)

Definition

Chronic autoimmune demyelinating disease of the CNS causing inflammation and sclerosis.

Pathogenesis

Autoimmune CD4+ T-cell (Th1/Th17)-mediated destruction of CNS myelin and oligodendrocytes.

Clinical Features
  • Optic neuritis (painful monocular visual loss)
  • Uhthoff phenomenon (worsening of symptoms with heat)
  • Lhermitte sign (electric shock-like sensation on neck flexion)
  • Sensory disturbances
  • Limb weakness
  • Diplopia
  • Ataxia
  • Spasticity
  • Bladder dysfunction.

Types
  • Relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS): Most common
  • Secondary progressive MS (SPMS): Progression following RRMS
  • Primary progressive MS (PPMS): Progressive disease from onset.

Diagnosis
  • McDonald criteria;
  • MRI shows Dawson's fingers with dissemination in space and time
  • CSF: Oligoclonal IgG bands positive.

Treatment
  • Acute relapse: High-dose IV methylprednisolone.
  • Disease-modifying therapies: Interferon-β, Glatiramer acetate, Dimethyl fumarate, Fingolimod, Natalizumab, Ocrelizumab, Alemtuzumab.

Brighton's criteria, IV Steroids (Option A): Brighton criteria are used for the diagnosis of Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), and corticosteroids are not recommended for its treatment.

Brighton's criteria, IV Immunoglobulin (Option B): Although IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) is a standard treatment for GBS, the MRI findings (Dawson's fingers) are characteristic of Multiple Sclerosis, not GBS.

McDonald's criteria, IV Immunoglobulin (Option D): McDonald's criteria are used to diagnose Multiple Sclerosis, but acute MS relapses are treated with high-dose IV methylprednisolone, not IVIG.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Pages 3462-3472

question: A 28-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of blurred vision and numbness of the right upper limb over the past year, with partial recovery after each episode. MRI brain (T2-FLAIR sagittal) shows the findings below. Based on the MRI finding, which of the following diagnostic criteria and corresponding treatment are most appropriate?

correctAnswer: B. Cerebral embolism with spontaneous reperfusion
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient has had spontaneous resolution of neurological symptoms in 2 hours, implying a transient ischemic attack. He has hypertension and atrial fibrillation as risk factors. The clot in the brain was spontaneously lysed due to the activity of plasmin/tissue plasminogen activator, and he escaped with a mini-stroke/TIA.
  • CT scan of the brain is normal, which rules out any hemorrhagic event. CT can be normal in AIS during the first 6 hours.

Spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage with resorption (Option A) would have nuchal rigidity, and CT would be abnormal.

Neuronal death due to cerebral anoxia (Option C) will cause symptoms to persist or have neurological deterioration.

Saturday night palsy due to neurapraxia (Option D) would occur when a person fell asleep on a couch with an overhanging arm and would present with tingling and paresthesias as well.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3448.

Saturday night palsy due to neurapraxia

question: A 68-year-old male presents to the ER with a sudden onset of headache and right-sided arm weakness that started while brushing his teeth in morning at 7 am. He is known case of hypertension and says he slept on couch last night while watching TV. On examination at 9 am he has irregularly irregular pulse, his arm weakness has improved significantly (power grade 4/5) and he can talk, drink water, chew food and walk normally. NCCT head is normal. Which of the following is the cause of this presentation?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Key finding is MRI showing hyperintensities over the occipital lobe in setting of postpartum female with history of eclampsia.
  • Cerebral edema explains the development of sudden onset headache and other focal deficits. With aggressive BP control pateint shows significant improvement and recovers.
  • This is seen in PRES.

Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (Option A) presents with sudden onset severe thunderclap headache (similar to SAH). It presents with severe new-onset hypertension. Cerebral Angiography reveals segmental narrowing and dilation of cerebral arteries (“string-of-beads” appearance), It is non-inflammatory diffuse vasccular changes that are reversible in 1-3 months.


CADASIL (Option B): Presents in the 5th-6th decade with stroke-like symptoms (small vessel syndrome). Lack of associated features like Migraine with aura, dementia makes this diagnosis unlikely.



Postpartum transient ischemic attack (TIA) (Option C): Usually symptoms last < 1 hour (definition: < 24 hours), although sudden onset headache with altered mentation makes TIA less likely.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2349, 2350.

question: A 30-year-old female who delivered a male baby via C-section owing to eclampsia developed a sudden onset headache, seizures, visual disturbances, and altered sensorium 2 days following delivery. BP is 180/120 mm Hg. An MRI head is shown. What is the likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • CADASIL - Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy is an inherited disorder characterized by small-vessel strokes.

CADASIL (Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy)

Description
  • Inherited disorder characterized by small-vessel strokes (Statement-2)

Etio- pathogenesis
  • Notch-3 gene (Statement-4)
  • Autosomal Dominant inheritance (Statement-1)
  • Notch-3 gene regulates Epidermal growth factor (EGF)

Clinical features
  • Age: 4th-5th decade
  • Small-vessel stroke
  • Progressive dementia
  • Migraine with aura: characteristic feature (Statement-3)

Diagnosis
  • MRI: Extensive symmetric white matter changes over anterior temporal lobe


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3448.
lessonTitle: Stroke, TIA and Image Based Questions
question:
Which among the following statements is/are false regarding CADASIL ?

1) Autosomal Dominant inheritance

2) Predominantly causes Large-vessel stroke

3) Characteristic symptom is Migraine with aura

4) Notch-3 gene is involved

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Cerebral angiography shows a “Puff of smoke” appearance which is suggestive of Moyamoya disease.
  • Moyamoya disease is a rare “Non-Inflammatory” neurological disorder characterized by occlusion predominantly involving internal carotid arteries.
  • It can present with both ischaemic - secondary to occlusion (in pediatric age group) and hemorrhagic features - secondary to burst of collaterals (in adult age group)

Moyamoya disease

Description

Isolated chronic, non-inflammatory (Option B) usually bilateral vasculopathy of undetermined etiology characterized by progressive narrowing of large arteries (Option A) - distal part of internal carotid artery (ICA), stem of middle cerebral (MCA) and anterior cerebral artery (ACA)

Management

Medical Management:

  • Aspirin 50-100mg: for maintenance
  • Anticoagulation: is usually contraindicated (Option C) as risk of collaterals induced hemorrhage can occur.

Surgical Management:

  • Revascularization procedures usually using superficial temporal artery bypass may be beneficial.


Reference:

question: Child presented with reccurent TIA events. Cerebral angiography was performed. Which among the following is false regarding this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Patient is having hypercoagulable state due to use of OCP and CT head shows empty delta sign. It indicates involvement of superior sagittal sinus where contrast outlines a triangular filling defect due to a thrombus.
  • The obstruction of superior sagittal sinus will cause raised ICP as absorption of CSF will be affected. The resultant cerebral edema can explain seizures
  • These features are suggestive of cerebral venous thrombosis.
  • Immediate anticoagulation with heparin is the first-line treatment, even in the presence of hemorrhagic infarcts.

Endovascular thrombolysis (Option A): Reserved for cases where anticoagulation fails or is contraindicated.

Oral warfarin immediately (Option C): Warfarin is used after heparin therapy, not as the initial treatment (effect takes a few days to develop so cannot be used for immediate anticoagulation, also it increases coagulation initially).

Blood pressure management for hypotension (Option D): Hypotension is not a common trigger for CVT and is not the primary treatment.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3447.

question: A 35 year old woman presents with sudden onset headache, seizures and focal neurological deficits. BP on admission is 160/100 mm Hg. She has a history of oral contraceptive use. CECT head is shown below. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?

correctAnswer: B. Perform urinary catheterisation for input output charting
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Routine urinary catheterisation is not recommended due to increased risk of infection and urethral trauma; it should be done only if clinically indicated.

  • Bleeding Risk: Thrombolytic agents (like tPA or TNK) induce a systemic lytic state. Inserting a catheter is an invasive procedure that can cause urethral trauma and significant mucosal bleeding.

  • Infection Risk: Catheters increase the risk of Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs), which can lead to post-stroke fever and worsen the neurological outcome.

  • It is recommended only in cases of acute urinary retention or incontinence threatening to pressure areas.

Monitor vitals and place in head end elevated position (Option A) helps prevent aspiration and cerebral edema.


Pneumatic compression stockings (Option C) are advised to prevent DVT in immobile stroke patients.


Give antipyretics to patients with fever (Option D) helps reduce infarct expansion and metabolic stress.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3441.

question: As an intern in the medicine ward, you are asked to guide the nursing staff about the various supportive care measures to improve the outcome in of Acute ischemic stroke patients who are managed with thrombolysis. Which among the following will you not advise?

correctAnswer: A. CT showing ischemic changes in &gt; 1/3 MCA territory
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Extensive early ischemic changes involving more than one-third of the MCA territory on CT scan are a major contraindication to thrombolysis.
  • This finding indicates a large infarct core with a high risk of hemorrhagic transformation if alteplase is administered.
  • Because the benefit of thrombolysis is low and the bleeding risk is very high, thrombolysis is not recommended in such patients.
  • Hence, this is a definite absolute contraindication.

Incorrect Options:

  • CT scan showing Hyperdense MCA sign (Option B): This indicates acute thrombus in MCA, which actually supports the diagnosis of acute ischemic stroke and is NOT a contraindication to thrombolysis. It often predicts a good response to early reperfusion.
  • Large hematochezia 10 days ago requiring banding (Option C): Although GI bleeding is a relative concern, thrombolysis is contraindicated only if there has been active internal bleeding within the last 21 days. A treated episode 10 days ago with no ongoing bleeding is considered a relative, not absolute, contraindication.
  • Recent epistaxis requiring nasal packing (Option D): Epistaxis especially if controlled with packing is not an absolute contraindication. Once the bleeding has stopped, thrombolysis can be considered. Only active, uncontrolled bleeding is a contraindication.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3441.

question: Which of the following is a contraindication to thrombolysis in a patient with acute ischemic stroke?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient is presenting with an acute ischemic stroke within the 4.5-hour window (sudden onset focal deficits, NCCT negative for hemorrhage).
  • Intravenous alteplase (thrombolysis) is the standard initial treatment to restore cerebral perfusion if there are no contraindications.

Antiplatelet therapy with aspirin (Option B) is indicated after thrombolysis or if thrombolysis is contraindicated, not as first-line within the window.

Mechanical thrombectomy (Option C) is reserved for large vessel occlusions and can be adjunctive to thrombolysis.

Immediate blood pressure reduction followed by alteplase (Option D) is incorrect; BP should only be lowered if >185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3441.

question: A 58 year old T2DM male with hypertension presents to the emergency department 2 hours after developing sudden onset of right sided arm weakness and face asymetry. His blood pressure is 170/90 mmHg, and a NCCT head shows no hemorrhage. He is on metformin, metoprolol and atorvastatin. What is the most appropriate initial treatment for this patient?

correctAnswer: A. Blood pressure of the patient should be reduced to &lt;140/90 with nicardipine
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient is having an intracerebral hemorrhage due to hypertensive crisis.
  • Hyperdensity is noted in the putamen and affects the internal capsule, causing a motor deficit.
  • According to current guidelines, BP of these patients should be aggressively lowered to < 140/90 mm Hg to reduce the chances of CNS bleeding.

Head end should be elevated, not flat (Option B) to reduce ICP.

Immediate intravenous thrombolysis is not indicated (Option C) because thrombolysis is contraindicated in hemorrhagic stroke.

Urgent BP lowering followed by thrombolysis (Option D) is incorrect as thrombolysis is contraindicated in hemorrhagic stroke.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3453.

question: A 50 year old male patient came to the ER with complaints of headache, blurring of vision and right sided hemiparesis for 2 hours. He is a known case of diabetes mellitus and hypertension. On examination pulse is 92/min with BP 190/110 mm Hg. What is the most appropriate statement regarding management of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The National Institute of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) is used to confirm the diagnosis of stroke. It has 15 parameters to do a structured neurological examination with a score ranging from 0 (Normal) to 42 (Severe stroke).
  • Components (11): Level of consciousness, gaze, visual fields, facial palsy, motor strength (arms/legs), limb ataxia, sensory, language, dysarthria, and extinction/inattention.
  • Score > 5 indicates need for intervention in the form of either thrombolysis or thrombectomy.

ABCD2 (Option A): This is used to predict the risk of a future stroke following a TIA (Transient Ischemic Attack). Since this patient has current, objective neurological deficits (weakness, slurred speech), he is having an active stroke, not just a TIA.

  • Components: Age (≥ 60), Blood Pressure (≥ 140/90), Clinical features (weakness/speech), Duration of symptoms, and Diabetes.

  • Scoring: 0 -7. A score ≥ 4 indicates moderate-to-high risk, usually requiring inpatient workup.

CHADS2VASc (Option B): This score is used specifically for patients with Atrial Fibrillation to determine their risk of thromboembolism and the need for long-term anticoagulation (Warfarin/DOACs). It is not a diagnostic tool for an acute stroke in progress.

  • Components: CHF, Hypertension, Age (≥ 75 is 2 pts), Diabetes, Stroke/TIA history (2 pts), Vascular disease, Age (65–74), and Sex Category (Female).

Agatson (Option D): This is a tool used in radiology to quantify coronary artery calcium on a CT scan to assess the risk of coronary artery disease (heart attacks). It has no role in acute stroke management.

  • Components: Based on the area and density of calcium deposits in the coronary arteries.

  • Scoring:

    • 0: No identifiable disease.

    • 1–100: Mild plaque.

    • > 400: Extensive plaque (high risk of Heart Attack).



Reference:

https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/stroke/assess-and-treat/nih-stroke-scale

question: A 65 year old male presents to the emergency department with a sudden onset of right sided weakness, slurred speech and facial drooping for the past 1 hour. NCCT head is normal. What is the appropriate scoring done to confirm the diagnosis of this patient?

explanationHtml:
• The ABCD² score is a clinical tool used to predict the risk of stroke following a transient ischemic attack (TIA). It includes clinical features of the TIA, not the past history of stroke.
  • It helps stratify patients into different risk categories to determine the likelihood of having a stroke in the short term, usually within 48 hours to 7 days after a TIA event.

The score is based on five clinical parameters:

  • Age: ≥ 60 years = 1 point
  • Blood Pressure: Systolic ≥ 140 mmHg or diastolic ≥ 90 mmHg = 1 point
  • Clinical Features:
    • Unilateral weakness = 2 points
    • Speech disturbance without weakness = 1 point
  • Duration of Symptoms:
    • ≥ 60 minutes = 2 points
    • 10-59 minutes = 1 point
  • Diabetes: History of diabetes = 1 point

ABCD2 Score Interpretation:

  • < 4 points: Low risk of stroke (1% risk of stroke within 2 days)
  • 4-5 points: Moderate risk of stroke (4% risk of stroke within 2 days)
  • > 5 points: High risk of stroke (8% risk of stroke within 2 days)



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3448.

question: A 70 year old woman presents to the ER with sudden-onset slurred speech and right-sided facial weakness that resolved after 90 minutes. The resident has asked you to calculate ABCD2 score. Which of the following is not a component of this score

correctAnswer: B. Rupture of penetrating arteries supplying internal capsule
explanationHtml:
• This patient's presentation is suggestive of a hemorrhagic stroke, with NCCT head showing hyperdensity involving the Putamen.
  • This is most commonly associated with long-standing hypertension, leading to rupture of penetrating arteries supplying the internal capsule.

Ruptured saccular aneurysm (Option A) will have nuchal rigidity.

Dural sinus thrombosis (Option C) is seen in a setting of a hypercoagulable state, while our case has hypertension.

Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (Option D) will cause cerebral edema involving the occipital lobes.

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3454.

question: A 45-year-old man with hypertension presents to the ER at 6 am in morning with excruciating headache and sudden onset face, arm and leg weakness. On examination GCS is 8 and blood pressure is 220/110 mmHg. NCCT head is shown. Cause of this presentation is?

explanationHtml:
• The patient presents with a left MCA territory stroke causing right-sided arm weakness and affecting the dominant hemisphere. That explains Broca's aphasia.
  • In a cortical stroke, the patient looks to the side of the lesion; hence, the patient is looking to the left. Reason is a destructive lesion in the left frontal eye field
  • Involvement of left optic radiations (MCA supplies parietal and temporal lobes) explains the right-sided homonymous hemianopia

Left MCA, Non-dominant hemisphere (Option A) will present with right-sided motor and sensory deficits and right homonymous hemianopia, without aphasia.

Left PCA, Dominant hemisphere (Option C) will present with Alexia without agraphia.

Right PCA, Non-Dominant hemisphere (Option D) will cause spatial neglect, map-reading issues and prosopagnosia.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 202, 3429.

question: A 60-year-old man is brought to ER with sudden onset of right-sided arm weakness and difficulty speaking. His gaze is deviated to the left, and he has a right homonymous hemianopia. Which of the following is the most likely location of the thrombus causing this patient's symptoms?

correctAnswer: B. CT perfusion with endovascular thrombectomy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of Acute ischemic stroke with symptoms persisting for > 6 hours. Hence, CT Perfusion will be done, followed by thrombectomy to remove the clot occluding the M2 segment of MCA.
  • The patient is outside the window period of thrombolysis of 4.5 hours.

Endovascular coiling (Option A) is used for the treatment of SAH.

Lower BP with Nicardipine followed by Tenecteplase (Option C) is done if thrombolysis is scheduled.

Lower BP with Nicardipine followed by Aspirin loading 325 mg (Option D) is wrong as aspirin is started after 24-48 hours of admission in AIS.

question: A 60 year old man presents with sudden onset right face deviation and arm weakness for last 8 hours. BP on admission is 185/110 mm Hg. NCCT head shows hypodensity in parietal lobe and CTA shows clot in M2 segment of MCA. Which is the best intervention for this patient?

correctAnswer: B. Sensory, motor, and autonomic fibres
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Peripheral neuropathies frequently involve a combination of sensory, motor, and autonomic nerve fibres, and a comprehensive clinical assessment will often reveal a mixed pattern of impairment.

This patient has poorly controlled diabetes with features of diabetic peripheral neuropathy, and his symptoms involve multiple fibre types:

1. Sensory fibre involvement

  • Stocking-and-glove numbness
  • Classic distal symmetric polyneuropathy
  • Due to the involvement of long sensory fibres (especially small fibres first)

2. Motor fibre involvement

  • Bilateral foot drop
  • Indicates weakness of dorsiflexors (deep peroneal nerve distribution)
  • Suggests motor fibre damage in advanced neuropathy

3. Autonomic fibre involvement

  • Recurrent dizziness on standing
  • Suggests orthostatic hypotension
  • Caused by autonomic (sympathetic) fibre dysfunction

Patients classically present initially with distal symmetric sensory loss. As the axonal degeneration progresses, it involves motor fibres (manifesting as distal weakness, such as foot drop) and autonomic fibres (leading to orthostatic hypotension, resting tachycardia, gastroparesis, or erectile dysfunction).

Therefore, the simultaneous presence of numbness, weakness, and orthostatic dizziness confirms the involvement of all three fibre types.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3594-3596.
question: A 55-year-old man with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus presents with a progressive stocking-and-glove numbness in his extremities. Recently, he has also developed bilateral foot drop and complains of recurrent dizzy spells upon standing. These clinical findings suggest impairment of which nerve fibres in peripheral neuropathy?

correctAnswer: C. Loss of joint position sense
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Disorders of autonomic function (dysautonomia) occur due to damage to the sympathetic and parasympathetic nerve fibres, which control involuntary bodily functions.
  • Loss of joint position sense (proprioception) is a manifestation of a somatic large-fibre sensory neuropathy, not an autonomic neuropathy.

Clinical manifestations of autonomic neuropathy include:

  • Cardiovascular: Unexplained orthostatic hypotension and resting tachycardia. (Option A ruled out)
  • Genitourinary: Impotence and bladder disorders such as urinary frequency, hesitancy, or incontinence. (Option B ruled out)
  • Gastrointestinal: Constipation, diarrhoea, bloating, nausea, vomiting of old food. (Option D ruled out)
  • Sudomotor: Altered sweating patterns, including hyperhidrosis or hypohidrosis (anhidrosis).
  • Other features: Syncope and sleep dysfunction.


Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3538-3540, 3595.
question: All of the following are characteristic clinical manifestations of autonomic neuropathy, except:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical picture of a strict vegan presenting with macrocytic anaemia and peripheral neuropathy is highly diagnostic of Vitamin B12 deficiency.

  • This deficiency leads to Subacute Combined Degeneration of the spinal cord (affecting the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts) and simultaneously causes a large fibre peripheral neuropathy.
  • Large, heavily myelinated nerve fibres (A-alpha and A-beta fibres) are responsible for transmitting proprioception and vibration sense.
  • Thus, untreated patients will develop a profound loss of joint position sense, leading to sensory ataxia and a positive Romberg's sign.

question: A 60-year-old strict vegan presents with progressive numbness in her hands and feet. Blood tests reveal a macrocytic anaemia and hypersegmented neutrophils. If this condition is left untreated, which of the following sensory modalities is most likely to be impaired first due to the involvement of large nerve fibres?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Peripheral neuropathies are classified according to the predominant nerve fiber involved.

  • Small-fibre neuropathies selectively affect thinly myelinated Aδ fibres and unmyelinated C fibres, producing:
    • Burning pain
    • Loss of pain and temperature sensation
    • Allodynia
    • Autonomic dysfunction
    • Preserved muscle strength, vibration sense, and deep tendon reflexes
  • Copper deficiency classically causes a myeloneuropathy that closely resembles vitamin B12 deficiency. It predominantly affects the dorsal columns and large myelinated sensory fibers, leading to:
    • Sensory ataxia
    • Loss of vibration and proprioception
    • Gait instability
    • Spasticity in advanced cases
  • Thus, copper deficiency is not a well-recognized cause of a predominant small-fibre neuropathy.

Conditions associated with small-fibre neuropathy

Category

Associated conditions

Metabolic & Endocrine

Diabetes mellitus, impaired glucose tolerance, hypothyroidism

Autoimmune & Inflammatory

Sjögren's syndrome, systemic lupus erythematosus, sarcoidosis, coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease (Option A ruled out)

Infectious

Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV), hepatitis C, Hansen's disease (leprosy), Lyme disease (Option D ruled out)

Genetic & Hereditary

Fabry disease, hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathies (HSAN), sodium channelopathies

Toxic & Pharmacological

Alcohol excess, chemotherapy (e.g., bortezomib, taxanes), metronidazole

Systemic & Infiltrative

Primary systemic amyloidosis, paraneoplastic syndromes (Option C ruled out)

Other

Idiopathic (accounts for up to 50% of cases)



Reference:
  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3612-3613.
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK582147/
question: Small-fibre neuropathies selectively affect thinly myelinated A-delta and unmyelinated C fibres, typically presenting with burning pain, temperature loss, and autonomic deficits while preserving deep tendon reflexes and muscle bulk. All of the following conditions are well-recognised causes of a prominent small-fibre neuropathy, EXCEPT:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Symmetric proximal and distal weakness in a patient who presents with both motor and sensory symptoms is the clinical hallmark of acquired immune demyelinating polyneuropathies, which include:

  • Acute form - Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS)
  • Chronic form - chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP).

Recognising this pattern is critical because it identifies a subset of patients who have a highly treatable neuropathic disorder. Most other classical polyneuropathies present with purely distal, length-dependent weakness.
