question: 40 year old woman is diagnosed with autoimmune demyelinating astrocytopathy. Which of the following areas of brain are targetted by AQP4 antibodies seen in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's presentation of progressive bilateral visual loss, temporal headaches, and neurological deficits, alongside the detection of aquaporin-4 antibodies, strongly indicates neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD).
  • Raised ICP is not a feature of NMOSD.
  • Lesion in hypothalamus will cause diencephalic syndrome causing severe emaciation/weight loss despite normal or increased appetite. (Option B)
  • Crossed hemiplegia is due to development of lesions in brainstem . Crossed means cranial nerve palsy will be ipsilateral to lesion along with contralateral hemiplegia. (Option A)

Radiological findings in NMOSD

Location

Characteristics

Spinal Cord
  • Longitudinally extensive lesions (≥3 vertebral segments)
  • Central/gray matter involvement
  • T1 hypointensity in acute lesions

[[figure-1]]

Brain
  • Periependymal lesions around the ventricular system
  • Hemispheric tumefactive lesions (Option C)
  • Cloud-like enhancing lesions.

[[figure-2]]

question: A 38-year-old African woman presents with four months of progressive bilateral visual loss and temporal headaches. Neurological examination reveals spastic paraplegia and brisk knee jerks and ankle jerks. Work up shows Anti- aquaporin-4 antibodies. Which of the following is not seen in this condition ?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This case is consistent with Multiple Sclerosis (Acute exacerbation)
    • Because of the patient's symptoms, including limb weakness, gait unsteadiness, paresthesias, and Lhermitte sign.
    • The MRI findings of multiple periventricular white matter lesions further support the diagnosis.
  • High-dose IV corticosteroids are the most appropriate treatment for acute exacerbations of MS, as they reduce inflammation and accelerate recovery from attacks.


Treatment Category

Interventions

Acute Exacerbations
  • High-dose IV corticosteroids
    • first-line treatment for acute flares (Option A)
  • Plasma exchange
    • for patients who do not respond to corticosteroids.

Disease-Modifying Therapies (Option B, C)
  • Natalizumab and Ocrelizumab are highly effective for patients who haven’t responded to other therapies.
    • Natalizumab: blocks integrin α4, preventing leukocyte adhesion to endothelial cells.
      • It has a risk of PML
    • Ocrelizumab: targets and depletes CD20-positive B cells.
  • Patients with less active disease may be started on oral medications like Dimethyl fumarate or Fingolimod (sphingosine-1-phosphate modulator)
  • β-interferon and Glatiramer have the highest safety profiles but lower effectiveness.

Symptomatic Therapy
  • Baclofen
    • used for spasticity (Option D)
  • Cholinergic
    • for urinary retention
  • Anticholinergics
    • for urinary incontinence
  • Carbamazepine, amitriptyline
    • for painful paresthesias
  • Antidepressants
  • Neurogenic bladder treatments
    • Catheterization, muscarinic antagonists, botulinum toxin injection
  • Spasticity treatments (GABA B receptor agonists)


Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3585.

question: A 36-year-old caucasian woman on medical tourism visit presents with a history of recent onset left lower limb weakness, gait unsteadiness, and paresthesias. She experiences an electric shock sensation that radiates down her spine when flexing her neck. An MRI of the brain is given below. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient’s condition?

correctAnswer: C. MRI of the brain and spinal cord
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This is a case of Multiple Sclerosis (MS), characterized by episodes of neurological symptoms. The patient's symptoms, including acute vision loss, weakness, and sensory disturbances, are consistent with MS.
  • MRI of the brain and spinal cord is the diagnostic test of choice because it can effectively identify the characteristic lesions associated with MS, particularly in the periventricular regions and spinal cord

Test

Description

MRI
  • Imaging modality of choice for MS
  • Shows multiple asymmetric, periventricular white matter lesions (Dawson fingers)

[[figure-1]]

Red arrowheads referred to as Dawson ﬁngers

  • Active lesions enhanced with gadolinium due to increased BBB permeability
  • Presence of plaques and black holes (T1-weighted)

Visual Evoked Potential
  • Assesses optic nerve damage (Option A)

CSF Analysis
  • ↑IgG index indicates intrathecal synthesis
  • Agarose electrophoresis: > 2 oligoclonal bands (not found in serum)

(Option D)

  • Lumbar puncture:
    • can provide supportive evidence (Option B)
    • > 5 cells/microliter; protein > 1g, cells > 75 suggests alternative diagnosis

question: A 30-year-old woman presents with a 2-day history of acute, painful vision loss in her left eye, associated with a dull ache that worsens with eye movement. She also reports episodes of leg weakness, difficulty maintaining balance, and tingling sensations in her arms. Her medical history includes recurrent episodes of blurred vision and fatigue, particularly worsening in warm conditions. What is the diagnostic test of choice for this condition?

correctAnswer: A. None, dissemination in space and in time are met
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In a person with 2 or more attacks and clinical evidence of 2 or more lesions, both dissemination in space (DIS) and dissemination in time (DIT) have already been established.
  • DIS is confirmed because multiple lesions exist in the central nervous system (CNS) regions
  • DIT is confirmed because multiple clinical attacks have occurred over time.
  • Therefore, no additional criteria are necessary to make the diagnosis of MS in this scenario

Scenario

Requirement for diagnosis

≥ 2 Clinical attacks + Objective evidence of ≥ 2 lesions

MS can be diagnosed – No further tests needed

≥2 attacks + 1 lesion

Dissemination in space required (MRI or new attack at different site)

1 attack + ≥ 2 lesions

Dissemination in time required (MRI or second clinical attack)

1 attack + 1 lesion

Need both DIS and DIT (Via MRI or clinical evidence)

Progressive neurological symptoms from onset (≥1 year)

Evidence of progression plus: 2 of 3

  1. DIS in brain
  2. DIS in spinal cord
  3. Positive CSF (oligoclonal bands or IgG index)

Abbreviations:

  • DIT = dissemination in time
  • DIS = dissemination in space
  • CNS = central nervous system
  • CSF = cerebrospinal fluid
  • T2 lesion = hyperintense lesion on T2 weighted MRI

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3583.

question: Which of the following statements regarding one and a half syndrome in multiple sclerosis is not true?

correctAnswer: C. Lesion in the left medial longitudinal fasciculus
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Based on the history of multiple sclerosis and the ocular findings, the diagnosis is internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO).
  • INO is caused by demyelination of the ipsilateral medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), a characteristic brainstem lesion in multiple sclerosis.
  • The left MLF connects the right abducens (VI) nucleus to the left oculomotor (III) nucleus, coordinating conjugate horizontal eye movements.
  • A left MLF lesion interrupts this pathway, resulting in:
    • Slowed/impaired adduction of the left eye on attempted right gaze.
    • Horizontal nystagmus of the abducting right eye, a characteristic finding of INO.
  • Bilateral INO is particularly suggestive of multiple sclerosis.

[[figure-1]]

Lesion in the right sixth cranial nerve (Option A): Causes impaired abduction of the right eye, not impaired adduction of the left eye.

Lesion in the left sixth cranial nerve (Option B): Causes impaired abduction of the left eye, not the findings seen here.

Lesion in the right medial longitudinal fasciculus (Option D): Causes impaired adduction of the right eye during left gaze, opposite to this patient's findings.

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3578.

question: A 45-year-old woman who is a known case of multiple sclerosis has come for follow up consultation. On examination, the left eye has slowed adduction when attempting to look to the right, and there is horizontal nystagmus in the right eye when it is abducting. Which of the following best explains the underlying pathology of this patient’s symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Uthoff's symptom refers to the temporary worsening of neurological symptoms due to increased body temperature, often triggered by heat exposure, such as spending time in a sauna.
  • This symptom is common in patients with multiple sclerosis.

Lhermitte’s symptom (Option A) : An electric shock-like sensation that radiates down the back into the legs. Typically induced by flexion or other movements of the neck.


Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (Option D) is caused by a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), and is characterized by impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye and nystagmus of the abducting contralateral eye.

question: A 34-year-old woman with a known diagnosis of multiple sclerosis visited a sauna in her gym. After the visit her vision becomes blurry and her leg weakness worsened that she had to be assisted by gym staff to her house. This presentation is called?

correctAnswer: C. Unilateral throbbing pain with phonophobia
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Unilateral throbbing pain with phonophobia meets the diagnostic criteria for migraines. It specifies unilateral pain, describes the pain as throbbing (a key characteristic), and includes phonophobia (sensitivity to sound), fulfilling the requirement for at least three features from the specified list.

Simplified Diagnostic Criteria for Migraine by International Headache Society

Repeated attacks of headache lasting 4–72h in patients with a normal physical examination, no other reasonable cause for the headache, and:

  • At least 2 of the following features:
    • Unilateral pain
    • Throbbing pain
    • Aggravation by movement
    • Moderate or severe intensity
  • Plus at least 1 of the following features:
    • Nausea/vomiting
    • Photophobia and phonophobia

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3466.

question: A 40-year-old woman reports experiencing recurrent headaches that last between 6 and 48 hours. She often feels fatigued and has mood changes before the headaches begin. According to the International Headache Society's criteria, which features are essential for diagnosing her condition as migraine?

correctAnswer: A. Amitriptyline, starting at 20 mg daily, with gradual increases as needed.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This patient likely has chronic tension-type headache (TTH), given her 9-month history of frequent headaches (at least 3 times per week).
  • The pain is described as a dull, bilateral ache, often associated with neck tension, stress, and fatigue, which are characteristic features of TTH.
  • Her report of difficulty concentrating and disrupted sleep further supports the chronic nature of the headaches, distinguishing them from episodic TTH.
  • Amitriptyline is the first-line treatment for chronic tension-type headaches (TTH). It is a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA) used for prevention, and it should be started at a low dose (10–25 mg daily) and increased gradually.

Combination of Ibuprofen 400 mg plus acetaminophen 1000 mg (Option B): Used for acute headache relief, not preventive therapy.

Aspirin and Botulinum toxin type A injections (Option C): Botulinum toxin is primarily used for chronic migraine, not tension-type headache.

Combination of massage therapy and acupuncture (Option D): Can be adjunctive, but not first-line preventive therapy.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3471.

question: A 35-year-old woman presents with a 9-month history of frequent headaches occurring at least 3 times per week. She describes the pain as a dull, bilateral ache that feels like a tight band around her head. The headaches are often accompanied by neck tension, stress, and fatigue. Which of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this patient's condition?

correctAnswer: B. Most commonly caused by vascular compression of the trigeminal nerve, often by the superior cerebellar artery.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient has trigeminal neuralgia (TN), characterized by sharp, electric shock-like pain affecting the maxillary (V2) and mandibular (V3) branches of the trigeminal nerve, triggered by light touch. The condition is most commonly caused by vascular compression, often by the superior cerebellar artery, leading to demyelination of the nerve.

Aspect Trigeminal Neuralgia Glossopharyngeal Neuralgia
About "Tic douloureux"; recurrent, brief electric shock-like pain; usually V2/V3; triggered by touch, chewing, cold air. Rare; brief sharp unilateral pain in jaw angle, ear, tonsillar fossa, tongue base; triggered by coughing, talking, swallowing (Option A).
Etiopathogenesis Mainly vascular compression (superior cerebellar artery); demyelination; also tumors or MS. Idiopathic or secondary: vascular compression, MS, infections, tumors, Eagle syndrome, rarely oropharyngeal cancer.
Clinical Features Unilateral, sharp, brief, multiple times/day; trigger zones; V1 rare autonomic signs (Option D). Intense, brief unilateral pain in ear/tongue/tonsil; may cause syncope/bradycardia; relapsing-remitting; weight loss.
Diagnosis Clinical ± MRI/MRA for vascular compression; ICHD criteria. Clinical ± MRI/MRA; CT/X-ray for Eagle syndrome; cardiac eval if syncope.
Treatment Pharmacologic: Carbamazepine/oxcarbazepine first-line (Option C); second-line: gabapentin, baclofen. Surgery: Microvascular decompression, rhizotomy, peripheral neurectomy. explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient presents with an acute onset of focal neurological deficits (left-sided facial paralysis and arm weakness), which is highly suggestive of an acute ischemic stroke. The CT head is normal, which is expected in early ischemic stroke, as changes may not be visible in the first few hours. The critical factor here is the time of onset, which is 8 hours, placing the patient outside the therapeutic window for IV thrombolysis (4.5 hours).

Stepwise Approach to Acute Ischemic Stroke:

  1. Confirm stroke type
    • Non-contrast CT: No hemorrhage
  2. Assess time window
    • IV thrombolysis (Alteplase) within 4.5 hours only
    • This patient: 8 hours (NOT eligible)
  3. Blood Pressure Management
    • BP = 160/100 mm Hg
    • In ischemic stroke (without thrombolysis):
      • Do NOT lower BP unless >220/120 mm Hg
      • Mildly elevated BP helps maintain cerebral perfusion (permissive hypertension)
  4. Next best step: Monitoring + urgent neurology consultation
    • Plan further evaluation (MRI, vascular imaging, secondary prevention)


IV labetalol (Option B) is not indicated here as BP is not severely elevated (>220/120 mm Hg). Aggressive BP reduction may worsen cerebral ischemia.


IV thrombolysis (Option C) is contraindicated because the patient is outside the 4.5-hour window.

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3453, 3454

question: A patient with left-sided facial paralysis and arm weakness for the last eight hours. BP on admission is 160/100 mm Hg. Her CT head is normal. What is the next step in the management of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient in question presents with a type of headache characterized by a duration of 5-240 seconds and a frequency of 3-200 attacks per day. These features align with SUNCT (Short-lasting Unilateral Neuralgiform headache attacks with Conjunctival injection and Tearing).

  • Duration: Very brief, 5–240 seconds per attack.
  • Frequency: High, 3–200 attacks/day, distinguishing it from cluster headaches (1–8/day).
  • Pain Quality: Unilateral, sharp or stabbing, similar to cluster headaches but shorter.
  • Treatment: IV lidocaine provides relief via sodium channel blockade.


High-flow oxygen (Option A) This treatment is effective for Cluster Headaches, as inhaling high-flow oxygen can significantly decrease the severity of the pain. However, it is not indicated for SUNCT, where the duration and frequency of attacks are much different.


Sumatriptan (Option B) Triptans, such as Sumatriptan, are typically used for the acute treatment of Cluster Headaches and are effective for relieving pain when used at the onset of an attack. However, they are not the first-line treatment for SUNCT and are generally less effective for this condition.


Verapamil (Option D) While preventive medications such as verapamil are commonly used for Cluster Headaches to reduce the frequency of attacks, they do not specifically address acute SUNCT episodes and are not the preferred initial treatment for this condition.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3473
question:
A 45-year-old male presents with a history of recurrent headaches. After a thorough evaluation, he is diagnosed with a headache that has a stinging character and characterized by the following features:

  • Duration: 5-240 seconds
  • Attacks: 3-200 attacks per day.

Which of the following treatments is most appropriate for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical features are suggestive of Giant cell Arteritis
  • Starting high-dose corticosteroids is the most appropriate next step in the management of Giant Cell Arteritis.
  • Prompt initiation of high-dose corticosteroids is crucial to prevent complications, particularly vision loss, which can occur if the condition progresses.

Perform temporal artery biopsy (Option B): While a temporal artery biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis and is often performed, it should ideally be done after the initiation of corticosteroids if the diagnosis of GCA is highly suspected, especially considering the risk of blindness.

Initiate aspirin therapy (Option C): Aspirin may be considered for vascular protection, but it is not the primary treatment for GCA. The immediate focus should be on controlling inflammation with corticosteroids.

Refer for imaging studies of the carotid arteries (Option D) While imaging can be helpful in assessing the extent of vascular involvement, it is not the immediate step when GCA is suspected. The clinical presentation and laboratory findings are sufficient to start treatment.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2903.

question: A 35-year-old man with a history of chronic migraines visits his physician to discuss treatment options. He is interested in triptans but has some health concerns that he wants to clarify. Which of the following is NOT a contraindication for triptans based on the provided information?

correctAnswer: C. To evaluate headache-related disability and its impact on daily activities.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The MIDAS questionnaire specifically measures how migraines affect a person's productivity in work, school, and social activities, providing insights into their overall disability.

MIDAS Test:

  • The MIDAS (Migraine Disability Assessment) is a self-administered questionnaire.
  • It assesses headache-related disability over the past three months.
  • The questionnaire consists of five questions about productivity loss and limitations in work, school, household, and social activities.
  • It includes a global question on migraine severity, rated from 0 (no pain) to 10 (very severe pain).
  • Additional questions gather information on headache frequency and intensity.
  • The MIDAS is a reliable and valid tool with good test-retest reliability and correlates with clinical needs for medical care.

Grading:

Total MIDAS scores categorize migraine-related disability into four grades:

  • Grade I: Little or no disability (0–5)
  • Grade II: Mild disability (6–10)
  • Grade III: Moderate disability (11–20)
  • Grade IV: Severe disability (≥ 21)


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3464, 3466.

Intracranial aneurysm rupture (Option B): Typically causes sudden thunderclap headache and subarachnoid hemorrhage, not basal ganglia bleed.

question: A newborn delivered by forceps has a high-pitched cry and bulging anterior fontanelle. The mother notes that the baby seems unusually irritable. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial diagnostic step and management?

correctAnswer: D. Venous bleeding with burr hole surgery
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This case presents classic features of chronic subdural hematoma due to the following reasons:

  • Risk factors: elderly, anticoagulation, brain atrophy, minor trauma
  • Gradual symptom progression over weeks (came at one month)
  • Nonspecific symptoms: confusion, gait issues, mild weakness
  • Left-sided concave hyperdensity with islands of hypodensity due to resorption of blood

Hence, the patient will require a Burr hole surgery. It will help in the evacuation of liquified hematoma

Arterial bleeding with craniotomy (Option A): Describes epidural hematoma, usually acute with rapid deterioration.

Arterial bleeding with craniotomy and ligation of bleeder (Option B): Relevant for epidural hematoma with arterial source, not chronic subdural.

Venous bleeding with craniotomy (Option C): Burr hole is less invasive and preferred for chronic subdural; craniotomy reserved for complicated cases.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3572, 3573.

question: A 75-year-old man with atrial fibrillation on warfarin presents with progressive confusion and unsteady gait over the past month. His wife reports he had a minor fall 6 weeks ago. On examination, he is confused, has mild right sided weakness. NCCT brain is given below. Which of the following is correct about this patient?

correctAnswer: C. Burr hole followed by craniotomy and ligation of the bleeder
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This case presents a classic epidural hematoma requiring emergency intervention because of:

  • Deteriorating consciousness
  • Focal neurological signs (pupillary dilation, hemiparesis)
  • Significant midline shift (>5mm)
  • Classic temporal location suggesting middle meningeal artery involvement

Other indications of Evacuation:

  • Clot >30cc volume
  • Thickness >15 mm
  • GCS <9

Epidural hematoma management:

  1. Immediate decompression (burr hole) to relieve pressure

  2. Definitive craniotomy to evacuate hematoma

  3. Ligation of the middle meningeal artery (the bleeder)

Observe and monitor neurological status (Option A): Incorrect because observation alone is dangerous in a deteriorating patient with significant mass effect.




Start mannitol and hyperventilate (Option B): Incorrect because while these measures may temporarily help, they are adjuncts to definitive surgical management.




Conservative management with anticonvulsants (Option D): Incorrect because conservative management is inappropriate for a large, symptomatic extradural hematoma.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3572.

question: A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department after being struck in the temporal region during a hockey game. Initially conscious at the scene, he now presents with decreasing consciousness, right-sided pupillary dilation, and left hemiparesis. CT head shows a lentiform hyperdense lesion in the right temporal region with 12mm midline shift. Which of the following is most appropriate treatment of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This case presents the classic scenario of an epidural hematoma as suggested by the presence of a lucid interval and CT showing a characteristic biconvex (lentiform) hyperdense lesion.
  • A lucid interval (LI) refers to a brief period of normal consciousness following an initial loss of consciousness, often seen in cerebral concussion or cerebral compression. In cases like epidural hematoma, the lucid interval occurs as the brain temporarily recovers before increased pressure from the hematoma leads to further deterioration.


Subdural hematoma (Option B): Usually crescent-shaped, crosses suture lines, and deterioration is more gradual, especially in elderly or anticoagulated patients.


Intraparenchymal hemorrhage (Option C): Typically spontaneous, often in hypertensive patients, not directly trauma-related.


Subarachnoid hemorrhage (Option D): Presents with sudden, severe “thunderclap” headache, not delayed deterioration.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3572
question: A 75-year-old man on warfarin (INR 2.5) falls and hits his head. He is initially alert and oriented, but after 2 hours, becomes progressively drowsy and confused. His CT scan is given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. 4-factor Prothrombin Complex Concentrate and Vitamin K 10mg IV
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient presents with classic features of warfarin-associated intracranial hemorrhage:

  • Patient is on warfarin therapy
  • Supratherapeutic INR 10.0
  • Acute neurological symptoms (headache, weakness, altered mental status)
  • Confirmed intraparenchymal hemorrhage on CT

This represents a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate reversal of anticoagulation by 4-factor Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC) & Vitamin K 10mg IV. Tranexamic acid may also be considered.


Vitamin K 10mg IV only (Option A): Too slow to reverse anticoagulation in acute hemorrhage.


Fast infusion of fresh frozen plasma (Option B): Works slower than PCC and requires large volume, may worsen intracranial pressure.


Fast infusion of fresh frozen plasma and urgent neurosurgery (Option C): Surgery cannot be safely done until coagulopathy is corrected; FFP alone is slower than PCC.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3455

question: A 52-year-old man presents with headache, left-sided facial, arm, and leg weakness. His sensorium is fast deteriorating, and he is a known case of rheumatic heart disease on warfarin. His INR is 10. The NCCT head is given below. Which of the following is correct about his management?

correctAnswer: C. Nicardipine to achieve target BP of 140/90 mm Hg or lesser
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Nicardipine is recommended as a first-line agent in the acute management of hemorrhagic stroke to reduce elevated blood pressure. According to the latest guidelines, blood pressure should be rapidly but safely lowered to a target of <140/90 mm Hg, as this has been shown to reduce the risk of re-bleeding without increasing the risk of ischemia.

Earlier guidelines advocated a more gradual reduction in blood pressure, but recent evidence supports early intensive control for better outcomes.


Mannitol (Option A) is generally contraindicated in active CNS bleeding unless there is evidence of raised intracranial pressure with herniation risk, as it may worsen bleeding by altering intracranial hemodynamics.


Immediate surgical evacuation (Option B): Indicated only for cerebellar hemorrhage, large lobar hemorrhage with mass effect, or deterioration, not all basal ganglia bleeds.


Sodium nitroprusside (Option D) is not preferred due to its tendency to cause a rapid and uncontrolled drop in blood pressure, which can lead to cerebral hypoperfusion and infarction, especially in patients with impaired cerebral autoregulation during hypertensive crises.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3453.

question: A 50-year-old hypertensive man suddenly develops facial asymetry and right arm weakness during a meeting. His BP on arrival is 220/130 mmHg. CT shows putaminal hemorrhage. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

correctAnswer: A. Superior division of left MCA
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The combination of:

  • Right facial weakness
  • Right arm weakness
  • Non-fluent (Broca's) aphasia
  • Preserved comprehension

This pattern suggests a superior division MCA stroke in the dominant (left) hemisphere, affecting the frontal opercular region and motor cortex.

Inferior division of left MCA (Option B) typically presents with Wernicke's (fluent) aphasia, Poor comprehension, Jargon speech, Superior quadrantanopia, usually no significant motor deficits

Main trunk of left MCA (Option C) would cause a complete MCA syndrome, more severe motor deficits including face, arm, and leg-Complete hemiparesis, both expressive and receptive language deficits-Global aphasia (if dominant hemisphere), hemisensory loss, hemianopia.

Lenticulostriate branches of left MCA (Option D) causes lacunar syndromes- pure motor stroke or sensory-motor stroke, affects internal capsule, no cortical symptoms like aphasia, affects internal capsule

question: A 65-year-old hypertensive male presents with sudden onset weakness of right face and arm, along with difficulty speaking. He is unable to form words properly but appears to understand commands. Brain imaging shows an acute infarct. Which division of the MCA is most likely involved?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Cerebral amyloid angiopathy fits the characteristic features of this patient:

  • Elderly patient (>60 years)
  • No history of hypertension
  • Multiple lobar hemorrhages in MRI
  • Acute neurological presentation

[[figure-1]]

Berry aneurysm rupture (Option B): Usually causes sudden subarachnoid hemorrhage, not multiple lobar hemorrhages.

Hypertensive crisis (Option C): Typically causes deep intracerebral hemorrhages (basal ganglia, thalamus) rather than lobar.

Venous sinus thrombosis (Option D): Can cause hemorrhagic infarcts, but usually associated with headache, seizures, and venous congestion rather than isolated lobar hemorrhages.

question: An 82-year-old normotensive, non-diabetic man presents with sudden onset confusion and headache. MRI shows multiple lobar hemorrhages. Which is the MOST likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The movement demonstrated is an intention (kinetic) tremor, a characteristic feature of cerebellar dysfunction.
  • Unlike resting tremor, an intention tremor is absent at rest and appears during voluntary movement, becoming increasingly prominent as the patient approaches a target during the finger-to-nose test or similar coordination tasks.
  • The cerebellum is responsible for coordination, precision, and timing of voluntary movements.
  • Lesions involving the cerebellar hemispheres impair the correction of ongoing movements, resulting in intention tremor, dysmetria (past-pointing), dysdiadochokinesia, hypotonia, rebound phenomenon, nystagmus, and an ataxic gait.
  • The tremor worsens near the endpoint of a movement because the cerebellum is unable to make the fine adjustments required for accurate motor control.

Basal ganglia (Option A) are involved in the initiation and modulation of voluntary movement. Disorders such as Parkinson disease produce a resting tremor, which is most prominent when the limb is relaxed and improves with voluntary movement. This is in contrast to the intention tremor demonstrated in the video, making basal ganglia dysfunction an unlikely explanation.

Subthalamic nucleus (Option C) is a component of the indirect basal ganglia pathway. Lesions involving the subthalamic nucleus classically produce hemiballismus, characterized by violent, flinging movements of the contralateral limbs. These involuntary movements are distinct from the slow, target-directed intention tremor observed in cerebellar disease.

Corticospinal tract (Option D) carries upper motor neuron fibers responsible for voluntary motor function. Lesions produce spastic weakness, hyperreflexia, increased muscle tone, clonus, and an extensor plantar (Babinski) response. Although voluntary movements become weak, intention tremor is not a feature of corticospinal tract lesions, making this option incorrect.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3508, 3509
question: A 34-year-old woman presents with progressive unsteadiness while walking and difficulty performing fine hand movements. During neurological examination, she is asked to perform the manoeuvre demonstrated in the attached video. This clinical finding most likely indicates a lesion involving which of the following?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • MRI shows Prominent cerebellar sulci and fissures and Mild atrophy of the brainstem suggesting MSA.
  • Midodrine is an alpha-1 adrenergic agonist that causes vasoconstriction, thereby increasing blood pressure.
  • It is a commonly used medication to treat symptomatic orthostatic hypotension, which aligns well with the patient's symptoms (dizzy spells, positive tilt table test) in the context of MSA.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1936.
question: 60 year old man with multiple system atrophy is having dizzy spells and tilt table test is positive. MRI head is shown below. Which of the following is most appropriate treatment for this case?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The involuntary movement shown is a resting tremor, one of the cardinal motor features of Parkinson disease. It is classically described as a "pill-rolling" tremor, occurring at a frequency of 4-6 Hz, most prominent when the affected limb is completely at rest, and diminishing with voluntary movement or during sleep.

  • Parkinson disease results from progressive degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dopamine deficiency within the nigrostriatal pathway.
  • The resulting imbalance between reduced dopaminergic activity and relative cholinergic overactivity in the basal ganglia produces the characteristic motor manifestations, including resting tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, and postural instability.
  • Neuropathologically, Parkinson disease is characterized by Lewy bodies, which are intracytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions composed predominantly of α-synuclein.
  • The mainstay of treatment is levodopa combined with carbidopa, along with dopamine agonists and other antiparkinsonian medications.

Serotonin (Option A) is an important neurotransmitter involved in the regulation of mood, sleep, appetite, and pain perception. Deficiency is primarily associated with depressive disorders and does not produce the characteristic resting tremor or other cardinal motor features of Parkinson disease.

Acetylcholine (Option C) is the principal neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction and plays a key role in cognitive function within the central nervous system. In Parkinson disease, there is relative cholinergic overactivity secondary to dopamine deficiency rather than acetylcholine deficiency. Anticholinergic drugs may reduce tremor by restoring the dopaminergic-cholinergic balance.

GABA (Option D): Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) is the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system. Disorders of GABAergic transmission are implicated in conditions such as epilepsy, anxiety disorders, and Huntington disease, but GABA deficiency is not the primary neurochemical abnormality responsible for the resting tremor of Parkinson disease.



Reference:
  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3405, 3406
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4913065/
question: A 68-year-old man presents with progressively worsening slowness of movements and difficulty initiating walking over the past year. During examination, the involuntary movement demonstrated in the attached video is observed while his hands are at rest. The neurotransmitter deficiency primarily responsible for this clinical finding is:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Frontotemporal dementia is often a tauopathy, characterized by the accumulation of hyperphosphorylated tau protein in neurons and glia.

  • Other tauopathies include progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration .

  • Alzheimer’s disease shows both β-amyloid plaques and tau tangles.

  • Lewy body dementia is an α-synucleinopathy.

  • Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease involves prion protein accumulation.

  • Tau and α-syn protein aggregation leads to neurotoxicity, resulting in: synaptic dysfunction and neuronal loss



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3486.

options.text: Prion protein accumulation in the brain

question: Which of the following pathological features is seen in Frontotemporal dementia?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • STN stimulation has been shown to improve tremor, bradykinesia, and rigidity in patients with Parkinson's disease.

Targeted Brain Structures in DBS

question: Involvement of the marked area of brain will result in which of the following disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The gait shown is a waddling gait, which is characteristic of proximal muscle weakness, particularly involving the pelvic (hip) girdle muscles, including the hip abductors and extensors.
  • Weakness of these muscles results in pelvic instability during walking, causing excessive side-to-side movement of the trunk and a broad-based, waddling appearance.
  • Patients commonly complain of difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a squatting position, getting up from a chair, or lifting themselves from the floor.
  • Waddling gait is seen in conditions affecting the proximal muscles, such as muscular dystrophies, inflammatory myopathies (e.g., polymyositis), metabolic myopathies, and advanced proximal muscle disorders.
  • Bilateral weakness of the hip abductors may also produce a positive Trendelenburg sign.

Distal limb muscles (Option A) are responsible for movements of the hands, feet, wrists, and ankles. Weakness of these muscles typically produces foot drop, high-stepping (steppage) gait, impaired grip, or difficulty with fine motor tasks, rather than the side-to-side waddling gait associated with proximal muscle weakness.

Cerebellar pathways (Option C) coordinate balance and voluntary movement. Cerebellar dysfunction produces an ataxic gait, characterized by a broad base, staggering, irregular steps, and difficulty with tandem walking. Although patients may appear unsteady, the gait lacks the pelvic swaying and trunk lurching that are typical of a waddling gait.

Dorsal columns (Option D) transmit proprioception, vibration sense, and fine touch. Lesions of the dorsal columns cause sensory ataxia, leading to an unsteady gait that worsens when visual input is removed, resulting in a positive Romberg sign. This differs from waddling gait, which results from muscle weakness rather than impaired proprioception.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 177-180

question: Which of the following clinical examination findings is associated with a lower motor neuron lesion?

correctAnswer: B. Motor nuclei of the lower cranial nerves
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient is presenting with the classic features of true bulbar palsy. This syndrome results from a lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion affecting the motor nuclei of the lower cranial nerves (CN IX, X, XI, and XII) located within the medulla oblongata.

  • Severe dysphagia → CN IX, X involvement
  • Nasal regurgitation → palatal weakness (CN IX, X)
  • Hoarse, breathy voice → laryngeal muscle paralysis (CN X)
  • Wasted, deeply furrowed tongue with fasciculations → LMN lesion of CN XII
  • Absent gag reflex → CN IX and X dysfunction

These findings indicate lower motor neuron damage to the cranial nerve nuclei, not corticobulbar tracts.

Key clinical features distinguishing it from its UMN counterpart include:

  • Tongue Appearance: Because it is an LMN lesion of the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), the tongue exhibits profound wasting (atrophy) and prominent fasciculations.
  • Reflexes: The gag and palatal reflexes are typically absent due to the disruption of the efferent motor arc.
  • Speech: The voice is characteristically breathy and nasal due to flaccid paralysis of the vocal cords and palate.

Bilateral corticobulbar tracts (Option A): Lesions here cause pseudobulbar palsy, an upper motor neuron disorder characterised by a spastic, unwasted tongue, a brisk gag reflex, an exaggerated jaw jerk, and emotional lability.

Anterior horn cells of the cervical spinal cord (Option C): Degeneration here would cause flaccid weakness and wasting in the upper limbs.

Upper motor neurons of the primary motor cortex (Option D): Unilateral lesions here rarely cause severe, lasting bulbar symptoms due to the bilateral cortical innervation of most lower cranial nerve nuclei (except the lower face and part of the tongue).



Reference:
  • https://litfl.com/bulbar-and-pseudobulbar-palsy/
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/medgen/898626

question: A 65-year-old patient presents with severe dysphagia, nasal regurgitation of liquids, and a hoarse, breathy voice. Examination reveals a wasted, deeply furrowed tongue that exhibits spontaneous fine twitches. The gag reflex is absent. This specific clinical syndrome is caused by a pathological lesion affecting which of the following structures?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of isolated spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses, combined with pseudobulbar signs (spastic dysarthria and dysphonia), is the hallmark of Primary Lateral Sclerosis (PLS).
  • It is a rare, idiopathic neurodegenerative disorder that selectively and exclusively targets the upper motor neurons (both the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts).

Degeneration of the corticobulbar tracts leads to:

  • Spastic dysarthria
  • Dysphonia
  • Dysphagia
  • Emotional lability
  • Brisk jaw jerk and gag reflex.

Because the anterior horn cells (lower motor neurons) are entirely spared, patients do not develop profound muscle wasting or fasciculations. Consequently, EMG shows no evidence of denervation, distinguishing it clearly from ALS.

Spinal muscular atrophy (Option A) is a genetically inherited disease that exclusively affects lower motor neurons, presenting with flaccid weakness, hypotonia, and areflexia.

Progressive muscular atrophy (Option B) is a sporadic motor neuron disease variant that, like SMA, is restricted purely to lower motor neuron degeneration and lacks any upper motor neuron signs.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Option D) is characterised by the simultaneous degeneration of both upper and lower motor neurons. EMG in ALS would show widespread active denervation and fasciculation potentials.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3519, 3525.
question: A 55-year-old woman presents with progressive limb stiffness, slurred speech, and a hoarse voice. Examination shows marked spasticity, hyperreflexia, a brisk jaw jerk, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Electromyography (EMG) reveals absolutely no evidence of muscle denervation. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Anterior horn cells and corticospinal tracts
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) is the most common form of progressive motor neuron disease. Pathologically, it is defined by the selective and simultaneous degeneration of two specific populations of motor neurons, while characteristically sparing sensory and autonomic pathways.

The features include:

  • Lower Motor Neuron Degeneration: There is a progressive loss of the anterior horn cells in the spinal cord and the motor nuclei of the lower cranial nerves in the brainstem. This results in the amyotrophic clinical signs: flaccid weakness, profound muscle atrophy, and fasciculations.
  • Upper Motor Neuron Degeneration: There is a loss of Betz cells in the motor cortex, leading to the demyelination and gliosis of the corticospinal tracts in the lateral funiculus. This results in the lateral sclerosis clinical signs: spasticity, hyperreflexia, and extensor plantar responses.

Anterior horn cells and spinothalamic tracts (Option A) are typically preserved in ALS; their involvement would suggest a condition like syringomyelia.

Dorsal root ganglia and corticospinal tracts (Option B) remain intact in ALS.

Substantia nigra and extrapyramidal tracts (Option D): Degeneration of the dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra is the defining pathology of Parkinson's disease.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3519, 3520.

options.text: Anterior horn cells and spinothalamic tracts
Dorsal root ganglia and corticospinal tracts
Anterior horn cells and corticospinal tracts

question: Which of the following neural structures are primarily involved in the pathophysiology of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical scenario describes Familial Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (FALS). While the majority of ALS cases are sporadic, approximately 10% are familial, usually following an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.

  • Progressive weakness and wasting of intrinsic hand muscles → LMN signs
  • Combination of upper and lower motor neuron signs → hallmark of ALS
  • Family history of similar disease in 40s → familial ALS
  • Adult onset (~40s)

Key genetic features of FALS include:

  • SOD1 Mutation: Mutations in the SOD1 gene (encoding the enzyme Copper-Zinc Superoxide Dismutase) were the first to be identified and account for approximately 20% of familial cases. This enzyme normally protects cells from oxidative stress by breaking down toxic superoxide radicals.
  • C9orf72: A hexanucleotide repeat expansion in this gene is now recognised as the most common genetic cause of both FALS and Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD).
  • TDP43: An RNA-binding protein encoded by TAR DNA-binding protein.

SMN1 (Option B): Mutations or deletions in the Survival Motor Neuron 1 gene cause Spinal Muscular Atrophy, a pure lower motor neuron disease affecting children and young adults.

PMP22 (Option C): Duplication of this gene is the cause of Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease Type 1A, a hereditary sensorimotor neuropathy.

Dystrophin (Option D): Mutations in this gene cause Duchenne or Becker Muscular Dystrophy, which are primary muscle disorders.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3521.
question: A 42-year-old man presents with progressive weakness and wasting of the intrinsic muscles of his hands. Examination reveals a combination of upper and lower motor neuron signs. explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Ophthalmoplegia is characteristically absent in ALS. Ocular motility is preserved even in the late stages of the disease because the motor neurons controlling eye movements (nuclei of CN III, IV, and VI) are resistant to the degenerative process.

Characteristic Clinical Features of ALS:

  • Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) Signs:
    • Weakness and Atrophy (Option A ruled out)
    • Fasciculations
    • Split-hand syndrome: Disproportionate wasting of the thenar and first dorsal interosseous muscles compared to the hypothenar muscles.
    • Head Drop: Weakness of cervical extensor muscles. (Option D ruled out)
  • Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) Signs:
    • Spasticity
    • Hyperreflexia
  • Bulbar/Corticobulbar Signs:
    • Dysarthria and Dysphagia
    • Pathological laughing or crying.
  • Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD) is seen predominantly in Familial ALS, characterised by early behavioural abnormalities with prominent behavioural features indicative of frontal lobe dysfunction. (Option C ruled out)

question: A 55-year-old male is referred for evaluation of progressive limb weakness. Which of the following clinical presentations would make a diagnosis of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis highly unlikely?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The diagnosis of ALS is fundamentally clinical, relying on the history and physical examination to demonstrate progressive motor deficits. Evidence of Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) and Lower Motor Neuron (LMN) degeneration in multiple body regions (bulbar, cervical, thoracic, lumbosacral) and the progression of symptoms over time, with the absence of other probable causes, is diagnostic of ALS.

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) Diagnosis

  1. Primary method:
    • ALS is a clinical diagnosis, based on progressive signs of both upper and lower motor neuron involvement in multiple regions, and exclusion of mimics.
    • Diagnostic frameworks: El Escorial / Awaji criteria (rely on clinical and EMG findings).
  2. Supporting tests:
    • Electromyography (EMG) → confirms LMN degeneration
    • MRI / labs → rule out mimics
    • Genetic testing → useful in familial cases, not required for sporadic ALS
    • CSF biomarkers/neurofilament light chains → under research; may support prognosis but not definitive

Genetic analyses (Option B) are useful for familial cases (10%), but since 90% of cases are sporadic, genetics cannot be the primary diagnostic tool for all patients.

Elevated neurofilament light chains (Option C): While a promising prognostic biomarker indicating axonal damage, it is not yet a standalone diagnostic test.

CSF biomarkers (Option D): CSF is typically normal in ALS; analysis is done to rule out other conditions.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3521.
question: A clinician suspects Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis in a patient with progressive weakness. The definitive diagnosis of ALS is primarily established based on:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Riluzole is the first-line disease-modifying drug in ALS and prolongs survival.

Mechanism of Action:

  • Inhibits glutamate release from presynaptic neurons
  • Blocks voltage-gated sodium channels
  • Reduces excitotoxic neuronal damage (key mechanism in ALS)

Another drug, Edaravone, has also been approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration based on a single 6-month study in a highly selected ALS population that demonstrated a modest reduction in the trajectory of worsening in ALS.

  • Free radical scavenger
  • Reduces oxidative stress-mediated neuronal injury
  • Protects motor neurons from degeneration

Baclofen (Option A): Treats spasticity (does not alter disease progression)

Pyridostigmine (Option C): Used in myasthenia gravis, not ALS

Memantine (Option D): NMDA antagonist, used in Alzheimer’s disease, not ALS



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3524.
question: Which of the following drugs can be used for the management of Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The child demonstrates Gowers' sign, in which he uses his hands to "climb up" his thighs in order to rise from the floor. This occurs due to proximal muscle weakness, particularly involving the hip and pelvic girdle muscles.

  • The most likely diagnosis is Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), an X-linked recessive disorder caused by mutations in the dystrophin gene on chromosome Xp21, resulting in the absence of functional dystrophin protein.
  • The disease typically presents between 2 and 5 years of age with delayed motor milestones, frequent falls, difficulty climbing stairs, waddling gait, toe walking, and progressive proximal muscle weakness.
  • Gowers' sign is one of its earliest and most characteristic clinical findings.
  • Other important features include calf pseudohypertrophy, markedly elevated serum creatine kinase (CK) levels, progressive cardiomyopathy, respiratory muscle weakness, and eventual loss of ambulation during early adolescence if untreated.
  • Genetic testing confirms the diagnosis, while muscle biopsy shows absent dystrophin expression on immunohistochemistry.

Becker muscular dystrophy (Option A) is also an X-linked dystrophinopathy, but it results from mutations that produce partially functional dystrophin. The onset is usually later in childhood or adolescence, progression is slower, and affected individuals remain ambulatory for a much longer period. Although Gowers' sign may be present, the early onset and severe progressive weakness in this child are more characteristic of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

Cerebral palsy (Option C) is a non-progressive disorder of movement and posture caused by injury to the developing brain. It commonly presents with spasticity, hyperreflexia, scissoring gait, and delayed motor development rather than progressive proximal muscle weakness. Gowers' sign is not a typical feature of cerebral palsy.

Myasthenia gravis (Option D) is an autoimmune disorder affecting the neuromuscular junction, characterized by fatigable muscle weakness that predominantly involves the ocular, bulbar, and proximal limb muscles. The weakness fluctuates and worsens with activity, while calf pseudohypertrophy and the characteristic progressive pattern seen in Duchenne muscular dystrophy are absent.



Reference:
  • Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3638
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK482346/
  • https://www.mda.org/disease/duchenne-muscular-dystrophy
question: A 7-year-old boy is brought to the outpatient clinic with progressive difficulty in running, climbing stairs, and getting up from the floor over the past 2 years. The child rises from the floor in the manner demonstrated in the attached video. The most likely diagnosis is:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical picture and video are consistent with Huntington disease, a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by chorea, psychiatric disturbances, and cognitive decline (dementia). It is caused by an expanded CAG trinucleotide repeat in the HTT gene (huntingtin gene) located on chromosome 4, leading to abnormal huntingtin protein accumulation and selective neuronal loss, especially in the caudate nucleus and putamen.

  • Huntington disease follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.
  • A key genetic feature is anticipation, where the disease manifests at an earlier age and often with increased severity in successive generations, particularly with paternal transmission due to expansion of CAG repeats during spermatogenesis.
  • Clinically, patients present with involuntary choreiform movements, behavioral changes such as irritability, depression, or psychosis, and progressive subcortical dementia.
  • MRI brain typically shows caudate nucleus atrophy with enlargement of the frontal horns of the lateral ventricles.

Autosomal recessive pattern (Option A) disorders require both alleles to be mutated and typically present in childhood or early adulthood with a higher likelihood of consanguinity. Examples include Wilson disease and phenylketonuria. Huntington disease does not follow this pattern and instead shows vertical transmission across generations.

X-linked recessive pattern (Option B) disorders predominantly affect males and are transmitted through carrier females, with no male-to-male transmission. Examples include Duchenne muscular dystrophy and hemophilia A. Huntington disease affects both males and females equally and shows vertical transmission, consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance.

Mitochondrial pattern (Option D) disorders are inherited exclusively from the mother due to mitochondrial DNA being maternally transmitted. They typically involve high-energy-demand tissues such as muscle and brain and show maternal inheritance patterns. Huntington disease is not maternally inherited and does not follow mitochondrial inheritance.



Reference:
  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3405
  • https://www.ninds.nih.gov/health-information/disorders/huntingtons-disease
  • https://www.movementdisorders.org/MDS/About/Movement-Disorder-Overviews/Chorea--Huntingtons-Disease.htm
question: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive involuntary jerky movements, personality changes, and difficulty concentrating over the past 2 years. A video demonstrates the characteristic involuntary movements affecting the face and limbs. The disorder shown is inherited in which of the following patterns?

correctAnswer: B. III, IV, V1, V2, and VI
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The combination of complete ophthalmoplegia, ptosis with fixed dilated pupil, facial pain, sensory loss over the forehead and cheek, and absent corneal reflex indicates involvement of multiple nerves in the cavernous sinus region (cavernous sinus syndrome).

Key findings and nerve involvement

  1. Complete ophthalmoplegia → paralysis of extraocular muscles
    • CN III (Oculomotor)
    • CN IV (Trochlear)
    • CN VI (Abducens)
  2. Fixed and dilated pupil + ptosis
    • CN III involvement
  3. Loss of sensation over the forehead and cheek
    • V1 (ophthalmic division of trigeminal) → forehead
    • V2 (maxillary division of trigeminal) → cheek
  4. Absent corneal reflex
    • Afferent limb → V1

Cavernous sinus contents:

  • Oculomotor nerve (III)
  • Trochlear nerve (IV)
  • Ophthalmic nerve(V1)
  • Maxillary nerve(V2)
  • Internal Carotid artery
  • Sympathetic plexus around the internal carotid artery
  • Abducens nerve (VI)

Key anatomical contents of the cavernous sinus include:

  • Lateral Wall: The oculomotor nerve (III), trochlear nerve (IV), and the ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) divisions of the trigeminal nerve traverse the lateral wall.
  • Central Portion: The abducens nerve (VI) runs freely through the centre of the sinus, adjacent to the internal carotid artery, making it particularly vulnerable to early compression or aneurysmal expansion.

[[figure-1]]



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3558.

III, IV, V2, V3, and VI

question: A 45-year-old patient with uncontrolled diabetes mellitus presents with an acute onset of right-sided facial pain, double vision, and drooping of the right eyelid. Examination reveals right-sided complete ophthalmoplegia, a fixed and dilated pupil, and loss of sensation over the right forehead and cheek. The corneal reflex is absent on the right. Which of the following combinations of cranial nerves is involved in this patient's pathological process?

correctAnswer: A. An extended segment of oligodendrocyte-derived myelin at its root entry zone
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient has secondary trigeminal neuralgia, which is more commonly associated with multiple sclerosis (MS) due to demyelination at the trigeminal nerve root entry zone. The proximal ~7 mm of the trigeminal nerve is covered by oligodendrocyte-derived central myelin, making it vulnerable to MS plaques.
  • Demyelination causes hyperexcitability and ephaptic transmission between large tactile fibres and adjacent pain fibres, so innocuous stimuli (e.g., washing the face, brushing teeth) trigger sudden, severe paroxysms of pain.

Selective autoimmune destruction of Schwann cells (Option B): Schwann cells are responsible for myelinating the peripheral nervous system. MS is strictly a disease of the central nervous system; Schwann cell-derived myelin is fundamentally spared.

Demyelination of the spinal tract (Option C): Trigeminal neuralgia in MS classically involves the root entry zone, not the spinal trigeminal tract in the cervical cord.

Microvascular compression (Option D): Compression of the nerve root by a blood vessel is the primary pathophysiological mechanism for classic trigeminal neuralgia in the general population.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3551-3552.

Selective autoimmune destruction of Schwann cells in the peripheral branches
Demyelination of the spinal tract of the fifth nerve in the upper cervical cord
Microvascular compression by the superior cerebellar artery at the pontine cistern

question: A 32-year-old woman with a known history of multiple sclerosis presents with severe, episodic, electric shock-like pain over her right cheek, which is triggered by applying makeup. Which of the following unique anatomical features of the trigeminal nerve is responsible for the condition seen in the woman?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Trigeminal neuralgia presents with brief, severe, electric shock–like facial pain triggered by light stimuli. The first-line medical treatment is a sodium channel–blocking anticonvulsant that stabilises hyperexcitable trigeminal neurons.

The pharmacological management of trigeminal neuralgia is as follows:

  • First-line Therapy: Carbamazepine is effective in ~50-75% of patients. It should be started as a single daily dose of 100 mg and increased gradually until substantial (>50%) pain relief is achieved. Most patients require a maintenance dose of 200 mg four times daily.
  • First-line Alternative: Oxcarbazepine is an alternative to carbamazepine that has less bone marrow toxicity and is probably equally efficacious.
  • Second-line Options: If these agents are not well tolerated or are ineffective, Phenytoin is another established option. (Option B ruled out)
  • Adjunctive Therapies: Other drugs such as Lamotrigine, Baclofen, or Topiramate are tried as adjuncts. Gabapentin may occasionally provide relief in refractory cases. (Options A and D ruled out)
  • Refractory Cases: If drug treatment fails, surgical interventions (e.g., microvascular decompression) are indicated.


Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3553.
question: Which of the following agents is the most appropriate first choice for the management of trigeminal neuralgia?

correctAnswer: D. 80% of patients have permanent deficits
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Approximately 80% of patients recover within a few weeks or months without significant residual deficits.
  • Bell’s palsy is an acute idiopathic LMN facial nerve (CN VII) paralysis that develops rapidly, often with retroauricular pain, and usually has a good prognosis, with most patients recovering completely.

Clinical Features of Bell's Palsy:

  • Risk factor: The incidence is increased in patients with diabetes mellitus and during pregnancy.
  • Onset: The onset is fairly abrupt, with maximal weakness typically being attained by 48 hours. (Option A ruled out)
  • Pain: Pain behind the ear frequently precedes the facial paralysis by a day or two. (Option C ruled out)
  • CSF Findings: In some cases, there is evidence of mild cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) lymphocytosis, reflecting an inflammatory process. (Option B ruled out)
  • Associated Symptoms: Unilateral loss of taste sensation and hyperacusis may be present.
  • Recurrence: Recurrences are reported in only ~7% of cases.


Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3554.

options.text: Maximal weakness is attained within 48 hours

question: Which of the following statements regarding the clinical presentation and course of Bell's palsy is incorrect?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Bell's palsy is an acute, unilateral, lower motor neuron paralysis of the facial nerve. Epidemiological evidence strongly suggests that the majority of cases are caused by the reactivation of Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1).
  • The virus lies dormant within the geniculate ganglion. Upon reactivation, it induces local inflammation, oedema, and subsequent ischaemic compression of the facial nerve within the narrow, bony Fallopian canal, leading to neuropraxia or axonotmesis.

Other causes of Bell’s palsy are:

  • Varicella zoster virus
  • SARS-CoV-2
  • HIV

Coxsackievirus (Option A) is known for causing hand, foot, and mouth disease or herpangina.

Borrelia burgdorferi (Option C): Lyme disease can cause a facial nerve palsy (often bilateral), which would typically present with a history of a tick bite or erythema migrans.

Human herpesvirus 6 (Option D): HHV-6 is the causative agent of Roseola infantum (exanthema subitum) in children.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3554.
question: Bell's palsy is most strongly linked to the reactivation of which of the following pathogens?

correctAnswer: B. Normal protective reflex unmasked by orbicularis oculi weakness.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical finding described is Bell's phenomenon. It is a completely normal, physiological defence mechanism designed to protect the cornea from exposure and trauma during blinking or sleep.

Key features of this phenomenon include:

  • When an individual attempts to close their eyes, the globes reflexively roll upwards and outwards.
  • In a healthy individual, this movement is hidden by the closed eyelids. However, in a lower motor neuron facial palsy (such as Bell's palsy), the orbicularis oculi muscle is paralysed, preventing complete eyelid closure. Consequently, the normal upward movement of the globe becomes visibly apparent to the examiner.

Confirms a concurrent lesion of the trochlear nerve (Option A): The trochlear nerve innervates the superior oblique muscle, which depresses and intorts the eye.

Indicates aberrant reinnervation following prior facial nerve trauma (Option C): Aberrant reinnervation typically results in synkinesis.

Pathognomonic sign of an upper motor neuron facial palsy (Option D): In UMN lesions, the upper face is largely spared due to bilateral cortical innervation.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3554.

options.text: Confirms a concurrent lesion of the trochlear nerve.
Normal protective reflex unmasked by orbicularis oculi weakness.
Indicates aberrant reinnervation following prior facial nerve trauma.
Pathognomonic sign of an upper motor neuron facial palsy.

question: A 50-year-old man presents with acute right-sided facial weakness. On attempting to forcefully close his eyes, his right eyelid remains partially open, revealing the cornea rotating superiorly beneath the upper lid. What is the clinical significance of this ocular movement?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The primary goals in the management of Bell's palsy are to hasten recovery and prevent corneal complications. Based on current clinical evidence and standard guidelines:

Stepwise Management of Bell's Palsy:

  • Eye Care:
    • Use of paper tape to depress the upper eyelid during sleep to prevent corneal drying. (Statement 3)
    • Frequent application of artificial tears during the day and lubricating ointment at night.
  • Physical Therapy:
    • Massage of the weakened muscles is a recommended symptomatic measure. (Statement 2 ruled out)
  • Pharmacotherapy:
    • Glucocorticoids: Prednisone (60-80 mg daily for the first 5 days, tapered over the next 5 days) is the mainstay of treatment. It modestly shortens the recovery period and improves long-term functional outcomes. (Statement 4 ruled out)
    • Antivirals: Acyclovir (400 mg five times daily) or Valacyclovir (1000 mg daily) are indicated only if there is evidence of Varicella Zoster virus infection (vesicles on the palate or external auditory canal). (Statement 1)
  • Surgical Management:
    • For patients with permanent paralysis, cosmetic surgical procedures may be considered to restore facial symmetry.


Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3555.
question:
Which of the following statements regarding the standard management of Bell's palsy are incorrect?

  1. Routine addition of acyclovir provides significant clinical benefit over corticosteroids alone.
  2. Symptomatic measures include massage of the weakened muscles.
  3. Paper tape should be used to keep the eyelid open during sleep to prevent infection.
  4. Glucocorticoids are administered to shorten recovery time and improve functional outcomes.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The image shows a right-sided lower motor neuron (LMN) facial nerve palsy, evidenced by:

  • Loss of forehead wrinkling on the right side (frontalis weakness)
  • Inability to close the right eye completely (orbicularis oculi weakness)
  • Flattening of the right nasolabial fold
  • Deviation of the angle of the mouth to the left (normal side) due to paralysis of the right facial muscles

The stylomastoid foramen is the site where the facial nerve exits the skull after giving off the greater petrosal nerve, nerve to stapedius, and chorda tympani.

  • Therefore, a lesion at this level causes isolated paralysis of the muscles of facial expression, while lacrimation, taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, salivation, and hearing remain intact.
  • This pattern of pure motor facial weakness without associated sensory or parasympathetic deficits localises the lesion to the stylomastoid foramen.

Facial motor nucleus in the pons (Option A): Produces an LMN facial palsy but is usually accompanied by other brainstem signs, such as abducens nerve palsy, contralateral hemiparesis, or sensory deficits.

Geniculate ganglion (Option C): Causes LMN facial palsy with loss of lacrimation, impaired taste over the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, hyperacusis, and may be associated with vesicular eruptions in Ramsay Hunt syndrome.

Internal acoustic meatus (Option D): Lesions at this level involve both the facial (CN VII) and vestibulocochlear (CN VIII) nerves, producing facial paralysis with sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, or vertigo.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3553-3555.

options.text: Facial motor nucleus in the pons

question: A 40-year-old man presents with the sudden onset of right-sided facial weakness, as shown in the image. On examination, there is an inability to close the right eye completely. There is no loss of taste, hyperacusis, or decreased lacrimation. The lesion is most likely located at which of the following sites?

correctAnswer: B. Patient X: Left UMN palsy; Patient Y: Left LMN palsy
explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: B) Patient X: Left UMN palsy; Patient Y: Left LMN palsy

Explanation:

Patient X:

  • Weakness involves only the lower face with forehead sparing.
  • Forehead muscles receive bilateral cortical innervation, so they are preserved in UMN lesions.
  • Right lower facial weakness indicates a contralateral corticobulbar lesion → Left UMN facial palsy.

Patient Y:

  • Entire left side of face is affected, including inability to wrinkle forehead and close eye.
  • This indicates involvement of the facial nerve itself → Left LMN facial palsy.
Feature UMN Facial Palsy LMN Facial Palsy
Facial involvement Lower face only Entire half of face
Forehead Spared Involved
Eye closure Preserved Impaired
Side affected Contralateral Ipsilateral
Common cause Stroke Bell’s palsy


Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3553-3555.

question:
Identify the correct diagnosis for the following two clinical scenarios:

Patient X: A 60-year-old hypertensive male with a sudden onset of slurred speech and drooping of the right corner of the mouth. He can raise both eyebrows symmetrically.

Patient Y: A 25-year-old female with sudden inability to close her left eye or smile on the left side. She cannot wrinkle her forehead on the left.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Simultaneous, bilateral, concurrent lower motor neuron (LMN) facial nerve paralysis is a rare presentation that strongly points toward an underlying systemic condition. The facial nerves are particularly susceptible to systemic demyelination, infection, or infiltration. Among the systemic conditions known to cause concurrent bilateral facial palsy, Guillain-Barré syndrome is the most common aetiology.

Causes of bilateral concurrent facial nerve palsy include:

  • Guillain-Barré syndrome (most common)
  • Lyme disease (infection with Borrelia burgdorferi)
  • Sarcoidosis
  • Cerebral lymphoma
  • Leukaemic infiltration
  • Infectious mononucleosis
  • Rabies
  • Moebius syndrome (congenital)

Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome (Option B) is characterised by alternating recurrent facial nerve palsy, recurrent facial or labial oedema, and a fissured tongue. It typically presents with sequential alternating episodes.

Cholesteatoma (Option C): Tumours that invade the temporal bone, such as cholesteatomas, carotid body tumours, or dermoids, produce a facial palsy by local compression. The onset is typically insidious, progressive, and strictly unilateral.

Ramsay Hunt syndrome (Option D) is caused by reactivation of the herpes zoster virus in the geniculate ganglion. It presents as a severe unilateral facial palsy accompanied by a characteristic vesicular eruption in the external auditory canal, pharynx, or other cranial integuments.



Reference:
  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3554, 3555.
  • Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Volume 2, Page 1391.
question: A 28-year-old patient presents to the emergency department with an acute onset of simultaneous weakness on both sides of the face, characterised by an inability to close both eyes and absent forehead wrinkles. Which of the following is the most common cause of this specific concurrent presentation?

correctAnswer: D. Visible Bell's phenomenon on the right side
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The presence of lower facial weakness with the sparing of the upper face confirms an Upper Motor Neuron or supranuclear facial palsy. UMN lesions spare the upper face because the portion of the facial nucleus supplying the frontalis and orbicularis oculi muscles receives bilateral corticobulbar innervation.
  • Bell's phenomenon, the upward and outward rolling of the eyeball during attempted eye closure, is a normal physiological reflex. It only becomes clinically visible when a patient has lagophthalmos, which is classic for a Lower Motor Neuron palsy. Because voluntary eye closure is intact in a UMN lesion, a clinically visible Bell's phenomenon is absent and unexpected.

Difference between UMN & LMN Facial Paralysis:

Feature

Supranuclear Lesion (UMN)

Lower Motor Neuron

Lesion Level

Corticobulbar tracts

Facial nerve (CN VII) distal to the nucleus

Side Affected

Contralateral

Ipsilateral

Facial Muscle Involved

Lower face only

Entire hemiface (Upper & Lower)

Forehead Wrinkling

Spared (Bilateral cortical innervation)

Involved (Cannot wrinkle forehead)

Eye Closure

Normal closure (Corneal reflex intact)

Impaired (Lagophthalmos present)

Nasolabial Fold

Flattened on the contralateral side

Flattened on the ipsilateral side

Emotional Response

Emotional incontinence (Pseudobulbar affect)

Absent / Lost

Associated Conditions

Hemiparesis, Aphasia, Dysarthria

Loss of taste, Hyperacusis, Vesicles (Ramsay Hunt)

Intact taste sensation on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue (Option A): Taste fibres travel via the chorda tympani, joining the facial nerve distally; a central UMN lesion will not impair these peripheral special sensory pathways.

Involuntary, uncontrollable laughing or crying (Option B): This represents emotional incontinence (pseudobulbar affect). UMN lesions disrupt the cortico-ponto-cerebellar modulatory pathways, leading to this expected finding of emotional dysmetria, disinhibition, or paradoxical excessive emotional output.

Normal corneal reflex (Option C): The ocular function is preserved in a UMN lesion due to the bilateral cortical representation of the upper facial muscles.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3553-3555.
