Visible Bell's phenomenon on the right side

question: A 62-year-old hypertensive male presents with an acute onset of right-sided facial weakness. On examination, the patient can symmetrically wrinkle his forehead and tightly close both eyes. Which of the following findings is least expected in this patient?

correctAnswer: C. Anomalous regeneration of salivary parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal gland
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • History of peripheral facial nerve palsy, occurring months later during recovery & tearing while eating (gustatory lacrimation) are suggestive of “Crocodile tears syndrome” (Bogorad syndrome).

Pathophysiology of Facial Synkinesis

After severe Lower Motor Neuron facial nerve injury, recovery may be incomplete due to axonal misdirection during regeneration. These troublesome phenomena result from the aberrant connection of regenerating fibres to incorrect target organs or muscle groups.

  • Crocodile Tears (Bogorad syndrome): Parasympathetic salivary fibres misdirect and reinnervate the lacrimal gland. Eating, which normally triggers salivation, now triggers involuntary tearing. (Option C)
  • Synkinesis: Motor fibres misdirect; e.g., fibres originally destined for the orbicularis oculi (eye) reinnervate the orbicularis oris (mouth). This causes involuntary mouth retraction when the patient closes their eyes. (Option B ruled out)
  • Hemifacial Spasm: Characterised by involuntary, diffuse contraction of facial muscles initiated by facial movements. This may manifest as narrowing of the palpebral fissure and deepening of the nasolabial fold. (Option D ruled out)
  • Jaw-winking: A synkinesia where jaw opening causes involuntary closure of the eyelids on the side of the palsy.

Incomplete remyelination of the motor branches of the facial nerve (Option A): Remyelination affects motor conduction, leading to residual weakness or mild synkinesis. It does not cause misdirection of autonomic secretomotor fibres, which are required for gustatory lacrimation.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3554.

options.text: Incomplete remyelination of the motor branches of the facial nerve
Fibres originally connected with orbicularis oculi, innervating orbicularis oris
Anomalous regeneration of salivary parasympathetic fibres to the lacrimal gland
Continuous diffuse contraction of the facial muscles

question: A 38-year-old female presents for follow-up 10 months after a severe episode of right-sided peripheral facial palsy. She complains of anomalous unilateral tearing from her right eye exclusively while eating. What is the precise pathophysiological mechanism underlying this specific phenomenon?

correctAnswer: C. Neurovascular compression at the pons is the most common aetiology
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hemifacial spasm is the involuntary contractions of muscles supplied by the facial nerve (CN VII) on one side of the face. It is caused most commonly by vascular compression of the facial nerve at its root exit zone in the pons.

Hemifacial Spasm:

  • Characterised by painless (Options A ruled out), irregular, involuntary unilateral (Options D ruled out) facial contractions.
  • Pathophysiology: Most commonly caused by neurovascular compression of the facial nerve at the root exit zone in the pons.
  • Other Etiologies: Compression by tumours (e.g., schwannoma), Multiple Sclerosis, or post-paralytic sequelae (post-Bell's palsy).
  • Management:
    • First-line: Local injections of botulinum toxin (effective for 3-4 months). (Option B ruled out)
    • Refractory: Surgical microvascular decompression.
    • Medical: Carbamazepine, gabapentin, or baclofen.


Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3555.

options.text: First-line management is oral carbamazepine therapy.
Neurovascular compression at the pons is the most common aetiology

question: Which of the following is true regarding hemifacial spasm?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome is a rare, classic triad consisting of:

  1. Recurrent facial nerve palsy
  2. Orofacial oedema (labial)
  3. Fissured tongue (lingua plicata)

[[figure-1]]

Heerfordt syndrome (Option A) is a manifestation of sarcoidosis consisting of the triad of uveitis, parotid gland enlargement, and facial nerve palsy.

Ramsay Hunt syndrome (Option B) caused by Varicella-zoster virus reactivation in the geniculate ganglion, manifesting as unilateral facial palsy, otalgia, and vesicular eruptions in the ear.

Moebius syndrome (Option D) is a congenital condition characterised by bilateral facial nerve palsy and congenital abducens nerve (CN VI) palsy, leading to an expressionless face and inability to move eyes laterally.



Reference:
  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3555.
  • Scott-Brown's Otorhinolaryngology and Head and Neck Surgery, 8th Edition, Volume 2, Pages 1391, 1392.
question: A 25-year-old patient presents with a triad of recurring facial palsy, persistent lip oedema, and a fissured tongue. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic term for this constellation of symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The diagnosis is Glossopharyngeal Neuralgia (CN IX Neuralgia). The condition is characterised by:

  • Paroxysmal Pain: Sudden, severe, lancinating, and electric-shock-like quality.
  • Distribution: Ipsilateral tonsillar fossa, posterior pharynx, base of the tongue, and the deep ear canal.
  • Triggers: Swallowing, chewing, yawning, talking, or clearing the throat.
  • Autonomic Involvement: Because the glossopharyngeal nerve provides the afferent limb for the carotid sinus reflex, excessive stimulation during a severe pain paroxysm can trigger a paradoxical vagal response. This leads to transient bradycardia, hypotension, or syncope.

Ipsilateral facial anhidrosis (Option A) is a key feature of Horner syndrome, reflecting damage to the sympathetic chain, which is anatomically and functionally distinct from the glossopharyngeal nerve.

Bilateral ptosis and miosis (Option C): Bilateral ptosis suggests a neuromuscular junction disorder like Myasthenia gravis. Miosis combined with ptosis (Horner syndrome) would be unilateral, not bilateral, and is unrelated to the pharyngeal distribution of CN IX.

Ipsilateral hyperacusis (Option D) is caused by paralysis of the stapedius muscle. It is a localising sign of a peripheral facial nerve (CN VII) lesion occurring proximal to the nerve's branch to the stapedius.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3555, 3556.
question: A 68-year-old patient presents with recurring episodes of severe, stabbing, lancinating pain in the tonsillar fossa and posterior pharynx, triggered by swallowing. During a particularly intense paroxysm of pain, which of the following autonomic manifestations is most likely to occur?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The manoeuvre shown is Kernig's sign, a classic meningeal irritation sign. It is considered positive when passive extension of the knee with the hip flexed at 90° produces pain or resistance, due to stretching of the inflamed meninges and spinal nerve roots. A positive Kernig's sign, in the presence of fever, severe headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness, strongly suggests acute bacterial meningitis.

  • Acute bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency characterized by inflammation of the meninges, most commonly caused by organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis in adults.
  • Patients typically present with the classical triad of fever, neck stiffness, and altered mental status, although all three may not always be present.
  • Prompt diagnosis with lumbar puncture (when not contraindicated) and immediate initiation of empirical intravenous antibiotics are essential to reduce morbidity and mortality.

Guillain-Barré syndrome (Option A) is an acute immune-mediated demyelinating polyneuropathy that presents with progressive, symmetrical ascending weakness, areflexia, and variable sensory symptoms, often following a preceding infection. Meningeal signs such as Kernig's sign are absent, making this diagnosis unlikely.

Transverse myelitis (Option C) is an inflammatory disorder involving the spinal cord that presents with bilateral motor weakness, sensory deficits, and autonomic dysfunction, including bowel and bladder involvement below the level of the lesion. Although neck or back pain may occur, Kernig's sign is not a feature, as the meninges are not primarily inflamed.

Cauda equina syndrome (Option D) results from compression of the lumbosacral nerve roots, commonly due to a large lumbar disc prolapse or spinal tumor. It presents with severe low back pain, saddle anesthesia, bowel and bladder dysfunction, and lower limb weakness. Kernig's sign is not associated with cauda equina syndrome, as it is a sign of meningeal irritation rather than nerve root compression.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1119
question: A 26-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with fever, intense headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness for the past 48 hours. During physical examination, the manoeuvre demonstrated in the attached video elicits pain and resistance on passive extension of the knee while the hip is flexed to 90°. This finding is most suggestive of which of the following conditions?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The MRI shows dilated perivascular (Virchow–Robin) spaces filled with gelatinous material—classically called “soap-bubble lesions”, seen in Cryptococcal meningitis, especially in AIDS patients with very low CD4 counts.
  • CSF findings (↑ opening pressure, lymphocytic pleocytosis, ↓ sugar, mildly ↑ protein) strongly support cryptococcal infection.

Tuberculous meningitis (Option A): Typically presents with a subacute onset, and CSF shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose, and high protein; encapsulated yeast is not seen.


Cytomegalovirus encephalitis (Option C): MRI brain will show periventricular and subependymal hyperintensities with contrast enhancement. Lots of time it will co-exist with CMV retinitis showing pizza pie retinopathy.


Toxoplasmosis (Option D): Usually presents with multiple ring-enhancing lesions on MRI, but does not involve encapsulated yeast or fungal elements in the CSF.

Staining

Imaging

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

India ink staining of Cryptococcus neoformans

[[figure-3]]



Gram staining of the CSF reveals clusters of thin-walled, encapsulated yeast forms of various sizes with narrow-based budding consistent with Cryptococcus.

[[figure-4]]

MRI showing “Soap bubble appearance” of C.Neoformans

David Sutton Textbook of Radiology and Imaging, 8th Edition, Page 1952.
question: A 32 year old HIV-positive truck driver presents with fever, headache and drowsiness. Lumbar puncture is performed, and CSF shows elevated opening pressure with 20 lymphocytes /cu.mm with low sugar and protein of 60 mg/dl. MRI of the brain is shown below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical triad of rapidly progressive dementia, myoclonus (intermittent, irregular jerky movements), and characteristic electroencephalogram (EEG) findings revealing the presence of generalised periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWC), which typically manifest as triphasic waves occurring synchronously at a frequency of 1 to 2 Hz, strongly points to sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD).

CJD is a fatal, transmissible spongiform encephalopathy caused by the accumulation of misfolded infectious prion proteins (PrPSc) in the brain.

  • Sporadic CJD - most common (~85%)
  • Familial CJD - PRNP gene mutation

Pathology

  • Spongiform degeneration of brain tissue
  • Neuronal loss and gliosis
  • No inflammation

[[figure-1]]

Spongiform degeneration

Clinical Features

  • Rapidly progressive dementia
  • Myoclonus (jerky movements)
  • Ataxia and visual disturbances
  • Behavioral changes
  • Progresses to akinetic mutism

Investigations

  • EEG: Periodic sharp wave complexes
  • MRI: Cortical ribboning and basal ganglia hyperintensity (DWI/FLAIR)
  • CSF: Increased 14-3-3 protein, RT-QuIC positive

[[figure-2]]

Cortical ribboning

Prognosis / Treatment

  • No curative treatment
  • Supportive care only
  • Fatal within ~1 year in most cases.

Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (Option A) presents with progressive dementia and myoclonus with periodic EEG complexes (Radermecker complexes). It almost exclusively affects children and adolescents.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (Option B), caused by the reactivation of the JC virus in severely immunocompromised individuals, causes progressive focal neurologic deficits, behavioural changes, and cognitive decline.

Neurosyphilis (Option D): Late-stage central nervous system infection by Treponema pallidum can manifest as general paresis, leading to progressive dementia, personality changes, and tremors.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3531, 3532.
question: A 65-year-old male presents with a gradually progressive cognitive decline over recent months and episodic, irregular jerky movements, with an EEG finding shown below. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In viral central nervous system infections, including Herpes simplex virus (HSV) encephalitis, the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) glucose level remains normal. Therefore, profoundly decreased glucose is an unexpected finding.

In Herpes Simplex Encephalitis, typical CSF findings include:

  • Mild-moderate lymphocytic pleocytosis (Option B ruled out)
  • Elevated protein (Option A ruled out)
  • Elevated RBC count due to hemorrhagic necrosis of the temporal lobes (Option C ruled out)
  • Normal glucose

A markedly low CSF glucose is the classic hallmark of acute pyogenic bacterial meningitis or tuberculous meningitis.

question: Which of the following findings would you not expect to see in a patient's CSF analysis with Herpes simplex virus encephalitis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of acute fever, confusion, and focal neurological signs (olfactory hallucinations) is highly characteristic of acute viral encephalitis caused by Herpes simplex virus (HSV) type 1. HSV has a predilection for the medial temporal lobes and inferior frontal lobes, where MRI typically shows hyperintensities due to hemorrhagic necrosis.

Clinical Features of HSV Encephalitis:

  • Focal Seizures: Often temporal lobe seizures, which may present with olfactory or gustatory auras (e.g., smelling burning rubber).
  • Altered Sensorium: Rapid onset of confusion, delirium, or lethargy.
  • Focal Neurological Deficits: Expressive aphasia (if the dominant hemisphere is involved) or hemiparesis.
  • Behavioural Changes: Personality alterations, hyperorality, profound memory loss, or bizarre psychiatric behaviour.

HSV-1 has a classic, strong tropism for the temporal lobes, which is the hallmark location for hemorrhagic and necrotising inflammation in this disease. MRI is the neuroimaging modality of choice and typically demonstrates oedema, haemorrhage, and hyperintensity primarily in this region.

[[figure-1]]

Bilateral cerebellar hemispheres (Option A): Lesions in this area are characteristic of acute cerebellar ataxia, which can be a post-viral autoimmune phenomenon following Varicella-zoster virus infection in children.

Basal ganglia and thalami (Option C): Bilateral involvement of the deep grey matter structures, such as the basal ganglia and thalami, is the classic neuroimaging hallmark of flavivirus infections, most notably Japanese encephalitis virus and West Nile virus.

Parieto-occipital cortex (Option D): Lesions predominantly affecting the posterior white matter are characteristic of Posterior Reversible Encephalopathy Syndrome (PRES) or Progressive Multifocal Leukoencephalopathy (PML) caused by the JC virus.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1499.
question: A 42-year-old male is brought to the emergency department with a 2-day history of high fever, confusion, and new-onset focal seizures preceded by the smell of burning rubber. Cerebrospinal fluid polymerase chain reaction is positive for a double-stranded DNA virus. MRI of the brain is most likely to reveal abnormal hyperintensities in which of the following areas?

correctAnswer: B. Lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose, markedly elevated protein
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of a 4-week history of fever, night sweats, cranial nerve palsy (double vision), and neuroimaging showing basal cistern enhancement with hydrocephalus is highly characteristic of subacute to chronic meningitis caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
  • Examination of cerebrospinal fluid reveals a high leukocyte count (up to 1000/μL), usually with a predominance of lymphocytes but sometimes with a predominance of neutrophils in the early stage; a protein content of 1-8 g/L (100-800 mg/dL); and a low glucose concentration. This classic lymphocytic, hypoglycorrhachic, and hyperproteinorrhachic profile confirms the diagnosis.

question: A 45-year-old male with a history of untreated HIV infection presents with a 4-week history of progressively worsening headache, low-grade fever, night sweats, and recent-onset double vision. MRI of the brain reveals hydrocephalus and abnormal enhancements of the basal cisterns. Which of the following CSF profiles is most consistent with this patient's likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

When acute bacterial meningitis is suspected, empirical therapy must be started immediately before culture results are available. The treatment should cover the most common pathogens:

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae
  • Neisseria meningitidis
  • Sometimes Haemophilus influenzae

Empirical antibiotic therapy for suspected meningococcal disease consists of a third-generation cephalosporin such as intravenous ceftriaxone (75-100 mg/kg per day) or cefotaxime. This is required to cover various other potentially penicillin-resistant bacteria.

  • Intravenous vancomycin is also recommended in combination with the cephalosporin for the empiric management of sepsis and suspected bacterial meningitis. The conventional duration for treating both meningococcal meningitis and septicemia is 7 days.
  • Once the organism is confirmed as Neisseria meningitidis, therapy can be de-escalated to penicillin G or ceftriaxone alone.

Intravenous Penicillin G (Option A): Reduced meningococcal sensitivity to penicillin has been increasingly reported. Therefore, the use of penicillin is only appropriate as definitive therapy once specific information on antimicrobial resistance patterns is available.

Oral Ciprofloxacin (Option C) is utilised for the eradication of nasopharyngeal carriage in close contacts.

Intravenous Cefotetan (Option D): Cefotetan is a second-generation cephamycin with primarily anti-anaerobic activity. It has poor cerebrospinal fluid penetration and is not indicated for the treatment of bacterial meningitis.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1249.
question: Which of the following is the most appropriate empirical treatment for a suspected case of meningococcal meningitis?

correctAnswer: B. Oral ciprofloxacin is the preferred agent for chemoprophylaxis in this patient.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's clinical presentation of fever, meningeal signs, and a characteristic petechial rash following exposure at a crowded gathering is highly suggestive of meningococcal meningitis caused by Neisseria meningitidis.
  • For chemoprophylaxis to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage in pregnant women, a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone is the preferred and safest agent.
  • Oral ciprofloxacin (a fluoroquinolone) is generally contraindicated in pregnancy due to potential risks to fetal cartilage development, making this statement false.

Meningococcal Meningitis

Causative organism: Neisseria meningitidis, an aerobic Gram-negative diplococcus (Option D ruled out).

  • Appears as kidney-shaped diplococci on Gram stain.
  • Often found intracellularly within neutrophils.

Transmission

  • Spread through respiratory droplets.
  • Common in crowded environments (hostels, schools, military barracks).

Risk factors:

  • Complement deficiency:
    • Terminal complement components (C5-C9) form the membrane attack complex (MAC).
    • Deficiency of C5-C9 increases susceptibility to Neisseria infections (Option A ruled out)
  • Asplenia

Clinical features

  • High fever
  • Severe headache
  • Neck stiffness
  • Altered mental status
  • Petechial or purpuric rash due to meningococcemia.

Complications

  • Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome
  • Septic shock
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)

Diagnosis

  • CSF examination showing neutrophilic pleocytosis.
  • Gram stain showing Gram-negative diplococci.
  • Blood and CSF cultures: With appropriate antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone or penicillin), CSF cultures often become sterile within 24 hours (Option C ruled out).

Management:

  • Treatment: Third-generation cephalosporins (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime) are first-line therapy.
  • Chemoprophylaxis
    • Given to close contacts of the patient.
    • Drugs include:
      • Rifampicin
      • Ciprofloxacin
      • Ceftriaxone
  • Meningococcal vaccines (MenACWY, MenB) help prevent outbreaks.


Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 1248, 1249.

question: A 26-year-old pregnant woman in her second trimester presents to the emergency department with a 2-day history of high-grade fever, severe headache, and vomiting. She recently attended a crowded indoor school gathering. On examination, she exhibits marked neck stiffness and a rapidly spreading petechial rash over her trunk and lower extremities. Which of the following statements is false regarding the disease she is most likely suffering from?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The most common pathogens implicated in healthcare-associated meningitis related to neurosurgical hardware are skin commensals.

Because these devices involve percutaneous entry and the presence of a foreign body, they are highly susceptible to colonisation by skin flora. Staphylococcus aureus and Coagulase-negative staphylococci (e.g., Staphylococcus epidermidis) are the predominant causative agents for long-term indwelling CNS device infections, such as Ommaya reservoirs and ventriculoperitoneal shunts.

  • These bacteria are skin commensals.
  • They easily adhere to prosthetic material.
  • They form biofilms on medical devices, making them the commonest cause of shunt/device infections.

Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option A) is the most common cause of community-acquired meningitis.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Option C) is a known cause of healthcare-associated meningitis, particularly following major neurosurgical procedures or trauma, but it is not the most common pathogen specifically isolated from indwelling reservoir devices.

Group B streptococci (Option D) are primarily associated with meningitis in neonates and specific immunocompromised adult populations (such as those with diabetes or malignancy).



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 583, 1119.
question: Which of the following is the most frequently identified pathogen responsible for meningitis following the implantation of an indwelling central nervous system device?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The diagnosis is acute bacterial meningitis, characterised by the classic triad of fever, neck rigidity, and headache.

In adults, Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most frequently identified pathogen.

The following are the most common causative organisms for community-acquired bacterial meningitis:

  • Streptococcus pneumoniae (~50%): The leading cause of bacterial meningitis in adults > 20 years.
  • Neisseria meningitidis (~25%): Often associated with epidemics of meningitis occurring every 8-12 years; frequent in adolescents and young adults. (Option B ruled out)
  • Group B streptococci (~15%)
  • Listeria monocytogenes (~10%): Common in neonates, elderly patients, and immunocompromised individuals. (Option D ruled out)
  • Haemophilus influenzae type b (<10%): Following widespread vaccination, this organism now accounts for a minor proportion of cases in most clinical series.

Staphylococcus aureus (Option A): This organism is rarely a cause of community-acquired meningitis; it is primarily associated with neurosurgical procedures, trauma, or hematogenous spread from endocarditis, otitis, mastoiditis, and sinusitis.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 1118, 1119.
question: A 30-year-old previously healthy male presents with the acute triad of high-grade fever, severe headache, and neck stiffness. Examination reveals positive Kernig’s and Brudzinski’s signs. Which of the following is the most common cause of community-acquired bacterial meningitis?

correctAnswer: B. Peripheral smear followed by IV Artensunate
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient is having high grade fever with evidence of brain parenchymal involvement (bilateral Babinski and brisk DTR).
  • Evidence of hemolysis is given in form on elevated LDH and low Hb.
  • HRP-2 card tesrt and peripheral smear must be done and empirical Artesunate can be started in this case pending investigations.
  • Presence of banana shaped gametocytes in peripheral smear with multiple ring stage will confirm the diagnosis of falciparum malaria.
  • The infection makes the RBC sticky causing microinfarctions in brain parenchyma that will explain the development of altered sensorium.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1763, 1768.

question: A 30-year-old man from the village is admitted with high-grade fever and altered sensorium. On examination, bilateral Babinski and exaggerated ankle jerks were noted. Nuchal rigidity is absent. Workup shows Hb:7 gm%, TLC: 10K/cu.mm, platelet count: 1.5 Lac/cu.mm, elevated LDH, LFT is normal, and Serum creatinine is 1.5mg/dl. What is the best course of action for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • MRI shows multiple sub-cortical hyperintense lesions in frontal, parietal and occipital lobes.
  • The patient’s symptoms, including progressive weakness in her right arm, blurred vision along with a low CD4+ T-cell count and MRI findings of non-enhancing hyperintense lesions, are consistent with progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) caused by the JC virus.
  • The JC virus in PML infects and destroys oligodendrocytes, leading to demyelination of subcortical white matter tracts. The specific neurological deficits—like visual loss and dysarthria—reflect the location of those demyelinating lesions:
  • The presence of JC virus DNA in the CSF is a key diagnostic marker for PML, with high specificity.

No enhancement and minimal mass effect distinguish it from toxoplasmosis (ring‑enhancing) or CMV (ventriculitis, periventricular enhancement). (Option C and D)



BK virus reactivation (Option B) is cause of graft failure after kidney transplantation.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1117, 1671.
question: A 42‑year‑old HIV positive man with CD4 count 80 cells/mm³ presents with 3 weeks of visual blurring, weakness in right arm and dysarthria. MRI brain (FLAIR sequence) shows multiple asymmetric hyperintense lesions in the frontal and parietal white matter, with no mass effect and no contrast enhancement. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

correctAnswer: A. Initiate treatment with sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine with leucovorin
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • MRI head shows ring-enhancing lesions seen in the basal ganglia and corticomedullary junction. They lack the eccentric scolex appearance of NCC or the target sign with the solid nodule appearance of TB meningitis. TBM also has leptomeningeal enhancement and hydrocephalus.
  • Ideally, we should do MR spectroscopy to distinguish them, but here, considering the options given, we will consider cerebral toxoplasmosis.
  • It is a common opportunistic infection in patients with advanced HIV/AIDS, especially with a CD4+ count <100 cells/μL.
  • Therefore, the appropriate initial management is to start treatment with sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine with leucovorin.

Perform a brain biopsy to confirm the diagnosis (Option B): Brain biopsy is definitive but is reserved for patients who fail 2-4 weeks of empiric therapy.


Order a chest X-ray to rule out tuberculosis (Option C): While TB is a concern in HIV patients, the acute neurological symptoms and MRI findings align more with cerebral toxoplasmosis. A chest X-ray is not the immediate priority here.


Start empiric treatment for bacterial meningitis (Option D): Bacterial meningitis could present similarly, but the MRI findings of ring-enhancing lesions are not typical for meningitis. The strong indication of cerebral toxoplasmosis suggests treating that condition first.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1803.

question: A 2-week-old infant presents with lethargy, poor feeding, irritability, and a bulging fontanelle. Born prematurely at 34 weeks with low birth weight, a lumbar puncture reveals cloudy cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) with high white blood cell count, decreased glucose, and elevated protein levels. Which is not a causative factor for this infant's condition?

correctAnswer: C. Liposomal amphotericin B plus 5 Flucytosine
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The diagnosis is cryptococcal meningitis because the patient's clinical presentation, including HIV with low CD4+ count, elevated CSF opening pressure, and the identification of encapsulated yeast in the CSF via India ink stain, is characteristic of Cryptococcus neoformans infection.
  • IV amphotericin B plus flucytosine is the standard initial treatment for cryptococcal meningitis to reduce fungal load and manage CNS infection.
  • Amphotericin should be continued until CSF culture is negative, followed by fluconazole (400 mg/d PO for 8 weeks, then 200 mg/d) until CD4+ T-cell count >200 cells/μL for 6 months.

Lumbar puncture shows elevated opening pressure, low glucose, normal protein and encapsulated yeast on India ink staining. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

Brudzinki sign (Option B): Assisted neck flexion will cause involuntary hip and knee joint flexion


Jolt accentuation (Option C): Ask patient to turn head left and right at 2-3 turns per second. This will cause worsening of headache.

question: A 45 y/o patient presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. On examination, the patient is lethargic and lumbar puncture reveals elevated CSF opening pressure, PMN leukocytosis, decreased glucose levels, and increased protein concentration. Which of the following will not be seen in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The diagnosis in this scenario is bacterial meningitis.

  • The correct treatment includes Ampicillin for Listeria coverage in addition to Ceftriaxone and Vancomycin for broad-spectrum bacterial coverage including Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis
  • For patients with hospital acquired menngitis, post traumatic meningitis, post neurosurgery or neutropenic patients Meropenem and Vancomycin (Option D) will be used

question: A 68 year old patient with diabetic nephropathy presents to the ER with fever, headache, and neck stiffness. Blood cultures are pending, and a lumbar puncture reveals elevated CSF protein, decreased glucose, and neutrophilic pleocytosis. Which of the following is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

correctAnswer: A. Lumbar puncture for CSF CBNAAT for MTB
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This immunocompromised patient is having ring enhanching lesions seen on MRI head.
  • Lesions show “Target sign” with solid central nodule.
  • First differential diagnosis in India - TB meningitis.
  • Due to raised ICP lumbar puncture cannot be performed in this patient as of now due to risk of brain herniation.
  • Empirical ATT with steroids will be started along with measures like Mannitol to lower raised ICP. (Option B,C and D)
  • Double vision is seen this case due to 6th nerve palsy seen in raised ICP.

Contraindications to Lumbar puncture

  1. Papilledema

  2. Focal neurologic deficit (esp. new onset)

  3. Midline shift or mass on CT/MRI

  4. Bleeding disorders / Anticoagulants

  5. Skin infection at site

  6. Uncontrolled seizures

  7. Signs of raised ICP with impending herniation

question: A 38 year old man presented to ER with inability to stand and sit up in bed since yesterday evening. He reports that the weakness began as slipping in stairs multiple times in last 3 days along with tingling in his fingertips. Explanation:

Treatment for NCC Stage wise

  1. Vesicular (Viable) : Albendazole (± praziquantel for heavy/multiple or subarachnoid disease) with steroids.
  2. Colloidal (degenerating, inflammatory): Commonly treated with albendazole + steroids to hasten resolution and reduce seizure recurrence.
  3. Granular–nodular : Parasite largely dead; many guidelines do not routinely give anti-helminthics.

question: A 30 year female presents with repeated episodes of GTCS since last 3 months. Neuroimaging is shown below. Which of the following treatment regimens is most appropriate?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's symptoms of progressive headaches, fever, weight loss, focal neurological deficits, and the presence of larger, conglomerated lesions on the CT scan suggest tuberculoma, which is commonly associated with meningitis.
  • Clinical manifestations of tuberculomas and tuberculous abscesses depend on their location.
    • Most are located in the supratentorial compartment, and
    • Present with headaches, seizures, papilledema and focal deficits occur.
  • They present months to years after primary infection.
  • CT - appear as low- or high-density round or lobulated masses with irregular walls showing homogenous enhancement after contrast administration.
    • May be solitary or multiple
    • Frontal and parietal lobe (most commonly affected)
    • Radiographic appearance depends on whether the lesion is noncaseating, caseating with a solid center or caseating with a liquid center.
    • Degree of perilesional edema is inversely proportional to the duration of the lesion.
    • “Target sign” with a central nidus of calcification surrounded by a ring of enhancement was once thought to be diagnostic of a tuberculoma, but is now known to be quite non specific.
    • Ring-enhancing lesions are usually seen on contrast imaging.
    • Magnetic resonance spectroscopy is used to distinguish tuberculomas from cysticercosis.
    • In patients with HIV, tuberculomas can cavitate and fill with fluid, turning into abscesses.
  • CSF - may be normal
  • Staining and culture for MTB would be normal if parenchyma only is involved.

question: A 30-year-old man presents with progressive headaches, fever, weight loss, and left arm weakness over the past month. He remembers taking a long duration of antibiotic course for a respiratory illness in his childhood, but the specific details he is unable to recall. CT head is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Neurocysticercosis is a parasitic infection of the central nervous system caused by the larvae of Taenia solium, presenting with seizures, headaches, and neurological deficits.
  • Diagnosis is typically confirmed through imaging (CT or MRI) showing cystic lesions, often with visible scolex, and supported by serological tests.
  • The vesicular Stage is characterized by cystic lesions containing a visible scolex, often described as having a "hole-with-dot" appearance on MRI.
  • There is no significant surrounding oedema or abnormal enhancement on gadolinium-enhanced MRI, which aligns with the findings described in the clinical scenario.

MRI (Gadolinium-Enhanced) Features in Neurocysticercosis:

Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is crucial for identifying and differentiating between the stages of neurocysticercosis.

Vesicular Stage: (Live stage)

  • Cystic lesions with a visible scolex ("hole-with-dot" appearance).
  • No significant surrounding oedema or abnormal enhancement on gadolinium-enhanced MRI.

Colloidal Stage: (Degenerating stage)

  • Lesions show peripheral ring enhancement after gadolinium contrast administration. (Option B ruled out)
  • Substantial surrounding oedema is visible, particularly on T2-weighted images.

Granulonodular Stage: (Degenerating stage)

  • Lesions exhibit homogeneous enhancement on post-contrast MRI. (Option C ruled out)
  • No surrounding oedema is present, as seen on FLAIR images.

Nodular-Calcified Stage: (Dead stage)

  • No significant enhancement on gadolinium MRI. (Option D ruled out)
  • Calcifications are better seen with susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI), as they may not enhance well on standard MRI.

[[figure-1]]

A: MRI of a vesicular cyst- Well-defined scolex, minimal contrast enhancement, and mass effect.

B: MRI of a colloidal cyst- Ring enhancement, loss of the scolex, and perilesional oedema.

C: MRI of the nodular/granular stage- Nodule with diffuse enhancement and no cystic component.

D: Noncontrast CT showing multiple punctuate calcifications.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1139.

question: 30-year-old biker is brought to the emergency room after a head injury. On examination, he is unconscious with an ipsilateral mid-dilated fixed pupil. NCCT head shows lenticular hyperdensity. Which of the following is the most likely cause and urgent next step?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Diffuse axonal injury occurs due to rapid acceleration-deceleration or rotational forces in high-impact trauma, causing shearing injury to the axons, especially in areas like the corpus callosum and brainstem.
  • The "retraction balls" represent swollen, broken ends of damaged axons, a hallmark microscopic finding in DAI.
  • Petechial hemorrhages in the corpus callosum and other white matter areas are caused by small vessel rupture during shearing injury.
  • Initial CT scans are often normal or show minimal findings despite severe injury, making early diagnosis challenging.

question: Adult patient involved in a high-speed road traffic accident had a normal CT scan on admission but died within 6 hours. Autopsy reveals petechial hemorrhages in the corpus callosum and retraction balls. The diagnosis is?

correctAnswer: A. Inhibition of the rubrospinal with overactivity of vestibulospinal and reticulospinal pathways
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Patient has extension in arms and legs seen in decerebrate posturing.
  • The key issue is damage below the red nucleus in the brainstem, which affects the balance of motor pathways controlling flexor and extensor muscles.
  • Flexors in arms are controlled by Rubrospinal tract, originating from the red nucleus in the midbrain. These are the ones damaged in decerebrate posturing where damage is below the level of red nucleus.
  • Extensor in arms and legs are controlled by Vestibulospinal tract and Pontine reticulospinal tract.
  • These extensor pathways remain intact and become overactive due to loss of inhibitory/facilitatory input from the damaged flexor pathways.

Intact or overactive rubrospinal tract with loss of extensor facilitation from vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts (Option C) describes a lesion above the red nucleus, where rubrospinal activity is preserved and drives upper-limb flexion while extensors act on the legs — the hallmark of decorticate posturing.

Loss of rubrospinal tract activity with strong extensor inhibition from vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts (Option D) is the opposite of decorticate mechanisms, with both rubrospinal and extensor systems suppressed, which would not result in a classical rigid posture but rather severe hypotonia.

correctAnswer: D. In ischemic stroke, BP should be reduced to &lt;140/90 mmHg immediately
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In ischemic stroke, BP should not be reduced to <140/90 mmHg immediately.
  • The correct management includes reducing the BP to <185/110 mmHg before administering thrombolytic therapy.
  • Lowering BP too aggressively could compromise cerebral perfusion, potentially worsening the ischemia and increasing infarct size.

Hemorrhagic Stroke:

  • BP should be lowered to <160/100 mmHg with antihypertensives to reduce the risk of rebleeding (Option A).
  • If SBP > 220 mmHg, aggressive use of IV antihypertensives is recommended (Option B).

Ischemic Stroke:

  • BP should only be reduced to <185/110 mmHg before thrombolysis.
  • If the BP is above this threshold and thrombolysis is considered, lowering it is necessary, but a reduction to <140/90 mmHg can worsen cerebral perfusion.

Emergency Management:

  • In a hypertensive emergency, multiple BP readings should be taken to ensure accurate assessment before starting antihypertensive therapy (Option C).
  • This is important to avoid over- or under-treatment.

question: Where is the site of the lesion that leads to the occurrence of hemiballismus in a patient displaying forceful, flinging movements?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hemiballismus is a hyperkinetic movement disorder characterised by violent, flinging, large-amplitude involuntary movements, predominantly affecting the proximal muscles on one side of the body.

  • It is considered a severe form of chorea.
  • When choreiform movements become large-amplitude and predominantly proximal, the term ballism is used.
  • The most common cause of hemiballismus is a lesion involving the contralateral subthalamic nucleus (STN), usually due to an infarct or hemorrhage.
  • The subthalamic nucleus is a key component of the indirect pathway of the basal ganglia, which normally suppresses unwanted movements.
  • Damage to the STN reduces inhibitory output from the basal ganglia, leading to excessive thalamocortical motor activity and the characteristic flinging movements.

The patient presents with acute ischemic stroke symptoms within the therapeutic window, non-contrast CT ruled out hemorrhage and is the initial imaging step. To identify a large vessel occlusion (LVO), CT angiography (CTA) is recommended as the next imaging modality.

  • CTA quickly visualizes intracranial and extracranial vessels to detect occlusions amenable to endovascular therapy.

  • Early identification of LVO allows timely planning for possible thrombectomy.

Workup for stroke

Initial Assessment and Stabilization
  • Upon arrival, ensure the ABCs (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) are stable.
  • Blood glucose levels should be checked quickly to address hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia.

Determining Stroke Type: Imaging is Key
  • A non-contrast CT scan is the primary imaging modality for differentiating between ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes.
  • Clinical features may suggest stroke type, but imaging is essential for confirmation as no clinical finding can definitively differentiate between the two.

Further Investigations: Uncovering the Cause
  • Detailed History and Physical Exam: Consider risk factors (hypertension, diabetes, smoking, atrial fibrillation, etc.) and perform a neurological exam to localize the affected brain area.
  • Laboratory Tests: Perform CBC, electrolytes, renal function, blood glucose, lipid profile, coagulation studies, ESR, and ECG (to detect arrhythmias and signs of recent MI).

Visualizing the Cerebral Vasculature: Imaging Techniques
  • CT Angiography (CTA): Assesses cerebral vasculature and identifies blockages/stenosis, but is performed after non-contrast CT has ruled out hemorrhage (not for stroke type differentiation).
  • CT Perfusion Imaging: Assesses blood flow, identifying reduced perfusion and ischemic penumbra.
  • MRI: Provides more detail but takes longer than CT and is not as widely available, thus not the first imaging choice for acute stroke evaluation. (Option B ruled out)
  • MRA: Offers detailed images of blood vessels, similar to CTA.
  • Cerebral Angiography: Gold standard for vessel evaluation, used when other techniques are inconclusive or before endovascular intervention.
  • Ultrasound Techniques: Carotid Duplex Ultrasonography assesses carotid stenosis but is not a first-line acute imaging modality; Transcranial Doppler (TCD) measures blood flow velocity in intracranial arteries.

Tailoring Investigations Based on Stroke Type
  • Ischemic Stroke: Focuses on identifying the source of the blockage (cardioembolic, artery-to-artery embolic, small vessel disease).
  • Hemorrhagic Stroke: Investigations focus on identifying causes of bleeding (e.g., hypertension, aneurysm, vascular malformation).

Tablet labetalol 10 mg stat (Option C): BP control alone does not address the underlying large vessel occlusion.

Thrombolysis (Option D) Should only be given after confirming eligibility and assessing vessel status; CT angiography helps guide this decision.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 3335-3340

correctAnswer: C. Doing EEG is mandatory for diagnosis of seizures
explanationHtml:
Doing EEG is not mandatory for diagnosis of seizures.

Electroencephalography (EEG):

  • Records electrical activity in the brain using electrodes placed on the scalp.
  • It is a dynamic test, EEG frequencies and distribution vary based on factors like brain maturation, age, alertness, and medication.
  • NICE Guidelines: Emphasize not relying solely on EEG for diagnosis. It should be used to:
    • Define seizure type and syndrome.
    • Guide treatment and prognosis.
  • EEG is critical when:
    • Non-convulsive status epilepticus is suspected.
    • Continuous Spike Wave in Slow Wave Sleep (CSWS) is suspected.
  • Avoid in Certain Cases:
    • EEG should not be requested for children with autistic regression.
    • EEG is not needed in developmentally/neurologically normal children with simple or complex febrile seizures.
  • Repeat EEG: Once a seizure type or syndrome has been diagnosed, repeat EEGs have limited value for monitoring treatment or deciding on drug withdrawal.

1-5% of the population can have epileptiform discharges (Option A): This statement is correct. These discharges are not specific to epilepsy, and even in known epilepsy cases, routine interictal EEG can be normal in 60% of cases. Therefore, EEG cannot establish the diagnosis of epilepsy in many individuals.

Scalp EEG may be useful in localizing frontal focal seizures (Option B): However, it is often misleading or normal, particularly when seizures arise from areas distant from the scalp, such as the inferior frontal or medial temporal lobe. In such cases, the EEG may not localize the seizures or may show non-specific activity.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PMLE) shows triphasic and slow waves on EEG (Option D): EEG in PMLE typically shows slow background activity and triphasic and slow waves, predominantly in the frontal regions.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Electroencephalography (EEG) is a noninvasive technique that records the electrical activity of the brain using electrodes placed on the scalp.

  • However, EEG is not mandatory for the diagnosis of epilepsy.
  • Epilepsy is primarily a clinical diagnosis, based on a detailed history and eyewitness descriptions of seizure events.
  • A normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy, and an abnormal EEG alone is insufficient to establish the diagnosis.

1–5% of the population can have epileptiform discharges (Option A): Epileptiform discharges may occur in healthy individuals without epilepsy and therefore, are not by themselves diagnostic of epilepsy.

Scalp EEG has limited accuracy in localising frontal lobe epilepsy (Option B): Frontal lobe seizures are often difficult to localise because scalp EEG recordings may be normal, obscured by movement artefacts, or fail to accurately represent deep frontal seizure foci.

Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy shows triphasic and slow waves on EEG (Option D): EEG findings in PML are generally nonspecific and commonly include diffuse slowing, with triphasic and slow-wave abnormalities reported in affected patients.

Hemisection of the spinal cord (as shown in the image) results in I/L loss of Dorsal and Pyramidal column tracts and C/L loss of Spinothalamic tract (STT) 2 segments below the level of lesion is known as Brown-Sequard syndrome, as STT (specifically Lateral STT) relays at the dorsal root ganglion and crosses over at 1-2 segments above the level of that spinal cord.

[[figure-2]]

Presentation of Brown-Sequard syndrome:

Ipsilateral (I/L)

Contralateral (C/L)

At the level of lesion
  • CST: LMN paralysis
  • Dorsal column: loss of vibration (Option D) and proprioception (Option B)
  • Radicular pain +
  • Muscles- fasciculation, areflexia

-

Below the level of lesion
  • CST: UMN paralysis
  • Dorsal column: Loss of vibration and proprioception
  • Spinothalamic tract: Loss of Pain and Temperature (Option C)

[[figure-3]]

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Page 3446

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The scenario here suggests overuse of analgesics and hence the diagnosis of medication overuse headache.

  • Medication overuse headache (MOH) is a secondary headache because it results from the frequent use of headache medication, unlike tension-type headaches, migraines, and primary stabbing headaches, which are all primary headaches.
  • This develops due to the overuse of analgesics for already-existing headaches.
  • This overuse induces MOH, which leads the patient to take more analgesics, thereby increasing the frequency of headaches, thus forming a vicious cycle.

Main Risk Factors for MOH:

  • Demographic
    • Age (less than 50 years)
    • Female
    • Low educational level
  • Self-reported complaints
    • Chronic musculoskeletal complaints
    • Gastrointestinal complaints
    • Anxiety or depression
  • Lifestyle
    • Smoking
    • Physical inactivity
    • Metabolic syndrome
    • High daily caffeine intake (greater than 540mg versus less than 240mg)
  • Medication
    • Tranquillizers
    • Aspirin
    • Ibuprofen
    • Opioids

Treatment of Medication Overuse Headache (MOH)

  • Patient Education and Prevention
    • Educate on appropriate medication use and risks of MOH.
    • Emphasize the importance of limiting acute headache medications to ≤2 days per week.
  • Medication Discontinuation Strategies
    • Stop overused medication abruptly (preferred for most patients) and start/optimize preventive therapy, titrated based on individual factors.
    • Gradual tapering: Useful for Opioids, Barbiturates, or Benzodiazepines (2-4 weeks for high doses; transdermal clonidine or phenobarbital may help with withdrawal).
  • Preventive Medications
    • Beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, TCAs, and anticonvulsants.
    • Topiramate and OnabotulinumtoxinA (useful, especially in chronic migraine with MOH).
  • Bridge Therapy
    • NSAIDs: Naproxen, Indomethacin, Ketorolac
    • Adjuncts: Tizanidine with NSAIDs, antiemetics (Prochlorperazine, Metoclopramide), and dihydroergotamine (DHE) for severe cases.
    • Raskin protocol: IV DHE + Metoclopramide every 8 hours.
  • Alternative Approaches
    • Withdrawal symptoms management: NSAIDs, hydration, antiemetics, magnesium, and lidocaine infusions.
    • Discontinuation first approach: Avoid starting preventive therapy for 2 months post-medication discontinuation (less tolerated).

Incorrect Options:

In tension headaches (Option B), the pain is described as a dull, bilateral ache, often associated with neck tension, stress, and fatigue.

Migraine (Option C) sufferers describe a prodrome of fatigue, neck discomfort, mood changes, increased urination and thirst, and cognitive impairment. Typical migraine symptoms include a strong, throbbing headache, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia, allodynia and vomiting.

Cluster headaches (Option D) are known for their unilateral, severe pain typically located around the eye, often described as retro-orbital pain. They are more common in males and can be associated with other symptoms such as nasal congestion and watering of the eyes.



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 3358
  2. Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 185

Correct Option B - Type 2 hypersensitivity reaction:

  • The type of hypersensitivity reaction seen in myasthenia gravis is a type 2 hypersensitivity reaction. Hypersensitivity reactions are exaggerated immune responses that can cause tissue damage and disease.
  • Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease, most commonly (80% of cases) caused by antibodies to acetylcholine receptors in the post-junctional membrane of the neuromuscular junction.
  • The autoantibodies in myasthenia gravis are primarily of the IgG subtype and lead to complement-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors.

Incorrect Options:

Option C - Type 3 hypersensitivity reaction: Examples of type 3 hypersensitivity reactions include systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis.

The low CSF/serum glucose ratio is also a characteristic finding in tubercular meningitis. But it is not the correct option.

  • The hypoglossal nerve is the 12th cranial nerve that controls the movement of the tongue.

Option C - Falling of the tongue: Falling back of the tongue” (airway obstruction) occurs mainly in bilateral hypoglossal palsy, not unilateral

correctAnswer: A. Ipsilateral upper and lower halves of the face
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Bell’s palsy is the most common cause of acute facial paralysis and represents an idiopathic lower motor neuron (LMN) lesion of the facial nerve (CN VII). It affects all muscles of facial expression on the same side, involving both the upper face (forehead and eye closure) and lower face (mouth).

  • It is thought to result from inflammation and edema of the facial nerve, most commonly due to reactivation of herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) in the geniculate ganglion.
  • Reactivation of varicella-zoster virus may also be responsible for some cases.

The onset is typically abrupt, with maximal weakness developing within 48 hours. Patients may experience:

  • Unilateral facial weakness
  • Inability to close the eye
  • Loss of forehead wrinkling
  • Drooping of the angle of the mouth
  • Loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
  • Hyperacusis
  • Pain behind the ear preceding the paralysis

UMN vs LMN Facial Palsy

Feature UMN (Supranuclear) Facial Palsy LMN Facial Palsy (Bell’s Palsy)
Forehead involvement Spared Involved
Eye closure Preserved Impaired
Lower face Contralateral weakness Ipsilateral weakness
Distribution Contralateral lower face only Ipsilateral upper and lower face
  • The forehead is spared in upper motor neuron lesions because the upper facial muscles receive bilateral corticobulbar innervation, whereas the lower facial muscles receive predominantly contralateral cortical innervation.

Contralateral upper and lower halves of the face (Option B): Complete paralysis of both the upper and lower face on the contralateral side is not the typical pattern of facial nerve lesions.

Ipsilateral lower half of the face (Option C): Bell’s palsy affects both the upper and lower facial muscles on the affected side. Isolated lower facial weakness is characteristic of an upper motor neuron lesion.

Contralateral lower half of the face (Option D): This is the classic pattern of a supranuclear (upper motor neuron) facial palsy, such as that caused by a stroke. The forehead is spared because of bilateral cortical innervation of the upper facial muscles.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3554, 3555

explanationHtml:
• The diagnosis for Myasthenia gravis is supported by the classic presentation of fatigable muscle weakness that worsens throughout the day (diurnal variation), ptosis, and positive response to neostigmine. The improvement with neostigmine, an Acetylcholinesterase inhibitor which increases acetylcholine availability at the neuromuscular junction, is particularly diagnostic of myasthenia gravis.

Clinical Features and Diagnosis of Myasthenia Gravis

Clinical Features
  • Diplopia, ptosis, dysarthria, dysphagia
  • Weakness in oculomotor, pharyngeal, limb, neck extensors
  • Fluctuation and fatigue worse with activity, improved by rest
  • Fatiguability increases as the day passes (diurnal variation)
  • Initial symptoms frequently ocular (diplopia/ptosis)
  • Facial weakness produces "snarling" expression

Physical Examination
  • Eye movements and ptosis
  • Assessment of muscle strength in neck and extremities
  • Weakness following repetitive muscle activation
  • Normal deep tendon reflexes
  • No sensory abnormalities
  • Symptoms relieved by Anticholinesterases

Diagnostic Tests
  • Anti-AChR antibodies (positive in ~85% generalized MG)
  • Anti-MuSK antibodies (in ~40% of AChR-negative cases)
  • Repetitive nerve stimulation
  • Single-fiber EMG
  • CT or MRI of chest (to evaluate thymus)

Clinical Tests
  • Edrophonium (Tensilon) test: 2mg + 8mg IV
  • Ice pack test for ptosis
  • Fatigue testing (repeated muscle activation)

Huntington chorea (Option B) is a genetic condition characterized by involuntary movements, cognitive decline, and psychiatric symptoms. It does not present with ptosis or show diurnal variation, nor does it respond to neostigmine.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Option C) presents with progressive muscle weakness, but lacks the characteristic diurnal variation seen in myasthenia gravis. ALS does not typically begin with ptosis and shows no improvement with neostigmine.

External ophthalmoplegia (Option D) can cause ptosis but does not demonstrate the distinctive pattern of fatigue and improvement with rest. Additionally, external ophthalmoplegia does not respond to neostigmine and lacks the diurnal variation characteristic of myasthenia gravis.



Reference:
  • Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 1141-1143
  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 3510-3513

explanationHtml:
• The clinical manifestations such as presence of characteristic headaches that worsen when lying down, papilledema on fundal examination, and the absence of focal neurological deficits indicate pseudotumor cerebri, also known as idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH). This condition is characterized by increased intracranial pressure without any identifiable cause such as a tumor. The patient's use of oral contraceptives is a notable risk factor, as hormonal medications can contribute to the development of this condition.

Pseudotumor Cerebri / Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension

Definition

A disorder associated with elevated CSF pressure without obvious cause, commonly affecting young, obese females

Key Symptoms
  • Headache (worse on waking and with recumbency)
  • Visual disturbances (may be transient)
  • Can occur without visual problems
  • Worse in morning or after lying down
  • Pulsatile tinnitus may be present

Diagnostic Criteria
  • Elevated CSF pressure (>20-25 cm H2O)
  • Normal MRI/MRV findings
  • Normal neurological examination (except for papilledema)
  • Papilledema may be present (but not required for diagnosis)

Initial Treatment
  • Acetazolamide (250-500 mg)
  • Weight loss (if overweight)
  • Serial lumbar punctures may be needed
  • Regular ophthalmologic monitoring

Secondary Treatment
  • Topiramate
  • Other carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
  • CSF shunting procedures (if needed)
  • Weight loss management programs

Monitoring
  • Regular visual field testing
  • Ophthalmic examination
  • CSF pressure monitoring
  • Weight monitoring
  • Headache diary

Important Considerations
  • Fundoscopic exam should be performed even without overt ophthalmic involvement
  • Consider diagnosis in chronic migraine cases
  • May require long-term management
  • Early intervention is crucial for preventing vision loss

Myasthenia gravis (Option A) primarily presents with muscle weakness and fatigue, particularly affecting ocular and bulbar muscles. The absence of muscle weakness/headache and the presence of papilledema make this diagnosis unlikely.

Temporal arteritis (Option B) typically affects older adults over 50 years and presents with temporal headache, jaw claudication, and scalp tenderness. Also, the patient's presentation of papilledema is not a typical feature of Temporal arteritis.

Chronic migraine (Option C) is characterized by headaches occurring on 15 or more days per month for at least three months. While the timeframe is similar, the presence of papilledema and positional nature of the headache are not typical features of migraine.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 20th Edition, Page 116
question: A woman presents with a history of headaches for the past 9 months that worsen in a recumbent position and improves as the day progresses. She also gives a history of taking oral contraceptives. Fundal examination shows papilledema. There are no focal neurological deficits. What is the probable cause of her headaches?

explanationHtml:
• The patient presents with classic features of Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), including antecedent respiratory tract infection, progressive ascending symmetrical weakness, and areflexia. GBS is an autoimmune polyradiculopathy causing patchy segmental demyelination of peripheral nerves and nerve roots. The temporal relationship with infection, pattern of weakness, and preserved sensory function are characteristic of GBS.

Category

Symptoms

Motor Symptoms
  • Progressive ascending paralysis (distal to proximal)
  • Areflexia
  • Weakness in the legs causes rubbery legs and instability to standing
  • Truncal paralysis, quadriplegia, neck floppiness
  • Bilateral 7th nerve palsy
  • Bulbar palsy
    • Difficulty in handling secretions leading to aspiration pneumonia
    • A leading cause of death due to pulmonary involvement.
  • Diaphragmatic paralysis
    • Ventilatory support is required in 30% of cases.
    • Increased carbon dioxide levels.

Sensory Symptoms
  • Glove-and-stocking distribution paresthesias
  • Proprioception loss (Preserved proprioception does NOT rule out GBS)
    • Difficulty in climbing stairs
    • Pain in the neck/arm/shoulder is similar to an over-exercised muscle
  • Sensory manifestations can occur before or along with motor manifestations.

Autonomic Symptoms
  • Autonomic dysregulation (e.g., orthostatic hypotension, bladder/bowel sparing/transient involvement)
  • Wide fluctuations of blood pressure, arrhythmias, postural hypotension
  • Reduced heart rate and blood pressure, neurogenic shock.

Myasthenia gravis (Option B): Weakness in myasthenia gravis typically worsens with repeated use of the affected muscles and improves with rest. Additionally, it often affects the muscles of the face and eyes before involving the limbs. The ascending pattern and areflexia are not typical features of myasthenia gravis.

Polymyositis (Option C): Polymyositis presents with symmetric proximal muscle weakness primarily affecting the shoulder and hip girdle muscles, making activities like climbing stairs or raising arms above the head difficult. Patients maintain normal reflexes and have no sensory involvement. The absence of proximal muscle pattern, presence of areflexia, and absence of ascending weakness pattern make polymyositis unlikely.

Multiple sclerosis (Option D): Multiple sclerosis typically follows a relapsing-remitting course with scattered neurological manifestations. Common presentations include visual symptoms like optic neuritis and sensory symptoms such as paresthesias and numbness. Patients often demonstrate hyperreflexia rather than areflexia.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principle of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 3501
question: A 26-year-old male with a history of respiratory tract infection 4 weeks ago is unable to stand or walk for the past 2 weeks and the weakness is progressive, ascending, and symmetrical in nature. The lower limbs were involved before and gradually the upper limbs were also affected. On examination you note areflexia. Pain and proprioception are preserved. Which of the following could be the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
• The presentation of sudden severe headache ("worst headache of my life"), hypertension, and nuchal rigidity, along with the CT scan showing characteristic "Star of Death" appearance due to blood accumulation in basal cisterns, are diagnostic of Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH).
  • This condition occurs when blood accumulates in the subarachnoid space between the brain and the thin tissues covering it, usually due to aneurysm rupture, and carries a 35% mortality rate if untreated.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage- Etiology, Risk factors and Pathophysiology

  • Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH): Blood accumulation in the subarachnoid space.

  • Causes: Often due to aneurysm rupture (~85%) or trauma.

  • Non-traumatic SAH is most commonly caused by the rupture of a saccular aneurysm.

  • Clinical Impact: High mortality and morbidity; often presents with a sudden, severe headache (worst headache of life).

  • Complications: Seizures, vasospasm, hydrocephalus, and delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI).

Epidemiology

  • Age: Most aSAH occurs between ages 40-60, mean rupture age 50-55 and slightly more prevalent in females.

  • Risk Factors: Smoking and history of ruptured aneurysms increase SAH risk.

Etiology

  • Aneurysmal SAH (aSAH):

    • Risk Factors: Hypertension, smoking, family history, alcohol use, sympathomimetic drugs, and estrogen deficiency.

    • Rupture Risk: (Option D)

      • Age >60

      • Posterior circulation aneurysms

      • Atherosclerosis

      • Aneurysm size

        • Aneurysms <10 mm: ~0.1% annual rupture risk.

        • Aneurysms ≥10 mm: 0.5–1% annual rupture risk.

        • Giant aneurysms (>2.5 cm): ~6% rupture risk in first year.

      • Family history

      • Previous SAH

      • ADPKD

  • Nonaneurysmal SAH (NASAH):

    • Perimesencephalic NASAH: Localized blood in perimesencephalic cisterns, normal angiography, benign course.

    • Occult Aneurysm: Small aneurysms missed on initial angiography, detectable on repeat imaging.

    • Vascular Malformations: Includes arteriovenous malformations (AVM) and dural arteriovenous fistulae. Treated with surgery or endovascular interventions.

    • Intracranial Arterial Dissection: Diagnosed by angiography, causes severe bleeding, treated with surgery or endovascular methods.

    • Other Causes: Cocaine abuse, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, cerebral venous thrombosis, sickle cell disorders, moyamoya disease, cerebral vasculitis, bleeding disorders.

Pathophysiology

  • Hemodynamic Stress: Central to intracranial aneurysm formation, especially at arterial bifurcations.

  • Aneurysm Rupture: Causes neurological damage through compression of adjacent brain tissue and ischemia from reduced blood flow.

    • Mechanisms: Hemodynamic stress and inflammation (matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-mediated degradation of extracellular matrix) weaken the arterial wall, promoting aneurysm formation and rupture.

    • Inflammatory Response: Macrophages and smooth muscle cells drive these degenerative processes.

Clinical Presentation

  • "Thunderclap headache" - worst headache of life

  • Sudden onset severe headache

  • Vomiting

  • Variable LOC

  • Meningismus

  • Retinal hemorrhages

  • Focal neurologic deficits

  • Nuchal rigidity

Diagnosis

[[figure-1]]

CT Head

  • Non-contrast CT is first-line

  • "Star sign" - blood in basal cisterns

  • Sensitivity: 98-100% in first 12 hours

Lumbar Puncture

  • If CT negative

  • Xanthochromia (takes 12h to develop)

  • Elevated opening pressure

Cluster headache (Option A): Cluster headaches are characterized by severe, unilateral pain centered around the eye often described as retro-orbital pain along with associated autonomic symptoms. They typically occur in clusters or cycles and do not present with nuchal rigidity or “Star sign” on CT findings.

Encephalitis (Option C): Encephalitis typically presents with fever, altered mental status, seizures, and focal neurological deficits. The absence of fever and presence of classic SAH findings on CT make encephalitis unlikely.

Meningitis (Option D): While meningitis can present with headache and nuchal rigidity, it typically includes fever and photophobia. The CT findings are not consistent with meningitis. Also, the characteristic "Star of Death" appearance on CT is pathognomonic of SAH.



Reference:
  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Edition, Page 3353, 3354
  • Subarachnoid Hemorrhage - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
question: A young patient presents with a severe headache. He has never experienced a headache of this severity before. He has hypertension and nuchal rigidity on examination. Which of the following could be the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
• The presentation including subacute fever with neck rigidity, characteristic CSF findings (lymphocytic predominance, low sugar, markedly elevated protein), cobweb coagulum formation, and chest X-ray showing upper lobe involvement with hilar lymphadenopathy, which are all classic features of tuberculous meningitis.

  • The negative Gram stain further supports mycobacterial infection rather than typical bacterial pathogens.

Tuberculous Meningitis

Symptoms and Clinical Features:

  • Headache, slight mental changes, and low-grade fever can develop over weeks, often accompanied by malaise, anorexia, and irritability.

  • More severe cases present with confusion, lethargy, neck rigidity, and altered sensorium.

  • Disease progression: evolves over 1–2 weeks, longer than bacterial meningitis.

  • Cranial nerve palsies, especially ocular nerves, are common due to inflammation at the base of the brain.

  • May result in coma, hydrocephalus, and intracranial hypertension if untreated.

  • Cerebral ischemia can result from the involvement of cerebral arteries.

  • Tuberculoma (space-occupying lesion) may cause seizures and focal neurological signs.

CSF Findings:

  • Elevated leukocyte count (up to 1000/μL, predominantly lymphocytes).

  • High protein content (1–8 g/L).

  • Cobweb Coagulum: Clear fluid in a test tube with a cobweb at the bottom

[[figure-1]]

  • Low glucose concentration.

Investigation of Choice:

  • Culture of CSF (gold standard, takes 4–8 weeks, positive in ~50%).

  • Smear for acid-fast bacilli (AFB) (low sensitivity, positive in 10–40%).

  • PCR for Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA (variable sensitivity).

Imaging:

  • CT/MRI may show hydrocephalus and abnormal enhancement of basal cisterns or ependyma.

  • Tuberculomas appear as contrast-enhanced ring lesions on imaging.

[[figure-2]]

MRI showing ring-enhanced lesions -tuberculoma

Treatment:

  • Empirical therapy is often initiated based on suspicion.

  • Initial drug regimen: isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol, and pyridoxine.

  • Duration: 6–12 months depending on response.

  • Dexamethasone (12–16 mg/day) for 3 weeks, tapered for 3 more weeks (recommended for HIV-negative patients).

  • Tuberculoma may require a biopsy for diagnosis.

Bacterial meningitis (Option B): Bacterial meningitis typically presents with acute onset (<24-48 hours), neutrophilic predominance in CSF, and positive Gram stain. The subacute presentation and lymphocytic CSF make bacterial meningitis unlikely.

Fungal meningitis (Option C): While fungal meningitis can present with similar CSF findings, including low glucose and high protein, it typically occurs in immunocompromised patients and does not usually present with characteristic upper lobe chest X-ray findings. The presence of pulmonary involvement strongly suggests tuberculosis.

Viral meningitis (Option D): Viral meningitis typically presents with normal to mildly elevated protein levels, normal glucose levels, and absence of cobweb coagulum. The markedly elevated protein (3000mg/dl) and low glucose are inconsistent with viral etiology.



Reference:

Classification of Dementia

Type of Dementia

Most common type of dementia, characterized by amyloid plaques and tau tangles in the brain.

Caused by abnormal protein deposits (Lewy bodies) in the brain, affecting cognitive and motor functions.

  • Memory impairment
  • REM sleep behavior disorder

Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD)

Characterized by degeneration in the frontal and temporal lobes, often with personality and behavioral changes.

(Option C)

  • Impaired coordination and motor function

(Option B)

  • Ataxia

A condition where excess cerebrospinal fluid accumulates in the brain ventricles, leading to cognitive decline.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is a form of traumatic brain injury caused by a blunt force injury to the brain, often from high-speed motor vehicle accidents.

Aetiology:

  • Cause: High-speed accidents, where accelerating and decelerating forces cause shearing of axons in the white matter of the brain.
  • Affected Areas: Primarily the corpus callosum, brainstem, and white matter tracts, especially at the junction of grey and white matter.

Pathophysiology:

  • Shearing forces disrupt neuronal connections, leading to brain dysfunction.
  • Common Deficits: Affect frontal and temporal white matter, corpus callosum, and brainstem.

Clinical Presentation:

  • Diagnosis: Clinical diagnosis, typically with a GCS of less than 8 lasting over six hours.
  • Symptoms:
    • Mild: Headache, dizziness, nausea, and fatigue.
    • Severe: Loss of consciousness, persistent vegetative state, potential long-term recovery for a few.
    • Dysautonomia: Tachycardia, tachypnea, hyperthermia, abnormal muscle tone, and posturing.

Evaluation:

  • CT: Small punctate haemorrhages to white matter tracts.
  • MRI: Investigation of choice
    • Small areas of cerebral microbleeds at the grey-white matter junction, corpus callosum, or the brainstem.

[[figure-1]]

Treatment/Management:

  • Goals: Prevent secondary injuries (e.g., hypoxia, hypotension, intracranial hypertension) and support recovery.
  • Initial Treatment: Focus on stabilization, including resuscitation and prevention of complications like cerebral oedema and elevated ICP.
  • ICP Monitoring: Recommended for GCS below 8 and for patients unable to be regularly evaluated neurologically.
  • Anticonvulsants: Short-term use (7 days) to prevent early seizures.
  • Emerging Therapies: Progesterone treatment shows promise but cannot be routinely recommended.

Incorrect Options:

Extensive subarachnoid haemorrhage (Option B) is a life-threatening condition due to the accumulation of blood between the arachnoid and pia mater.

Hypoxic cerebral injury (Option C) refers to injury of the brain due to a lack of oxygen delivery enough to support metabolic needs. This is caused due to conditions like cardiac arrest, strangulation, severe anaemia, systemic hypotension, etc.

Multiple hemorrhagic contusions (Option D) are traumatic brain injuries which are the most disabling type of traumatic phenomenon. These can be caused by falls, road traffic accidents, aggression, sports injuries, cyclists, etc. These appear as several localized areas of bleeding.



Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK448102/

In this scenario of Compressive Myelopathy, knee clonus supports the diagnosis because it is an upper motor neuron sign seen below the level of spinal cord compression.

Compressive myelopathy is spinal cord compression, commonly from a mass, disc herniation, tumor, or degeneration → Produce upper motor neuron signs below the lesion.

Upper motor neuron signs include:

Lower motor neuron signs (hypotonia, hyporeflexia, muscle wasting) are typically seen at the level of the lesion, not below it. (Option A ruled out)
Normal cremasteric reflex (Option D) is not typically affected in compressive myelopathy.

• The clinical features of unilateral headache, nausea, photophobia, and phonophobia are classic signs of an acute migraine attack.
  • Migraine is a common episodic headache disorder, more frequent in females, and often triggered by stimuli such as bright lights, hunger, or stress.

  • The given clinical scenario, along with CSF findings of mononuclear cytosis, elevated proteins, low sugars, and the characteristic cobweb-like clot, strongly suggests tuberculous meningitis (TBM).

Features of Tuberculous Meningitis (TBM):

  • Etiology: Caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spreading hematogenously or via rupture of subependymal tubercles into the subarachnoid space.
  • Presentation: Subacute infection with fever, headache, neck stiffness, and cranial nerve palsies (commonly ocular nerves due to basal meningeal involvement).

Diagnosis:

  • Gold Standard: CSF culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
  • Supportive Tests: Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain, PCR for tuberculosis, or CSF ADA levels.

Management:

  • Steroids to reduce inflammation.
