explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Berry aneurysms primarily develop due to disruption of the internal elastic lamina of cerebral blood vessels. The internal elastic lamina is a critical structural component that provides tensile strength and elasticity to blood vessels. When this layer is compromised, the vessel wall becomes weakened and less able to withstand normal hemodynamic stresses, leading to outward bulging and eventual aneurysm formation.

Berry Aneurysm

Definition
  • Saccular outpouching of intracranial arterial wall
  • Represents 90% of cerebral aneurysms
  • Primary location: Circle of Willis
  • Most common sites:
    • Anterior communicating/anterior cerebral junction
    • Posterior communicating/internal carotid junction
    • Middle cerebral artery bifurcation
    • Basilar apex

Pathophysiological Mechanisms

Structural Changes:

  • Most important- Internal elastic lamina disruption
  • Media layer thinning
  • Adventitial layer remodeling

Molecular Mechanisms:

  • Inflammatory mediator activation
  • Matrix metalloproteinase upregulation
  • Vessel wall extracellular matrix degradation

Hemodynamic Factors:

  • Wall shear stress elevation
  • Flow-related endothelial injury
  • Intramural stress distribution alterations

Histopathological Classification

1. Mycotic:

  • Infectious arterial wall damage
  • Distal vessel predilection
  • Inflammatory cell infiltration

2. Arteriosclerotic:

  • Intimal hyperplasia
  • Media degeneration
  • Elastic fiber fragmentation

3. Traumatic:

  • Transmural disruption
  • False lumen formation
  • Adventitial hemorrhage

Rupture Risk Stratification

Morphological Criteria:

  • Size >7mm: high risk
  • Aspect ratio >1.6
  • Daughter sac presence
  • Wall irregularity

Hemodynamic Factors:

  • Systolic BP >140 mmHg
  • Flow pattern alterations
  • Intrasaccular pressure gradients

Genetic Markers:

  • Collagen deficiency
  • Elastic fiber abnormalities
  • Matrix metalloproteinase polymorphisms

Clinical Manifestations

Subarachnoid Hemorrhage:

  • Hunt-Hess grading scale correlation
  • Fisher scale for CT findings
  • Modified Rankin Scale outcomes

Mass Effect:

  • Cranial nerve compression syndromes
  • Brainstem compression sequelae
  • Hydrocephalus development

Thromboembolic Events:

  • Watershed infarction patterns
  • Perforator occlusion syndromes
  • Distal embolization phenomena

Endothelial injury due to HTN (Option A) while hypertension can exacerbate aneurysm formation and increase rupture risk, it is not the primary underlying cause of berry aneurysms. Hypertension acts as a contributing factor rather than the initiating defect.

Endothelial layer defect (Option C) although the endothelium can be involved in aneurysm progression, the primary defect occurs in the internal elastic lamina rather than the endothelial layer. The endothelial dysfunction is usually secondary to the underlying structural abnormality.

Adventitia defect (Option D) the adventitial layer is the outer layer of blood vessels and is not the primary site of berry aneurysm formation. The key pathology begins in the internal elastic lamina and medial layer of the vessel wall.



Reference:
  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page: 3353-3355
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557480/

Explanation:

  • Based on the given clinical presentation, the probable diagnosis in this case is Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA).

Transient Ischaemic Attack (TIA)

  • Defined as a transient episode of neurologic dysfunction due to the focal brain, spinal cord, or retinal ischemia without acute infarction or tissue injury.
  • A TIA typically lasts less than an hour, more often minutes.
  • Usually resolves within 24 hours.
  • Risk is highest in the first 48 hours following a transient ischemic attack.

Etiology:

  • Common risk factors for all TIA include diabetes, hypertension, age, smoking, obesity, alcoholism, unhealthy diet, psychosocial stress, and lack of regular physical activity.
  • A previous history of stroke or TIA will increase substantially the subsequent risk of recurrent stroke or TIA.

Pathophysiology:

TIA subtypes, classified according to the pathophysiological mechanisms

  • Large artery atherothrombosis (M/C): This may be intracranial or extracranial atherothrombosis. The mechanism may be a lack of blood flow distal to the site of arterial stenosis or an artery-to-artery embolism.
  • Small vessel ischemic diseases: The underlying pathology is either lipohyalinosis or small vessel arteriolosclerosis. The commonest risk factor is hypertension, followed by diabetes and age.
  • Cardiac embolism: A clot in the cardiac chamber, most commonly in the left atrium, is secondary to atrial fibrillation.
  • Cryptogenic: This is usually a cortical pattern of ischemia without any identifiable large artery atherothrombosis or cardiac source of emboli. More recently it is often referred to as ESUS (embolic stroke of unknown source).
  • Other uncommon causes such as arterial dissection or vasculitis.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given image represents the patient suffering from hemispatial neglect where there are missing details in the left side of the line drawing.

Hemispatial Neglect:

  • Hemispatial neglect is the inability to report, respond, and orient to stimuli in one-half of the space despite having no motor or sensory deficits.

Types and location of lesions:

  • Contralesional Hemispatial Neglect:
    • Result of damage to cortical or subcortical components of the spatial attention network.
    • Not always caused by parietal lobe lesions, as traditionally believed.
  • Spatial Attention Model:
    • Right hemisphere: Directs attention to the entire extrapersonal space.
    • Left hemisphere: Directs attention mostly to the right hemispace (contralateral).
    • Left hemisphere lesions: Minor neglect, as the right hemisphere compensates.
    • Right hemisphere lesions: Severe neglect of the left hemispace due to lack of ipsilateral attentional mechanisms in the left hemisphere.

Clinical Examination:

  • Patients may neglect grooming, eating, and reading on the left side.
  • Line drawing and writing often have missing details on the left side.
  • Tests for neglect:
    • Simultaneous Bilateral Stimulation: Patients fail to detect bilateral stimuli and experience extinction (only detecting stimuli from the right side).
    • Target Detection Task: Difficulty detecting targets on the left side, reflecting a motor and attentional deficit rather than sensory input loss (hemianopia).
  • Some patients may deny the existence of hemiparesis or even the paralyzed limb (anosognosia).

Clinical Observation:

  • Neglect is more common, severe, and long-lasting after right hemisphere damage.
  • Severe neglect of the right hemispace is rare even with left hemisphere lesions.

Confabulation (Option A) is a phenomenon in which the patient fills in memory gaps with made-up stories and inaccurate facts.

Kinetic apraxia (Option C) is the inability to perform a fine movement or task despite having the desire and physical capability to do it. The lesion lies in the paracentral cortex.

Asterixis (Option D) is a type of negative myoclonus where irregular lapses of the posture of body parts are noted.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page: 199, 200.

  • Neisseria meningitidis is a gram negative diplococci.
  • Fulminant meningococcemia presents with a very high fever and hemorrhagic rash.

Acute Bacterial Meningitis

  • Definition: Acute purulent infection in the subarachnoid space (SAS) leading to CNS inflammation.
  • Causes:
    • Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitides are the primary causes.
    • Listeria monocytogenes is a significant risk in adults over 50, especially in those with diabetes, alcoholism, or weakened immune systems.
  • Presentation: Can be acute and fulminant or subacute, with the classic triad of symptoms:
    • Fever
    • Headache
    • Nuchal rigidity (stiff neck)

Clinical features

Description

Consciousness

Decreased level of consciousness occurs in >75% of cases, ranging from lethargy to coma.

Kernig's Sign

Positive when passive extension of the knee elicits pain; indicative of meningeal irritation.

Brudzinski's Sign

Positive when passive flexion of the neck results in spontaneous flexion of the hips and knees; also indicative of meningeal irritation.

Pupils

May present as dilated and poorly reactive due to increased intracranial pressure (ICP).

Posturing

Possible decerebrate posturing as a sign of severe CNS dysfunction.

Signs of Increased ICP

Includes elevated CSF opening pressure (>180 mmH2O), papilledema, and potential cerebral herniation (1–8% incidence).

Additional Symptoms

Nausea, vomiting, photophobia; seizures in 15–40% (focal or generalized).

Meningococcemia Rash

Erythematous maculopapular rash that quickly becomes petechial, commonly on the trunk and lower extremities.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Option B) is a gram-negative rod-shaped bacteria.

Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option C) is a gram-positive, spherical bacteria.

E. Coli (Option D) is a gram-negative rod-shaped bacteria.

explanationHtml:
• The patient's progressive bilateral limb weakness, muscle wasting, positive Babinski sign, absent deep tendon reflexes, and absence of sensory or autonomic dysfunction are consistent with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS).

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS):

  • ALS is the most common progressive motor neuron disease and a prime example of neurodegenerative disorders.
  • Genetic Causes:
    • Mutant Proteins: SOD1, ubiquilin-1/-2, and p62 mutations disrupt protein degradation.
    • RNA Processing: C9orf72, TDP43, and FUS mutations affect RNA transport/processing.
    • Axonal Transport: Mutations in dynactin and profilin-1 affect axonal transport.
  • Pathology:
    • The hallmark of ALS is the death of both lower motor neurons (anterior horn cells and brainstem motor neurons) and upper motor neurons (corticospinal neurons).
    • ALS involves both denervation and muscle atrophy, particularly in proximal muscles, and results in selective loss of motor neurons.
  • Clinical Manifestations:
    • Lower Motor Neuron Dysfunction: Asymmetric muscle weakness, muscle cramping, fasciculations, muscle atrophy and bulbar palsy.
    • Upper Motor Neuron Dysfunction: Reflex hyperactivity, muscle stiffness, spasticity and pseudobulbar palsy.
    • Corticobulbar Projection Degeneration: Results in dysarthria (speech difficulty) and pseudobulbar affect (excessive weeping or laughing).
    • Symmetric Muscle Involvement: Over time, more muscle groups become involved, leading to a symmetric distribution of the disorder in all regions.
    • Preserved Sensory and Cognitive Functions: Sensory, bowel and bladder, and cognitive functions are preserved even in the late stages.
    • Ocular Motility Sparing: Ocular motility remains unaffected until the very late stages of ALS.
  • Treatment:
    • No treatment halts the underlying ALS pathology.
    • Riluzole: Reduces excitotoxicity via decreased glutamate release.
    • Edaravone: Acts as an antioxidant and it modestly reduces disability progression.
    • Phenylbutyrate and Taurursodiol: Oral combination shown to slow disease progression and extend survival by improving mitochondrial and endoplasmic reticulum function.

Multiple sclerosis (Option A) typically presents with relapsing-remitting episodes, optic neuritis, and a combination of upper motor neuron (UMN) and sensory deficits, which are absent in this case, and the patient lacks the characteristic visual and brainstem symptoms like ataxia and nystagmus.

Guillain-barre syndrome (Option C) causes rapidly progressive ascending paralysis with areflexia, sensory involvement, and autonomic dysfunction, which this patient does not exhibit, as the weakness is bilateral and progressive over a longer period without sensory loss.

Tropical spastic paraparesis (Option D) is associated with spastic paraparesis, sensory deficits, and bladder disturbances but no lower motor neuron (LMN) involvement, which contrasts with this patient's presentation of muscle wasting (suggestive of LMN involvement) and absence of bladder dysfunction.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 3410-3415

NPH is often idiopathic but can result from prior injuries affecting cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dynamics, such as subarachnoid hemorrhage.

Clinical Triad

  • Gait disturbance: Progressive difficulties in walking
  • Urinary issues: Urgency or incontinence
  • Cognitive impairment: Decline in cognitive functions

Imaging Characteristics

  • Ventriculomegaly is typically seen
  • Evans ratio: the ratio of the maximum width of frontal horns to inner table width of more than 0.31 is often used for evaluation but has low diagnostic accuracy.
  • An acute callosal angle (less than 90°) on coronal MR images is another measurement used, also with limited accuracy.
  • A disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus is seen having ventriculomegaly combined with sulcal effacement at the vertex and scattered enlarged sulci.
  • CSF flow study shows hyper-dynamism with a streak of flow void through cerebral aqueduct.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Frontotemporal dementia (Option B) (FTD) primarily affects personality, behavior, and language, often presenting with early changes such as disinhibition, apathy, and loss of empathy. Urinary incontinence is not a typical early feature of FTD, and gait disturbances or falls are also not commonly seen at the onset, making it less likely in this case.

Parkinson's disease (Option C) primarily presents with motor symptoms such as bradykinesia, resting tremor, rigidity, and postural instability. While dementia and falls can occur in the later stages, urinary incontinence is not a typical early feature, and the behavioral changes in Parkinson's disease are usually associated with the later stages or due to medication effects, which makes it less consistent with the initial presentation.

Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (Option D) (CJD) is a rapidly progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by prions, characterized by rapidly progressing dementia, myoclonus, ataxia, and other neurological signs. While behavioral changes can occur, urinary incontinence and multiple falls are not typical presenting features of CJD.

explanationHtml:
Explanation: The slowing of conduction in multiple sclerosis is due to the loss of myelin sheath.

Multiple sclerosis

  • Multiple sclerosis (MS) is an autoimmune disease of the central nervous system characterized by chronic inflammation, demyelination, gliosis (plaques or scarring), and neuronal loss.
  • The course can be relapsing or progressive.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Immune hypothesis: Increased T lymphocytes in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and higher immunoglobulin synthesis in the CNS
    • Blood-brain barrier (BBB) injury: Activated T lymphocytes cross the blood-brain barrier, recognize myelin antigens on nervous system antigen-presenting cells (microglia) and proliferate
    • Demyelination:
      • Inflammatory cascade releases cytokines, leading to oligodendrocyte- myelin destruction by macrophages
      • Lesions: disintegration of myelin, lymphocyte/macrophage infiltration, and perivascular inflammation
      • Ectopic lymphoid follicles are linked to demyelination and neuronal loss in the cerebral cortex
      • Diffusible factors from these lymphoid cells may cause demyelination and neurodegeneration
    • Axonal damage:
      • Demyelination reduces trophic support for axons, redistributes ion channels, and destabilizes action potential membrane potentials
      • Neuronal and axonal death may result from glutamate excitotoxicity, oxidative injury, iron accumulation, and mitochondrial failure
      • Inflammatory mediators like nitric oxide initiate and worsen axonal damage
      • Axons can adapt initially to these injuries, but over time, distal and retrograde degeneration (“dying-back” axonopathy) occurs
      • Axonal loss accumulates over time due to repeated attacks and lack of neurotrophic factors from oligodendrocytes
    • Plaque formation:
      • After acute attacks, gliosis occurs by astrocyte cells, forming scars.
      • Surviving oligodendrocytes partially remyelinate axons causing shadow plaques.
    • Oligodendrocyte precursor cells often fail to differentiate into myelin-producing cells.
    • Long-term myelin loss leads to reduced impulse propagation and conduction block, impairing CNS functions.

[[figure-1]]

Gliosis (Option A): This refers to the proliferation of glial cells (especially astrocytes) in response to central nervous system injury. While gliosis occurs in MS as part of the tissue response to demyelination and inflammation, it is not the primary cause of slowed conduction. Instead, it is a secondary effect resulting from the damage.

Defect at the Node of Ranvier (Option C): Nodes of Ranvier are small gaps in the myelin sheath where voltage-gated sodium channels are concentrated, allowing for the rapid "jumping" of action potentials (saltatory conduction). Although defects at these nodes can disrupt impulse propagation, in multiple sclerosis the main problem is the loss of myelin rather than a defect in the nodes themselves.

Leaky Na⁺ Channels (Option D): In demyelinated axons, the redistribution or abnormal functioning of sodium channels can occur, which may contribute to conduction issues. However, this change is a consequence of myelin loss rather than a primary cause of conduction slowing. The loss of the insulating myelin sheath is the key factor impairing the proper function of these channels.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principle of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 3462, 3464, 3465

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Wallenberg syndrome presents with pain, numbness, impaired sensation over one half of the face, horner syndrome, diplopia, numbness of the ipsilateral arm, trunk and leg. Occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebral artery is responsible for Wallenberg syndrome as it supplies the lateral medulla.

Blood Supply of the Brain:

  • The brain is primarily supplied by two systems: the anterior circulation from the internal carotid arteries and the posterior circulation from the vertebral arteries. These arteries anastomose to form the Circle of Willis, providing collateral circulation between the anterior and posterior blood supplies.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

1. Internal Carotid Artery (ICA)

  • Branches:
    • Ophthalmic artery: Supplies the eye and orbital structures.
    • Posterior communicating artery (PCoA): Connects the internal carotid artery with the posterior cerebral artery.
    • Anterior cerebral artery (ACA): Supplies medial portions of the frontal and parietal lobes.
    • Middle cerebral artery (MCA): The largest branch, supplies the lateral aspect of the brain.
  • Internal carotid artery occlusion can cause ischemia in MCA or ACA territory or a watershed (border zone) infarct between these areas.

2. Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA)

  • Supply: Medial portions of the frontal and parietal lobes, including the superior portion of the motor and sensory cortices (leg area).
  • ACA Stroke:
    • Contralateral weakness and sensory loss, primarily affecting the lower limb (leg > arm).
    • Frontal lobe symptoms, including abulia (lack of initiative) and personality changes.
    • Urinary incontinence due to damage to the medial frontal lobes.

3. Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA)

  • Supply: Lateral surface of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes; basal ganglia; and internal capsule.
  • MCA Stroke:
    • Contralateral hemiparesis and hemisensory loss (face and arm > leg).
    • Aphasia if the dominant hemisphere (usually left) is affected.
    • Hemineglect if the non-dominant hemisphere is involved.
    • Homonymous hemianopia due to optic radiation involvement.

4. Posterior Cerebral Artery (PCA)

  • Supply: Occipital lobe (visual cortex), inferior temporal lobe, thalamus, and parts of the midbrain.
  • PCA Stroke:
    • Contralateral homonymous hemianopia (loss of the same side of the visual field in both eyes).
    • Thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome) if the thalamus is involved, leading to contralateral sensory loss followed by chronic pain.
    • Memory disturbances if the temporal lobe is affected.

5. Vertebral Arteries

  • Branches:
    • Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA): Supplies the cerebellum and lateral medulla.
    • PICA Stroke: Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome): Causes ipsilateral facial numbness, contralateral body numbness, ataxia, vertigo, and dysphagia.

6. Basilar Artery (Option D)

  • Supply: Pons, midbrain, occipital lobes, and cerebellum.
  • Branches:
    • Anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA): Supplies the cerebellum and parts of the brainstem.
    • Superior cerebellar artery (SCA): Supplies the superior cerebellum and parts of the midbrain.
    • Posterior cerebral arteries (PCA): Terminal branches that supply the occipital lobe.
  • Basilar Artery Stroke:
    • Locked-in syndrome: Quadriplegia with preserved consciousness and vertical eye movements due to damage to the pons.
    • Cranial nerve palsies (especially those involving eye movements like the oculomotor nerve).
    • Ataxia, vertigo, and dysarthria due to cerebellar involvement.

7. Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (AICA) (Option C)

  • Supply: Anterior inferior portion of the cerebellum, the lateral pons, and parts of the internal auditory canal.
  • AICA Stroke:
    • Ipsilateral ataxia, vertigo, hearing loss (due to involvement of the inner ear via the labyrinthine artery), facial weakness, and contralateral sensory loss.

8. Superior Cerebellar Artery (SCA) (Option B)

  • Supply: Superior part of the cerebellum and parts of the midbrain.
  • SCA Stroke:
    • Ipsilateral cerebellar ataxia, nausea, vomiting, and dysarthria.

9. Anterior Spinal Artery

  • Supply: Anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord and parts of the medulla.
  • Anterior Spinal Artery Syndrome:
    • Medial medullary syndrome: Results in contralateral hemiparesis, loss of proprioception, and ipsilateral hypoglossal nerve dysfunction (tongue deviation).

Clinical Features of Myasthenia Gravis

  • Fatigable muscle weakness: Muscle strength decreases with continued use, especially:
    • Later in the day
    • After exercise
  • No sensory or CNS involvement, distinguishing it from other neurological disorders.

Common Initial Symptoms

  • Ptosis (drooping eyelid)
  • Diplopia (double vision)

    • Chewing, swallowing, and speaking muscles

Affected Muscles

Ocular muscles

Mimics central eye movement disorders.

Cogan's lid twitch sign

Shoulder girdle muscles

Respiratory muscles

Weakness may cause respiratory failure and aspiration risks.
  • Ventilatory support: Essential for severe respiratory weakness.
  • Ineffective coughing: Increases aspiration risk.

Incorrect Options:

Lamberton-Eaton syndrome (Option B) involves muscle weakness and autonomic dysfunctions like a dry mouth. The muscle weakness improves with use in contrast to myasthenia gravis.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy (Option C) presents with weakness, difficulty in walking, fractures in ambulatory patients, lumbar lordosis, episodes of aspiration, nasal regurgitation, etc. The weakness does not improve on resting or exercise. It is also associated with intellectual disability and often presents in the first few years of life.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option D) presents with a characteristic malar rash with musculoskeletal symptoms like joint pain with synovitis of more than 2 joints leading to deformities.

question: A 30-year-old man presented with excessive fatiguability towards the end of the day that improved with rest. He also gives a history of ptosis and difficulty in speech and swallowing. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: D. Subacute combined degeneration of the cord
explanationHtml:
• The clinical features described in this case—sensory loss, weakness of limbs, angular stomatitis, loss of proprioception and vibration sensation, UMN-type weakness, and absent ankle reflexes—are highly suggestive of subacute combined degeneration of the cord (SACD), which is a condition caused by vitamin B12 deficiency.

Subacute Combined Degeneration of the Cord (SACD)

Neurological disorder due to vitamin B12 deficiency, causing demyelination of the posterior columns and lateral corticospinal tracts.

Etiology

Vitamin B12 Deficiency:

  • Pernicious anemia.
  • Gastrectomy or ileal resection.
  • Diphyllobothrium latum infestation.
  • Long-term use of metformin or PPIs.

Affected Areas

  • Posterior columns: Loss of proprioception and vibration sense.
  • Lateral corticospinal tracts: Spasticity and UMN-type weakness.

[[figure-1]]

Clinical Features

Sensory Symptoms:

  • Loss of proprioception and vibration sense: Begins in lower limbs, may progress to upper limbs.
  • Sensory ataxia: Positive Romberg’s test (difficulty standing with eyes closed).
  • Paresthesia: Tingling or numbness in extremities, typically in a glove-and-stocking distribution.

Motor Symptoms:

  • Upper motor neuron signs: Weakness, spasticity, and hyperreflexia.
  • Spastic weakness: Due to lateral corticospinal tract involvement.
  • Absent ankle reflex: A key finding, coexisting with UMN signs due to concurrent peripheral neuropathy.

Signs:

  • Lhermitte's Sign: Electric shock-like sensation down the spine on neck flexion.
  • Angular stomatitis
  • Optic neuropathy

Non-neurological Features:

  • Megaloblastic anemia: fatigue, pallor, glossitis, and jaundice.

Psychiatric Symptoms:

  • Irritability, dementia, psychosis.
  • Depression and memory loss.

Treatment

  • Vitamin B12 Replacement:
    • IM cyanocobalamin or hydroxocobalamin.
    • Oral B12 for maintenance.
  • Address underlying causes (e.g., anemia, parasitic infestation).

Extradural cord compression (Option A), caused by a space-occupying lesion (e.g., tumor or abscess), typically presents with localized back pain, radicular symptoms, and bladder/bowel dysfunction. It typically causes asymmetric neurological deficits, unlike the symmetrical loss of proprioception, vibration, and UMN signs seen in subacute combined degeneration. Additionally, it does not cause angular stomatitis, which is indicative of vitamin B12 deficiency

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Option B) primarily affects lower motor neurons and upper motor neurons. It presents with fasciculations, muscle cramps, muscle weakness, and atrophy, as well as bulbar palsy symptoms (dysarthria, dysphagia). Absence of sensory loss is a key differentiator here, as ALS does not typically affect sensory pathways.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) (Option C): MS is an autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system, affecting both white matter in the brain and spinal cord. It commonly presents with symptoms like paresthesia, optical neuritis, weakness, and gait disturbances. Lhermitte’s sign (pain down the back with neck flexion) and Uhthoff's sign (worsening of symptoms with heat) are classic, but the sensory loss and angular stomatitis here point more toward vitamin B12 deficiency rather than MS.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page: 3454, 568, 3411, 3412, 3462, 3463.

Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page: 651.

Explanation:

Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4, the enzyme that metabolizes Carbamazepine, leading to elevated carbamazepine levels and resulting in toxicity, with ataxia being a common symptom.

  • MOA: Inhibits high-frequency neuronal discharges and modulates voltage-gated sodium channels.
  • Uses:
    • Trigeminal neuralgia
    • GTCS (generalized tonic clonic seizures)
    • Partial seizures
    • Bipolar disorder.
  • Interactions:
    • Metabolism of carbamazepine is induced by phenobarbitone, phenytoin, and vice versa.
    • Erythromycin, fluoxetine, and isoniazid inhibit the metabolism of carbamazepine. (Option A)

Adverse Effects

Description

Neurotoxicity

Sedation, dizziness, vertigo, diplopia, and ataxia

Gastrointestinal Effects

Vomiting and diarrhoea occur with higher doses.

Acute Intoxication

Coma, convulsions, cardiovascular collapse.

Haematological

Agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia.

Hypersensitivity Reactions

Rashes, photosensitivity, hepatitis, lupus-like syndrome.

Water Retention and Hyponatremia

Due to enhanced antidiuretic hormone (ADH) action, it is more common in the elderly.

Teratogenicity

Increased incidence of minor fetal malformations.

Incorrect Options:

Erythromycin toxicity (Option B) is not the cause, as it rarely causes ataxia. Its main role here is as a CYP3A4 inhibitor, which increases carbamazepine levels and leads to toxicity.

Worsening of the underlying disease (Option C) can cause ataxia, but the timing after starting erythromycin points to a drug interaction, making this less likely.

A separate, unrelated neurological condition (Option D) is unlikely, as the timing with carbamazepine and erythromycin use suggests a drug interaction rather than a new, unrelated diagnosis.



Reference:

K D Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8th Edition, Page 442.

  • The clinical presentation of resting tremors, bradykinesia, and postural instability is characteristic of Parkinson's disease.
  • Lewy bodies are the pathological hallmark of this condition, representing eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions containing both neurofilaments and α-synuclein.
  • The disease is characterized by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to reduced striatal dopamine. These pathological changes manifest as the classic motor symptoms seen in this patient.

Pathophysiology of Parkinson’s Disease

Initial Damage

Damage to substantia nigra

Consequence

Loss of dopaminergic neurons in substantia nigra (pars compacta)

Effect

Decrease in dopamine production

Autopsy findings

Depigmentation of substantia nigra

Microscopic findings

Inclusion bodies called Lewy bodies

Composition of Lewy Bodies

Composed of α-synuclein (intracellular eosinophilic inclusions)

Hirano bodies (Option B): These inclusions are typically observed in ALS and Parkinsonism-dementia complex, not in classic Parkinson's disease.

Guarneri bodies (Option C): These are cytoplasmic inclusions found specifically in cells infected with smallpox or vaccinia virus. They have no association with movement disorders or neurological conditions like Parkinson's disease.

Negri bodies (Option D): These are eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions found in neurons infected with rabies virus, containing viral proteins and RNA. They are diagnostic of rabies infection.

  • When differentiating between tuberculoma and neurocysticercosis in cases of ring-enhancing lesions, NMR Spectroscopy (Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy) provides detailed metabolic and chemical information about the brain lesions. Option A - CBNAAT of CSF:

It confirms the presence of tuberculosis but does not provide biochemical information about the lesion itself.

Option B - PET Scan:

Option D - MRI aerial scan:

  • This term is not a standard diagnostic modality in clinical practice. MRI is used to visualize lesions and their characteristics but does not provide specific confirmation of tuberculoma or neurocysticercosis.   • Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome is a genetic condition characterized by the development of various tumors, including brain tumors (often hemangioblastomas), kidney tumors (renal cell carcinoma), and other tumors like pheochromocytomas. The family history of both brain and kidney tumors aligns with VHL syndrome. This condition is due to mutations in the VHL gene.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Neurofibromatosis: Neurofibromatosis (NF) has two main types: NF1 and NF2. NF1 is associated with cutaneous neurofibromas, café-au-lait spots, and optic nerve tumors, while NF2 is associated with bilateral vestibular schwannomas (acoustic neuromas) and other central nervous system tumors. Although brain tumors are present, NF does not typically present with kidney tumors.

Option B - Li-Fraumeni syndrome: Li-Fraumeni syndrome is a hereditary condition associated with a higher risk of several cancers, including breast cancer, sarcomas, brain tumors, and adrenal cortex tumors. While it is associated with brain tumors, it is not typically associated with kidney tumors. The syndrome is caused by mutations in the TP53 gene.

Option D - Churg-Strauss syndrome: Churg-Strauss syndrome, now known as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA), is an autoimmune condition that affects small and medium-sized blood vessels. It primarily involves respiratory symptoms, asthma, and vasculitis, but it is not associated with brain and kidney tumors.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has:

  • Left-sided arm and leg weakness → Contralateral hemiparesis
  • Right-sided facial paralysis → Ipsilateral CN VII involvement
  • Difficulty with horizontal eye movements → Ipsilateral PPRF/abducens nucleus involvement

This combination localizes the lesion to the dorsal pons (pontine tegmentum) and is characteristic of Foville syndrome.

Foville Syndrome

Site of Lesion: Dorsal pontine tegmentum

Structures commonly involved:

  • Abducens nucleus (CN VI)
  • Paramedian pontine reticular formation (PPRF)
  • Facial nerve fascicles (CN VII)
  • Corticospinal tract

Clinical Features

Ipsilateral Findings:

  • CN VI Nucleus / PPRF Lesion
    • Horizontal gaze palsy
    • Inability to look toward the side of the lesion
  • CN VII Fascicle Lesion: Ipsilateral LMN facial paralysis

Contralateral Findings: Corticospinal Tract Involvement - Contralateral hemiparesis/hemiplegia

Classical Triad

Structure Involved Clinical Finding
PPRF / Abducens nucleus Horizontal gaze palsy
Facial nerve fascicle Ipsilateral facial paralysis
Corticospinal tract Contralateral hemiparesis

Benedict Syndrome (Option B): Midbrain lesion involving oculomotor nerve (CN III) and red nucleus. Features:

  • Ipsilateral CN III palsy
  • Contralateral tremor/choreoathetosis/ataxia

Millard-Gubler Syndrome (Option C): Structures involved are facial nerve fascicle (CN VII), corticospinal tract, and sometimes abducens fascicle. Features:

  • Ipsilateral LMN facial palsy
  • Contralateral hemiparesis
  • Horizontal gaze palsy is not a defining feature, because the PPRF/abducens nucleus is spared.

Wallenberg Syndrome (Option D): It is a lateral medullary syndrome, usually due to PICA occlusion. Features

  • Dysphagia, hoarseness
  • Vertigo, nystagmus
  • Ipsilateral facial pain-temperature loss
  • Contralateral body pain-temperature loss
  • Horner syndrome

The characteristic CSF findings in bacterial meningitis are:

  • Markedly elevated white blood cell count (predominantly neutrophils)
  • Elevated protein
  • Decreased glucose (typically CSF glucose <40 mg/dL or CSF:serum glucose ratio <0.4)
  • Increased opening pressure

Bacterial Meningitis

Common Causative Organisms:

Age Group Common Organisms
Neonates Group B Streptococcus, E. coli, Listeria monocytogenes
Children Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis
Adults Streptococcus pneumoniae (most common), Neisseria meningitidis
Elderly (>50 years) S. pneumoniae, Listeria monocytogenes, Gram-negative bacilli
Post-neurosurgery Staphylococcus aureus, Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Pathophysiology: Bacterial invasion of the meninges leads to:

  • Intense neutrophilic inflammation
  • Increased blood-brain barrier permeability → ↑ protein
  • Consumption of glucose by bacteria and inflammatory cells → ↓ glucose
  • Increased intracranial pressure

Clinical Features

  • Fever
  • Neck stiffness
  • Altered mental status
  • Headache
  • Photophobia
  • Vomiting
  • Seizures
  • Positive Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs

Diagnosis:

Lumbar Puncture and CSF Analysis (Investigation of Choice)

  • Opening pressure ↑
  • Neutrophilic pleocytosis
  • Protein ↑
  • Glucose ↓
  • CSF:Serum glucose ratio <0.4

Confirmatory Tests

  • CSF Gram stain (rapid)
  • CSF culture (Gold Standard)
  • PCR-based tests (if available)
  • Blood cultures (often positive)

Neuroimaging: CT/MRI brain before LP if:

  • Papilledema
  • Focal neurological deficit
  • New-onset seizures
  • Immunocompromised patient

Treatment

Empiric Antibiotic Therapy

Indication Empirical Antibiotic Therapy
Preterm infants to infants < 1 month Ampicillin + Cefotaxime
Infants 1-3 months Ampicillin + Cefotaxime or Ceftriaxone
Immunocompetent children > 3 months and adults < 55 years Cefotaxime, Ceftriaxone, or Cefepime + Vancomycin
Adults > 55 years and adults of any age with alcoholism or other debilitating illnesses Ampicillin + Cefotaxime, Ceftriaxone, or Cefepime + Vancomycin
Hospital-acquired meningitis, post-traumatic or post-neurosurgery meningitis, neutropenic patients, or patients with impaired cell-mediated immunity Ampicillin + Ceftazidime or Meropenem + Vancomycin

Adjunctive Therapy: Dexamethasone (before or with first antibiotic dose)

Supportive Care

  • IV fluids
  • Antipyretics
  • Seizure management
  • Raised ICP management

correctAnswer: B. Plasmapheresis is not preferred in refractory cases
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Plasmapheresis is actually preferred in refractory cases of Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS), especially when the condition does not improve after initial treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG).
  • The standard treatment for GBS involves the use of either IVIG or plasmapheresis, depending on the patient's condition and response to initial therapy.

Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS)

  • Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute autoimmune disorder that affects the peripheral nervous system.
  • It often leads to ascending paralysis, starting from the lower limbs and spreading upwards.
  • GBS is considered a neurological emergency due to its potential to cause respiratory failure, autonomic dysfunction, and death without timely treatment.
  • Incidence: GBS occurs in 1–2 cases per 100,000 individuals annually.
  • Preceding Infections: In about two-thirds of AIDP cases, a preceding infection triggers an autoimmune response. Common infections include:
    • Campylobacter jejuni
    • Cytomegalovirus (CMV)
    • Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)
    • Zika virus
    • Influenza
  • These infections lead to molecular mimicry, where the immune system attacks nerve structures, particularly the myelin sheath, causing demyelination.

Variants of Guillain-Barré Syndrome:

Variant

Description

Autoantibodies

Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (AIDP)

Most common in Europe and North America, marked by segmental demyelination.

IgG Anti-GM1, IgG Anti-GQ1b

Axonal Variants (AMAN/AMSAN)

More prevalent in China and Japan, often linked with Campylobacter jejuni infection.

IgG Anti-GM1

Miller Fisher Syndrome

Characterized by a triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, and areflexia, the best-recognized variant.

Anti-GQ1b

Autoantibodies in Guillain-Barré Syndrome:

  • Diversity: GBS patients exhibit a range of autoantibodies targeting nerve cells and structures.
  • Common Antibodies: The most common are anti-ganglioside antibodies, which appear in up to 50% of GBS cases.
  • Prognostic Implications: The presence of anti-GM1 antibodies correlates with poorer clinical outcomes, especially in pure motor variants and Miller Fisher Syndrome.

Clinical Features:

Motor Symptoms
  • Progressive ascending paralysis (distal to proximal)
  • Areflexia
  • Weakness in legs, causing rubbery legs and instability to stand
  • Truncal paralysis, quadriplegia
  • Difficulty handling secretions leading to aspiration pneumonia
  • Diaphragmatic paralysis or bulbar palsy leading to respiratory failure within hours, Ventilatory support required in 30% of cases

Sensory Symptoms
  • Glove-and-stocking distribution paresthesias
  • Loss of proprioception
  • Pain in neck/shoulders similar to over-exercised muscles

Autonomic Symptoms
  • Orthostatic hypotension
  • Wide fluctuations of blood pressure
  • Arrhythmias
  • Neurogenic shock

Diagnostic Findings:

Category

Findings

Lumbar Puncture

Elevated CSF protein (100-1000 mg/dL) with normal WBC count (albuminocytologic dissociation)

CSF Timing

Normal findings (<48 hours), protein rise seen by 7 days

Electrodiagnostic Testing

Prolonged F-wave latencies, indicating demyelination (early in AIDP)

Brighton Criteria for Diagnosis of GBS:

Mnemonic: FAME

Flaccid Bilateral Weakness

Areflexia (Option A)

CytoAlbuminologic dissociation (Elevated CSF protein, normal WBC) (Option D)

Monophasic Illness (Symptoms develop over 12 hours to 28 days)

Electrodiagnostic findings consistent with demyelination

Treatment:

  • IVIG (Intravenous Immunoglobulin) (Option C):
    • First-line treatment.
    • It modulates the immune response and helps reduce inflammation.
  • Plasmapheresis (Plasma Exchange):
    • Equally effective as IVIG.
    • It removes harmful antibodies from the blood; preferred in refractory cases.
  • Glucocorticoids:
    • Not useful in GBS treatment, as they do not improve outcomes.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 3504

question: A patient presents with sudden-onset aphasia and right-sided arm weakness for the past 4 hours. After stabilizing the patient and confirming the diagnosis of ischemic stroke with urgent neuroimaging, which investigation is most appropriate to determine the etiology of this stroke?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient has:

  • Sudden-onset aphasia
  • Right upper limb weakness
  • Acute ischemic stroke (left MCA territory)

After confirming the diagnosis with urgent neuroimaging, the next step is to identify the source of embolism.

Atrial fibrillation is the most common cause of cardioembolic ischemic stroke.

TEE is superior to Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE)for detecting:

  • Left atrial appendage thrombus
  • Atrial thrombi
  • Patent foramen ovale (PFO)
  • Atrial septal defects
  • Valvular vegetations
  • Aortic arch atheroma

Therefore, TEE is the most sensitive investigation for identifying a cardioembolic source of stroke

Evaluation of Ischemic Stroke Etiology

Cardioembolic Causes

  • Atrial fibrillation (Most common)
  • Recent myocardial infarction
  • Dilated cardiomyopathy
  • Prosthetic valves
  • Infective endocarditis

Transthoracic Echocardiography (TTE) (Option A): Less sensitive than TEE. May miss:

  • Left atrial appendage thrombi
  • Small vegetations
  • PFO

Carotid Doppler (Option B): Detects extracranial carotid stenosis. Useful in atherosclerotic stroke. However, for embolic etiology (AF-related stroke), TEE is preferred.

MRI brain (Option D): Helps confirm infarct location and extent. Does not determine the source/etiology of the embolus



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3444, 3445, 1949.
question: A patient presents with sudden-onset aphasia and right-sided arm weakness for the past 4 hours. Which of the following investigations is most appropriate to determine the etiology of this stroke?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Mutism and altered sensorium after rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia is suggestive of Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome (Central Pontine Myelinolysis).

The investigation of choice is MRI Brain (Head), which demonstrates characteristic demyelinating lesions in the pons and sometimes extrapontine regions.

Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome (Central Pontine Myelinolysis)

A demyelinating disorder caused by rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia, resulting in osmotic injury to oligodendrocytes.

Pathophysiology

Chronic Hyponatremia: The brain adapts by losing intracellular osmolytes to prevent cerebral edema.

Rapid Sodium Correction: When serum sodium rises too quickly:

  • Water rapidly leaves brain cells
  • Oligodendrocytes are injured
  • Demyelination occurs
  • Most commonly in:
    • Central pons
    • Basal ganglia
    • Thalamus
    • Cerebellum

Safe Rate of Sodium Correction

Situation Maximum Correction
General population ≤8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours
High-risk patients (alcoholism, malnutrition, liver disease) ≤8 mEq/L in 24 hours

The patient's sodium increased:

  • 98 → 110 mEq/L
  • Increase = 12 mEq/L in 24 hours

This exceeds the recommended correction rate.

Clinical Features

Symptoms usually appear 2-6 days after correction, but suspicion should arise immediately when new neurological deficits develop.

Features

  • Dysarthria
  • Dysphagia
  • Mutism
  • Altered sensorium
  • Quadriparesis
  • Pseudobulbar palsy
  • Locked-in syndrome (severe cases)

Investigation of Choice: MRI Brain

Management

  • Correct hyponatremia slowly
  • Frequent sodium monitoring

Established ODS

  • Supportive care
  • Rehabilitation
  • Some cases may benefit from relowering sodium if recognized very early

LP for CSF Biochemistry (Option B): CSF analysis is not useful for diagnosing osmotic demyelination. Used for meningitis, encephalitis, and inflammatory CNS disorders

Brainstem Evoked Potentials (Option C): May show brainstem dysfunction but are not diagnostic and are not the preferred investigation.

EEG (Option D): Useful for seizures, non-convulsive status epilepticus, encephalopathy assessment. Does not diagnose central pontine myelinolysis.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2348, 2349.
question: Patient came with severe headache and seizures. Sodium on admission was 98 meq/L. We have started correction with 3% saline and now after 24 hours of infusion sodium is 110 meq/L. Patient develops mutism and altered sensorium. Which investigation will you perform now?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The presence of Gram-negative diplococci in the CSF is characteristic of Neisseria meningitidis, a common cause of acute bacterial meningitis.

  • Rifampicin is used for chemoprophylaxis of close contacts of patients with meningococcal meningitis.
  • Alternative agents include:
    • Ciprofloxacin (single-dose regimen in adults)
    • Ceftriaxone (preferred in pregnancy)
  • Because meningococci colonise the nasopharynx and spread through respiratory secretions, close contacts of affected patients are at increased risk of developing invasive disease.
  • Therefore, chemoprophylaxis is recommended to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage and prevent secondary cases.
  • Chemoprophylaxis is recommended for:
    • Household contacts
    • Daycare contacts
    • Individuals directly exposed to oral secretions (e.g., kissing, mouth-to-mouth resuscitation)
    • Healthcare workers with significant exposure to respiratory secretions

Amoxicillin (Option A): Used for infections such as Listeria monocytogenes meningitis, but does not eradicate meningococcal nasopharyngeal carriage and is not used for prophylaxis.

Doxycycline (Option B): Has no established role in chemoprophylaxis of meningococcal disease.

Ethambutol (Option C): An antitubercular drug used in the treatment of tuberculosis and has no role in meningococcal prophylaxis.

Explanation:

  • The typical hand movements shown in the image are known as asterixis or "flapping tremors. These characteristic hand movements are seen in patients of toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, potentially due to hypercarbia.

The 3 causes of toxic-metabolic encephalopathy include:

  • Hepatic encephalopathy (Increased level of ammonia)
  • Uremic encephalopathy (Increased level of urea)
  • Hypercarbia (Increased level of CO2)

This condition occurs frequently in patients with chronic CO2 retention, particularly those receiving oxygen therapy for emphysema or chronic pulmonary disease. The flapping movement is elicited by having patients extend their arms and bend their wrists back.

Thyrotoxicosis (Option A) presents with fine tremors. The tremor pattern is distinctly different from the coarse flapping movements seen in asterixis.

Hemiballismus (Option C) manifests with wild, flinging movements at the shoulder joint. These movements are abrupt and unilateral compared to the bilateral wrist movements seen in asterixis.

Hypoxia (Option D) typically causes disorientation and mental status changes with O2 saturation <90%. While it can cause neurological symptoms, it does not specifically produce the characteristic flapping tremor seen in this case.

question: The patient is having the following hand movements. In which of the following conditions would this be seen?

correctAnswer: C. Loss of color perception and depth perception is proportional to visual loss
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In optic neuritis (often seen in MS), color vision (especially red) and depth perception can be disproportionately affected compared to overall visual acuity. A patient may have mild visual acuity loss but significant dyschromatopsia (color desaturation) or depth perception difficulties.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) Clinical features:

  • Abrupt or insidious onset of symptoms

Sensory symptoms
  • Paresthesias: tingling, prickling sensations, “pins and needles,” or painful burning.
  • Hypesthesia: reduced sensation, numbness, or a “dead” feeling.
  • Unpleasant sensations: feelings that body parts are swollen, wet, raw, or tightly wrapped.
  • Pain is a common symptom of MS.

Optic neuritis (ON)

  • Diminished visual acuity.
  • Decreased colour perception in the central field of vision.
  • May progress to severe visual loss.
  • Periorbital pain.
  • Fundoscopic examination: normal or optic disc swelling (papillitis), pallor of the optic disc (optic atrophy).

Weakness of the limbs
  • Loss of strength, speed, dexterity, and gait disturbance.
  • Exercise-induced weakness is a characteristic symptom of MS.
  • Upper motor neuron type weakness accompanied by other pyramidal signs.

Facial weakness
  • Lesion in the pons may resemble idiopathic Bell’s palsy.

Spasticity
  • Spontaneous and movement-induced muscle spasms.
  • Painful spasms.

Visual blurring
  • Due to ON (optic neuritis) or diplopia.
  • Diplopia is caused by internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) or palsy of the sixth cranial nerve.
  • Bilateral INO is particularly suggestive of MS.
  • Other gaze disturbances in MS:
    • Horizontal gaze palsy
    • One-and-a-half syndrome (horizontal gaze palsy plus an INO)
    • Acquired pendular nystagmus

Ataxia
  • Cerebellar tremors.
  • Cerebellar dysarthria.

Vertigo
  • Lesion in the brainstem.

Ancillary symptoms

Paroxysmal symptoms

Brief duration (10s to 2 min), high frequency (5–40 episodes per day), no change of consciousness or change in background electroencephalogram during episodes, and a self-limited course.

Lhermitte’s symptom

An electric shock-like sensation that radiates down the back into the legs.

Typically induced by flexion or other movements of the neck.

Trigeminal neuralgia, hemifacial spasm, and glossopharyngeal neuralgia

Demyelinating lesions involve the root entry or exit zone of the fifth, seventh, and ninth cranial nerve, respectively.

Facial myokymia

Persistent rapid flickering contractions of the facial musculature

Slow spread of contraction across the face.

Heat sensitivity

Uthoff symptoms: Neurological symptoms develop from heat exposure, such as steam baths and saunas.

Bladder dysfunction

Present in >90% of MS patients.

Detrusor hyperreflexia.

Detrusor sphincter dyssynergia - hesitancy, urinary retention, overflow incontinence, and recurrent infection.

Bowel dysfunction

Constipation, faecal urgency or bowel incontinence.

Cognitive dysfunction

Memory loss.

Impaired attention.

Psychiatric symptom

Depression.

Fatigue

90% of patients experience fatigue.

It causes work-related disability.

Incorrect Options:

70% of patients with MS develop optic neuritis during course of illness (Option A): Optic neuritis is a common presenting symptom and complication of MS. Around 70% of patients develop it at some point during the disease. It often causes painful vision loss, especially on eye movement.

Oral steroids are given for acute relapses (Option B): High-dose intravenous steroids (e.g., methylprednisolone) are preferred for acute relapses, but oral steroids (like oral prednisolone or tapering doses after IV) can also be used in certain cases. So, oral steroids are indeed part of acute relapse management, especially during recovery or tapering phases.

Examination of fundus can be normal and can show papillitis (Option D): In optic neuritis, retrobulbar neuritis often shows a normal fundus because the inflammation is behind the globe. However, in some cases, papillitis (optic disc swelling) may be seen. Both scenarios are possible in MS-related optic neuritis.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principle of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 3462, 3463, 3468-3474.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • SAH often presents with sudden severe headache, vomiting, photophobia, and meningeal signs. CT may miss early or small bleeds, and CSF can be normal if bleeding is minimal or delayed. Hydrocephalus suggests impaired CSF drainage due to subarachnoid blood.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage
  • Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH): Blood accumulation in the subarachnoid space.
  • Causes: Often due to aneurysm rupture (~85%) or trauma.
  • Non-traumatic SAH is most commonly caused by the rupture of a saccular aneurysm.
  • Clinical Impact: High mortality and morbidity; often presents with a sudden, severe headache (worst headache of life).
  • Complications: Seizures, vasospasm, hydrocephalus, and delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI).

Epidemiology:

  • Age/ Gender: Most of the SAH occurs between age of 40-60, mean rupture age 50-55 and slightly more prevalent in females.
  • Risk Factors: Smoking and history of ruptured aneurysms increase SAH risk.

Etiology:

  • Aneurysmal SAH (aSAH):
    • Risk Factors: Hypertension, smoking, family history, alcohol use, sympathomimetic drugs, and estrogen deficiency.
    • Rupture Risk: (Option D)
      • Age >60
      • Posterior circulation aneurysms
      • Atherosclerosis
      • Aneurysm size
        • Aneurysms <10 mm: ~0.1% annual rupture risk.
        • Aneurysms ≥10 mm: 0.5–1% annual rupture risk.
        • Giant aneurysms (>2.5 cm): ~6% rupture risk in first year.
      • Family history
      • Previous SAH
      • ADPKD
  • Nonaneurysmal SAH (NASAH):
    • Perimesencephalic NASAH: Localized blood in perimesencephalic cisterns, normal angiography, benign course.
    • Occult Aneurysm: Small aneurysms missed on initial angiography, detectable on repeat imaging.
    • Vascular Malformations: Includes arteriovenous malformations (AVM) and dural arteriovenous fistulae. Treated with surgery or endovascular interventions.
    • Intracranial Arterial Dissection: Diagnosed by angiography, causes severe bleeding, treated with surgery or endovascular methods.
    • Other Causes: Cocaine abuse, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, cerebral venous thrombosis, sickle cell disorders, moyamoya disease, cerebral vasculitis, bleeding disorders.

Pathophysiology:

  • Hemodynamic Stress: Central to intracranial aneurysm formation, especially at arterial bifurcations.
  • Aneurysm Rupture: Causes neurological damage through compression of adjacent brain tissue and ischemia from reduced blood flow.
    • Mechanisms: Hemodynamic stress and inflammation (matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-mediated degradation of extracellular matrix) weaken the arterial wall, promoting aneurysm formation and rupture.
    • Inflammatory Response: Macrophages and smooth muscle cells drive these degenerative processes.

Clinical features:

  • Sudden, severe "thunderclap" headache (hallmark)
  • Loss of consciousness: Increase in intracranial pressure.
    • It presses the reticular activating system.
    • Leads to the development of stupor and coma.
  • Worst headache of the life
  • Nuchal rigidity is due to blood but no fever.
  • Vomiting
  • Sentinel bleed: microbleeds from the berry Aneurysm

Investigations:

  • Non-contrast CT head: "Hyperdense" blood in the subarachnoid space ("SAH star")
  • Lumbar puncture: Xanthochromia (yellowish discoloration) of CSF after 12 hours
  • Cerebral angiography: Identifies aneurysms or AVMs
  • CT angiography or MR angiography: Non-invasive methods to detect vascular abnormalities

Incorrect Options:

Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) (Option A): Presents with triad: dementia, gait disturbance, urinary incontinence—not acute meningeal symptoms.

Bacterial Meningitis (Option B): Would show abnormal CSF: high protein, low glucose, and neutrophilic pleocytosis.

Viral Encephalitis (Option C): Presents with altered sensorium, seizures, and abnormal CSF (lymphocytic pleocytosis), not just headache and normal CSF.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Edition, Page 3353, 3354

question: Which of the following is one of the earliest presenting symptoms in a patient with Multiple Sclerosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The basal ganglia, particularly the putamen, are the most common site of spontaneous hypertensive intracerebral haemorrhage (ICH).

  • Haemorrhage in this region frequently involves or compresses the adjacent posterior limb of the internal capsule, through which the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts pass.
  • As a result, patients classically present with contralateral weakness of the face, arm, and leg.
  • Common clinical manifestations of basal ganglia haemorrhage include:
    • Contralateral hemiparesis involving the face, arm, and leg
    • Contralateral hemisensory deficits
    • Aphasia (dominant hemisphere involvement)
    • Hemineglect (nondominant hemisphere involvement)
    • Headache, nausea, vomiting, and decreased consciousness in larger haemorrhages
  • Hypertension is the most important risk factor, and rupture of small penetrating arteries supplying the basal ganglia is the usual mechanism.

[[figure-1]]

Midbrain (Option B): Midbrain haemorrhages typically produce crossed brainstem syndromes, characterised by ipsilateral cranial nerve deficits (especially oculomotor nerve palsy) with contralateral motor weakness.

Pons (Option C): Pontine haemorrhage usually presents with coma, pinpoint pupils, quadriplegia, gaze abnormalities, and respiratory dysfunction. Severe brainstem signs predominate rather than isolated contralateral hemiparesis.

Medulla (Option D): Medullary haemorrhages are rare and generally produce crossed neurological deficits involving cranial nerves and long tracts, rather than pure contralateral weakness of the face, arm, and leg.



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11889578/
question: A patient presents with contralateral face, arm, and leg weakness. NCCT shows intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). What is the most likely location of the CNS bleed?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hypsarrhythmia is the characteristic EEG finding of West syndrome (Infantile Epileptic Spasms Syndrome, IESS).

  • The classical triad consists of:
    • Infantile spasms
    • Hypsarrhythmia on EEG
    • Developmental delay or developmental regression
  • Infantile spasms typically occur during the first year of life and often present as clusters of brief flexor, extensor, or mixed spasms.
  • ACTH (Adrenocorticotropic Hormone) is considered a standard first-line treatment for infantile spasms and has been shown to be superior to vigabatrin for short-term spasm control in most patients.
  • ACTH suppresses spasms, improves EEG abnormalities, and may improve developmental outcomes when initiated early.

[[figure-1]]

Vigabatrin (Option B): Vigabatrin is an effective treatment for infantile spasms and is particularly effective in children with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), where it is considered the drug of choice. However, for most other cases of West syndrome, ACTH remains the preferred initial therapy.

Valproate (Option C): Valproate is used for several generalised and focal epilepsies, but is not considered a first-line treatment for infantile spasms and is less effective than ACTH or vigabatrin in controlling spasms.

Carbamazepine (Option D): Carbamazepine is mainly used for focal seizures and may aggravate certain generalised epileptic syndromes. It has no established role in the treatment of infantile spasms



Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537251/
question: The infant is being evaluated for recurrent episodes of seizures. ECG shows Hypsarrhythmia. Which drug is preferred for management?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Diffuse axonal injury (DAI):

Explanation:

  • Diffuse axonal injury is a primary brain injury caused by shearing forces during high-velocity trauma (e.g., RTA).
  • These forces disrupt axons in the white matter, corpus callosum, and brainstem.
  • On initial imaging, NCCT may be normal or show only tiny petechial hemorrhages; the condition is often diagnosed clinically or via MRI.
  • Histopathology (or biopsy) reveals multiple punctate hemorrhages in deep white matter tracts.
  • DAI often leads to immediate or prolonged coma without a lucid interval and carries a high mortality rate.

[[figure-1]]

Incorrect Options:

Ischemic injury (Option A): Usually presents with territorial infarcts and hypoxic changes, not punctate hemorrhages in white matter.

Intraventricular bleeding (Option C): Would be evident on CT and localized to ventricular system, not diffuse white matter punctate hemorrhages.

Subdural hemorrhage (Option D): Characterized by crescent-shaped collection on CT, caused by tearing of bridging veins — not microscopic hemorrhages.



Reference:

question: A patient had a road traffic accident (RTA). NCCT head was normal on admission. The patient later died after several days in the ICU due to coma. Brain biopsy revealed multiple punctate hemorrhages. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Horner syndrome:

Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of miosis, anhidrosis, mild ptosis, and a persistent small pupil even in low light is suggestive of Horner syndrome. Ptosis is a result of the weakness of Müller muscle and miosis due to the unopposed action of the sphincter pupillae with resultant anisocoria.
  • Pancoast tumor can compress the sympathetic nerves, leading to the classic triad of symptoms seen in Horner syndrome: ptosis, miosis (constricted pupil), and ipsilateral facial anhidrosis (lack of sweating).

Acquired Neurogenic Ptosis: Acquired ptosis with drooping of the upper eyelid caused by a disruption in the nerve supply to the muscles responsible for elevating the eyelid.

Causes:

  • Third Cranial (Oculomotor) Nerve Palsy: The third nerve can be damaged by trauma, ischemia, infection, tumor, or compression, causing ptosis and diplopia.Oculomotor nerve palsy causes ptosis as it supplies the levator palpebrae superioris muscle.

The ptotic eyelid can be elevated with a frontalis sling or levator aponeurosis advancement.

  • Horner's Syndrome: Involves a lesion in the sympathetic pathway, affecting the Müller’s muscle, leading to mild ptosis accompanied by miosis (pupil constriction) and anhidrosis (loss of sweating).
  • Ophthalmoplegic migraine
  • Multiple Sclerosis

Diagnosis:

  • Topical apraclonidine test is now considered the test of choice. Apraclonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that also acts as a very weak alpha 1-adrenergic agonist; when topically applied in Horner’s syndrome, it causes dilation of the affected pupil and possibly lid elevation, without change to the normal pupil.

Incorrect Options:

Adie’s tonic people (Option A) It is a unilateral condition and is characterized by anisocoria (different size of pupil) and direct light reflex is sluggish or absent.

Marcus gunn pupil (Option C) Aka relative afferent pupillary defect is characterized by paradoxical dilatation of both the pupil when light is flashed on the diseased eye.

Argyll Robertson pupil (Option D) It is a specific sign of late-stage syphilis. The bilaterally small pupils do not constrict when exposed to bright light.
question: What is the probable diagnosis for a patient who exhibits miosis, anhidrosis, mild ptosis, and a persistent small pupil even in low light conditions?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B – Oxygen:

Explanation:

  • High-flow 100% oxygen is the most effective acute abortive therapy for cluster headaches, rapidly relieving pain within 15–20 minutes in most cases. It is safe, well-tolerated, and works faster than most medications.
  • Cluster headaches are severe unilateral headaches with autonomic features. Acute attacks require rapid-acting treatment — high-flow oxygen via a non-rebreather mask or subcutaneous sumatriptan are first-line.
  • Oxygen relieves pain by causing vasoconstriction and possibly modulating trigeminal-autonomic reflexes. Prophylaxis (e.g., verapamil, lithium) is started later to prevent recurrences, but during an acute attack, oxygen is the gold standard.

Cluster Headache:

Feature

Cluster Headache

Pain

Severe, unilateral, retro-orbital/temporal

Duration

15–180 minutes per attack

Frequency

Up to 8/day during cluster periods

Autonomic signs

Lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, ptosis, miosis

Triggers

Alcohol, histamine, nitroglycerin during cluster period

Acute treatment

100% O₂ (12–15 L/min), subcutaneous sumatriptan

Prophylaxis

Verapamil (drug of choice), lithium, topiramate

Incorrect Options:

Verapamil (Option A): Used for prophylaxis, not acute attack.

Lithium (Option C): Alternative prophylactic agent in refractory cases.

Topiramate (Option D): Used in prophylaxis for migraine and sometimes cluster headache, not acute management.
question: A 30-year-old male presents with deep-seated retro-orbital pain of cluster headache. What is the best management?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Demyelination of A, B-fibers:

Explanation:

Guillain–Barré Syndrome (GBS) is an acute immune-mediated polyneuropathy, most often triggered by infections like Campylobacter jejuni. It primarily affects myelinated large-diameter motor and sensory fibers (A and B fibers), leading to weakness and areflexia.

A- and B-fibers are myelinated nerve fibers responsible for motor function and some sensory modalities. In GBS, autoantibodies and immune cells attack the myelin sheath, impairing conduction. This demyelination disrupts both motor signals (causing weakness) and reflex arcs (causing areflexia).

Guillain–Barré Syndrome:

  • Trigger: Often post-infectious (e.g., Campylobacter jejuni, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma).
  • Pathophysiology: Autoimmune-mediated demyelination of peripheral nerves and nerve roots.
  • Clinical features: Symmetrical ascending weakness, areflexia, minimal sensory loss; may involve cranial nerves (bilateral facial palsy).
  • Complications: Respiratory muscle involvement → respiratory failure; autonomic instability.
  • Diagnosis: CSF shows albuminocytologic dissociation (↑ protein, normal cell count); NCS shows slowed conduction velocity.
  • Treatment: IVIG or plasmapheresis; avoid steroids.
  • Prognosis: Most recover fully, but some have residual deficits.

Fiber types affected in GBS:

Fiber Type

Myelination

Function

A fibers

Myelinated

Motor + sensory

B fibers

Myelinated

Preganglionic autonomic

C fibers

Unmyelinated

Pain + temperature

Incorrect Options:

Demyelination of B-fibers (Option B) – B-fibers are affected, but not in isolation; A-fibers are also involved.

Demyelination of the spinal cord (Option C) – GBS is a peripheral neuropathy, not a central spinal cord disorder.

Cord inflammation (Option D) – Suggestive of myelitis, which presents with UMN signs and sensory level, not typical in GBS.
question: A patient presents with symmetrical leg weakness and areflexia. He had developed diarrhoea 2 weeks ago. He was diagnosed as having GBS. What is the cause?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - ALS (Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis)

Explanation:

ALS is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder involving both upper motor neurons (UMN) and lower motor neurons (LMN), leading to weakness, hypertonia, and fasciculations, while sparing the sensory system. The presence of UMN signs (hypertonia) and LMN signs (fasciculations) together is characteristic.

ALS affects motor neurons in the motor cortex, brainstem, and spinal cord.

  • UMN involvement → spasticity, hyperreflexia
  • LMN involvement → muscle atrophy, fasciculations, weakness.
  • Sensory pathways are usually preserved, helping differentiate from other neuropathies.
  • Onset is insidious and relentlessly progressive, leading to respiratory failure.

ALS:

  • Epidemiology: Usually presents in middle age; more common in men.
  • Pathophysiology: Degeneration of corticospinal tracts (UMN) and anterior horn cells (LMN).
  • Clinical features: Combination of UMN + LMN signs in multiple regions, no sensory loss.
  • Diagnosis: Clinical (exclusion of mimics), EMG shows denervation and reinnervation.
  • Prognosis: Progressive; most patients die within 3–5 years from respiratory failure.
  • Treatment: Riluzole (glutamate inhibitor) modestly prolongs survival; supportive care is key.

LMN and UMN signs in ALS:

Feature

UMN signs

LMN signs

Tone

Spasticity

Hypotonia

Reflexes

Hyperreflexia, Babinski+

Hyporeflexia

Muscle bulk

Normal initially

Atrophy

Fasciculations

Rare

Common

Incorrect Options:

Spinal muscular atrophy (Option B) – Pure LMN disease; no UMN signs like hypertonia.

question: A 35-year-old female with progressive limb weakness for the past 1 year. On examination, muscle fasciculations and hypertonia are noted, and the sensory system is intact. What is the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Thrombolysis:

  • Thrombolysis, also known as clot-busting therapy, involves administering medications to dissolve blood clots. It is typically used in the treatment of ischemic strokes (caused by a blood clot blocking a blood vessel in the brain). However, in this case, the patient's presentation and brain imaging findings suggest a hemorrhagic stroke, which is characterized by bleeding into the brain tissue. Administering thrombolytic therapy in a hemorrhagic stroke could exacerbate the bleeding and worsen the patient's condition, which is why thrombolysis is contraindicated in this scenario.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - BP Control: High blood pressure (hypertension) is a risk factor for both ischemic and hemorrhagic strokes. In the context of a hemorrhagic stroke, controlling blood pressure is crucial to prevent further bleeding and manage the patient's overall condition. So, BP control is an essential part of the management.

Option C - Edema Management: Brain edema (swelling) can occur following a stroke, and it can lead to increased intracranial pressure, potentially causing further damage. Edema management might involve measures such as elevating the head of the bed, using osmotic agents, and closely monitoring the patient's neurological status. This is an important aspect of stroke management.

Option D - Elective Hyperventilation: Elective hyperventilation, which involves intentionally increasing breathing rate, can lead to a decrease in carbon dioxide levels in the blood. This can lead to constriction of blood vessels in the brain (vasoconstriction) and reduction of cerebral blood flow. While it was previously used in the management of elevated intracranial pressure, it is generally not recommended due to the risk of worsening cerebral ischemia. Instead, other methods for intracranial pressure control are preferred.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The patient's presentation of difficulty expressing emotions, lack of participation in daily activities, resting tremors, and rigidity is highly suggestive of Parkinson's disease.

Parkinson's disease results from degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, leading to dysfunction of the basal ganglia motor circuits.

The basal ganglia is a group of nuclei in the brain involved in motor control, as well as cognitive and emotional functions. The degeneration of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra disrupts the communication between the basal ganglia and other parts of the brain, resulting in the characteristic motor and non-motor symptoms seen in Parkinson's disease.

Parkinson's Disease

  • Parkinson's disease is caused by degeneration of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta of the midbrain, resulting in dysfunction of the basal ganglia motor circuits.
  • This degeneration results in reduced dopamine production, which affects the motor control pathways, leading to the hallmark symptoms of rigidity, tremors, and bradykinesia.

Clinical Features

Motor Features Other Motor Features Non-Motor Features
  • Tremor at rest ("pill-rolling"): Involuntary, rhythmic shaking that occurs when the muscles are relaxed.
  • Rigidity (lead-pipe/cogwheel): Increased muscle tone causing resistance to passive movement.
  • Bradykinesia: Slowness of movement, making daily tasks more difficult.
  • Postural instability
  • Micrographia
  • Masked facies (hypomimia)
  • Reduced eye blinking
  • Drooling
  • Soft voice (hypophonia)
  • Dysphagia
  • Freezing
  • Falling
  • Cognitive impairment/dementia
  • Visual hallucinations
  • Depression
  • Constipation
  • REM sleep behavior disorder
  • Autonomic dysfunction

Hippocampus (Option B): The hippocampus is primarily involved in memory formation, learning, and spatial navigation, and lesions here can lead to issues with memory and emotional behavior. However, it is not primarily associated with the motor symptoms seen in Parkinson's disease.

Cerebellum (Option C): The cerebellum is responsible for coordinating voluntary movement and balance. Lesions in the cerebellum typically cause ataxia, intention tremors, and gait disturbances, but not the resting tremors or rigidity characteristic of Parkinson's disease.

Premotor cortex (Option D): The premotor cortex is involved in the planning and preparation of movements, particularly in coordinating postural adjustments for voluntary movements. While damage here can affect motor planning, it is not typically associated with the specific motor symptoms seen in Parkinson's disease.

  • Disinhibition and deficits in concentration, orientation, judgment
  • May have reemergence of primitive reflexes.

  • Eyes look away from the side of the lesion.

    • Parkinson disease: Resting tremor, rigidity, bradykinesi a

    • Athetosis: Slow writhing movements

Mammillary Bodies (Bilateral)
  • Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome: Confusion, ataxia, nystagmus, ophthalmoplegia, memory loss (anterograde and retrograde amnesia), confabulation, personality changes.

  • Klüver-Bucy syndrome: Disinhibited behavior (eg, hyperphagia, hypersexuality, hyperorality).
  • Eg: HSV-1 encephalitis

  • Parinaud syndrome: Paralysis of conjugate vertical gaze (rostral interstitial nucleus also involved).
  • Eg: Stroke, hydrocephalus, pinealoma.

Reticular Activating System (Midbrain)
  • Reduced levels of arousal and wakefulness (eg, coma).

Cerebellar Hemisphere
  • Intention tremor, limb ataxia, loss of balance; damage to cerebellum → Ipsilateral deficits; fall toward side of lesion.
  • (Cerebellar hemispheres are laterally located and affect lateral limbs)

Cerebellar Vermis
  • Truncal ataxia
  • Dysarthria
  • (Vermis is centrally located and affects central body)

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The inability to identify objects and the ability to determine the colour, texture, and shape of objects refer to visual agnosia, which is caused by lesions involving the temporal lobe.

Features of Left Temporal Lobe Stroke

Features of Right Temporal Lobe Stroke
  • Impaired language and memory: Difficulty with spoken language and remembering verbal information.
  • Fluent (Wernicke’s) aphasia: Fluent speech with incorrect words, affecting language comprehension.
  • Poor visual memory and spatial awareness: Difficulty recognizing visual patterns and spatial information.
  • Prosopagnosia: Inability to recognize faces, including familiar ones.

General Features of Temporal Lobe Stroke
  • Poor memory: Difficulty recalling memories and learning new information.
  • Prosopagnosia: Trouble recognizing faces and objects.
  • Fluent aphasia: Specifically in left-sided strokes, affecting speech fluency but with incorrect word use.
  • Visual perception difficulties: Challenges with interpreting the visual field and surroundings.
  • Trouble processing sound: Inability to differentiate or process sounds correctly.
  • Visual agnosia: Inability to recognize visually presented objects despite otherwise normal visual field, acuity, colour vision, brightness, discrimination, language, and memory.
  • Emotional and behavioural changes: Varying behaviours due to damage to the amygdala, such as aggression, passiveness, or difficulty interpreting facial cues.

Incorrect Options:

Lesions in a patient's Frontal lobe (Option A) can lead to certain symptoms such as trouble with learning, deficits in visual-motor function, executive dysfunction and problems with attention (planning, focusing, and inhibition).

Parietal lobe (Option B): Right - Damage to this area can cause visuospatial deficits (e.g., the patient may have difficulty finding their way around new, or even familiar, places).

Parietal Lobe, Left: Damage to this area may disrupt a person's ability to understand spoken and/or written language.

Unilateral Occipital lobe (Option D) lesion causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia. It is a visual field defect on the same side of both eyes contralateral to the site of the lesion - lesions of the occipital lobe due to the posterior cerebral artery infarct cause homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

question: A 30-year-old patient presents with high-grade fever for the past week. On examination neck stiffness and Kernig's sign were positive. CSF analysis showed lymphocytosis protein - 8 g/L, glucose - 20 mg/dl while RBS = 140 mg/dl. What is your diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - (IgG):

  • Acute Inflammatory Demyelinating Polyneuropathy (AIDP) is commonly known as Guillain-Barré Syndrome (GBS). GBS is an autoimmune disorder where the immune system mistakenly attacks the peripheral nervous system, leading to inflammation and demyelination of nerves. In the context of GBS, the antibodies produced against components of peripheral nerves belong primarily to the IgG class.
  • IgG is the correct answer because IgG antibodies are the most involved immunoglobulins in GBS. These antibodies target myelin, which is the protective covering of nerve fibers, leading to impaired nerve conduction and the characteristic symptoms of muscle weakness, tingling, and paralysis seen in GBS patients.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - IgM: While IgM antibodies can be involved in certain autoimmune diseases, they are not typically associated with GBS. IgM antibodies are usually associated with early immune responses and are not as commonly found in autoimmune disorders affecting the nervous system.

Option C - IgE: IgE antibodies are primarily associated with allergic reactions and parasitic infections. They are not a characteristic component of the immune response seen in GBS.

Option D - IgA: IgA antibodies are mainly found in mucosal secretions and play a role in defending mucous membranes. They are not typically associated with the immune response involved in GBS.
