question: Which of the following vasculitis syndromes is not classified as an ANCA-associated vasculitis according to the Chapel Hill Classification?

correctAnswer: B. Glomerulonephritis, hematochezia and palpable purpura
explanationHtml:
Option B: Glomerulonephritis, hematochezia and palpable purpura

  • Henoch – schonlein purpura:
    • Henoch- Schonlein Purpura is a type of vasculitis that affects small vessels.
    • It is also called Non-thrombocytopenic purpura.
    • Henoch Schonlein purpura is the most prevalent form of childhood systemic vasculitis.
    • It affects males more than females.
    • Children are affected more than adults.
  • Symptoms:
    • The following features characterize it:
    • It is a form of vasculitis with glomerulonephritis as a key feature.
    • Glomerulonephritis can present as proteinuria, hematuria, and acute renal failure.
    • Gastrointestinal presentation of HSP includes intermittent, colicky abdominal pain and hemorrhage into the bowels, which presents as hematochezia.
    • Skin involvement in HSP presents as blotchy purple spots on the skin, the purpura.
    • Purpura on the skin is palpable.
    • There is also non-deforming polyarthritis, marked at the hips, knees, and ankles.
  • Diagnosis:
    • On skin biopsy, there is leukocytoclastic vasculitis with IgA and C3 deposition in the vessel wall.
  • Treatment:
    • Treatment for Henoch Schonlein purpura is usually supportive.
    • Steroids are also used for severe or renal diseases.

Option A: Erythromelalgia

  • Erythromelalgia is a very rare condition.
  • It has features of severe, burning pain in the limbs it affects.
  • It has diffuse red discolouration but does not necessarily have a pattern.
  • There is no rash of Erythromelalgia.
  • Erythromelalgia is seen in conditions such as thrombocythemia and polycythemia Vera.
  • In some cases, it can be treated with Aspirin.

Option C: Lhermitte's sign

  • Lhermitte's sign is also called Lhermitte's phenomenon.
  • It is a feeling of a gradient-like electric sensation that goes down the spine upon flexion of the neck.
  • It is seen in cases of Multiple sclerosis.
  • It is a sequela of neurologic disorders.
  • Multiple sclerosis is a chronic relapsing and remitting type of autoimmune disease.
  • In multiple sclerosis, the myelin destruction and destruction of oligodendrocytes are the main pathologies.

Option D: Virchow's triad

  • Virchow's triad includes three factors:
  • Intravascular damage of vessels, stasis in blood flow, hypercoagulable state.
  • It may lead a person to develop thrombosis of veins
  • Thrombosis means there is a formation of clots in blood vessels.
  • Virchow's triad determines whether a person is at risk of developing thrombotic disorders.
  • Thromboembolic events could include cerebrovascular disorders, pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis.


Reference:

Harrison 20th edition page no : 2586
question: A 4-year-old kid comes to your clinic with his mother. His mother complains that he has had an acute fever and abdominal pain for 2 days. You examine the child and find out that the skin on the buttocks and extensor surfaces of arms and legs are covered with small round patches of blue-purple discoloration. You also find out that the kid has hematuria. You have diagnosed it as a case of Henoch Schonlein Purpura. Henoch-Schonlein purpura, a vasculitis, is characterized by which of the following symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A young woman with arm claudication, unequal blood pressures, diminished pulse, and elevated ESR indicates an inflammatory large-vessel vasculitis involving the aortic arch and its branches. These clinical features and investigations are suggestive of Takayasu arteritis.

  • Takayasu arteritis is correctly classified as a large-vessel vasculitis characterised by granulomatous inflammation of the aorta and its major branches, especially the aortic arch.
  • Large-vessel vasculitides primarily involve the aorta and major arterial branches.

Vasculitis is classified based on the predominant size of affected vessels: large, medium, or small vessels.

Vessel Size

Vasculitis Syndrome

Key Vessel Characteristics & Pathologic Features

Large Vessel

Takayasu Arteritis

Inflammatory disease of large-sized arteries with a strong predilection for the aortic arch and its branches.

Giant Cell Arteritis

Inflammation of medium- and large-sized arteries characteristically involves branches of the carotid artery (e.g., temporal artery) and the aorta.

Medium Vessel

Polyarteritis Nodosa (Option A)

Necrotising vasculitis of small- and medium-sized muscular arteries (involving renal and visceral arteries); notably spares pulmonary arteries, capillaries, and venules (no glomerulonephritis).

Kawasaki Disease

Vasculitis of the coronary arteries (medium-sized vessels), often associated with aneurysms, typically affects children.

Small Vessel

Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (Wegener's) (Option B)

Necrotising vasculitis of small arteries and veins is characterised by granuloma formation and glomerulonephritis.

Microscopic Polyangiitis

Necrotising vasculitis affecting small vessels (capillaries, venules, or arterioles); rarely involves small- and medium-sized arteries; glomerulonephritis is very common.

Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (Churg-Strauss)

Necrotising vasculitis of small vessels associated with extravascular granulomas and eosinophilic infiltration.

IgA-Vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein) (Option D)

Small-vessel vasculitis predominantly affects postcapillary venules and is characterised by palpable purpura and IgA immune complex deposition.

Cryoglobulinemic Vasculitis

Vasculitis of small vessels (primarily postcapillary venules); associated with cryoprecipitable immunoglobulins.

Cutaneous Leukocytoclastic Angiitis

Inflammation of small vessels (postcapillary venules, capillaries, and arterioles) confined to the dermis.

Variable Vessel

Behçet’s Disease

Can involve vessels of any size (small, medium, or large) and any type (arteries or veins) in any organ.

Cogan’s Syndrome

Systemic vasculitis that may involve large vessels (aortitis) or vessels of other sizes.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2903, 2904.
question: A 24 y/o woman presents with fatigue, arm claudication, and dizziness. Blood pressure is 150/90 mmHg in the right arm and 110/70 mmHg in the left arm. On examination, the left radial pulse is diminished. ESR is elevated. Which of the following primary vasculitides is classified as a large-vessel vasculitis with a strong predilection for the aortic arch and its branches?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) is a small-vessel vasculitis characterised by necrotising granulomatous inflammation of the upper and lower respiratory tracts with associated glomerulonephritis.
  • Granulomatous vasculitis refers to vasculitis in which granuloma formation (organised collections of macrophages and multinucleated giant cells) occurs within or around vessel walls.
  • GPA is described as a distinct clinicopathologic entity defined by:
    • Necrotizing granulomas
    • Small- to medium-vessel vasculitis
    • Respiratory tract involvement
    • Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
  • GPA is strongly associated with c-ANCA (PR3-ANCA).
  • Among primary vasculitides, true granulomatous vasculitis of small vessels is classically seen in the following:
    • Granulomatosis with polyangiitis
    • Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
  • Histologic distinction:
    • GPA → necrotizing granulomas + vasculitis
    • Other ANCA-associated vasculitides → vasculitis without granulomas

Microscopic polyangiitis (Option A): Small-vessel necrotising vasculitis without granulomatous inflammation.

Polyarteritis nodosa (Option B): Medium-vessel necrotising vasculitis. Does not form granulomas and spares small vessels.

IgA vasculitis (Option D): Immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis. Primarily affects postcapillary venules.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2896, 2897.
question: Which of the following small-vessel vasculitides is histopathologically distinguished by necrotising granulomatous inflammation involving the upper and lower respiratory tracts?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Upper airway involvement (sinusitis, epistaxis), lung cavitary nodules, renal involvement (RBC casts), and a c-ANCA pattern strongly point to Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA). The c-ANCA antibody is directed against Proteinase-3 (PR3).

  • c-ANCA produces a diffuse cytoplasmic staining pattern on immunofluorescence.
  • c-ANCA-associated vasculitis is strongly linked to:
    • Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
    • Necrotising granulomatous inflammation
    • Upper airway + lung + kidney involvement
  • Pathogenesis:
    • Anti-PR3 antibodies bind neutrophils
    • Neutrophil activation → endothelial injury
    • Small-vessel necrotising vasculitis ± granulomas
  • ANCA-associated vasculitides are classified as pauci-immune small-vessel vasculitides, meaning minimal immune complex deposition on biopsy
  • Classic triad of GPA:
    • Upper respiratory tract disease
    • Pulmonary nodules/cavitation
    • Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis

Myeloperoxidase (Option A): Target of p-ANCA (perinuclear pattern).

Glomerular basement membrane (Option C): Seen in anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease.

Double-stranded DNA (Option D): Specific for systemic lupus erythematosus.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2894.
question: A 48 y/o man presents with chronic sinusitis, epistaxis, hemoptysis, and fatigue. Labs show creatinine at 2.8 mg/dL and urinalysis with red blood cell casts. Chest CT demonstrates multiple bilateral cavitary nodules. Serum immunofluorescence shows a cytoplasmic ANCA (c-ANCA) pattern. The autoantibody in this patient is most likely directed against which antigen?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) occurs in ~40-50% of patients with giant cell arteritis and represents a related clinical manifestation of the same inflammatory disease spectrum.

Giant cell arteritis (GCA):

  • It is a large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis affecting branches of the external carotid artery, especially the temporal artery.
  • GCA is characterised by:
    • Age >50 years
    • New headache
    • Jaw claudication
    • Visual symptoms (risk of blindness)
    • Elevated ESR/CRP
  • Pathogenesis:
    • T-cell-mediated granulomatous inflammation
    • Multinucleated giant cells
    • Intimal hyperplasia → luminal narrowing → ischemia
  • Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) features:
    • Proximal muscle stiffness (neck, shoulder, hip girdles)
    • No true muscle weakness
    • Dramatic response to low-dose corticosteroids
  • Conversely, 10-20% of patients initially diagnosed with PMR later develop GCA.
  • PMR and GCA are closely linked conditions within the same large-vessel inflammatory disease spectrum.

Rheumatoid arthritis (Option A): Chronic autoimmune synovitis with RF/anti-CCP.

Systemic lupus erythematosus (Option B): An immune-complex-mediated systemic disease.

Polyarteritis nodosa (Option D): Medium-vessel necrotising vasculitis.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2902.
question: Which of the following rheumatic disorders occurs in approximately Giant cell arteritis and is considered part of the same disease spectrum?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

An elderly patient with new-onset unilateral temporal headache, scalp tenderness, visual symptoms, elevated ESR, and anaemia strongly indicates Giant Cell Arteritis.

A temporal artery biopsy is the gold-standard diagnostic test for Giant Cell Arteritis, confirming the diagnosis through characteristic histopathologic findings.

  • Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) is a large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis affecting branches of the external carotid artery, especially the temporal artery
  • Histopathologic findings on biopsy:
    • Granulomatous inflammation of the vessel wall
    • Multinucleated giant cells
    • Disruption of the internal elastic lamina
    • Intimal thickening with luminal narrowing
  • Biopsy remains definitive because:
    • Imaging suggests inflammation, but cannot confirm granulomatous pathology
    • Tissue diagnosis differentiates GCA from other vasculitides
  • Skip lesions may occur → obtain a long biopsy segment.
  • Treatment (high-dose corticosteroids) should begin immediately if suspected, even before biopsy, to prevent irreversible vision loss.

Colour Doppler ultrasonography of the temporal arteries (Option A): May show “halo sign” suggesting vessel wall oedema.

Magnetic resonance angiography (Option B): Demonstrates luminal narrowing or vessel inflammation.

CT angiography of the aortic arch (Option D): Useful for assessing large-vessel (aortic) involvement.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2902.

options.text: Colour Doppler ultrasonography of the temporal arteries
CT angiography of the aortic arch

question: A 72 y/o woman presents with a 2-week history of severe unilateral temporal headache, scalp tenderness, and fatigue. She reports a transient episode of right-eye vision loss one day prior. Examination reveals a thickened, tender temporal artery with decreased pulsation. ESR is 85 mm/h, and labs show normochromic anaemia. Which of the following is the most definitive diagnostic procedure to confirm the suspected diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Giant cell arteritis is a large-vessel vasculitis that can involve the aorta and its major branches, even years after apparent remission. Chronic inflammation of the aortic wall predisposes patients to thoracic aortic aneurysm and dissection, which may occur long after initial treatment.

  • GCA is a large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis that not only affects cranial arteries but may also involve the aorta and its major branches
  • Pathophysiology of late complications:
    • Chronic granulomatous inflammation of the aortic wall
    • Destruction of elastic tissue
    • Progressive medial weakening
    • Predisposition to aneurysm formation, dissection, or rupture
  • Aortic involvement may be clinically silent or detected years after initial diagnosis
  • Long-term monitoring:
    • Periodic imaging (CTA, MRA, or echocardiography)
    • Surveillance for dilation of the thoracic aorta
  • Association with GCA emphasises that this disease extends beyond cranial arteritis and has systemic large-vessel implications.

Coronary artery aneurysms (Option A): Classic complication of Kawasaki disease.

Renal cell carcinoma (Option C): No established strong epidemiologic link with GCA.

Interstitial lung disease (Option D): Seen in connective tissue diseases (e.g., systemic sclerosis, RA).



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2903.
question: A 76 y/o woman with giant cell arteritis (GCA) treated successfully 6 years ago presents for routine follow-up. Despite remission, she remains at significantly increased risk for a serious late complication and requires long-term surveillance. Which of the following complications is most strongly associated with prior GCA?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A young woman with arm claudication, diminished radial pulse, BP discrepancy, elevated ESR, and aortic arch branch stenosis is classic for Takayasu arteritis (“pulseless disease”).

The subclavian artery is involved in approximately 93% of Takayasu arteritis cases, making it the most frequently affected vessel.

  • Takayasu arteritis is a granulomatous large-vessel vasculitis involving the aorta and its major branches
  • Predominant vessel involvement
    • Subclavian artery → ~93% (most common)
    • Common carotid → ~58%
    • Abdominal aorta → ~47%
    • Renal artery → ~38%
    • Vertebral artery → ~35%
  • Clinical correlation:
    • Subclavian stenosis → diminished pulses (“pulseless disease”)
    • Arm claudication
    • Blood pressure asymmetry
    • Raynaud phenomenon
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Granulomatous inflammation of the media and adventitia
    • Intimal proliferation → stenosis
    • May also cause aneurysm formation
  • Recognition of the most commonly involved artery explains the classic upper-extremity ischemic symptoms in Takayasu.

Abdominal aorta (Option A): Less frequent than subclavian involvement.

Renal artery (Option B): Can cause renovascular hypertension, but it is not the most common.

Common carotid artery (Option D): Second most commonly involved (~58%).



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2903.
question: A 24 y/o woman presents with progressive fatigue and left arm claudication. Examination reveals diminished left radial pulse and a blood pressure discrepancy between arms. ESR is elevated. Angiography demonstrates stenotic lesions involving branches of the aortic arch. Which vessel is most frequently involved?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A young woman with constitutional symptoms (fatigue, night sweats, myalgias), arm claudication, blood pressure discrepancy between arms, diminished pulse, supraclavicular bruit, and elevated ESR indicates a large-vessel vasculitis involving the aortic arch branches: Takayasu arteritis.

  • Takayasu arteritis is a large-vessel granulomatous vasculitis affecting the aorta and its major branches, classically presenting in young women with arm claudication, pulse deficits, and blood pressure discrepancies.
  • Takayasu arteritis is described as an inflammatory disease of large arteries predominantly affecting adolescent girls and young women, involving the aortic arch and its branches
  • Clinical phases:
    • Early (“pre-pulseless”) phase → constitutional symptoms (fatigue, fever, night sweats, ↑ESR)
    • Late occlusive phase → vascular insufficiency (arm claudication, bruits, pulse deficits)
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Granulomatous inflammation of the media and adventitia
    • Intimal proliferation → stenosis
    • Leads to diminished pulses (“pulseless disease”)
  • Classic examination findings:
  • Inter-arm blood pressure discrepancy
  • Subclavian bruit
  • Upper extremity claudication

Giant cell arteritis (Option A): Large-vessel vasculitis that occurs in patients >50 years.

Polyarteritis nodosa (Option B): Does not primarily affect aortic arch branches.

Coarctation of the aorta (Option D): Causes upper vs. lower extremity BP differences, not inter-arm discrepancy with systemic inflammation.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2903.
question: A 26 y/o woman presents with 4 months of fatigue, night sweats, and diffuse myalgias. She now reports left-arm heaviness when blow-drying her hair. Blood pressure is 135/75 mmHg in the right arm and 105/60 mmHg in the left arm. The left radial pulse is diminished, and a bruit is heard over the left supraclavicular area. ESR is 85 mm/h. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Recurrent oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis are suggestive of Behçet disease.

A positive pathergy test is defined as the development of a sterile papule or pustule at the needle insertion site within 24-48 hours, reflecting an exaggerated inflammatory response. It assesses nonspecific skin hyperreactivity.

Behçet disease: Multisystem inflammatory vasculitis characterised by:

  • Recurrent oral aphthous ulcers (required feature)
    • Genital ulcers
    • Uveitis
    • Skin lesions
  • A positive pathergy reaction is one of the diagnostic criteria and reflects exaggerated neutrophilic inflammation at sites of minor trauma
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Abnormal innate immune activation
    • Neutrophil hyperreactivity
    • Sterile inflammatory pustule formation
  • The pathergy test is supportive, not mandatory, but increases diagnostic specificity in appropriate clinical settings.

Wheal and flare reaction (Option A): Represents immediate (Type I) hypersensitivity.

Indurated area >10 mm (Option B): Seen in delayed-type hypersensitivity (e.g., tuberculin test).

Localised ecchymosis (Option D): Reflects vascular injury or trauma.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2908.
question: A patient presents with recurrent painful oral ulcers, genital ulcers, and episodic blurred vision due to uveitis. A pathergy test is performed by inserting a sterile needle into the dermis. Which of the following findings observed 24-48 hours later constitutes a positive test result?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis, acneiform lesions, positive pathergy, and now venous thrombosis point to multisystem vasculitis: Behçet disease.

Behçet disease is classically associated with:

  • Venous thrombosis
  • Pulmonary artery aneurysms (potentially fatal due to rupture → massive hemoptysis)

Behçet disease: Multisystem inflammatory vasculitis affecting arteries and veins of all sizes

  • Associations of Behçet disease:
    • Recurrent oral aphthous ulcers (hallmark)
    • Genital ulcers with scarring
    • Uveitis
    • Acneiform or erythema nodosum-like lesions
    • Positive pathergy test
  • Vascular involvement:
    • Venous thrombosis is common (DVT, superficial thrombophlebitis)
    • Strong association between venous thrombosis and pulmonary artery aneurysms
    • Pulmonary artery aneurysms may rupture → massive hemoptysis → high mortality (~20-25% over 5 years)
  • Pathogenesis:
    • Neutrophilic inflammation
    • Endothelial dysfunction
    • Immune-mediated vessel wall destruction
  • Recognition of this vascular clustering is critical because it alters the monitoring and management strategy.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm (Option A): Can occur in large-vessel vasculitides (e.g., GCA).

Renal artery stenosis (Option C): Seen in Takayasu arteritis or PAN.

Temporal artery dissection (Option D): Characteristic of Giant Cell Arteritis.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2909.
question: A 28 y/o man presents with acute right calf swelling. He has a 4-year history of recurrent painful oral ulcers, genital ulcers with scarring, episodic uveitis, acneiform skin lesions, and a positive pathergy test. Given his risk for venous thrombosis, he should be urgently evaluated for which life-threatening vascular complication is classically associated with this disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

PAN causes necrotising inflammation of small- and medium-sized muscular arteries, typically spares the pulmonary circulation, and does not cause glomerulonephritis (renal involvement occurs via renal artery vasculitis, not glomerular capillaries).

  • PAN is classified under medium-vessel vasculitis, involving muscular arteries but not arterioles, capillaries, or venules
  • Key distinguishing features of PAN:
    • Necrotising transmural inflammation
    • Segmental arterial lesions (“skip lesions")
    • No pulmonary involvement
    • No primary glomerulonephritis (renal ischemia due to artery involvement, not glomerular inflammation)
  • Clinical manifestations:
    • Abdominal pain (mesenteric ischemia)
    • Renal artery involvement → hypertension
    • Peripheral neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex)
    • Livedo reticularis
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Immune-mediated injury of medium arteries
    • Microaneurysm formation
    • Organ ischemia
  • In contrast to small-vessel vasculitis, PAN does not cause pulmonary capillaritis or crescentic glomerulonephritis.

Clinical Manifestations Related to Organ System Involvement in Polyarteritis Nodosa

ORGAN SYSTEM

CLINICAL MANIFESTATIONS

Renal

Renal failure, hypertension

Musculoskeletal

Arthritis, arthralgia, myalgia

Peripheral nervous system

Peripheral neuropathy, mononeuritis multiplex

Gastrointestinal tract

Abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, bleeding, bowel infarction and perforation, cholecystitis, hepatic infarction, pancreatic infarction

Skin

Rash, purpura, nodules, cutaneous infarcts, livedo reticularis, Raynaud’s phenomenon

Cardiac

Congestive heart failure, myocardial infarction, pericarditis

Genitourinary

Testicular, ovarian, or epididymal pain

Central nervous system

Cerebral vascular accident, altered mental status, seizure


Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Option A): Small-vessel vasculitis with pulmonary involvement.

Microscopic polyangiitis (Option B): Associated with pulmonary capillaritis and glomerulonephritis.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Option D): Immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2901.
question: Which of the following syndromes is characterised by necrotising inflammation of small- and medium-sized muscular arteries that typically spares the pulmonary circulation and does not cause glomerulonephritis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient has digital ischemia (black fingertips), weight loss, postprandial abdominal pain (mesenteric ischemia), neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex), hypertension (renal artery involvement), elevated ESR, and negative ANCA, classic for Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN).

Renal involvement in PAN affects renal arteries, causing hypertension and mild proteinuria, but does not cause glomerulonephritis (hence no RBC casts).

  • Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN):
    • Necrotising inflammation of small- and medium-sized muscular arteries
    • Segmental (“skip”) lesions
    • No pulmonary artery involvement
    • No primary glomerulonephritis
  • Mechanism of digital gangrene:
    • Medium-artery inflammation → luminal narrowing
    • Thrombosis → distal ischemia → tissue necrosis
  • Systemic associations:
    • Renal artery involvement → hypertension
    • Mesenteric artery involvement → postprandial abdominal pain
    • Peripheral nerve ischemia → mononeuritis multiplex
    • Livedo reticularis due to cutaneous vessel involvement
  • Important diagnostic distinction:
    • ANCA negative
    • Absence of pulmonary capillaritis
    • Urinalysis lacks RBC casts (no GN)

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Option A): Small-vessel vasculitis with pulmonary involvement.

Microscopic polyangiitis (Option B): Associated with pulmonary capillaritis and glomerulonephritis.

Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Option D): Immune-complex small-vessel vasculitis.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2901.
question: A 42 y/o man presents with painful black discolouration of fingertips for one week, as shown below. He reports 3 months of weight loss, postprandial abdominal pain, and numbness in his left foot. Blood pressure is 165/95 mmHg. ESR is elevated. ANCA testing is negative. Urinalysis reveals mild proteinuria without red blood cell casts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Bifurcations and branchings of arteries
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Histopathological features of Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) show segmental, transmural necrotising inflammation of medium-sized muscular arteries.

The lesions characteristically occur at arterial bifurcations and branch points, where turbulent blood flow predisposes to immune complex deposition and vascular injury.

  • Polyarteritis Nodosa is a medium-vessel necrotising vasculitis involving small- and medium-sized muscular arteries
  • Histopathologic features:
    • Transmural inflammation
    • Fibrinoid necrosis
    • Segmental (“skip”) lesions
    • Predilection for arterial bifurcations

[[figure-1]]

Fibrinoid necrosis

  • Consequences of branch-point involvement:
    • Microaneurysm formation
    • Thrombosis
    • Downstream ischemia
    • Organ infarction
  • PAN does not involve:
    • Capillaries
    • Venules
    • Pulmonary arteries
  • This distribution pattern explains the renal artery microaneurysms, mesenteric ischemia, and peripheral neuropathy.

The vasa vasorum of the adventitia (Option A): More characteristic of large-vessel vasculitis (e.g., GCA, Takayasu).

The subendothelial space of capillaries (Option B): Seen in small-vessel vasculitis (e.g., microscopic polyangiitis).

The internal elastic lamina of the aortic arch (Option D): Classic for giant cell arteritis.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2901.

options.text: The vasa vasorum of the adventitia
The internal elastic lamina of the aortic arch

question: Histopathologically, the segmental necrotising lesions of Polyarteritis Nodosa have a specific predilection for which anatomical location within the arterial tree?

correctAnswer: B. Infiltration of polymorphonuclear neutrophils into all layers of the vessel wall
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The acute stage of PAN is defined by transmural infiltration of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (panarteritis), producing necrotising inflammation of medium-sized muscular arteries.

  • The core pathology of PAN:
    • Segmental transmural inflammation
    • Neutrophil predominance in the acute phase
    • Fibrinoid necrosis of the vessel wall
    • Intimal proliferation
    • Perivascular inflammatory infiltrates
  • Acute phase → neutrophils dominate.
  • Subacute/chronic phase → mononuclear cells replace neutrophils → fibrosis.
  • PAN is classified as a medium-vessel necrotising vasculitis
  • Important distinguishing features:
    • No granulomas
    • No capillary or venule involvement
    • No pulmonary artery involvement
    • No glomerulonephritis

[[figure-1]]

Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), Acute phase: neutrophilic vasculitis

Granulomatous inflammation involving the media and adventitia (Option A): More characteristic of large-vessel vasculitides (e.g., GCA, Takayasu).

Predominantly lymphocytic infiltration with numerous eosinophils (Option C): Suggests Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis.

Leukocytoclastic vasculitis restricted to postcapillary venules (Option D): Small-vessel vasculitis. PAN affects muscular arteries, not venules.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2901.

Infiltration of polymorphonuclear neutrophils into all layers of the vessel wall
Predominantly lymphocytic infiltration with numerous eosinophils
Leukocytoclastic vasculitis restricted to postcapillary venules

question: Which of the following descriptions accurately characterises the histologic findings in the acute stage of vascular lesions in polyarteritis nodosa?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein purpura) is the most common vasculitis in children and classically presents with the tetrad of palpable purpura, arthralgia, abdominal pain, and renal involvement.

  • It is classified as a small-vessel immune complex-mediated vasculitis
  • Typical age group: Most common between ages 4 and 7 years.
  • Core pathologic mechanism:
    • IgA-containing immune complex deposition
    • Leukocytoclastic vasculitis of small vessels
    • Mesangial IgA deposition in the kidneys
  • Classic tetrad:
    • Palpable purpura (buttocks and lower extremities)
    • Arthralgias/arthritis
    • Colicky abdominal pain ± GI bleeding
    • Glomerulonephritis (hematuria, mild proteinuria)
  • Often follows an upper respiratory infection.
  • Emphasised in Harrison as the most common pediatric vasculitis

Kawasaki disease (Option A): Medium-vessel vasculitis with coronary artery aneurysms.

Polyarteritis nodosa (Option C): Medium-vessel necrotising vasculitis. Rare in children

Takayasu arteritis (Option D): Large-vessel vasculitis. Occurs in adolescents/young women



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2904
question: Which of the following vasculitides is most frequently observed in children (typically ages 4-7 years) and is clinically characterised by the tetrad of palpable purpura, arthralgias, gastrointestinal symptoms, and glomerulonephritis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of fatigue, joint pain, photosensitive rash, mouth ulcers, hair loss, positive ANA and anti-dsDNA antibodies suggest systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
  • Elevated levels of IFN-α play a crucial role in SLE pathogenesis by promoting B cell activation and increasing antibody production, particularly autoantibodies such as anti-dsDNA.

Decreased B cell activation (Option A): IFN-α promotes B cell activation and survival, not decreases it. This contributes to autoantibody production in SLE.


Enhanced clearance of apoptotic cells (Option B): In SLE, clearance is defective, contributing to accumulation of nuclear debris → triggers autoimmunity.


Suppression of T cell activity (Option C): IFN-α activates dendritic cells and promotes T cell activation, not suppression.



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2737
  2. Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 1034
question:
A 25-year-old woman presents with fatigue, joint pain, and a photosensitive rash. She reports mouth ulcers and hair loss. Laboratory tests show positive ANA and elevated anti-ds DNA antibodies. Further examination reveals elevated levels of IFN-α.

Which of the following is a consequence of elevated IFN-α in this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's symptoms of recurrent fever, myalgia, photosensitivity, and joint pain, along with erythematous plaques with adherent scales on the face and scalp, suggest Discoid Lupus Erythematosus (DLE), a chronic cutaneous form of lupus.
  • It is characterised by round, scaly, slightly raised, erythematous plaques with hyperpigmented rims and depigmented centres that occur due to damage to all the dermal appendages.

Mucocutaneous symptoms of SLE
  • Malar rash/ Butterfly rash is photosensitive and involves the cheeks and nose, sparing the nasolabial folds. (Option B)

[[figure-1]]

  • Discoid lupus erythematosus

[[figure-2]]

  • Subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus are scaly, red, circular or flat, annular lesions, similar to psoriasis (Option C)

[[figure-3]]

  • Ulcers
  • Lichen planus

[[figure-4]]

  • Urticarial eruptions are red or skin-coloured, raised, and surrounded by a halo of redness (Option A)

[[figure-5]]



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2740
  2. Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 1035
question: A 30-year-old woman presents with a history of recurrent fever, myalgia, photosensitivity, and joint pain. On examination, multiple erythematous plaques with adherent scales are noted on her face and scalp. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's presentation of chest pain that worsens with deep breathing, along with a history of fatigue, joint pain, photosensitivity, and positive autoimmune markers (ANA, anti-dsDNA), suggests Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
  • Pleuritis is the most common pulmonary manifestation of SLE, and it can present with or without effusion.

Pulmonary Systemic Involvement in SLE
  • Pleuritis (most common): Prevalence (30 - 50%)
  • Pneumonitis
  • Atelectasis
  • Reduced lung volume and
  • Pulmonary ﬁbrosis
  • Shrinking lung syndrome, (< 5%) (Option B ruled out)
  • Intra-alveolar hemorrhage
  • Pulmonary HTN (< 5 %) (Option C ruled out)
  • Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) (< 5%) (Option A ruled out)



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2740, 2741, 2742, 2743.
question:
A 26-year-old woman presents with chest pain worsened by deep breathing, shortness of breath, fatigue, joint pain, and a photosensitive facial rash. Physical examination reveals tenderness over the chest wall and mild joint swelling. Laboratory tests show positive ANA and elevated anti-dsDNA antibodies. A chest X-ray shows mild pleural effusion. Which of the following pulmonary complications is most likely associated with her condition?

(ARDS: Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome)

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Antihistone antibodies are the most specific antibodies for diagnosing drug-induced lupus.

Antibodies

Clinical significance

Anti-C1q

(Option C ruled out)

Associated with active lupus nephritis, it is non-specific for SLE and can be used to correlate with disease activity. Deficiency predisposes SLE.

Anti-RNP (Option B ruled out)

Non-specific to SLE and is associated with syndromes that overlap with rheumatic syndromes

Anti-Ro (SS-A) (Option A ruled out)

Not very specific, it is associated with sicca syndrome and neonatal lupus (congenital heart block)



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2738
question: A 28-year-old woman presents with joint pain and skin rashes after being treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a recent infection. She has a history of Systemic lupus erythematosus. Laboratory tests reveal positive anti-dsDNA antibodies. Which of the following antibodies would be more specific for diagnosing the cause of her symptoms?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Though GI and ocular symptoms are part of SLE manifestations, they aren't included in the EULAR/ACR Classification Criteria for SLE.
  • This classification includes both clinical & immunological criteria; the patient must fulfil at least one clinical criterion, and ≥10 points are classified.
  • ANA positive ( titer of ≥ 1:80 on Hep-2 cells) is the required entry criteria to classify SLE.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2741, 2740.
question: A 27-year-old woman presents with joint pain, fatigue, and a malar rash. Laboratory tests reveal positive ANA and anti-dsDNA antibodies. According to the EULAR/ACR classification criteria, which of the following criteria is not required for diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Renal biopsy indicating lupus with lupus autoantibodies is sufficient
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The SLICC (Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinics) criteria state that SLE can be diagnosed if a patient meets 4 criteria, including at least 1 clinical and 1 immunological criterion.
  • However, SLE can also be diagnosed if a renal biopsy shows lupus nephritis and the patient has positive ANA or anti-dsDNA antibodies, regardless of meeting other clinical or immunological criteria.

Systemic Lupus International Collaborating Clinic (SLICC) Criteria

Clinical Manifestations

Immunological Manifestations

Skin:

  • Acute cutaneous lupus erythematosus (photosensitive, malar, maculopapular, bullous)
  • Chronic cutaneous lupus erythematosus (discoid lupus, panniculitis, lichen planus-like, hypertrophic verrucous, chill blains)
  • ANA > reference negative value
  • Anti-dsDNA > reference

(if by ELISA, 2× reference)

  • Anti-Sm
  • Antiphospholipid antibodies
  • Lupus anticoagulant
  • Anticardiolipin
  • Anti–β2-glycoprotein1
  • Low serum complement (C3, C4, or CH50)
  • Positive direct Coombs test
  • Oral or nasal ulcers
  • Nonscarring alopecia
  • Synovitis involving ≥2 joints
  • Serositis (Pleurisy or pericarditis)

Renal:

  • Protein-to-creatinine ratio (Prot/Cr) ≥0.5
  • RBC casts
  • Renal biopsy indicating lupus (Wire-loop lesions)

Neurologic:

  • Seizures
  • Psychosis
  • Mononeuritis & myelitis
  • Peripheral/Cranial neuropathies
  • Acute confusional state

Hematology:

  • Hemolytic anemia
  • Leukopenia (<4000/μL)
  • Lymphopenia (<1000/μL)
  • Thrombocytopenia (<100,000/μL)

Classification Criteria:

  • At least 4 criteria must be present, with at least 1 from the clinical manifestations and 1 from the immunologic manifestations. (Option A, C and D ruled out)
  • A renal biopsy indicating lupus nephritis qualifies as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) if any lupus autoantibodies are present, even if the total criteria are < 4. (Option B)


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2739, 2740

options.text: Four clinical criteria must be met to confirm SLE
Renal biopsy indicating lupus with lupus autoantibodies is sufficient
At least 2 clinical criteria with one antibody confirms SLE
Presence of Anti-ds, Anti-Sm and ANA confirms SLE

question: A 25-year-old woman presents with fatigue, a malar rash, and joint pain. Laboratory tests show positive anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith antibodies, and a positive ANA. She undergoes a renal biopsy that reveals features consistent with lupus nephritis. Based on the SLICC criteria, which of the following statements is true?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's renal biopsy shows diffuse glomerular inflammation involving over 50% of glomeruli corresponds to Class IV lupus nephritis.

Classification of Lupus nephritis

Class II: Mesangial Proliferative Lupus Nephritis

(Option B ruled out)
  • Light microscopy: Mesangial hypercellularity (or) matrix expansion
  • Mesangial immune deposits
  • Subepithelial or subendothelial deposits may be present.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]

Class III: Focal Lupus Nephritis

  • Class III (A): Active lesions—focal proliferative lupus nephritis.
  • Class III (C): Chronic inactive lesions—focal sclerosing lupus nephritis.
  • Class III (A/C): Active and chronic lesions

(Option C ruled out)
  • Active or inactive glomerulonephritis involving ≤50% of all glomeruli.
  • Focal subendothelial immune deposits and possible mesangial alterations

[[figure-3]]

Class IV: Diffuse Lupus Nephritis

  • Class IV-S: Diffuse segmental lupus nephritis (≥50% of involved glomeruli have segmental lesions).
  • Class IV-G: Diffuse global lupus nephritis (≥50% of involved glomeruli have global lesions).
  • Class IV (A): Active lesion
  • Class IV (A/C): Active and chronic lesion
  • Class IV (C): Chronic inactive lesions with scars

(Option D)
  • Active or inactive glomerulonephritis involving ≥50% of all glomeruli.
  • Diffuse subendothelial immune deposits and possible mesangial alterations.
  • Wire-loop lesions in IF

[[figure-4]]

[[figure-5]]

Class V: Membranous Lupus Nephritis

(Option A ruled out)
  • Global or segmental subepithelial immune deposits.
  • Morphologic sequelae are observable by light microscopy, immunofluorescence, or electron microscopy, with or without mesangial alterations.
  • It may coexist with class III or IV LN.

[[figure-6]]

[[figure-7]]

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2739
question: A 32-year-old woman with known systemic lupus erythematosus presents with new-onset hypertension and elevated creatinine. Urinalysis shows hematuria and proteinuria. Renal biopsy reveals glomerular inflammation involving >50% of glomeruli. Which class of lupus nephritis does this most likely represent?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • For SLE patients with severe disease presenting with significant organ involvement, the most appropriate management strategy is high-dose glucocorticoids and cyclophosphamide.

Hydroxychloroquine and NSAIDs (Option B): Appropriate for mild, non–organ-threatening SLE, not adequate here.

Low-dose glucocorticoids + azathioprine (Option C): Used for maintenance or moderate disease, not strong enough for acute severe disease.

Conservative management (Option D): Unsafe, as supportive care alone risks progression and organ failure.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2746, 2747

Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 1036, 1037

Conservative management with close monitoring and supportive care

question: A 28-year-old woman with a history of SLE presents with increased fatigue, severe joint pain and pleuritis with features suggestive of coronary artery disease. Laboratory tests indicate elevated serum creatinine. Which of the following management strategies is most appropriate for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Hydralazine is a known trigger for drug-induced lupus, especially in patients with a history of hypertension.
  • It is associated with positive anti-histone antibodies and symptoms consistent with lupus erythematosus.
  • Common offending agents for drug-induced lupus: (Options A, B and D ruled out)
    • Antiarrhythmics: Procainamide, disopyramide, propafenone
    • Antihypertensives: Hydralazine
    • Antithyroid: Propylthiouracil
    • Antipsychotics: Chlorpromazine, lithium

question: A 45-year-old man with TB on ATT isoniazid therapy presents with fatigue, fever, joint pain, and a rash. Explanation:

  • The clinical scenario of a woman with recurrent miscarriages and deep vein thrombosis (DVT), along with elevated anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies, suggests antiphospholipid syndrome (APS).
  • In APS, increased endothelial cell apoptosis exposes negatively charged phospholipids, promoting the formation of antiphospholipid antibodies.

Impaired fibrinolysis (Option C): APS is mainly characterised by increased coagulation and platelet activation rather than a failure to break down clots.

question: A 35-year-old woman with a history of recurrent miscarriages and recent episodes of deep vein thrombosis is found to have elevated anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies. Which of the following pathophysiological mechanisms is primarily responsible for her condition?

correctAnswer: C. Positive titer for APLA antibodies on a single occasion
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Laboratory criteria for diagnosing Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APLA) include the presence of a positive titer for APLA antibodies on two occasions 12 weeks apart.

APLA antibodies include

  • Lupus antibody
  • Anticardiolipin
  • Anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I

Diagnosis of antiphospholipid syndrome

Clinical criteria

  • Vascular thrombosis - one or more clinical episodes of arterial, venous or small vessel thrombosis (Option A ruled out)
  • Pregnancy morbidity (anyone)
    • One or more unexplained deaths of a normal fetus at or after 10 weeks of gestation (Option D ruled out)
    • One or more premature births of a normal neonate before 34 weeks of gestation due to eclampsia, severe pre-eclampsia or placental insufficiency
    • Three or more unexplained consecutive miscarriages before 10 weeks of gestation (Option B ruled out)

Lab criteria

Intermediate or high titer of any one of the following antibodies on two occasions 12 weeks apart. (Option C)

  • Lupus antibody
  • Anticardiolipin
  • Anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I

Diagnosis of APLA: One clinical + one laboratory criterion in the absence of other thrombophilia


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2750

question: A 30-year-old woman presents with a history of recurrent miscarriages, having experienced three miscarriages before 10 weeks of gestation and an unprovoked deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in her left leg six months ago, which required anticoagulation therapy. She is diagnosed with antiphospholipid syndrome. Which of the following is not a diagnostic criterion of antiphospholipid syndrome?

correctAnswer: B. Increase the dose of warfarin with a target INR of 3.0 to 4.0
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Since this patient has experienced arterial thrombosis, the target INR should be raised from the standard range of 2.0-3.0 to 3.0-4.0.
  • This adjustment can be achieved by increasing the dosage of warfarin.

Treatment of antiphospholipid syndrome

After the first venous thrombosis
  • Warfarin - Lifelong with a target INR 2.0-3.0
  • Consider Direct thrombin inhibitors if there is a contraindication to warfarin or failure to achieve target INR *

Arterial thrombosis

  • Increase warfarin dose with target INR 3.0-4.0 or (Option B)
  • Maintain INR 2.0-3.0 and low-dose aspirin (LDA) 70-100 mg/day

Pregnant woman with APLA
  • LDA + Prophylactic dose of LMWH (Option D ruled out)
  • If thrombosis occurs - LDA + therapeutic dose of LMWH

Recurrent obstetric complications, even after standard treatment

  • LDA + therapeutic dose of LMWH
  • Oral hydroxychloroquine 400 mg / day (Option A ruled out)
  • IV immunoglobulin 400 mg/kg for 5 days

Asymptomatic patients with high-risk antiphospholipid profile

  • Prophylactic low-dose aspirin

Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS)
  • Combination therapy
    • Glucocorticoid
    • Heparin
    • Plasmapheresis or IV immunoglobulin

Refractory CAPS
  • B-cell depletion therapy with rituximab
  • Complement inhibition with Eculizumab

* Avoid direct thrombin inhibitors in cases of prior arterial thrombosis or triple positive APLA (Option C ruled out)


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2750-2751

Test

Interpretation

correctAnswer: B. Presence of HLA-DR β 1 is strongly associated with this condition
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Rheumatoid arthritis has a strong genetic association with HLA-DRB1 alleles, which contribute to autoimmune activation and chronic synovial inflammation.

  • Crystal deposition in the joint spaces leads to joint inflammation (Option A): Characteristic of gout or pseudogout, not RA.

question: A 45-year-old male presents to the clinic with joint pain and morning stiffness lasting more than one hour. Based on the EULAR classification criteria for rheumatoid arthritis, which of the following combinations of clinical, serological, and laboratory findings is most likely to lead to a definitive diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's history of a joint condition, likely rheumatoid arthritis (given the positive HLA-DR4), combined with long-term occupational exposure to coal dust and the presence of rounded lung nodules on X-ray and biopsy, suggests Caplan syndrome.
  • It is characterised by the formation of multiple well-defined pulmonary nodules, with pathological features similar to rheumatoid nodules, including central necrosis, surrounding palisading histiocytes, and a peripheral rim of lymphocytes and plasma cells.

[[figure-1]]

Secondary Sjögren's Syndrome (Option B) occurs in individuals with a pre-existing autoimmune disease, such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus. It primarily involves dryness of the eyes and mouth (sicca symptoms) due to autoimmune destruction of the lacrimal and salivary glands.


Felty syndrome (Option C) is a rare complication of longstanding rheumatoid arthritis, characterised by the triad of RA, splenomegaly, and neutropenia. It does not involve pulmonary opacities or occupational exposure, pulmonary nodules, or occupational lung exposure.


Lofgren syndrome (Option D) is an acute presentation of sarcoidosis, marked by the triad of erythema nodosum, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, and arthritis (usually in the ankles). It is not related to the patient’s coal mining history or lung opacities.

question: A 60-year-old male with a history of working in coal mines presents with progressive shortness of breath and a chronic cough. He reports that years ago, he was diagnosed with a joint condition that caused swelling and stiffness, particularly in his hands and wrists. Laboratory testing reveals he is positive for HLA-DR4. A chest X-ray shows multiple rounded opacities in both lung fields. A lung biopsy showed the following picture. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient’s presentation suggests a diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis (RA). Common extra-articular manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis include subcutaneous nodules, erythema nodosum, and ocular complications (keratoconjunctivitis sicca due to secondary Sjögren’s syndrome).

Rheumatoid/subcutaneous nodules are the most common extra-articular manifestation of RA.

[[figure-1]]

Uveitis (Option B): More commonly seen in seronegative spondyloarthropathies, not RA.

Iritis (Option C): Typically associated with ankylosing spondylitis or juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

Iridocyclitis (Option D): Also more common in spondyloarthropathies, not RA.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2752
question: A 32-year-old male presents with multiple subcutaneous nodules on his arms and back, along with joint pain and stiffness primarily affecting his hands and knees. He has erythema nodosum and a positive family history of similar conditions. Which of the following is a common ocular extra-articular manifestation associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation suggests rheumatoid arthritis (RA), characterised by morning stiffness, symmetrical joint involvement, and synovitis in the hands. The most appropriate initial investigation to support this diagnosis is the anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibody test, which is highly specific for rheumatoid arthritis.

  • Anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) test (Option A) is primarily used to diagnose systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and other connective tissue diseases, not RA. Although ANA can occasionally be positive in RA, it is not a specific or reliable test for this condition.
  • Synovial fluid analysis (Option C) helps rule out other conditions, such as infection or crystal arthropathy but is not the initial investigation for rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Ultrasound or magnetic resonance imaging (Option D): To establish diagnosis

question: A 52-year-old man presents with bilateral pain, swelling, and stiffness in his hands and wrists for the past 4 months. His symptoms are worse in the morning and improve throughout the day. The physical exam shows synovitis in the metacarpophalangeal joints. Considering the high specificity for rheumatoid arthritis, which initial investigation is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Methotrexate is the first-line DMARD for rheumatoid arthritis, especially in patients with high disease activity (DAS28 >5.1) who have not responded to NSAIDs or lifestyle measures.

  • Sulfasalazine (Option A): Used in mild to moderate RA or in combination therapy.

  • Leflunomide (Option C): Alternative to methotrexate if contraindicated, not first-line.

  • Hydroxychloroquine (Option D): Typically used in mild RA or combination therapy, not in high disease activity alone.

question: A 55-year-old female patient presents with significant joint pain, stiffness, and swelling affecting multiple joints. Her Disease Activity Score (DAS28) is 5.4, indicating high disease activity. She has not responded adequately to lifestyle modifications and NSAIDs. Which medication is considered this patient's first-line disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD)?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In patients with high disease activity despite methotrexate monotherapy, oral triple DMARD therapy (methotrexate + sulfasalazine + hydroxychloroquine) is recommended before considering biologic agents.

Management Algorithm of Rheumatoid Arthritis:

[[figure-1]]

Increase the dose of methotrexate (Option A): May help, but patient is already on an adequate dose for 6 months.


Switch from methotrexate to leflunomide (Option C): Considered if methotrexate intolerance or contraindication, not first step.


Continue methotrexate for 3 more months (Option D): Not appropriate for persistent high disease activity; requires escalation.

≤1 mg/dL (Option C)

≤1 (on a 0–10 scale) (Option D)

≤3.3

question: A 62-year-old man presents with sudden, severe pain in his right big toe, waking him from sleep. The joint is swollen, red, and extremely tender. He has a history of high uric acid levels and recently consumed protein-rich meals. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. Impaired renal excretion of uric acid
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation, along with an increased intake of red meat, suggests gouty arthritis due to increased uric acid levels.
  • Impaired renal excretion is a common cause of hyperuricemia, which can lead to the formation of monosodium urate crystals and gout attacks.

Etiopathogenesis of Gout:

[[figure-1]]

Increased renal tubular secretion of uric acid (Option A), Decreased production of purines (Option B), Increased breakdown of uric acid (Option D): All of these will lead to lower uric acid levels and decrease gout risk formation. Hence, incorrect options.

question: A 43-year-old man presents with severe pain in his right big toe, redness, and swelling, as shown in the image. He has a history of hypertension and recently increased her consumption of red meat. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiological process leading to her condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation with increased uric acid levels points towards gout.
  • The patient is currently symptom-free after her previous acute attack, indicating she is in the intercritical stage of gout, characterised by intervals between episodes of acute gout.

Stages of Gout Progression:

Stage 1: Asymptomatic Hyperuricemia

(Option A ruled out)
  • Elevated serum uric acid levels without any symptoms.
  • It can last for years & individuals may be unaware of their condition.

Stage 2: Acute Gout Attack

(Option B ruled out)
  • A sudden onset of severe pain, redness, and swelling in a joint, most commonly the MTP joint, typically lasts 1–2 weeks.
  • Symptoms usually resolve spontaneously.

Stage 3: Intercritical Gout

(Option C)
  • Periods between acute attacks when the patient is symptom-free & intervals vary from weeks to years.
  • No symptoms, but the risk of future attacks remains.

Stage 4: Chronic Gouty Arthritis

(Option D ruled out)
  • Persistent joint inflammation and damage due to repeated attacks.
  • Chronic pain and swelling, joint deformities & formation of tophi (urate crystal deposits)



Reference:
  1. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK546606/

question: A 60-year-old woman with a history of elevated uric acid levels reports that she experienced a painful episode in her right big toe two months ago. Since that time, she has had no symptoms and feels completely normal. She is concerned about the possibility of future attacks. What stage of the associated condition is this patient most likely experiencing now?

correctAnswer: C. Needle-shaped crystals exhibiting negative birefringence
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Gout is characterized by the identification of needle-shaped monosodium urate (MSU) crystals exhibiting negative birefringence under polarised light.

Rhomboid-shaped crystals (Option A) are characteristic of calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate (CPPD) crystals, which are associated with pseudogout, not gout.

Elevated white blood cell count with neutrophilic predominance (Option B) can occur in gout due to inflammation, but it is not specific to gout.


Thickened synovial fluid with a high percentage of lymphocytes (Option D) is more indicative of conditions like rheumatoid arthritis or other inflammatory arthritis rather than the acute inflammatory process typically seen in gout.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2863,2864

question: A 58-year-old man presents with a sudden onset of severe pain in his left knee, accompanied by swelling and redness. He has a history of elevated uric acid levels. question: A 46-year-old man presents to the OPD with severe pain, redness, and swelling in his right knee. Examination reveals tender swelling and redness at the base of the right 1st toe. Serum urate levels are normal, but arthrocentesis reveals negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals under polarised light. Which of the following is the drug of choice for this acute attack?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Allopurinol is the first-line treatment for the prevention of gouty arthritis, particularly in patients who are overproducers of uric acid.
  • The initial dose is typically 100 mg daily, with a target urate level of <5-6 mg/dL and can be titrated up to 800 mg as needed.

question: A 48-year-old man had an acute gout attack treated successfully with NSAIDs. His labs show markedly elevated serum uric acid and high 24-hour urinary uric acid excretion. Which drug is the best choice for long-term management?

explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: C) Febuxostat

Explanation:

  • Febuxostat is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor that undergoes hepatic metabolism; thus, no dose adjustment is required for renal impairment.

Probenecid (Option A) is a uricosuric second-line agent for gout.

  • It can be used as monotherapy or in combination with allopurinol.
  • But it is ineffective in patients with renal insufficiency.

Allopurinol (Option B) is a xanthine oxidase inhibitor and the first-line treatment for gout prevention.

  • However, it is not safe for renal insufficiency due to its renal excretion, which increases the risk of severe cutaneous adverse reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.


Lesinurad (Option D) is a renal urate transporter inhibitor that targets URAT1 and OAT4

  • However, it is associated with elevated serum creatinine levels, making it contraindicated in patients with renal insufficiency.

question: A 45-year-old male with stage 2 chronic kidney disease presents with painful swelling at the base of his left big toe. He was diagnosed with an acute gouty attack and treated with oral glucocorticoids. Which anti-gout medication can be used to reduce the risk of another attack without dose modification?

correctAnswer: B. Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in cartilage matrix vesicles
explanationHtml:
The clinical presentation and polarised light microscopy findings of rhomboid-shaped crystals with positive birefringence indicate Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (CPPD) or ‘Pseudogout’ in which deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in cartilage matrix vesicles is seen.

Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease

Aetiology

  • Ageing
  • Osteoarthritis
  • Post Meniscectomy or joint trauma
  • Familial-genetic
  • Hemochromatosis
  • Hypophosphatasia
  • Hypomagnesemia
  • Certain drugs: Thiazide and loop diuretics
  • Malabsorption
  • Gitelman’s syndrome
  • Gout
  • X-linked hypophosphatemic rickets
  • Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia

Pathogenesis

  • Mutation in ANKH gene ➜ Increased extracellular transportation of pyrophosphate.
  • Decreased levels of glycosaminoglycans in the cartilage, which results in
    • Increased inorganic pyrophosphate in the cartilage matrix.
    • Calcium combines with this pyrophosphate to form excess CCP.
    • Phagocytosis of CCP crystals by neutrophils and macrophage inflammation.

Clinical features

  • Acute attack may follow surgery (especially parathyroidectomy) and trauma
    • Systemic signs can occur during the attack, such as fever and chills.
    • Joint swelling, redness and pain.
      • Most commonly affected joint: Knees.
      • Rarely affected: First metatarsophalangeal joint.
  • Chronic:
    • Symmetrical Polyarticular arthritis with severe joint damage.
    • Chondrocalcinosis can occur.

Diagnosis

X-ray: Punctate or linear radiodense deposits within fibrocartilaginous joint meniscus or articular hyaline cartilage.

Arthrocentesis: Positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped crystals under polarised light



Excessive mechanical wear and tear of the articular cartilage (Option A) is seen with osteoarthritis, leading to cartilage degradation, bone spurs, and reduced joint space. It typically presents with asymmetrical joint involvement and does not usually show any crystal deposition in the joints.


Excess purine production causes crystal deposition in the joints (Option C), which causes gout. Urate crystals are strongly negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals under polarised light.


Autoimmune reaction leading to pannus formation in the joint (Option D) is seen in rheumatoid arthritis, a CD4+ mediated autoimmune condition. RA presents with symmetrical small joint pain and stiffness, especially in the morning, which improves during the day. During microscopy of synovial fluid, it does not show any form of crystal.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2865-2866

Deposition of calcium pyrophosphate crystals in cartilage matrix vesicles
Excess purine production causes crystal deposition in the joints
Autoimmune reaction leading to pannus formation in the joint

question: A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden swelling, redness, and severe pain in both knees. He has experienced intermittent joint pain for the past few months. Polarised light microscopy of joint aspiration reveals rhomboid-shaped crystals exhibiting positive birefringence. Which statement best explains the pathogenesis of his condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Calcium apatite (basic calcium phosphate) crystals are very small, non-birefringent microcrystals that cannot be seen clearly under polarised light microscopy. They often appear as “shiny, broad, clumped aggregates” (also called calcific debris). This is characteristic of calcific tendinitis and calcium apatite deposition disease.

Microscopy of synovial fluid

Gout

(Monosodium urate)

Negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals (Option C ruled out)

Pseudogout

(Calcium pyrophosphate)

Positively birefringent rhomboid-shaped crystals (Option A ruled out)

Calcium Apatite deposition disease

Microcrystals of apatite in the synovial fluid show no birefringence under polarised light.

Calcium oxalate deposition disease

  • Variable shape and variable birefringence
  • The most easily recognisable crystals are strong birefringent bipyramidal crystals. (Option B ruled out)


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2864-2867

Explanation:

  • The patient’s symptoms - thickened and tight skin on the fingers, painful fingertip ulcers, shiny facial skin, and limited neck extension - are characteristic of systemic sclerosis (scleroderma).

  • Hyperpigmentation in sun-exposed areas is not typically associated with systemic sclerosis.
  • Instead, patients often exhibit early diffuse tanning without sun exposure or a "salt-and-pepper" appearance, particularly in darker-skinned individuals.

Dermal Manifestations of Systemic Sclerosis (SSc):

  1. Bilateral Symmetrical Skin Thickening: Begins distally in the fingers and progresses proximally. (Option A ruled out)
  2. Fixed Contractures: Affects wrists, elbows, and knees due to skin and tendon fibrosis. (Option C ruled out)

question: A 45-year-old lady presents with skin changes, reporting that her fingers have become thick and tight. She has developed painful ulcers on her fingertips that heal slowly. The physician notes shiny, taut skin on her face and limited neck extension. The given image shows the patient's facial features. Which of the following findings is not typically associated with the skin changes observed in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Statement 1 correctly describes the pathologic findings in the skin (Image A), which include thickened dermis and loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue due to collagen accumulation.
  • Statement 3 accurately reflects the findings in the kidneys (Image B), which include vascular lesions and ischemic changes.

Systemic Sclerosis:

Organ/System

Pathologic Findings

Skin
  • Thickened dermis due to collagen accumulation and atrophic adnexal glands.
  • Loss of subcutaneous adipose tissue replaced by collagen.

[[figure-1]]

Kidneys
  • Vascular lesions in interlobular and arcuate arteries; ischemic glomerular changes.
  • Scleroderma renal crisis shows fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles, intimal proliferation, and thrombotic microangiopathy-like changes.

[[figure-2]]

question:
Which of the following statements about the histopathological examination (HPE) of the images is correct?

A)

B)

  1. Image A shows a thickened dermis with collagen accumulation and loss of adipose tissue.
  2. Image B demonstrates normal glomerular architecture with no signs of injury.
  3. Image B shows vascular lesions and ischemic glomerular changes.
  4. Image A is characterized by alveolar septal fibrosis leading to gas exchange impairment.

correctAnswer: C. Pulmonary arterial hypertension; Constrictive pericarditis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's skin changes, including thickened skin and telangiectasia, suggest systemic sclerosis, which often leads to pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) and constrictive pericarditis due to vascular involvement and fibrosis.

Tuberculosis; Congestive cardiac failure (Option A): Tuberculosis is not associated with systemic sclerosis (SSc). Congestive cardiac failure can occur due to various conditions but is not specific to SSc.

Cavitation; Pericarditis (Option B): Cavitation is linked to infections, not SSc. Pericarditis can occur in SSc, but this option does not represent a key pulmonary feature.

Non-caseating granuloma; Atrial myxoma (Option D): Non-caseating granulomas are associated with sarcoidosis, not SSc. Atrial myxoma is unrelated to SSc, making this option incorrect.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2780-2782
question: A 52-year-old woman presents with skin changes, including thickened and tight skin on her fingers, as well as pain and ulcerations at the fingertips. On examination, she has a shiny appearance to her skin and visible telangiectasia on her face. Which of the following options includes one pulmonary and one cardiac manifestation correctly associated with her clinical features?

correctAnswer: C. Anti-centromere antibodies increase the risk of scleroderma renal crisis.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Anti-centromere antibodies are associated with a lower risk of scleroderma renal crisis.
  • Commonly presents with severe accelerated hypertension (>150/90 mmHg) and oliguric acute renal failure; ~10% are normotensive but have poor outcomes. (Option A ruled out)
  • Raynaud’s Phenomenon is the most common extracutaneous feature in SSc. (Option B ruled out)
  • Nailfold Capillaroscopy (Option D ruled out):
    • Primary Raynaud’s: Evenly spaced parallel capillary loops.
    • Secondary Raynaud’s: Distorted, widened, irregular capillary loops, dilated lumen, microhemorrhages, and vascular dropout.

[[figure-1]]

[[figure-2]]



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2778, 2782
  2. Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 1037, 1038

question: A 45-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis presents with new-onset hypertension and episodes of cold-induced finger discoloration. Which statement about her renal and vascular manifestations is false?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's symptoms, including skin thickening, fatigue, and shortness of breath, suggest systemic sclerosis with severe skin and pulmonary involvement.
  • Topoisomerase I (Scl-70) is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc and linked to severe skin involvement, interstitial lung disease (ILD), and renal crisis.

Auto-Antibody

Prominent Characteristic

Topoisomerase I (Scl-70)
  • Speckled pattern

[[figure-1]]

  • Tendon friction rubs, digital ischemic ulcers, scleroderma, extensive skin involvement, early ILD, cardiac involvement, scleroderma renal crisis

Centromere proteins
  • Discrete speckled (centromere) pattern

[[figure-2]]

  • Digital ischemic ulcers, calcinosis cutis, isolated PAH; renal crisis rare (Option A ruled out)

RNA polymerase III
  • Speckled pattern
  • Rapidly progressive skin involvement, tendon friction rubs, joint contractures, GAVE, renal crisis, contemporaneous cancers; digital ulcers rare (Option C ruled out)

U1-RNP
  • Speckled pattern
  • PAH, inflammatory arthritis, myositis overlap (Option D ruled out)

question: A 45-year-old woman presents with symptoms including skin thickening on her fingers, fatigue, and shortness of breath with episodes of painful swelling in her fingertips and difficulty swallowing. During her examination, a specific immunofluorescence test is performed, revealing the presence of several autoantibodies. Which of the following auto-antibodies is most likely associated with severe skin involvement and interstitial lung disease in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Given the patient's presentation (including symptoms of Raynaud’s phenomenon, dyspnea on exertion, and gastrointestinal issues such as heartburn) and positive anti-Scl-70 antibodies with no visible skin thickening, the most likely diagnosis is Sine Sclerosis.

Limited Scleroderma (Option A ruled out):

  • Most common type of scleroderma.
  • Skin thickening is usually limited to fingers, hands, forearms, or face.

Diffuse Scleroderma (Option B): Skin thickening over large body areas (fingers, hands, arms, anterior trunk, legs, and face).

Sjögren's Syndrome (Option D) is an autoimmune disorder primarily affecting moisture-producing glands, leading to dry mouth and eyes.

question: A 60-year-old woman presents with severe fatigue, dry mouth, difficulty swallowing, and episodes of coldness and color changes in her fingers. She reports dyspnea on exertion and has a history of gastrointestinal reflux. There is no visible skin thickening. Laboratory tests show positive anti-nuclear antibodies and anti-Scl-70 antibodies. Which condition is she most likely experiencing?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient has Primary Raynaud's phenomenon because:

  • Young female (age 20-40 years, female: male ratio 5:1)
  • Classic triphasic color changes
  • No underlying condition
  • Normal nail fold capillaroscopy showing regular hairpin loops
  • Symmetric involvement
  • Cold trigger

Secondary Raynaud's Due To Scleroderma (Option A): There are no signs of scleroderma-like skin tightening, sclerodactyly, or internal organ involvement, and is associated with digital ulcers and tissue loss

Acrocyanosis (Option C): Acrocyanosis is persistent rather than episodic, does not show triphasic color changes, discoloration extends proximally from digits, and no blanching occurs.

Secondary Raynaud's Due To SLE (Option D): Only about 20% of SLE patients develop Raynaud's, other systemic symptoms of SLE would be present, and may have associated antibodies.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles Of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Volume I, Page. 2112, 2113
question: A 25-year-old female presents with episodes of sequential color changes in her fingers (white, blue, and red) triggered by cold exposure. She has no underlying conditions, normal nail fold capillaroscopy, and symmetric involvement. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis

correctAnswer: B. Immediate initiation of short-acting ACE inhibitors
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Short-acting ACE inhibitors are the first-line treatment for scleroderma renal crisis.
  • This is a medical emergency requiring:
    • Immediate hospitalization
    • Prompt initiation of ACE inhibitors
    • Rapid blood pressure normalization

Start calcium channel blockers and taper steroids (Option A): While useful for Raynaud's phenomenon, calcium channel blockers are not the first-line treatment for scleroderma renal crisis.


Start plasmapheresis for suspected TTP (Option C): While the presentation might mimic TTP with microangiopathic hemolysis and thrombocytopenia, this is characteristic of Scleroderma renal crisis.


Increase steroid dose to control inflammation (Option D): This would worsen the condition as glucocorticoids are a risk factor for scleroderma renal crisis. high-dose steroids (>10 mg/day) should be avoided in high-risk patients.



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles Of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Volume I, Page 2782, 2786
  2. https://www.researchgate.net/figure/UKSSG-guidelines-on-the-diagnosis-and-management-of-scleroderma-renal-crisis-Reproduced_fig3_361015939

Immediate initiation of short-acting ACE inhibitors
