question: A 30-year-old man presents to the clinic for evaluation of elevated liver enzymes. He reports feeling fatigued and has noticed some jaundice. His medical history is significant for recent unprotected sexual contact with a partner who is Hepatitis B positive. Laboratory tests reveal that HBsAg is positive, and further testing shows the presence of HBeAg. Which of the following does the presence of HBeAg indicate in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This patient has symptoms of acute Hepatitis B (fatigue, anorexia, jaundice) following recent exposure. Although HBsAg is negative, this can occur during the window period, when both HBsAg and anti-HBs are undetectable.
  • During this period, the only positive marker is IgM anti-HBc, which is the most reliable indicator of a recent HBV infection.
  • It confirms early acute Hepatitis B even when other markers are not yet detectable.

Positive anti-HBs only (Option A): Indicates recovery or vaccination, not an acute infection; cannot appear during symptoms or the window period.


Positive IgG anti-HBc (Option B): Indicates a past, resolved infection or chronic infection; not a marker of recent exposure.


Positive HBcAg (Option D): The core antigen is intracellular and never detected in serum; only antibodies to it (IgM/IgG anti-HBc) are measurable.



Reference:

Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 873-875
question: A 28-year-old woman presents to the clinic with fatigue, loss of appetite, and mild jaundice. She reports that she had a recent exposure to a friend who was diagnosed with Hepatitis B. Laboratory tests reveal that HBsAg is negative, but her liver enzymes are elevated. Which of the following is the most likely finding in this patient’s blood tests?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is responsible for more than half of all cases of fulminant viral hepatitis due to its ability to trigger severe immune-mediated hepatocellular destruction and massive hepatic necrosis.
  • Cause of fulminant hepatitis
    • Fulminant hepatitis refers to:
      • Rapid development of acute liver failure
      • Severe hepatocellular necrosis
      • Hepatic encephalopathy
      • Coagulopathy occurring within weeks of acute hepatitis
  • Major viral causes of fulminant hepatitis
    • Primarily associated with:
      • HBV
      • HDV coinfection/superinfection
      • HEV
      • Rarely HAV
  • HBV commonly causes fulminant hepatitis:
    • Severe host immune response against infected hepatocytes
    • Extensive hepatocyte apoptosis and necrosis
    • Massive hepatic dysfunction
  • Clinical manifestations
    • Rapid jaundice progression
    • Markedly elevated aminotransferases
    • Coagulopathy (↑ PT/INR)
    • Hepatic encephalopathy
    • Cerebral oedema in severe cases
  • Important prognostic indicators
    • Prolonged prothrombin time
    • Elevated bilirubin
    • Encephalopathy
    • Renal dysfunction
  • Role of HDV
    • HBV with hepatitis D coinfection or superinfection markedly increases:
      • Severity of hepatitis
      • Risk of fulminant hepatic failure
  • Complications of fulminant hepatitis
    • Cerebral edema
    • Sepsis
    • Hepatorenal syndrome
    • Multiorgan failure

Hepatitis A virus (HAV) (Option A): Rarely causes fulminant hepatitis and accounts for only a small proportion of overall cases.

Hepatitis C virus (HCV) (Option C): Fulminant hepatitis is exceedingly uncommon in acute HCV infection. More commonly progresses to chronic hepatitis

Hepatitis E virus (HEV) (Option D): HEV can cause severe fulminant hepatitis, especially in pregnancy, but does not account for most cases overall.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2659, 2660.
question: Which hepatitis virus accounts for more than 50% of cases of fulminant viral hepatitis worldwide?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Baseline NS5A resistance-associated substitutions (RASs) markedly reduce the efficacy of elbasvir-grazoprevir in genotype 1a HCV infection, decreasing sustained virologic response rates and historically necessitating pretreatment RAS testing with treatment extension and ribavirin addition.

  • NS5A inhibitors: Direct-acting antivirals that:
    • Block HCV replication complex assembly
    • Inhibit viral RNA replication
    • Interfere with virion assembly
  • Common NS5A inhibitors
    • Elbasvir
    • Ledipasvir
    • Velpatasvir
    • Pibrentasvir
  • Characteristics of NS5A inhibitors
    • Highly potent antiviral activity
    • Important component of pangenotypic regimens
    • Low genetic barrier to resistance compared with some other DAAs
  • Resistance-associated substitutions (RASs)
    • Viral mutations that reduce DAA susceptibility
    • Most clinically important in:
      • Genotype 1a infection
      • Treatment-experienced patients
  • Elbasvir-grazoprevir and NS5A RASs
    • Baseline NS5A RASs significantly reduce treatment efficacy
    • Historically:
      • Baseline RAS testing was mandatory in genotype 1a
      • Positive RASs required:
        • 16-week therapy
        • Addition of ribavirin
  • Mechanism of regimen components
    • Elbasvir: NS5A inhibitor
    • Grazoprevir: NS3/4A protease inhibitor
  • Other important HCV regimens
    • Sofosbuvir-velpatasvir:
      • Pangenotypic
      • Minimal impact from baseline NS5A RASs
    • Glecaprevir-pibrentasvir:
      • Protease inhibitor + NS5A inhibitor
      • High cure rates across genotypes
  • Pretreatment evaluation before DAAs
    • Fibrosis staging
    • Drug-drug interaction review
    • Viral genotype determination
    • HBV screening
  • Modern DAAs achieve cure rates >95% in most treatment-naïve patients

Sofosbuvir-velpatasvir (Option A) Baseline NS5A RASs generally do not significantly affect treatment response.

Sofosbuvir-ledipasvir (Option B) Baseline RASs usually have minimal clinical impact in treatment-naïve patients.

Glecaprevir-pibrentasvir (Option D) NS5A RASs may slightly reduce efficacy in some treatment-experienced patients, but not to the dramatic extent seen with elbasvir-grazoprevir.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2690, 2691.
question: A 60 y/o man with chronic hepatitis C genotype 1a and compensated cirrhosis is being evaluated for direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy. For which of the following regimens do baseline NS5A RASs significantly reduce efficacy in genotype 1a patients, possible treatment extension with ribavirin?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Sofosbuvir-containing regimens are contraindicated with amiodarone because they can cause severe symptomatic bradycardia and potentially fatal cardiac conduction abnormalities.

  • Treatment regimen for hepatitis C
    • Modern HCV treatment relies on: Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs)
    • DAAs target:
      • Viral replication proteins
      • NS3/4A protease
      • NS5A protein
      • NS5B polymerase
  • Sofosbuvir: NS5B RNA polymerase inhibitor commonly combined with Velpatasvir, Ledipasvir, Velpatasvir/voxilaprevir
  • Major drug interaction with amiodarone
    • Can cause severe bradycardia, syncope, heart block, sudden cardiac death
    • Risk increases with Beta-blocker coadministration & underlying cardiac disease
  • Important pretreatment evaluation before DAA therapy
    • HCV genotype
    • Fibrosis staging
    • Drug-drug interaction review
    • HBV screening
    • Renal function assessment
  • Goals of HCV treatment
    • Achieve sustained virologic response (SVR)
    • Prevent:
      • Cirrhosis
      • Hepatocellular carcinoma
      • Hepatic decompensation
  • Monitoring during therapy
    • HCV RNA levels
    • Liver function tests
    • Adverse drug interactions

Glecaprevir (Option A): Does not have the characteristic life-threatening bradycardia interaction seen with sofosbuvir and amiodarone.

Pibrentasvir (Option B): Important DAA component but not specifically associated with severe amiodarone-induced bradycardia.

Elbasvir (Option D): Requires interaction review but lacks the classic dangerous interaction seen with sofosbuvir.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2690, 2691.
question: A 58 y/o man with chronic hepatitis C genotype 1a is being evaluated for direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy. His medical history is significant for cardiac arrhythmia treated with amiodarone. Which DAA component must be avoided because of interaction with amiodarone?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

HIV co-infection accelerates fibrosis progression in chronic hepatitis C by increasing viral replication, impairing immune regulation, and promoting more rapid hepatic inflammation and cirrhosis development.

Predictors of fibrosis progression in HCV

  • Chronic hepatitis C progression varies significantly among patients.
  • Important determinants include:
    • Viral factors
    • Host metabolic factors
    • Coinfections
    • Alcohol exposure
  • Major predictors of rapid fibrosis progression
    • HIV co-infection
    • Alcohol-associated liver disease
    • Obesity
    • Hepatic steatosis
    • Chronic HBV co-infection
    • Increased hepatic iron stores
  • Impact of HIV co-infection
    • Faster fibrosis progression
    • Earlier cirrhosis
    • Increased hepatic decompensation risk
    • Increased hepatocellular carcinoma risk
  • Mechanisms contributing to progression
    • Persistent hepatic inflammation
    • Immune dysregulation
    • Increased oxidative stress
    • Enhanced fibrogenesis
  • Importance of antiviral therapy
    • Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs):
      • Achieve cure rates >95%
      • Reduce fibrosis progression
      • Lower HCC risk
  • Monitoring chronic HCV patients
    • Liver fibrosis assessment
    • HCC surveillance in cirrhosis
    • Evaluation of coinfections and metabolic risk factors

Hepatitis A virus (HAV) co-infection (Option A): HAV does not cause chronic liver disease in immunocompetent individuals and is not a major predictor of HCV fibrosis progression.

Uncomplicated cholelithiasis (Option C): Gallstone disease does not significantly influence HCV-related fibrosis progression.

Primary biliary cholangitis (Option D): Although it is a chronic liver disease, it is not specifically recognised as a classic predictor of fibrosis acceleration in chronic HCV.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2685, 2686.
question: Which of the following concomitant conditions is recognised as an important factor that accelerates fibrosis progression in patients with chronic hepatitis C infection?

correctAnswer: B. All adolescents and adults aged 18-79 years
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

CDC and USPSTF guidelines recommend one-time universal HCV screening for all adults aged 18-79 years because many infected individuals remain asymptomatic for years, and early diagnosis significantly reduces cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma, and transmission risk.

  • Indications for Hepatitis C screening
    • HCV screening aims to:
      • Detect asymptomatic infection
      • Initiate early antiviral therapy
      • Prevent chronic liver disease progression
      • Reduce transmission
  • Current universal screening recommendation:
    • Screen: All adults aged 18-79 years
    • Regardless of risk factor status
  • Why was universal screening adopted?
    • A large number of undiagnosed chronic infections
    • Effective curative direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy available
    • Chronic HCV often remains clinically silent for decades
  • High-risk groups requiring screening:
    • Injection drug users
    • Patients on hemodialysis
    • HIV-positive individuals
    • Recipients of blood transfusions before 1992
    • Children born to HCV-positive mothers
  • Previous recommendation:
    • Earlier guidelines focused mainly on: Persons born between 1945-1965 (“baby boomer cohort”)
    • Updated recommendations expanded to universal adult screening
  • Screening tests:
    • Initial test: Anti-HCV antibody
    • Confirmation: HCV RNA testing
  • Complications prevented by early diagnosis:
    • Cirrhosis
    • Hepatocellular carcinoma
    • Portal hypertension
    • Liver failure

All persons born between 1945 and 1965 only (Option A): This was the older recommendation and has now been replaced by broader universal adult screening.

All adults older than 50 years (Option C): Current recommendations are not restricted to this age group.

All children and adolescents aged 12-21 years (Option D): This does not represent the current universal screening guideline.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2654, 2655.

options.text: All persons born between 1945 and 1965 only
All adolescents and adults aged 18-79 years
All children and adolescents aged 12-21 years

question: According to current CDC and USPSTF recommendations, which of the following groups should undergo universal screening for hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection regardless of traditional risk factors?

correctAnswer: C. Ultrasound of the liver at 6- to 12-month intervals
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Liver ultrasound performed every 6-12 months is the recommended screening modality for HCC surveillance because it is noninvasive, cost-effective, widely available, and effective for early tumour detection in high-risk cirrhotic patients.

  • Surveillance for HCC is recommended in:
    • Patients with cirrhosis
    • Selected chronic HBV patients, even without cirrhosis
    • High-risk chronic liver disease populations
  • Recommended surveillance strategy
    • Primary modality: Liver ultrasound (US)
    • Surveillance interval:
      • Every 6 months (preferred)
      • Acceptable range: 6-12 months
  • Early detection improves:
    • Curative treatment eligibility
    • Surgical resection outcomes
    • Liver transplantation success
    • Overall survival
  • Common high-risk groups requiring surveillance
    • Viral hepatitis-related cirrhosis
    • Alcohol-associated cirrhosis
    • MASLD/MASH-related cirrhosis
    • Autoimmune hepatitis with cirrhosis
  • Advantages of ultrasound
    • Noninvasive
    • No radiation exposure
    • Relatively inexpensive
    • Good sensitivity for surveillance
  • Role of CT and MRI - Used primarily for:
    • Lesion characterization
    • Staging
    • Diagnostic confirmation after abnormal screening US
  • Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP):
    • Sometimes combined with ultrasound
    • Limited sensitivity and specificity alone
  • Important HCC risk factors
    • Cirrhosis
    • Chronic HBV infection
    • Chronic HCV infection
    • Alcohol-related liver disease
    • MASLD/MASH
  • Surveillance detect small, early-stage tumours amenable to:
    • Resection
    • Ablation
    • Liver transplantation

Contrast-enhanced CT scan every 2 years (Option A): CT is not recommended as the routine primary surveillance tool because of radiation exposure and cost.

MRI of the liver every 1-2 years (Option B): MRI is highly sensitive but reserved mainly for lesion characterisation or high-risk special cases rather than standard surveillance.

Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) annually (Option D): EUS is primarily used for gastrointestinal and pancreatic evaluation, not routine HCC surveillance.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2632, 2633.

options.text: MRI of the liver every 1-2 years
Ultrasound of the liver at 6- to 12-month intervals

question: What is the recommended primary imaging modality and surveillance interval for screening hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in patients with cirrhosis?

correctAnswer: B. Entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), and tenofovir alafenamide (TAF)
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Entecavir, TDF, and TAF are recommended first-line therapies because they provide potent suppression of HBV DNA with a high genetic barrier to antiviral resistance and excellent long-term efficacy.

  • 1st line therapy in chronic HBV - Goals of chronic HBV treatment:
    • Suppress HBV replication
    • Reduce hepatic inflammation
    • Prevent cirrhosis
    • Prevent hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)
    • Reduce liver-related mortality
  • Current preferred first-line agents: Oral nucleos(t)ide analogues:
    • Entecavir
    • Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF)
    • Tenofovir alafenamide (TAF)
  • Advantages of first-line oral agents
    • Potent antiviral activity
    • Durable HBV DNA suppression
    • Low resistance rates
    • Once-daily oral dosing
  • Tenofovir preparations
    • TDF: Highly effective, possible renal and bone toxicity with prolonged use
    • TAF: Similar antiviral efficacy, lower renal and bone adverse effects
  • Entecavir: Effective against wild-type HBV, high resistance barrier in treatment-naïve patients
  • Pegylated interferon (PEG-IFN)
    • Also considered a first-line option in selected patients
    • Advantages: Finite duration therapy
    • Limitations:
      • Injectable
      • Significant adverse effects
  • Older HBV therapies
    • Lamivudine
    • Adefovir
    • Telbivudine
    • Less preferred because of:
      • High resistance rates
      • Inferior long-term efficacy
  • Monitoring during therapy
    • HBV DNA levels
    • ALT levels
    • HBeAg seroconversion
    • Renal function with tenofovir
  • Complications prevented by therapy
    • Cirrhosis
    • Liver failure
    • Hepatocellular carcinoma

Lamivudine and adefovir dipivoxil (Option A): Older agents associated with significant antiviral resistance are no longer preferred as first-line therapy.

Telbivudine and emtricitabine (Option C): Telbivudine has high resistance rates, and emtricitabine is not approved as standard HBV monotherapy.

Standard interferon-α and ribavirin (Option D): Ribavirin is used primarily for hepatitis C; standard interferon has largely been replaced by pegylated interferon formulations.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2675, 2676.

options.text: Entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), and tenofovir alafenamide (TAF)

question: Which of the following medications are currently recommended as first-line oral agents for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B infection?

correctAnswer: C. The immunoglobulin class of anti-HBc (IgM versus IgG)
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The immunoglobulin class of anti-HBc differentiates acute HBV-HDV coinfection from HDV superinfection because IgM anti-HBc indicates recent acute HBV infection, whereas IgG anti-HBc indicates pre-existing chronic HBV infection with subsequent HDV superinfection.

  • HBV superinfection and coinfection
    • HDV is a defective RNA virus that requires HBsAg for replication and transmission
    • HDV infection occurs only in patients infected with HBV
  • Types of HDV infection
    • Coinfection: Simultaneous acute HBV + HDV infection
      • Usually, IgM anti-HBc positive; Acute hepatitis presentation
    • Superinfection: HDV infection in a patient with chronic HBV
      • Usually, IgG anti-HBc positive; More severe liver disease
  • Important serologic distinction
    • Acute HBV infection: IgM anti-HBc predominates
    • Chronic HBV infection: IgG anti-HBc predominates
  • Clinical significance of HDV superinfection
    • Associated with:
      • Severe hepatitis
      • Fulminant hepatic failure
      • Rapid progression to cirrhosis
  • HBV markers commonly present in both conditions
    • HBsAg: Positive in both coinfection and superinfection
    • HDV RNA: Detectable in both active infections
  • HDV cannot replicate independently because it requires HBV surface antigen envelope
  • Diagnostic approach
    • Evaluate:
      • HBsAg
      • Anti-HBc class
      • HDV RNA
      • Anti-HDV antibodies
  • Clinical outcomes
    • Coinfection: Often self-limited
    • Superinfection: Higher risk of chronic liver disease and hepatic decompensation

Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) (Option A): Present in both coinfection and superinfection and cannot distinguish between them.

HDV RNA (Option B): Indicates active HDV replication but does not determine whether HBV infection is acute or chronic.

Anti-HBs (Option D): Marker of immunity or recovery and is not present during active HBV-HDV infection.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2658, 2659.

options.text: The immunoglobulin class of anti-HBc (IgM versus IgG)

question: Which of the following serologic markers is most useful for distinguishing acute hepatitis D virus (HDV) co-infection with hepatitis B virus (HBV) from acute HDV superinfection in a patient with chronic HBV infection?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

IgM anti-HBc is the most reliable marker of recent acute HBV infection because it appears early during acute infection and declines over time, distinguishing acute disease from remote or chronic infection.

  • Most reliable indicator of HBV infection - HBV serology is used to determine:
    • Acute infection
    • Chronic infection
    • Recovery
    • Immunity
    • Viral replication status
  • Role of IgM anti-HBc
    • Appears during:
      • Acute HBV infection
      • Early symptomatic phase
    • Indicates:
      • Recent infection
      • Acute hepatitis B
  • Clinical importance of IgM anti-HBc
    • Helps distinguish:
      • Acute infection
      • Chronic HBV
      • Remote resolved infection
    • Particularly useful during the “window period”
  • Window period:
    • Interval when HBsAg disappears & Anti-HBs not yet detectable
    • IgM anti-HBc may be the only positive serologic marker
  • Other important HBV markers
    • HBsAg: Indicates active infection; Does not differentiate acute vs chronic disease
    • Anti-HBs: Indicates recovery or vaccination-induced immunity
    • HBeAg: Marker of active viral replication and infectivity
    • IgG anti-HBc: Indicates past exposure or chronic infection
  • Interpretation:
    • Acute HBV: HBsAg positive; IgM anti-HBc positive
    • Chronic HBV: HBsAg positive >6 months; IgG anti-HBc positive
    • Resolved infection: Anti-HBs positive; IgG anti-HBc positive
  • HBV is a DNA virus that replicates via reverse transcription through an RNA intermediate.

[[figure-1]]

Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) (Option A) indicates current HBV infection but cannot reliably distinguish acute from chronic infection.

Anti-HBs (Option B) reflects immunity following recovery or vaccination, not recent acute infection.

Hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) (Option D) is a marker of viral replication and infectivity rather than infection timing.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2658, 2659.
question: Which of the following serologic markers is the most reliable indicator for distinguishing a recent acute hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection from a remote past infection?

correctAnswer: B. Anti-HBe positivity with detectable replicating HBV DNA
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Precore mutant HBV contains mutations that prevent HBeAg synthesis despite continued active viral replication, resulting in anti-HBe positivity with detectable HBV DNA levels.

  • Types of hepatitis B mutants
    • HBV mutants arise due to:
      • Viral replication errors
      • Immune selection pressure
      • Antiviral therapy exposure
  • Precore mutant HBV
    • Common mutation: G→A substitution at nucleotide 1896
    • Creates: Premature stop codon
    • Consequence: Failure to produce HBeAg
  • Characteristic serologic profile
    • HBsAg positive
    • Anti-HBc positive
    • Anti-HBe positive
    • Detectable HBV DNA
    • Active hepatitis despite absent HBeAg
  • Clinical significance of precore mutants - Associated with:
    • Severe chronic hepatitis B
    • Persistent hepatic inflammation
    • Progressive fibrosis and cirrhosis risk
  • Interpretation:
    • Absence of HBeAg does not always indicate inactive disease
    • HBV DNA quantification is essential to assess true viral replication
  • Other important HBV mutants
    • Core promoter mutants
    • Surface antigen escape mutants
    • Polymerase-resistant mutants
  • HBV serology
    • HBsAg: Active infection
    • HBeAg: Viral replication/infectivity
    • Anti-HBe: Reduced infectivity in typical strains
    • Anti-HBc: Evidence of exposure
  • Clinical implication: Patients with precore mutants may appear less infectious serologically while still having significant viral activity and liver injury.

[[figure-1]]

HBeAg positivity with undetectable HBV DNA (Option A): Active HBeAg positivity usually correlates with viral replication, not the absence of HBV DNA.

Loss of HBsAg with simultaneous appearance of anti-HBs (Option C): This pattern indicates recovery and immunity, not precore mutant infection.

Absence of both HBsAg and anti-HBc despite active hepatitis (Option D): Active HBV infection characteristically produces detectable viral antigens or antibodies.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2647, 2648.

options.text: HBeAg positivity with undetectable HBV DNA
Anti-HBe positivity with detectable replicating HBV DNA
Loss of HBsAg with simultaneous appearance of anti-HBs
Absence of both HBsAg and anti-HBc despite active hepatitis

question: A patient with chronic hepatitis B infection undergoes serologic testing. The laboratory report demonstrates detectable HBV DNA with active viral replication despite the absence of HBeAg and the presence of anti-HBe antibodies. Which of the following is most characteristic of an HBV precore mutant infection?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hemochromatosis causes progressive iron overload within hepatocytes, leading to chronic inflammation, fibrosis, and eventually cirrhosis if untreated.

  • Causes of cirrhosis
    • Cirrhosis represents the end stage of chronic liver injury, characterised by:
      • Diffuse fibrosis
      • Regenerative nodules
      • Distortion of hepatic architecture
  • Major causes of cirrhosis
    • Chronic viral hepatitis (HBV, HCV)
    • Alcohol-related liver disease
    • MASLD/MASH
    • Autoimmune hepatitis
    • Cholestatic liver disease
    • Inherited metabolic disorders
  • Inherited metabolic disorders causing cirrhosis
    • Hemochromatosis
    • Wilson disease
    • α1-antitrypsin deficiency
    • Cystic fibrosis–associated liver disease
  • Pathophysiology of hemochromatosis
    • Excess intestinal iron absorption
    • Progressive iron accumulation in the liver, pancreas, heart, and skin
    • Hepatic iron deposition leads to:
      • Oxidative injury
      • Fibrosis
      • Cirrhosis
      • Increased hepatocellular carcinoma risk
  • Clinical features of hereditary hemochromatosis
    • Hepatomegaly
    • Diabetes mellitus
    • Skin hyperpigmentation (“bronze diabetes”)
    • Cardiomyopathy
    • Arthropathy
  • Interpretation:
    • Elevated ferritin and transferrin saturation suggest iron overload
    • Liver biopsy or MRI may assess hepatic iron burden
    • Early phlebotomy can prevent progression to cirrhosis

Gilbert syndrome (Option A): Benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to reduced bilirubin conjugation; it does not cause fibrosis or cirrhosis.

Dubin-Johnson syndrome (Option C): Benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with pigmented liver but no progression to cirrhosis.

Rotor syndrome (Option D): Benign hereditary conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal liver histology and no cirrhosis.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2712.
question: Which of the following inherited metabolic disorders is a well-recognised cause of cirrhosis due to progressive hepatic iron deposition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The major cause of death in hepatitis E infection is fulminant hepatitis with massive hepatic necrosis, leading to acute liver failure and severe hepatic dysfunction.

  • Fatality due to hepatitis E
    • Hepatitis E virus (HEV):
      • Enterically transmitted RNA virus
      • Usually causes self-limited acute hepatitis
      • Endemic in developing regions with poor sanitation
  • Fulminant hepatitis in HEV
    • Characterised by:
      • Rapid hepatocellular necrosis
      • Acute liver failure
      • Hepatic encephalopathy
      • Coagulopathy
    • Represents the most feared complication of acute viral hepatitis
  • Mortality pattern
    • General mortality:
      • Approximately 1-2%
    • Pregnancy-associated mortality:
      • Can reach up to 20%
      • Especially during the third trimester
  • Clinical features of fulminant hepatitis
    • Jaundice
    • Markedly elevated aminotransferases
    • Prolonged prothrombin time
    • Encephalopathy
    • Cerebral oedema in severe cases
  • Why pregnant women are at high risk
    • Altered immune response
    • Hormonal influences
    • Increased susceptibility to severe hepatic injury
  • Chronicity and long-term complications
    • HEV usually does not progress to:
      • Chronic hepatitis
      • Cirrhosis
      • Hepatocellular carcinoma
    • Chronic infection may occur in immunocompromised hosts
  • Interpretation: Although acute-on-chronic liver failure may occur in patients with preexisting liver disease, fulminant hepatic failure remains the principal mechanism responsible for HEV-related fatalities

Ruptured hepatocellular carcinoma (Option B): HEV does not typically cause chronic liver disease leading to HCC in immunocompetent individuals.

Secondary biliary cirrhosis (Option C): This is not a recognised complication of acute HEV infection.

Acute-on-chronic liver failure due to underlying hepatitis B (Option D): This can occur in selected patients with underlying liver disease, but it is not the primary mechanism responsible for overall HEV mortality.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2659, 2660.

options.text: Acute-on-chronic liver failure due to underlying hepatitis B

question: Fatalities associated with hepatitis E virus (HEV) infection are most commonly caused by which severe complication?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hepatitis E virus (HEV) is primarily transmitted by the faecal-oral route through contaminated water supplies, especially during outbreaks associated with poor sanitation and flooding.

  • Routes of transmission of hepatitis E
    • HEV is:
      • An enterically transmitted RNA virus
      • A major cause of acute viral hepatitis in developing countries
      • Commonly associated with waterborne epidemics
  • Epidemiology of HEV
    • Endemic in: India, Southeast Asia, Africa, Central America
    • Large outbreaks often occur after:
      • Monsoon flooding
      • Sewage contamination
      • Unsafe drinking water exposure
  • Primary transmission route
    • Faecal-oral spread via:
      • Contaminated water
      • Poor sanitation systems
      • Community water outbreaks
  • Morphology: HEV is:
    • A non-enveloped RNA virus
    • Usually self-limited
    • Similar to HAV epidemiologically
  • Clinical features
    • Jaundice
    • Malaise
    • Fever
    • Nausea
    • Elevated aminotransferases
  • High-risk population
    • Pregnant women, especially during the third trimester:
      • Increased risk of fulminant hepatitis
      • High maternal mortality
  • Transmission patterns compared with HBV/HCV
    • HEV: Primarily enteric
    • HBV/HCV: Primarily, bloodborne and sexual transmission
  • Chronic infection
    • Rare in immunocompetent individuals
    • May occur in immunosuppressed patients

Percutaneous exposure through shared needles (Option A): Bloodborne transmission is characteristic of HBV and HCV, not the predominant route for HEV.

Intimate sexual contact (Option C): Sexual transmission is uncommon and not a major epidemiologic route for HEV.

Perinatal transmission from mother to infant (Option D): Vertical transmission may occur rarely, but it is not the principal mode of spread in endemic regions.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2652, 2653.

options.text: Perinatal transmission from mother to infant

question: Which of the following is the most common mode of transmission of the hepatitis E virus (HEV) in highly endemic regions such as India, Asia, Africa, and Central America?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

HBcAg is an intracellular nucleocapsid core protein that remains enclosed within hepatocytes and viral particles; naked HBcAg does not freely circulate in serum, so routine clinical testing measures anti-HBc antibodies instead of the antigen itself.

  • DNA virus causing hepatitis
    • Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is:
      • A partially double-stranded DNA virus
      • Member of the Hepadnaviridae family
      • The major DNA virus causing viral hepatitis in humans
  • Important HBV antigens
    • HBsAg
      • Surface envelope protein
      • The earliest marker of active infection
      • Freely circulates in the blood
    • HBeAg
      • Secreted nucleocapsid-associated protein
      • Marker of active viral replication and infectivity
    • HBcAg
      • Intracellular core protein
      • Located within infected hepatocytes
      • Not detectable directly in serum
    • HBx protein
      • Regulatory transcriptional protein
      • Plays a role in viral replication and hepatocarcinogenesis
  • Serologic interpretation of HBV infection
    • HBsAg positive: Current HBV infection
    • Anti-HBs positive: Recovery or vaccination
    • IgM anti-HBc: Acute infection
    • IgG anti-HBc: Prior exposure or chronic infection

[[figure-1]]

  • Why HBcAg is not routinely assayed
    • Core particles are:
      • Intracellular
      • Covered by HBsAg envelope in circulation
    • Therefore:
      • Direct serum detection is impractical
      • Anti-HBc antibody testing is clinically used instead
  • Clinical significance of anti-HBc
    • Important during:
      • Acute infection
      • Window period
      • Chronic HBV assessment
    • HBV replicates through an RNA intermediate using reverse transcriptase despite being a DNA virus.

Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) (Option A): Freely circulates in serum and is the primary marker used to diagnose active HBV infection.

Hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) (Option B): Secreted into circulation and serves as a marker of viral replication and infectivity.

Hepatitis B x antigen (HBxAg (Option D): Regulatory protein involved in transcriptional activation and oncogenesis, but not the intracellular core antigen described in the question.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2644, 2645.
question: During the evaluation of acute hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, several viral antigens and antibodies are assessed serologically. Which of the following HBV proteins is an intracellular core protein that does not circulate freely in serum and therefore is not routinely measured directly in clinical practice?

correctAnswer: C. Lifestyle modification with a healthy diet and regular exercise
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Lifestyle modification with dietary changes and regular physical activity is the cornerstone and first-line therapy for MASH because sustained weight reduction improves hepatic steatosis, inflammation, and fibrosis progression.

  • 1st-line therapy for MASH
    • Metabolic dysfunction–associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) and MASH are strongly associated with:
      • Obesity
      • Type 2 diabetes mellitus
      • Insulin resistance
      • Metabolic syndrome
  • Goals of first-line treatment
    • Reduce hepatic fat accumulation
    • Improve insulin sensitivity
    • Decrease hepatic inflammation
    • Prevent progression to fibrosis and cirrhosis
  • Role of weight loss
    • Weight reduction is the most effective nonpharmacologic intervention
    • Clinical benefits:
      • 3–5% weight loss → improves steatosis
      • 7–10% weight loss → improves steatohepatitis and fibrosis
  • Recommended lifestyle interventions
    • Calorie-restricted healthy diet
    • Mediterranean-style diet
    • Reduction in fructose and processed foods
    • Routine aerobic exercise
    • Resistance training
  • Importance of exercise
    • Improves:
      • Insulin sensitivity
      • Hepatic lipid metabolism
      • Cardiometabolic risk
    • Benefits may occur even without major weight loss
  • Pharmacologic therapy in MASH
    • Reserved for selected high-risk patients
    • Includes:
      • Pioglitazone
      • Vitamin E
      • GLP-1 receptor agonists (selected patients)
  • Disease progression without treatment
    • Persistent inflammation may lead to:
      • Advanced fibrosis
      • Cirrhosis
      • Portal hypertension
      • Hepatocellular carcinoma
  • Important interpretation concept
    • Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of mortality in MASLD/MASH patients, making lifestyle therapy critically important.

Bariatric surgery (Option A): Useful in selected obese patients but not considered universal first-line therapy for all MASH patients.

Vitamin E supplementation (Option B): May improve histology in selected non-diabetic patients, but is not a foundational therapy.

Pioglitazone (Option D): Can improve steatohepatitis but is generally reserved for selected patients because of adverse effects and long-term concerns.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2705, 2706.

options.text: Lifestyle modification with a healthy diet and regular exercise

question: Which of the following is considered the foundational first-line treatment for patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH)?

correctAnswer: B. Corticosteroids reduce 28-day mortality compared with pentoxifylline or placebo
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Corticosteroids have demonstrated a short-term survival benefit in severe alcoholic hepatitis and significantly reduce 28-day mortality when compared with pentoxifylline or placebo.

  • Pentoxifylline for the management of severe alcoholic hepatitis
    • Severe alcoholic hepatitis is characterised by:
      • Acute hepatic inflammation
      • Jaundice
      • Coagulopathy
      • High short-term mortality
  • Role of corticosteroids
    • Prednisolone is the standard pharmacologic therapy in eligible patients
    • Mechanism:
      • Suppression of inflammatory cytokines
      • Reduction in hepatic inflammatory injury
    • Demonstrated benefit:
      • Improved 28-day survival
  • Role of pentoxifylline
    • Pentoxifylline is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor that reduces TNF-α production.
    • Previously studied as an alternative therapy.
    • Current evidence does not support a significant mortality reduction compared with corticosteroids
  • Key findings from the Louvet et al. meta-analysis
    • Corticosteroids: Reduced short-term mortality
    • Pentoxifylline: No significant survival advantage over placebo
    • Therefore, Pentoxifylline is no longer routinely recommended as primary therapy
  • Assessment of severe alcoholic hepatitis
    • Maddrey Discriminant Function (DF)
    • MELD score
    • Lille score for steroid response
  • Important treatment considerations
    • Corticosteroids should be avoided in:
      • Active infection
      • GI bleeding
      • Severe renal failure
      • Uncontrolled sepsis
  • Major complications of severe alcoholic hepatitis
    • Hepatic encephalopathy
    • Hepatorenal syndrome
    • Sepsis
    • Acute-on-chronic liver failure

Pentoxifylline significantly reduces 28-day mortality compared with corticosteroids (Option A): Pentoxifylline did not demonstrate a superior short-term survival benefit compared with corticosteroids.

Pentoxifylline and corticosteroids provide identical mortality benefit compared with placebo (Option C): Corticosteroids showed superior short-term mortality reduction.

Neither corticosteroids nor pentoxifylline improves 28-day mortality compared with placebo (Option D): Corticosteroids do improve 28-day survival in selected patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2700.

options.text: Pentoxifylline significantly reduces 28-day mortality compared with corticosteroids
Corticosteroids reduce 28-day mortality compared with pentoxifylline or placebo
Pentoxifylline and corticosteroids provide identical mortality benefit compared with placebo
Neither corticosteroids nor pentoxifylline improves 28-day mortality compared with placebo

question: Which of the following best summarises the effect of corticosteroid therapy on 28-day mortality in severe alcoholic hepatitis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency causes abnormal accumulation of misfolded alpha-1 antitrypsin protein within hepatocytes, leading to chronic hepatocellular injury, fibrosis, and cirrhosis.

  • Types of cirrhosis
    • Cirrhosis is the end-stage consequence of chronic liver injury characterised by:
      • Diffuse fibrosis
      • Regenerative nodules
      • Distortion of hepatic architecture
  • Etiologic categories of cirrhosis
    • Alcohol-related liver disease
    • Chronic viral hepatitis (HBV, HCV)
    • MASLD/MASH
    • Autoimmune liver disease
    • Cholestatic liver disease
    • Inherited metabolic liver diseases
  • Inherited metabolic causes of cirrhosis
    • Hemochromatosis
    • Wilson disease
    • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
    • Cystic fibrosis–associated liver disease
  • Pathophysiology of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
    • Defective folding of the alpha-1 antitrypsin protein
    • Retention of abnormal protein in hepatocyte endoplasmic reticulum
    • Progressive hepatocyte injury and fibrosis
  • Clinical manifestations
    • Chronic hepatitis
    • Cirrhosis
    • Portal hypertension
    • Increased hepatocellular carcinoma risk
    • Associated with early-onset emphysema
  • Histopathology: PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules in hepatocytes

[[figure-1]]

  • Innterpretation:
    • Liver involvement severity varies widely
    • Disease may present in:
      • Neonates
      • Children
      • Adults with chronic liver disease

Gilbert syndrome (Option B).Benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to reduced bilirubin conjugation without fibrosis or cirrhosis.

Dubin-Johnson syndrome (Option C) Benign conjugated hyperbilirubinemia caused by impaired bilirubin excretion; does not progress to cirrhosis.

Crigler-Najjar syndrome (Option D) Severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia due to UDP-glucuronyl transferase deficiency, not a fibrosing liver disease.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2707, 2708.
question: Which of the following inherited metabolic liver diseases is a recognised cause of progressive hepatic fibrosis and cirrhosis?

correctAnswer: B. Have people annoyed you by criticising your drinking?
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The “A” in the CAGE questionnaire stands for “Annoyed,” referring to whether the patient has been annoyed by criticism of their drinking habits.

  • CAGE questionnaire
    • The CAGE questionnaire is a rapid screening tool used to identify:
      • Alcohol misuse
      • Alcohol dependence
      • Problematic drinking behaviours
  • Components of the CAGE questionnaire
    • C - Cut down
      • “Have you ever felt you should cut down on your drinking?”
    • A - Annoyed
      • “Have people annoyed you by criticising your drinking?”
    • G - Guilty
      • “Have you ever felt guilty about your drinking?”
    • E - Eye-opener
      • “Have you ever had a drink first thing in the morning to steady your nerves or get rid of a hang


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2629.

options.text: Have you ever experienced blackouts after drinking alcohol?
Have people annoyed you by criticising your drinking?
Have you ever been angry about your need to drink?
Are you drinking alone more often than you used to?

question: A 52 y/o man presents with vague right upper quadrant discomfort. He reports drinking several beers nightly. During screening for alcohol misuse, he admits feeling guilty about his drinking and occasionally requiring a morning drink to relieve a hangover. On the CAGE questionnaire, which of the following represents the “A” component of the CAGE questionnaire?

correctAnswer: B. Alcohol-induced deficiency of pyridoxal phosphate
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Chronic alcohol use causes pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6) deficiency, which reduces hepatic ALT activity and leads to disproportionately low or normal serum ALT levels in alcohol-related liver disease.

  • Specific markers for alcoholism
    • Alcohol-related liver disease classically demonstrates:
      • AST predominance over ALT
      • AST: ALT ratio >2:1
      • Elevated GGT
      • Macrocytosis (↑ MCV)
  • Mechanism of AST predominance
    • Alcohol causes:
      • Mitochondrial injury → increased AST release
      • Pyridoxal phosphate deficiency → impaired ALT activity
    • Result:
      • ALT remains relatively low
      • AST becomes disproportionately elevated
  • Typical laboratory profile in alcohol-related liver disease
    • AST: ALT ratio >2:1 is strongly suggestive
    • AST: ALT ratio >3:1 is highly suggestive
    • AST usually <300 IU/L
    • Elevated GGT is common due to enzyme induction
  • Pyridoxal phosphate matters
    • Pyridoxal phosphate is a cofactor required for ALT synthesis and activity
    • Alcoholism commonly causes a nutritional deficiency of vitamin B6
    • This selectively suppresses ALT levels
  • Other laboratory markers associated with alcoholism
    • Elevated GGT
    • Macrocytosis
    • Hypertriglyceridemia
    • Mild thrombocytopenia in advanced disease
  • Clinical significance
    • AST predominance helps distinguish alcohol-related liver disease from:
      • Viral hepatitis
      • MASLD
      • Drug-induced hepatotoxicity
    • In most nonalcoholic hepatocellular disorders:
      • ALT ≥ AST

Rapid renal clearance of ALT in the presence of ethanol (Option A): ALT reduction in alcoholism is not due to altered renal excretion.

Exclusive synthesis of ALT in cardiac and skeletal muscle (Option C): ALT is predominantly localized to hepatocytes, not muscle tissue.

Direct inhibition of ALT gene transcription by acetaldehyde (Option D): This mechanism is not the established explanation for low ALT in alcohol-related liver disease.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2635, 2636

question: In alcohol-related liver disease, what is the primary mechanism responsible for the characteristically low or normal serum alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels despite ongoing hepatocellular injury?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is a functional renal failure that occurs in advanced cirrhosis due to severe circulatory dysfunction.

Sequence:

  1. Cytokine release (TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8, and increased nitric oxide production)
    • Portal hypertension and bacterial translocation promote systemic inflammation and release of inflammatory mediators.
  2. Systemic vasodilation (predominantly splanchnic arterial vasodilation)
    • Nitric oxide and other vasodilators reduce the effective arterial blood volume despite an increased total blood volume.
  3. Vasopressin release (along with activation of the RAAS and sympathetic nervous system)
    • These compensatory mechanisms are triggered to maintain arterial pressure and circulating volume.
  4. Renal vasoconstriction → decreased renal blood flow and GFR
    • Persistent neurohormonal activation causes marked renal vasoconstriction, leading to functional renal failure without intrinsic kidney damage.

Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS)

Definition

Functional acute kidney injury in advanced cirrhosis due to severe renal vasoconstriction

Pathophysiology

Cytokine release → Splanchnic vasodilation → RAAS/SNS + Vasopressin activation → Renal vasoconstriction

Clinical Features

Oliguria, rising serum creatinine, low urine sodium (<20 mEq/L), bland urine sediment, advanced cirrhosis with ascites

Diagnosis

Cirrhosis with ascites, AKI not responding to albumin and diuretic withdrawal, absence of shock, nephrotoxins, or structural kidney disease

Treatment

Albumin + Terlipressin (first-line), norepinephrine (ICU alternative), liver transplantation (definitive), TIPS in selected patients



Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430856/

question: Which of the following is not a feature of hepatorenal syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient likely has Hepatorenal Syndrome (HRS), a complication of advanced liver disease characterized by renal dysfunction due to splanchnic vasodilation and reduced renal perfusion.
  • HRS is diagnosed based on clinical features, including worsening renal function, low urine sodium (<10 mEq/L), and exclusion of other causes of acute kidney injury (e.g., hypovolemia, nephrotoxicity).
  • The recommended dosage of albumin infusion in HRS is 1 g/kg per day, up to a maximum of 100 g/day, to expand intravascular volume and improve renal perfusion.
  • Treatment is with vasoconstrictors such as terlipressin or, if not available, low-dose norepinephrine, which requires intensive care unit monitoring.
  • Higher doses (e.g., 2-5 g/kg/day) are avoided due to risks such as pulmonary edema.

question: Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of Type 1 hepatorenal syndrome?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's history of chronic liver disease(cirrhosis), positional dyspnea (platypnea-orthodeoxia), the presence of spider angiomas, and hypoxemia are classic findings in hepatopulmonary syndrome (HPS).
  • Hepatopulmonary Syndrome (HPS): It is defined as reduced arterial oxygen saturation due to dilated pulmonary vasculature in the presence of advanced liver disease or portal hypertension.

Atelectasis (Option B):

  • Presents with localized lung findings such as decreased breath sounds, dullness to percussion and potentially an opaque area on a chest X-ray.
  • There is no positional dyspnea or bubble study findings associated with atelectasis.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) (Option C):

  • Present with a history of smoking, chronic cough, and progressive shortness of breath without the positional changes described in this patient.
  • The bubble study result is inconsistent with COPD.

Recurrent pulmonary emboli (Option D):

  • Present with sudden-onset shortness of breath, pleuritic chest pain and sometimes hemoptysis.
  • A bubble study would not show the delayed appearance of bubbles in the left atrium seen in HPS.

question: A 52-year-old male with a long history of cirrhosis presents to the clinic with worsening shortness of breath over the past few months. He reports that his breathlessness worsens when standing and improves when lying down. Physical examination reveals spider angiomas. Pulse oximetry shows an oxygen saturation of 85% on room air. A contrast-enhanced echocardiogram (bubble study) is performed, and delayed bubbles are seen in the left atrium. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • HPS leads to intrapulmonary shunting due to intrapulmonary vascular dilations, where blood bypasses the alveoli, resulting in poor oxygen exchange and hypoxemia.
  • Hepatopulmonary Syndrome (HPS): It is defined as reduced arterial oxygen saturation due to dilated pulmonary vasculature in the presence of advanced liver disease or portal hypertension.

Portopulmonary hypertension (Option B): Causes elevated pulmonary artery pressures but does not result in intrapulmonary shunting. The pathology is related to increased vascular resistance, not shunting.

Recurrent pulmonary emboli (Option C): Causes vascular obstruction, leading to ventilation-perfusion mismatch (dead space), not intrapulmonary shunting.

Pneumonia (Option D): Can cause impaired gas exchange and fluid accumulation in alveoli, but this results in ventilation-perfusion mismatch, not the intrapulmonary shunting seen in HPS.



Reference:

www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK562169/

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Mallory-Denk bodies: These are characteristic of alcoholic hepatitis.

Histopathology:

The classical histological features include:

  • Mallory-Denk bodies: Cytoplasmic inclusions composed of aggregated intermediate filaments particularly keratin (CK8/18) and other proteins.

  • Hepatocellular ballooning representing steatohepatitis
  • Cholestasis
  • Chicken-wire fibrosis

  • These are eosinophilic globules found in plasma cells, associated with conditions like multiple myeloma and chronic inflammatory states, not alcoholic hepatitis

[[figure-2]]

Dutcher bodies (Option B):

  • These are found in the nuclei of plasma cells and are associated with multiple myeloma.
  • They are not related to liver pathology.

[[figure-3]]

Kamino bodies (Option D):

question:
A 52-year-old man with a history of heavy alcohol consumption presents with jaundice, abdominal pain, and fatigue. A liver biopsy is performed to assess the extent of liver damage. Which of the following findings is most characteristic of this condition?

Histopathology image given below:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Asterixis (flapping tremors) is a classical physical examination finding highly suggestive of hepatic encephalopathy.

[[figure-1]]

Hepatic encephalopathy:

  • Portosystemic encephalopathy is a serious complication of chronic liver disease and is broadly defined as an alteration in mental status and cognitive function occurring in the presence of liver failure.
  • Symptoms include confusion, personality changes, violent behavior, or excessive sleepiness, making the patient difficult to manage or rouse.
  • Asterixis: A flapping tremor seen in hepatic encephalopathy.
    • Elicited by having the patient extend arms and bend wrists back (producing a “liver flap”).
  • Other features like hyperbilirubinemia, ascites or gynaecomastia are suggestive of a liver pathology but not indicative of Hepatic encephalopathy.

question: A 50-year-old male with a history of heavy alcohol use presents with jaundice and altered sensorium. Laboratory tests reveal elevated bilirubin, AST > ALT, hypoalbuminemia, and prolonged PT/INR. Which of the following findings is most suggestive of the presence of hepatic encephalopathy in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The AST/ALT ratio is the most specific biochemical marker for alcoholic liver disease among the options. A ratio >2:1 is highly suggestive of alcohol-induced injury, and a ratio >3:1 is even more specific. This occurs because alcoholics often have a deficiency of pyridoxal-5'-phosphate (Vitamin B6), which is a necessary co-factor for ALT synthesis, causing ALT to be disproportionately lower than AST.


γ-glutamyl transferase assay (Option A): While GGT is a sensitive marker for alcohol ingestion due to enzyme induction, it is not specific. It is frequently elevated in NAFLD, cholestasis, and with the use of various medications.


PT/INR (Option B): This is a marker of liver synthetic function and is used to calculate the MELD score, but it does not identify the specific cause of liver disease.


Serum bilirubin (Option C): Indicates the degree of cholestasis or hepatocellular failure and is used for prognostic scoring (e.g., Maddrey’s Discriminant Function), but it is not etiology-specific.


PT/INR (Option B): Reflects liver synthetic failure but is not specific for alcoholic liver disease.


Serum bilirubin (Option C): Indicates cholestasis or hepatocellular dysfunction but not specific to alcohol.


AST/ALT ratio (Option D): Suggestive when >2, but still not specific, as it can be seen in other liver diseases.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2618

question: Which among the following is not a component of Liver FibroTest?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This 12-year-old girl has marked transaminase elevation with polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia, negative viral hepatitis markers, and an association with another autoimmune condition (vitiligo), pointing toward autoimmune hepatitis. The absence of ANA and ASMA makes type 1 AIH unlikely. In children and adolescents, this pattern is characteristic of type 2 autoimmune hepatitis, for which anti-liver kidney microsome type 1 (anti-LKM1) antibodies are the most specific.

  • Type II autoimmune hepatitis is classically associated with anti-LKM1 antibodies, which target cytochrome P450 2D6 and are most commonly seen in children and adolescents, often with concurrent autoimmune diseases.
  • Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is diagnosed using a combination of criteria, not a single test:
    • Hepatocellular pattern of liver injury with markedly elevated AST and ALT
    • Elevated serum IgG or polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia
    • Characteristic autoantibodies (ANA, ASMA, anti-LKM1, anti-SLA, depending on subtype)
    • Exclusion of viral hepatitis, drug-induced, and metabolic liver disease
    • Compatible liver histology showing interface hepatitis with plasma cell-rich infiltrates
  • Subtype distinction:
    • Type I AIH: ANA, ASMA, anti-SLA; all ages
    • Type II AIH: anti-LKM1; predominantly pediatric population

AMA (Option A): Marker of primary biliary cholangitis, not AIH.

Anti-SLA (Option C): Seen in Type I AIH, often severe disease.

pANCA (Option D): Nonspecific; seen in Type I AIH and PSC.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2694, 2695.
question: A 12 y/o girl has elevated liver enzymes. She has vitiligo and is asymptomatic. Labs show ALT 320 U/L, AST 280 U/L, negative ANA and ASMA, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. Viral hepatitis serologies are negative. Which of the following autoantibodies is most specific for this subtype?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • pANCA is positive in approximately 60-70% of patients with PSC, making it the most commonly associated autoantibody and a useful supportive marker in the correct clinical context.
  • Key features of Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis:
    • Chronic cholestatic liver disease affecting intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts
    • Strong association with ulcerative colitis
    • Cholestatic enzyme pattern (↑ ALP, ↑ GGT)
    • pANCA positivity (supportive, not diagnostic)
    • Diagnosis confirmed by cholangiography showing multifocal strictures (“beading”)
    • Increased risk of cholangiocarcinoma and colorectal cancer

AMA (Option A): Hallmark antibody of primary biliary cholangitis, not PSC.

ASMA (Options B): Associated with Type I autoimmune hepatitis.

Anti-LKM1 (Option D): Marker of Type II autoimmune hepatitis, usually pediatric.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2711, 2712.
question: Which of the following autoantibodies is found in approximately 65% of patients with primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC) and can aid in distinguishing it from other cholestatic liver diseases?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In a middle-aged woman with pruritus, fatigue, cholestatic enzymes (↑ ALP), and normal biliary imaging, testing for AMA is the key next step; AMA is present in ~90-95% of PBC cases and establishes the diagnosis when combined with cholestatic labs.
  • Diagnostic framework for PBC:
    • Persistent elevation of alkaline phosphatase
    • Positive AMA (diagnostic in the appropriate clinical setting)
    • Exclusion of extrahepatic biliary obstruction (normal ultrasound)
    • Liver biopsy not required if AMA is positive and labs are typical; reserved for AMA-negative PBC or overlap syndromes
  • Associated features supporting PBC:
    • Female predominance; association with other autoimmune diseases
    • Mild AST/ALT elevation; bilirubin often normal early
    • Possible ANA positivity (nonspecific).

ERCP (Option A): Invasive; used for obstruction or PSC, not first-line in suspected PBC.

Percutaneous liver biopsy (Options C): Reserved for AMA-negative cases or diagnostic uncertainty.

IgG4 level (Option D): Evaluates IgG4-related cholangitis, not typical PBC.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2711.
question: A 48 y/o woman has 6 months of fatigue and nocturnal pruritus and has Hashimoto thyroiditis. The exam shows excoriations and xanthelasma. Ultrasound reveals a normal biliary tree. Labs show: Alkaline phosphatase: 450 U/L (↑↑), AST: 55 U/L, ALT: 60 U/L, Total bilirubin: 1.0 mg/dL, ANA: positive (1:40). What is the most appropriate next step to confirm the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Obeticholic acid is a validated second-line therapy for PBC patients who have an inadequate biochemical response to UDCA, with studies showing significant improvement in cholestatic markers in a substantial proportion of nonresponders.
  • Stepwise management of PBC:
    • First-line therapy: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA)
    • Treatment goal: Reduction in alkaline phosphatase and bilirubin to improve transplant-free survival
    • UDCA-refractory PBC (30-40% of patients):
      • Add or switch to obeticholic acid
      • Emerging alternatives include PPAR agonists (e.g., elafibranor, seladelpar)
    • These agents target bile acid metabolism and cholestatic injury pathways

Azathioprine (Option A) and Prednisone (Option B): Core therapies for autoimmune hepatitis, not standard treatment for PBC.

Ribavirin (Option D): Antiviral used in hepatitis C/E, not cholestatic liver disease.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2711, 2712.
question: A patient with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC) fails to achieve an adequate biochemical response to first-line therapy with ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA). Which of the following agents is an established second-line treatment shown to produce significant biochemical improvement in this subset of patients?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A middle-aged woman with pruritus, xanthelasma, and a cholestatic enzyme pattern (marked ↑ ALP and GGT with mild AST/ALT elevation) is classic for PBC, and AMA is the hallmark serologic marker, present in ~90-95% of cases.

Characteristic laboratory findings in PBC:

  • Cholestatic pattern: Disproportionate ↑ alkaline phosphatase and GGT

  • Mild to moderate AST and ALT elevation

  • Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) positivity

  • Elevated IgM levels

  • Hyperlipidemia → xanthelasma/xanthomas

  • Bilirubin is often normal early; it rises late with disease progression

Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)

  • Chronic, progressive autoimmune cholestatic liver disease causes destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts.

  • Epidemiology: Middle-aged women (female predominance)

  • Pathogenesis: Immune-mediated bile duct injury → cholestasis → fibrosis → cirrhosis

  • Autoantibody: Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) in ~90-95% (diagnostic hallmark)

  • Biochemistry: ↑ ALP and GGT (cholestatic pattern), mild ↑ transaminases

  • Clinical features: Often asymptomatic early, detected via cholestatic labs

    • Fatigue - the most common and debilitating symptom

    • Pruritus - due to chronic cholestasis and bile acid retention

  • Associated conditions: Other autoimmune diseases (Sjögren syndrome, autoimmune thyroid disease)

  • Complications: Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, osteoporosis, portal hypertension

  • Treatment: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) first-line; obeticholic acid if UDCA is inadequate

  • Prognosis: Variable; untreated disease may progress to cirrhosis and liver failure

ANA (Option A) and ASMA(Option C): Typical of Type I autoimmune hepatitis, not PBC.

pANCA (Option D): Associated with primary sclerosing cholangitis and ulcerative colitis.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2711.
question: A 52 y/o woman presents with progressive fatigue and generalised pruritus, worse in the evening. Examination shows excoriations and xanthelasma. Laboratory results are as follows: Total bilirubin: 1.2 mg/dL, Alkaline phosphatase: 580 U/L (↑↑), AST: 65 U/L, ALT: 72 U/L, GGT: 350 U/L. Which of the following serologic markers is most likely to be positive?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Symptomatic PBC is classically characterised by profound fatigue (often disproportionate to disease severity) and pruritus, which is present in approximately half of patients at diagnosis and may precede jaundice.

Primary Biliary Cholangitis (PBC)

  • Chronic, progressive autoimmune cholestatic liver disease causing destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts

  • Epidemiology: Middle-aged women (female predominance)

  • Pathogenesis: Immune-mediated bile duct injury → cholestasis → fibrosis → cirrhosis

  • Autoantibody: Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) in ~90-95% (diagnostic hallmark)

  • Biochemistry: ↑ ALP and GGT (cholestatic pattern), mild ↑ transaminases

  • Clinical features:

    • Often asymptomatic early, detected via cholestatic labs

    • Fatigue - the most common and debilitating symptom

    • Pruritus - due to chronic cholestasis and bile acid retention

    • Jaundice - typically a late manifestation

    • Associated with hyperlipidemia, leading to xanthelasma/xanthomas

    • Strong association with other autoimmune diseases (e.g., Sjögren syndrome, thyroid disease)

  • Associated conditions: Other autoimmune diseases (Sjögren syndrome, autoimmune thyroid disease)

  • Complications: Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency, osteoporosis, portal hypertension

  • Diagnosis: Cholestatic labs + AMA (biopsy if unclear)

  • Treatment: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) first-line; obeticholic acid if UDCA is inadequate

  • Prognosis: Variable; untreated disease may progress to cirrhosis and liver failure

RUQ pain & fever (Option A): Suggest acute cholangitis (Charcot triad), not chronic PBC.

Arthralgias & rash (Option C): More typical of autoimmune hepatitis or viral prodromes.

Nausea & vomiting (Option D): Nonspecific; no defining features of PBC.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2711.

options.text: Right upper quadrant pain and fever

question: Which of the following pairs of symptoms represents the most prominent and characteristic clinical manifestations in symptomatic patients with primary biliary cholangitis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Anti-SLA antibodies identify a subset of autoimmune hepatitis patients who are reported to have a more aggressive disease course and worse prognosis, even when classified within the Type I AIH spectrum.

  • Poor prognostic markers in AIH include:
    • Anti-SLA positivity
    • High aminotransferase and IgG levels at presentation
    • Advanced fibrosis or cirrhosis on biopsy
    • Delayed response or nonresponse to immunosuppressive therapy
    • Younger age at onset in aggressive subtypes
  • Role of serologic markers in AIH prognosis:
    • Autoantibodies help with classification and risk stratification
    • Anti-SLA is highly specific for AIH and associated with severe disease, frequent relapse, and poorer long-term outcomes
    • ANA and ASMA are useful diagnostically, but do not independently predict prognosis

ANA (Option A) and ASMA (Option B): Common in Type I AIH; not linked to worse prognosis.

Anti-LKM1 (Option D): Marker of Type II AIH; subtype distinction, not prognostic severity.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2695.
question: Which of the following autoantibodies detected in patients with autoimmune hepatitis is specifically associated with a worse prognosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) is the recommended second-line agent and the next drug of choice in patients with AIH who are nonresponsive to or intolerant of azathioprine.

Stepwise management approach in AIH:

  • First-line induction: Prednisone (or budesonide in mild disease) ± azathioprine
  • Maintenance: Azathioprine-based immunosuppression
  • Steroid-refractory or azathioprine-intolerant disease: Mycophenolate mofetil
  • MMF suppresses lymphocyte proliferation and has a favourable efficacy-toxicity profile
  • Role of MMF:
    • Effective in inducing and maintaining remission
    • Preferred before calcineurin inhibitors due to better tolerability
    • Commonly used when azathioprine causes cytopenias or hepatotoxicity

Methotrexate (Option A): Limited evidence; not standard second-line therapy in AIH.

Cyclosporine (Option B): Reserved for refractory cases; higher toxicity burden.

Ursodeoxycholic acid (Option D): Used in primary biliary cholangitis, not AIH.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2696.
question: A patient with autoimmune hepatitis is treated with standard first-line therapy, including corticosteroids and azathioprine, but fails to achieve biochemical remission. The clinician plans to escalate immunosuppressive therapy. Which of the following agents is the next drug of choice in this setting?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Budesonide is recommended as an alternative first-line corticosteroid for mild AIH because its extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism limits systemic glucocorticoid exposure while maintaining intrahepatic anti-inflammatory activity.
  • Principles of first-line therapy in AIH:
    • Goal: Induce remission (normalise aminotransferases and IgG, improve histology)
    • Standard first-line regimen: Prednisone (or prednisolone) ± azathioprine
    • Mild disease (low transaminase elevation, no cirrhosis): Budesonide can substitute for prednisone to reduce steroid-related adverse effects
    • Contraindication: Budesonide should not be used in patients with cirrhosis or portal hypertension due to reduced first-pass metabolism

Dexamethasone (Option A): Potent systemic steroid; not recommended as first-line AIH therapy.

Methylprednisolone (Option B): Used IV when oral therapy isn’t possible; not preferred for mild AIH.

Hydrocortisone (Option D): Short-acting; not standard for AIH induction therapy.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2696.
question: A patient with mild autoimmune hepatitis (aminotransferases <2× the upper limit of normal) requires initial corticosteroid therapy with minimal systemic effects. Which of the following corticosteroids is an alternative first-line option in this setting?

Explanation:

  • IgG anti-HBc indicates chronic hepatitis B infection; when HDV infection occurs on this background, it confirms HDV superinfection, not coinfection.
  • Key serologic principle in hepatitis differentiation:
    • HBsAg indicates active HBV infection
    • IgM anti-HBc → acute HBV infection
    • IgG anti-HBc → chronic HBV infection
    • HDV requires HBV (HBsAg) for replication
  • HDV infection patterns:
    • Coinfection: Acute HBV + acute HDV → IgM anti-HBc positive
    • Superinfection: Chronic HBV + acute HDV → IgG anti-HBc positive
    • Superinfection is associated with more severe disease and a higher risk of chronic liver failure.

IgM anti-HBc (Option A): Indicates acute HBV, consistent with coinfection, not superinfection.

Anti-HBs (Option C): Marker of recovery or immunity, not present with active HBsAg positivity.

IgM anti-HAV (Option D): Indicates acute hepatitis A, unrelated to HBV/HDV.

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2657, 2658.
question: A patient with acute hepatitis is HBsAg positive with anti-HDV antibodies. To represent HDV superinfection on chronic hepatitis B rather than HBV-HDV coinfection. Which antibody profile confirms HDV superinfection?

correctAnswer: C. Anti-liver kidney microsome type 1 antibody (anti-LKM1)
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Type II autoimmune hepatitis is defined by the presence of anti-LKM1 antibodies, which target cytochrome P450 2D6 and are most commonly seen in children and adolescents, often with negative ANA and ASMA.
  • Serologic markers are central to the diagnosis and subtyping of AIH, alongside elevated aminotransferases, increased IgG levels, exclusion of viral hepatitis, and compatible histology.
  • Key serologic patterns in AIH:
    • Type I AIH: ANA and/or ASMA (most common form; all age groups)
    • Type II AIH: anti-LKM1 (pediatric predominance; more aggressive disease)
    • Anti-SLA: Highly specific for AIH, usually grouped with Type I, often associated with severe disease

ANA (Option A) and ASMA (Option B): Hallmark antibodies of Type I AIH, not Type II.

Anti-SLA (Option D): Seen in a subset of Type I AIH, especially ANA/ASMA-negative cases.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2694, 2695.
question: Which of the following autoantibodies is considered the serologic hallmark of Type II autoimmune hepatitis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Nitrofurantoin is a classic cause of drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis, producing a chronic hepatocellular injury with ANA and ASMA positivity and histology identical to idiopathic AIH, particularly with prolonged use.
  • Drug-induced autoimmune hepatitis (DIAIH) is characterised by:
    • Chronic hepatocellular enzyme elevation (AST/ALT predominant)
    • Development of autoantibodies (ANA, ASMA)
    • Hypergammaglobulinemia
    • Interface hepatitis with plasma cells on biopsy
    • Clinical and histologic indistinguishability from idiopathic AIH
    • Improvement after drug withdrawal ± immunosuppression
  • Nitrofurantoin and minocycline are the most strongly implicated drugs in DIAIH, especially with long-term exposure.

Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Option A): Common cause of DILI, but typically cholestatic or mixed injury, not autoimmune hepatitis.

Erythromycin estolate (Option B): Causes inflammatory cholestasis, not an autoimmune phenotype.

Ciprofloxacin (Option C): Produces idiosyncratic hepatocellular injury, usually acute and non-autoimmune.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 2670, 2671.
question: A patient on long-term antibiotic therapy develops chronic hepatitis with elevated aminotransferases. Serologic testing reveals positive ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibodies. Which antimicrobial agent is associated with this pattern of hepatotoxicity?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Type 1 Autoimmune Hepatitis is characterized by the presence of ANA and ASMA antibodies, along with the typical histological findings of interface hepatitis and plasma cell infiltration.
  • It is the most common form of autoimmune hepatitis and is often seen in women.

Types of Autoimmune hepatitis:

Type 1 Autoimmune Hepatitis (Option A)

Type 2 Autoimmune Hepatitis (Option B)

More common in females (2nd-3rd decade)

More common in children

Associated with:

  • ANA (also seen in SLE) - hence, lupoid hepatitis
  • Anti SMA (Anti smooth muscle antibody) - against actin
  • Anti-soluble liver antigen
  • Atypical p-ANCA (x-ANCA)

Associated with:

  • ANA absent
  • Anti LKM1 (Liver kidney microsome type 1)
  • Anti-liver cytosol - 1 antibody

Primary Biliary Cholangitis (Option C): It is a chronic disease that targets the small intrahepatic bile ducts rather than the hepatocytes. The diagnostic hallmark is the Anti-Mitochondrial Antibody (AMA). Florid duct lesions and granulomas are seen on biopsy, which differ significantly from the plasma cell-rich inflammation seen in AIH.


Drug-Induced Liver Injury (Option D): While it can cause interface hepatitis, it is a diagnosis of exclusion. The presence of specific high-titer ASMA/ANA strongly favors a primary autoimmune etiology over a transient drug reaction.

Management Aspect

Details

question: A 35-year-old man presents with complaints of nausea and abdominal pain after ingesting 20 paracetamol tablets approximately 8 hours ago. His vital signs are stable, but he has mild jaundice. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

correctAnswer: A. Glutathione depletion with NAPQI buildup
explanationHtml:
Correct Answer: A) Glutathione depletion with NAPQI buildup

Explanation:

  • Acetaminophen is metabolized in the liver to form the toxic metabolite NAPQI, which is normally detoxified by glutathione.
  • In overdose situations, excessive NAPQI depletes glutathione, leading to its accumulation and binding to hepatocyte proteins.
  • This results in oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and hepatocyte necrosis.
  • The patient's symptoms of fatigue, jaundice, and elevated aminotransferases indicate significant liver injury.

Metabolism of Acetaminophen
  • Acetaminophen is mainly metabolized via phase II reactions into harmless sulfate and glucuronide metabolites.(Option B)
  • A small portion undergoes phase I metabolism by CYP2E1 (Option D), forming the hepatotoxic metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone-imine (NAPQI).

Detoxification of NAPQI

  • NAPQI is neutralized by binding to glutathione, forming water-soluble mercapturic acid, which is excreted via the kidneys.

Glutathione Depletion (Option C)

  • When excessive NAPQI is produced, or glutathione is depleted (Option A), NAPQI binds to hepatocyte macromolecules, forming acetaminophen-protein adducts, causing hepatocyte necrosis.


Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2588
  2. https://www.msdmanuals.com/professional/injuries-poisoning/poisoning/acetaminophen-poisoning

Increased risk of renal toxicity (Option A): Acetaminophen is primarily associated with hepatotoxicity, not renal toxicity.

Decreased effectiveness of acetaminophen (Option B): Opioid tolerance affects the efficacy of opioids, not acetaminophen. The effectiveness of acetaminophen remains unchanged.

Development of opioid dependency (Option D): While chronic use of opioids can lead to dependency, this risk is not specifically tied to the combination with acetaminophen and can occur independently.
