question: A 50-year-old individual who is a chronic smoker came with complaints of recurrent episodes of coughing up blood without any accompanying symptoms of fever or weight loss. On chest x-ray there were no abnormalities seen, and the sputum test is also negative for acid-fast bacilli (AFB). Which of the following options could be the next effective diagnostic test?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is defined by resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin, the two most potent first-line anti-TB drugs.

Drug-Sensitive Tuberculosis (DSTB)

Tuberculosis that is susceptible to the first-line anti-TB drugs, such as isoniazid and rifampin.

Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis (DR-TB)

TB caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains that are resistant to at least one first-line anti-TB drug.

Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB)

TB caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains that are resistant to at least isoniazid and rifampin, the two most potent first-line anti-TB drugs.

Extensively Drug-Resistant Tuberculosis (XDR-TB)

A more severe form of MDR-TB resistant to isoniazid, rifampin, fluoroquinolones, and at least one of the second-line injectable drugs (e.g., amikacin, kanamycin, or capreomycin).


Reference:
  • Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Pages 961, 1359, 1369, 1372, 1372, 1376-1378.
  • Goodman & Gillman's The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics, 13th Edition, Page: 761, 1068, 1070, 1071, 1072, 1073, 1074.
  • https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557666/
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4561400/
question: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) tuberculosis shows resistance to which of the following drugs?

explanationHtml:
• The clinical scenario of a patient with dyspnea, bilateral pitting pedal edema, abdominal distension, elevated jugular venous pulse (JVP), and a palpable liver strongly suggests right ventricular (RV) failure. Chronic smoking is a key risk factor for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), which can lead to cor pulmonale, a condition where the right ventricle fails due to prolonged lung disease. Therefore, the abnormality lies in the right ventricle, as indicated in option D.

Cor Pulmonale:

  • Alteration in the structure and function of the right ventricle (RV) caused by a primary respiratory disorder leading to pulmonary hypertension.
  • Etiology:
    • Lung Diseases: COPD, interstitial lung disease, scleroderma, cystic fibrosis, obesity hypoventilation syndrome.
    • Vascular Disorders: Idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension.
    • Upper Airway: Obstructive sleep apnea.
    • Chest Wall Disorders: Kyphoscoliosis.
    • Massive Pulmonary Embolism: Leading cause of acute cor pulmonale, may mimic myocardial infarction with elevated troponins and chest pain.
    • COPD: Most common cause of chronic cor pulmonale.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Chronic hypoxemia leads to pulmonary vasoconstriction and smooth muscle proliferation in small pulmonary arteries.
    • Increased pulmonary vascular resistance causes right ventricular enlargement (thickening, dilation).
  • Symptoms:
    • Dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, lethargy, exertional syncope, chest pain, abdominal edema, and lower extremity edema.
    • Clinical signs appear later, after pulmonary hypertension develops
  • Physical Findings:
    • Jugular Venous Distension: Prominent jugular V wave (tricuspid regurgitation).
    • Peripheral Edema: Non-specific but common in right heart failure.
    • Cardiovascular: Parasternal lift, loud S2, narrow S2 splitting, holosystolic murmur of tricuspid regurgitation, right-sided S4 heart sound.
    • Abdomen: Hepatomegaly, ascites.
  • Investigations:
    • Chest Radiograph: Pulmonary artery enlargement, right ventricular cardiomegaly.
    • ECG: Right ventricular hypertrophy/enlargement.
    • Chest CT Angiography: Rules out pulmonary embolism, pulmonary artery diameter >29 mm.
  • Management:
    • Oxygen Therapy: Improves oxygenation, reduces pulmonary vasoconstriction, enhances cardiac output.
    • Diuretics: Reduces RV filling volume in chronic cor pulmonale.


Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK430739/
question: A chronic smoker presented with shortness of breath, bilateral pitting pedal edema, and abdominal distension. On examination, jugular venous pulse was found to be elevated and liver was palpable 8 cm below the costal margin. An abnormality in which of the following structures is responsible for the patient’s symptoms?

correctAnswer: A. Non-invasive PPV should be given
explanationHtml:
• Initial Management and Assessment:
    • Home management: Increased bronchodilator therapy, short course of oral glucocorticoids, and possibly antibiotics.
    • Hospital referral indicators:
      • Cyanosis
      • Peripheral oedema
      • Altered consciousness
    • Comprehensive assessment upon admission:
      • Level of consciousness (response to commands, ability to cough)
      • Signs of CO2 retention (warm peripheries, bounding pulse, flapping tremor)
      • Airway obstruction assessment (wheeze, prolonged expiration)
      • Signs of cor pulmonale (peripheral oedema, raised JVP)
      • Background functional status and quality of life
      • Precipitating causes (e.g., infection, environmental factors)

Investigations:

Investigation

Purpose/Findings

Arterial blood gases

Assess severity of hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, acidaemia; guide oxygen therapy and ventilation.

Chest X-ray

Identify complications such as pneumonia, pneumothorax, or pleural effusion.

Management Strategies:

Management

Details

Oxygen Therapy
  • Administer controlled oxygen at 24% or 28% to maintain PaO2 > 8 kPa (60 mmHg) or SaO2 > 90%.
  • Regular arterial blood gas monitoring to adjust therapy.

Non-Invasive Ventilation (NIV)
  • Safe for mild to moderate respiratory acidosis; helps reduce intubation need and mortality.
  • Not suitable for patients unable to protect their airway.

Bronchodilators
  • Use nebulised short-acting β2-agonists (e.g., salbutamol, terbutaline) with anticholinergics (e.g., ipratropium).
  • If oxygen sensitivity is a concern, use compressed air for nebulisation.

Glucocorticoids
  • Administer oral prednisolone (30 mg for 10 days) to reduce symptoms and improve lung function.Reduces frequency and severity of exacerbations.
  • Consider osteoporosis prophylaxis for repeated courses.

Antibiotic Therapy
  • Indicated for increased sputum purulence, volume, or breathlessness.
  • Use simple regimens (aminopenicillin, tetracycline, macrolide); co-amoxiclav in areas with β-lactamase organisms.

Mechanical Ventilation (Option B)
  • Consider if there is a reversible cause, no prior respiratory failure, or if NIV has failed/contraindicated.
  • Decisions should involve the patient, family, and GP.

Additional Therapy
  • Diuretics for peripheral oedema.
  • Limited evidence for intravenous aminophylline; consider arrhythmia risk.
  • Doxapram may be used short-term for low respiratory rates.
  • Discharge and Follow-Up:
    • Discharge criteria:
      • Clinically stable on maintenance medication.
      • Off nebulised therapy for at least 24 hours.
      • PEF reaches 75% of predicted or personal best.
    • Post-exacerbation follow-up:
      • Identify and avoid trigger factors.
      • Provide asthma education and a written self-management plan.

IV corticosteroids should be administered (Option C): Systemic corticosteroids are helpful in treating acute COPD exacerbations by reducing airway inflammation and improving lung function over time, but their effects are not immediate. Non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIPPV), on the other hand, provides immediate respiratory support, reducing the work of breathing and stabilizing the patient's condition, making it the priority in the initial management.

Permissive hypercapnia is allowed (Option D): Permissive hypercapnia involves allowing elevated carbon dioxide levels to avoid lung injury from over-ventilation, but this is not an approach used in the initial management of acute COPD exacerbations. The goal during the acute phase is to normalize blood gases and relieve respiratory distress, which is best achieved with NIPPV. Permissive hypercapnia is typically considered only after NIPPV fails and invasive positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) is required.



Reference:

Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 577, 578

question: High anion gap acidosis with low bicarbonate levels is seen in all of the following conditions except:

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • As the patient's chest X-ray reveals a significant amount of fluid accumulation on the left thorax and as the patient is also intubated, ultrasound-guided aspiration may be a reasonable next step. It is often done to improve respiratory function and prevent complications associated with accumulation of fluid in the lungs.
  • Ultrasound serves a complementary role in chest imaging, particularly in evaluating fluid collections.

Applications of Ultrasound:

  • Pleural Effusion: Used for detection and guiding the drainage of fluid collections.
  • Pericardial Effusion: Evaluates the presence of fluid around the heart and for assessing cardiac function.

Suctioning (Option A) is a routine procedure used to clear the airway of secretions or foreign material. While suctioning may be necessary for some intubated patients, it is not a next specific step. The appropriateness of suctioning would depend on the patient's clinical condition and the presence of indications for suctioning.

Chest physiotherapy (Option B) techniques, such as postural drainage, percussion, and vibration, are often used to help mobilize secretions and improve airway clearance. While these techniques may be beneficial in certain cases, they are not the next specific steps for this patient.

Starting antibiotics and sending samples for culture (Option C) may be appropriate in certain situations, such as suspected or confirmed respiratory infection. However, the decision to start antibiotics and send samples for culture should be based on a comprehensive evaluation of the patient's clinical presentation, including signs and symptoms of infection. It cannot be determined solely based on the information of an X-ray finding.



Reference:

Grainger & Allison's Diagnostic Radiology, 7th edition, Page 27-31,43

question: An intubated patient in the ICU had a chest X-ray taken to evaluate for fever spikes over the last 24-48 hours. The radiograph is given below. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?

correctAnswer: D. Consider admission in a non-ICU setting
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's symptoms, such as productive cough, tachypnea, and hypotension, align with the diagnosis of pneumonia.
  • The CURB-65 score of this patient is 2 (age >/= 65 and urea > 19mg/dl); hence, the patient can be considered for admission to a non-ICU setting for further management.

Treatment for Lobar Pneumonia

  • Treatment depends on severity; assess if inpatient or outpatient management is needed.
  • CURB-65 Score: Used to stratify patients with the following factors:

CURB-65

Symptom

Score

(C) Confusion

1

(U) Urea: BUN >19mg/dL (>7 mmol/L)

1

(R) Respiratory rate ≥30/min

1

(B) Blood Pressure – Systolic BP ≤90 mmHg or diastolic BP ≤60 mmHg

1

(65) Age ≥65 years

1
  • Hospitalization Criteria:
    • CURB-65 score 1 or 2: Indicates hospitalization
    • A score ≥3: Indicates ICU admission and more intensive therapy. (Option B and C)
  • Empiric Therapy:
    • Outpatient: (Option A)
      • When no symptoms in the CURB-65 scoring system are present.
      • No comorbidities: Monotherapy with macrolides (Azithromycin, Clarithromycin).
      • With comorbidities (chronic lung/heart disease, diabetes, smoking, HIV): Newer Fluoroquinolones (Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin, Gemifloxacin) or a combination of beta-lactam (e.g., Amoxicillin) and a macrolide.
    • Inpatient Non-ICU:
      • Newer Fluoroquinolones (Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin) alone or a combination of beta-lactam (e.g., Ampicillin, Ceftriaxone) and a macrolide.
    • Inpatient ICU:
      • Combination of macrolide (Azithromycin) or newer fluoroquinolone (Levofloxacin) with beta-lactam (e.g., Ampicillin-sulbactam, Ertapenem).
      • If risk of aspiration, consider ampicillin-sulbactam or ertapenem; for Pseudomonas infection, use anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (e.g., Piperacillin-tazobactam) with anti-pseudomonal fluoroquinolone (e.g., Ciprofloxacin).
      • For MRSA, add vancomycin or linezolid.
  • Duration of Therapy: Typically 5 to 7 days, extended if clinical response is delayed.
  • Influenza Treatment: All hospitalized patients testing positive for influenza should receive Oseltamivir, regardless of illness onset.


Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page: 1012.
  2. Typical Bacterial Pneumonia - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

question: A 68-year-old man presents with a cough with yellowish sputum. Auscultation revealed bronchial breath sounds. He is hemodynamically stable and not confused. On examination, his respiratory rate is 20/min, and his blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg. Lab reports show urea levels of 44 mg/dL. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical features of hyperventilation leading to carpal spasm are caused due to respiratory alkalosis.

  • Respiratory alkalosis occurs when there is a decrease in carbon dioxide (CO2) levels in the blood, leading to an increase in alkalinity.
  • Hyperventilation causes excessive elimination of carbon dioxide, leading to decreased blood CO2 levels. This results in respiratory alkalosis

Clinical features of respiratory alkalosis will include:

  • Tachypnea
  • Symptoms of hypocapnia
  • Paresthesias from decreased ionized calcium due to alkalemia
  • Reduced cerebral blood flow from hypocapnia
  • Decreased ionized calcium causing tetany/carpopedal spasms

Respiratory alkalosis- Clinical Features & Management

Category

Features

Cause

Neurological
  • Dizziness
  • Mental confusion
  • Paresthesias
  • Circumoral numbness
  • Seizures (severe cases)
  • Due to reduced cerebral blood flow
  • From rapid ↓ PaCO2
  • May occur without hypoxemia

Cardiovascular
  • Chest tightness/pain
  • Palpitations
  • Arrhythmias
  • Possible ECG changes
  • Due to coronary vasoconstriction
  • ↓ ionized calcium effects
  • Bohr effect on O2 delivery

Neuromuscular
  • Carpopedal spasms
  • Tetany
  • Muscle twitching
  • Weakness
  • From ↓ ionized calcium
  • Enhanced nerve excitability
  • Similar to hypocalcemia

Laboratory
  • ↑ pH
  • ↓ PaCO2
  • ↓ Ionized calcium
  • ↓ K+, ↓ PO4
  • Acute: ↓ HCO3- by 2 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↓ PaCO2
  • Chronic: ↓ HCO3- by 4-5 mEq/L per 10 mmHg ↓ PaCO2
  • Electrolyte shifts into cells

Management

Underlying Disease:

  • Treat primary condition
  • Address anxiety if present
  • Manage sepsis if present

Hyperventilation Syndrome:

  • Reassurance
  • Rebreathing techniques
  • Paper bag breathing if needed
  • β-blockers if needed
  • Primary focus on the underlying cause
  • Avoid sedatives for anxiety
  • Monitor during mechanical ventilation
  • Adjust ventilator settings if needed
  • Regular monitoring of blood gases
  • Address psychological factors

Incorrect Options:

Respiratory acidosis (Option A) results from impaired ventilation due to pulmonary disease, respiratory muscle fatigue, or abnormalities in ventilatory control. Some examples of these are drugs, alcohol, motor neuron diseases, skeletal muscle disease, etc.

Metabolic acidosis (Option B) is caused by methanol, uremia, diabetic ketoacidosis, iron tablets, isoniazid, etc and not by hyperventilation.

Metabolic alkalosis (Option D) is caused by exogenous bicarbonate loads, hypertension, K+ deficiency, mineralocorticoid excess, etc.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page: 368.
question: A woman with hysteria who was hyperventilating developed carpo-pedal spasms. What could be the likely cause for this?

correctAnswer: D. Mixed disorder: Vomiting + Early DKA
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

ABG shows alkalemia (pH 7.52) with high HCO₃⁻ (30) → metabolic alkalosis from vomiting.

  • However:
  • PaCO₂ = 20 mmHg is too low for compensation → separate respiratory alkalosis.
  • Anion gap = 26 (high) → presence of high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, most consistent with early DKA in a diabetic.
  • Vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis, but it cannot cause low PCO₂ or high AG.
  • Thus, this is a triple acid–base disorder:
    • Metabolic alkalosis – from vomiting
    • High-anion-gap metabolic acidosis – from early DKA
    • Respiratory alkalosis – from tachypnea due to dehydration
  • This combination is classic for “ketoalkalosis,” where DKA is masked by vomiting.

Isolated vomiting induced metabolic alkalosis (Option A ): Vomiting explains metabolic alkalosis but cannot account for the high anion gap (36 mEq/L). Pure vomiting causes normal AG metabolic alkalosis, not mixed disorders.

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) (Option B): DKA causes high anion gap metabolic acidosis, so pH is low or near-normal if compensated. But this patient has alkalemia (pH 7.52) and elevated HCO₃⁻, which DKA alone cannot produce.


Septic shock (Option C) can lead to multiple organ dysfunction and a state of metabolic acidosis. The pH of 7.52 in the ABG report suggests alkalosis rather than acidosis, so septic shock is unlikely to be the cause.



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page: 365, 366, 367.
  2. Arterial Blood Gases - Physiopedia
question:
A diabetic woman presents with persistent vomiting after eating outside food. Her BP is 90/60 mmHg. ABG shows:

  • pH: 7.52
  • HCO₃⁻: 30 mEq/L
  • PaCO₂: 20 mmHg
  • Na⁺: 123 mEq/L
  • K⁺: 3.2 mEq/L
  • Cl⁻: 67 mEq/L

What is the most likely cause of these ABG findings?

correctAnswer: A. pH-7.14, pCO2-20 mmHg, HCO3- 5 mEq/L
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The low pH and HCO3 levels in the blood show metabolic acidosis.

Metabolic acidosis

Definition
  • Primary decrease in HCO3⁻ or increase in H⁺ ions
  • Characterized by ↓ pH and ↓ HCO3⁻
  • Compensatory mechanism: ↓ PaCO2 through hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing)

Types

High anion gap (AG > 12 mEq/L)

Normal anion gap (AG 6-12 mEq/L)

Causes

(Mnemonic: MUDPILES)

  • M: Methanol
  • U: Uremia (Renal failure)
  • D: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
  • P: Paraldehyde, Phenformin, Propylene glycol
  • I: Iron tablets, Isoniazid
  • L: Lactic acidosis
  • E: Ethylene glycol
  • S: Salicylates (late phase)

(Mnemonic: HARD UP)

  • H: Hyperalimentation (TPN)
  • A: Acetazolamide
  • R: Renal Tubular Acidosis
  • D: Diarrhea
  • U: Ureteral diversion
  • P: Pancreatic fistula
  • GIT fistulas

Clinical Features

General Features:

  • Lethargy
  • Confusion
  • Fatigue
  • Nausea/vomiting
  • Deep, rapid breathing (Kussmaul)

Specific Features:

  • DKA: Fruity breath, polyuria, polydipsia
  • Uremia: Itching, volume overload
  • Lactic acidosis: Shock, hypotension
  • Toxic ingestion: Visual disturbances (methanol), oxalate crystals (ethylene glycol)

Incorrect Options:

pH-7.14, pCO2-20 mmHg, HCO3- 34 mEq/L (Option B): Although the pH and pCO₂ suggest acidemia with respiratory compensation, the high HCO₃⁻ (34 mEq/L) is inconsistent with metabolic acidosis. A high bicarbonate would be seen in metabolic alkalosis, which does not fit this clinical picture.

pH-7.54, HCO3- 27 mEq/L, pCO2- 34 mmHg (Option C): This option shows a high pH (7.54), indicating alkalosis. The pCO₂ is slightly low, suggesting respiratory alkalosis, while the HCO₃⁻ is near normal. This acid-base picture does not match the metabolic acidosis expected in a dialysis patient with hyperkalemia.

pH-7.4, HCO3- 27 mEq/L, pCO2- 40 mmHg (Option D): This combination of normal pH, normal pCO2, and normal HCO3- does not indicate any significant acid-base imbalance. Therefore, this option is less likely to be the correct acid-base imbalance in this case.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles Of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Volume I, Page: 361, 362, 364.
question: A middle-aged man with chronic renal failure on dialysis presents with sudden collapse to the casualty with laboured breathing. ECG shows tall, tented T waves. What is the most likely acid-base imbalance that can be seen in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The given scenario is of pneumonia in an AIDS-infected child. The most common organism causing fever, and productive cough, with given examination findings, is Streptococcus pneumonia.

Pneumonia Etiology and Common Pathogens

  • Main Pathogens: Bacteria, viruses, fungi, and protozoa.
    • Typical Bacteria: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA).
    • Atypical Bacteria: Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Legionella species
    • Viruses: Influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), coronaviruses (e.g., SARS-CoV-2).

Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP)

Atypical Pneumonia

Outpatients

Hospitalised Patients

Includes M.pneumoniae C.pneumoniae, and Legionella species.

Common causes:

S.pneumoniae, M.pneumoniae

H. influenzae, C.pneumoniae, Respiratory viruses (influenza, RSV).

Non-ICU

ICU Patients

Similar pathogens to outpatients, plus Legionella species.

Pathogens include S.pneumoniae, S. aureus (including MRSA), Legionella species, gram-negative bacilli, and H. influenzae.

Specific Pathogens in Certain Conditions:

Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA):
  • It can cause CAP, often complicating influenza infections.
  • Community-acquired MRSA (CA-MRSA) has emerged as a significant cause of necrotizing pneumonia.

Pneumococcal Pneumonia:
  • Higher risk in elderly patients, and those with comorbidities like dementia, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, alcoholism, smoking, COPD, and HIV infection.

CA-MRSA Pneumonia:
  • More likely in patients with prior skin infections or following viral illnesses.

Enterobacteriaceae:
  • Common in patients recently hospitalized, those treated with antibiotics, or those with comorbidities like alcoholism, heart failure, or renal failure.

Pseudomonas aeruginosa:
  • Found in patients with severe structural lung diseases such as bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis, or advanced COPD.

Legionella Infection:
  • Associated with risk factors like diabetes, hematologic malignancies, cancer, severe renal disease, HIV, smoking, male gender, and recent travel (air conditioners, showers, hotels, cruise ships). It is an important cause of atypical pneumonia.

Pneumocystis jirovecii (Option A) pneumonia (PJP) is a common opportunistic infection in patients with AIDS. However, it typically presents with non-productive cough, shortness of breath, and bilateral diffuse infiltrates on chest X-ray.

Staphylococcus aureus (Option C) is another bacterium that can cause pneumonia in immunocompromised individuals, including those with AIDS. It is known for causing severe infections, including necrotizing pneumonia, but not the most common cause.

Mycoplasma pneumoniae (Option D) is an atypical bacterium that can cause pneumonia, particularly in children and young adults. It often presents with a milder respiratory illness, including a persistent cough, headache, sore throat, and patchy infiltrates rather than lobar consolidation in the chest X-ray.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page: 1010, 1011.
question: A 10-year-old child with AIDS presented with a fever and productive cough. On auscultation, bronchial breath sounds and crepitations were heard in the right infra-scapular region. Chest x-ray showed right lower lobe consolidation. The CD4 count was 55 cells/mm3. What is the most common causative organism for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The nocturnal cough, fever, breathlessness, and wheezing with eosinophilia of >5000/µL and miliary pattern in chest X-ray all point to the diagnosis of tropical pulmonary eosinophilia.

Tropical pulmonary eosinophilia (TPE)

  • TPE is a pulmonary hyperreactive condition triggered by trapped microfilariae in lung tissue, leading to symptoms like nocturnal cough, dyspnea, and wheezing.

Pathophysiology:

  • Eosinophils are key in the pathogenesis, triggered by microfilariae released from the lymphatic system that become trapped in pulmonary microcirculation.
  • Eosinophils degranulate, releasing proteins to clear microfilariae and cause lung damage.
  • IL-4 promotes airway hyperactivity, while IFN-gamma suppresses it.
  • An overactive TH2 response increases IL-4, IL-5, and specific IgG, IgM, and IgE antibodies, leading to eosinophilia.

Clinical features:

  • History of travel or residence in filarial endemic areas.
  • Symptoms:
    • Dry, paroxysmal, nocturnal cough
    • Dyspnea
    • Systemic signs (fever, malaise, weight loss)
    • Peripheral eosinophilia (>3,000/mm³)
    • Extrapulmonary signs: Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly
  • Physical Findings: Wheezing, crepitations, organomegaly, enlarged lymph nodes.

Investigations:

  • Blood Tests: Leukocytosis with eosinophilia, elevated IgE, filarial antibody titers.
  • Stool Test: Rule out other parasitic causes.
  • Imaging:
    • Chest X-ray: Reticulonodular opacities, miliary mottling, or normal in 20-30% of cases.
    • Chest CT: Bronchiectasis, lymphadenopathy, pleural effusion in unclear cases.
  • Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs): Mixed restrictive and mild to moderate obstructive patterns.

[[figure-1]]

Management:

  • First-line:
    • Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) for 21 days.
    • It targets both microfilariae and adults, leading to dramatic symptom improvement.
  • Adjunctive:
    • Corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation, particularly in chronic cases.
  • Alternative Drugs:
    • Ivermectin and albendazole target microfilariae and adult worms, though there is limited data.

Incorrect Options:

Bronchial asthma (Option A) is a chronic respiratory condition characterized by inflammation and narrowing of the airways, leading to symptoms such as wheezing, coughing (often nocturnal), breathlessness, and occasionally fever. However, the presence of a miliary pattern on chest X-ray is not typical of bronchial asthma.

Miliary tuberculosis (Option B) is a severe form of tuberculosis (TB) in which the infection spreads throughout the body, including the lungs. It is characterized by the dissemination of tiny, millimetre-sized lesions throughout various organs, including the lungs, giving a miliary pattern on chest X-ray. The elevated absolute eosinophil count is not typical of miliary tuberculosis.

Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (HP) (Option D), also known as extrinsic allergic alveolitis, is an immune-mediated lung disease caused by the inhalation of various organic substances such as dust, moulds, or animal proteins. The absolute eosinophil count can be elevated in some cases. However, the presence of a miliary pattern on chest X-ray is not typical of HP.



Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557524/
question: A patient presents with fever, nocturnal cough, breathlessness, and wheezing for 4 weeks. The absolute eosinophil count is >5000/µL. Chest x-ray shows a miliary pattern. What is the likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: A. Hypoventilation causing decreased CO2 washout
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • For metabolic acidosis with HCO₃⁻ = 10, the expected compensatory PaCO₂ is:
    • 1.5×10+8=23±2 mmHg (Using Winter's formula)
    • Expected PaCO₂ = 21–25 mmHg
  • But the actual PaCO₂ = 30 mmHg → higher than expected.
  • If the patient were hyperventilating, PaCO₂ would drop below the expected value.
  • Instead, it is elevated, meaning CO₂ is being retained.
  • So the secondary disorder is a respiratory acidosis due to hypoventilation.

Hyperventilation causing decreased CO₂ washout (Option B): Would lower PaCO₂, but here PaCO₂ is elevated, so hyperventilation is ruled out.


Increased tubular reabsorption of HCO₃⁻ (Option C): Renal compensation for respiratory acidosis, not metabolic acidosis.


Increased excretion of H⁺ (Option D) Slow renal compensation for metabolic acidosis and does not explain the elevated PaCO₂.

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Pages 359-367

• In patients with class II (low risk) pulmonary hypertension and a negative vasoreactive test, the next step in management is the use of ambrisentan, an endothelin receptor antagonist.

Vasoreactivity Testing in PAH:

  • Indication: Vasoreactivity testing is primarily reserved for patients with idiopathic or hereditary PAH.
  • Preferred Vasodilators: Short-acting vasodilators such as inhaled nitric oxide (NO) or inhaled epoprostenol are preferred for the test.
  • Positive Response: A decrease in mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) by ≥10 mmHg to an absolute level of ≤40 mmHg without a decrease in cardiac output (CO) is considered a positive vasoreactivity response.
  • Treatment for Responders:
    • Patients with a positive vasoreactivity response are considered for long-term treatment with calcium channel blockers (nifedipine, diltiazem or amlodipine). (Option C)
  • Negative Vasoreactivity: Treatment approach depends on clinical risk.
    • Low- or Intermediate-Risk Patients (class II, III): Initial treatment includes combination oral therapy, typically involving an endothelin receptor antagonist (ambrisentan, sitaxsentan or bosentan) and a phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor (sildenafil or tadalafil).
    • High-Risk Patients (Class IV): Patients with advanced heart failure or syncope are treated with combination drug therapy, which includes intravenous prostacyclin therapy (epoprostenol, treprostinil or iloprost). (Option A & D)

Classification of PAH:

  • Group 1: Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH)
  • Group 2: Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease
  • Group 3: Pulmonary hypertension due to lung disease or hypoxia
  • Group 4: Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
  • Group 5: Pulmonary hypertension due to unclear and/multifactorial mechanisms

explanationHtml:
• The A-a gradient measures the difference between the oxygen concentration in the alveoli (PAO2) and the oxygen concentration in the arterial system (PaO2).
  • Helps narrow the differential diagnosis for hypoxemia.
  • A-a Gradient Formula:
    A-a Gradient = PAO2 – PaO2
    (PAO2 = Alveolar oxygen tension, PaO2 = Arterial oxygen tension).
  • Hypoventilation and A-a Gradient:
  • Hypoventilation occurs when there is inadequate ventilation of the lungs, leading to decreased oxygen levels in the arterial system.
  • Causes of Hypoventilation:
    • CNS depression.
    • Neuromuscular diseases (e.g., myasthenia gravis).
    • Poor chest elasticity (e.g., kyphoscoliosis).
    • Vertebral fractures and other factors.
  • Hypoventilation affects both arterial oxygen tension (PaO₂) and alveolar oxygen tension (AₐO₂), resulting in decreased oxygen levels in both the respiratory and circulatory systems.
  • The A-a gradient (the difference between alveolar and arterial oxygen tensions) remains normal in hypoventilation because both PaO₂ and AₐO₂ decrease in proportion.

Right to left shunt (Option A): In a right-to-left shunt, oxygenated blood bypasses the alveoli, mixing with deoxygenated blood and causing hypoxemia. This leads to an increased A-a gradient, as diffusion between capillaries and alveoli remains unaffected, but the lack of oxygenation of the shunted blood worsens the oxygenation process.

Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) mismatch (Option B) leads to a disparity between ventilation and perfusion in the lungs, resulting in an increased A-a gradient. This is because some areas of the lung are either under-ventilated or under-perfused, impairing the gas exchange process and increasing the gradient.

Alveolar membrane damage (Option D), seen in conditions like ARDS or pulmonary fibrosis, impairs the diffusion of oxygen across the alveolar-capillary barrier. This causes an increased A-a gradient as oxygen fails to transfer efficiently from the alveoli into the bloodstream, leading to hypoxemia.



Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK545153/#
question: A patient came with hypoxemia and a normal alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient. What can be the cause?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most likely diagnosis of this patient is Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS).
  • ARDS is a severe lung condition characterized by widespread inflammation and damage to the alveoli (air sacs) in the lungs. It can be triggered by various factors, including infection, sepsis, trauma, or inhalation injury. The key features of ARDS include acute onset of severe hypoxemia (low oxygen levels) that is refractory to supplemental oxygen, bilateral pulmonary infiltrates on imaging (such as the chest X-ray), and impaired lung compliance.

Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS):

  • ARDS is a diffuse neutrophilic alveolitis caused by infective & non-infective triggers.

Berlin definition of ARDS:

  • Onset within 1 week of a known clinical insult, or new or worsening respiratory symptoms
  • Bilateral opacities on chest X-ray, not fully explained by effusions, lobar/lung collapse or nodules
  • Respiratory failure not fully explained by cardiac failure or fluid overload.
  • Objective assessment (e.g. by echocardiography) must exclude hydrostatic oedema if no risk factor is present Impaired oxygenation

Pathophysiology:

  • Activated neutrophils & macrophages → capillary permeability ↑ → alveolar damage
  • Protein-rich exudate accumulation → hyaline membrane formation
  • Cytokine & chemokine release → inflammatory cell recruitment
  • Surfactant loss → alveolar collapse & ↓ lung compliance
  • Hypoxaemia & hypercapnia due to ventilation-perfusion mismatch

ARDS Severity (PaO2/FiO2 Ratio in kPa):

  • Mild: 40–26.6 kPa (300–200 mmHg)
  • Moderate: 26.6–13.3 kPa (200–100 mmHg)
  • Severe: ≤ 13.3 kPa (≤ 100 mmHg)
    (Measured on ≥5 cmH₂O PEEP or CPAP)

(CPAP = continuous positive airway pressure; PEEP = positive end-expiratory pressure)

Management:

  • Supportive care: Lung-protective mechanical ventilation, negative fluid balance, and treat underlying cause
  • Severe ARDS: Requires prone positioning, extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO)

Atelectasis (Option A) refers to the collapse or incomplete expansion of lung tissue. It can result from blockage of the airways, compression of the lung, or surfactant deficiency. While atelectasis can cause localized or segmental lung collapse, it typically does not lead to widespread bilateral infiltrates and severe hypoxemia.

Pulmonary fibrosis (Option C) typically presents with a gradual onset of symptoms, such as shortness of breath and cough, and the chest X-ray findings would show a reticular or honeycomb pattern.



Reference:

Davidson's principles and practice of medicine, 24th edition, Page 198, 199

What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The elevated pH (>7.45) and increased bicarbonate (HCO3-) (32 mEq/L), indicates a primary metabolic alkalosis.

Metabolic Alkalosis

  • Metabolic alkalosis is characterized by an increase in arterial pH, elevated serum bicarbonate [HCO3−], and increased PaCO2 due to compensatory hypoventilation.
  • Often presents with hypochloremia and hypokalemia.
  • Occurs as a mixed disorder with respiratory or metabolic acidosis or alkalosis.
  • Causes
    • Exogenous Bicarbonate Loads
      • Acute alkali administration
      • Milk-alkali syndrome
    • Effective ECFV Contraction (Normotension, K+ Deficiency, Secondary Hyperreninemic Hyperaldosteronism)
      • Gastrointestinal Origin: Vomiting, gastric aspiration, congenital chloridorrhea, gastrocystoplasty, villous adenoma
      • Renal Origin: Diuretic use (thiazides, loop diuretics), posthypercapnic state, hypercalcemia/hypoparathyroidism, recovery from acidosis, non-resorbable anions (e.g., penicillin), Mg²⁺ deficiency, K⁺ depletion, Bartter's syndrome, Gitelman's syndrome
    • ECFV Expansion, Hypertension, K+ Deficiency, and Mineralocorticoid Excess
      • High Renin: Renal artery stenosis, accelerated hypertension, renin-secreting tumor, estrogen therapy
      • Low Renin: Primary aldosteronism (adenoma, hyperplasia, carcinoma), adrenal enzyme defects (11β-hydroxylase, 17α-hydroxylase deficiency), Cushing’s syndrome, substances like licorice, carbenoxolone
    • Genetic Sodium Channel Mutation (Liddle's Syndrome)
    • Gain-of-function mutation in the distal convoluted tubule, causing ECFV expansion, hypertension, K⁺ deficiency, and hypo-reninemic-hypoaldosteronism
  • Clinical Features
    • Neurological: Mental confusion, obtundation, potential seizures
    • Peripheral Nervous System: Paresthesias, muscle cramps, tetany (similar to hypocalcemia effects)
    • Cardiovascular: Aggravation of arrhythmias, particularly in COPD patients
  • Electrolyte Imbalances
    • Potassium (K⁺): Hypokalemia, especially in cases involving secondary hyperaldosteronism or diuretic use.
    • Chloride (Cl⁻): Hypochloremia, frequently accompanying alkalosis, especially in cases of vomiting or diuretic use.
    • Calcium (Ca²⁺): Symptoms may mimic hypocalcemia despite normal levels.

Metabolic acidosis (Option A) would show a low pH and low bicarbonate levels.

Respiratory acidosis (Option C) is characterized by a low pH and elevated PaCO₂

Respiratory alkalosis (Option D) would show a high pH with low PaCO₂.



Reference:
  • Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Page 365 - 367
  • Arterial Blood Gases - Physiopedia
question: A 45-year-old female presents to the emergency department with the following arterial blood gas (ABG) results: pH 7.55, PaCO2 40 mmHg, HCO3- 32 mEq/L. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for these findings?

correctAnswer: A. Pleural: Serum protein ratio &gt; 0.5, pleural: Serum LDH ratio &gt; 0.6 or pleural LDH &gt; ⅔ of serum LDH
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

To classify the effusion as transudative or exudative, we apply Light's criteria:

  • Pleural fluid protein/serum protein > 0.5
  • Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH > 0.6
  • Pleural fluid LDH exceeds two-thirds of the normal upper limit for serum LDH

Investigation of pleural fluid

Radiological investigation

X-ray:

  • 200 mL of fluid is needed for detection on the posteroanterior (PA) view.
  • 50 mL of fluid may lead to blunting of the costophrenic angle on the lateral view.
  • A homogeneous opacity with obliteration of the costophrenic angle is typical.
  • This appearance is marked by a curved upper border, known as the Ellis S-shaped curve.
  • Obliteration of cardiophrenic angle.

Ultrasound: More effective than X-ray in detecting fluid presence, showing a clear hypoechoic space indicative of transudate and moving densities suggesting exudate.

Pleural fluid Analysis

Light's Criteria

Differentiates transudative from exudative pleural effusions based on LDH and protein levels in pleural fluid.

  • An exudative pleural effusion meets at least one of the following:
    1. Pleural fluid protein/serum protein > 0.5
    2. Pleural fluid LDH/serum LDH > 0.6
    3. Pleural fluid LDH exceeds two-thirds of the normal upper limit for serum.
  • ~25% of transudates may be misidentified as exudates.
  • If exudative criteria are met but a transudative condition is suspected, measure protein difference; if >31 g/L (3.1 g/dL), likely transudative.

Additional Tests for Exudative Effusions
  • Appearance description
  • Glucose level, If Glucose <60 mg/dL Consider:
    • Malignancy
    • Bacterial infections (empyema)
    • Rheumatoid pleuritis
  • Differential cell count
  • Microbiologic studies
  • Cytology

Standard Peculiarities

  • Heart Failure: NT-proBNP level > 1500 pg/mL indicates effusion due to congestive heart failure
  • Parapneumonic Effusion: Key criteria include:
    • Loculated pleural fluid
    • Pleural fluid pH < 7.20
    • Pleural fluid glucose < 3.3 mmol/L (< 60 mg/dL) ( Option B, C)
    • Positive Gram stain or culture results
    • Presence of visible pus
  • Tuberculous Pleuritis: Diagnosis confirmed by high TB markers in pleural fluid (adenosine deaminase > 40 IU/L or interferon γ > 140 pg/mL)

Since the criteria suggest an exudate, which is often associated with other conditions like malignancy or infection rather than just congestive heart failure (Option D).



Reference:
  • Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Page 2198, 2199
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4753987/#sec4

Explanation:

  • The presence of crepitus after chest trauma suggests air leakage into the subcutaneous tissue, indicating subcutaneous emphysema.

Subcutaneous Emphysema:

  • Air accumulation in the subcutaneous tissue, which lies beneath the dermis.
  • Can spread into deeper tissues, leading to pneumomediastinum, pneumothorax, pneumoperitoneum, or pneumoretroperitoneum.
  • Causes:
    • Traumatic: Blunt or penetrating injuries, barotrauma, bowel perforation, pulmonary blebs.
    • Iatrogenic:
      • Ventilator circuit malfunction or disruption.
      • Improper pop-off valve closure.
      • Valsalva maneuvres that increase thoracic pressure.
      • Trauma to the airway.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Crepitus on palpation (crackling sensation or sound).
    • Swelling in the chest, neck, or face; distorted facial appearance; vocal changes; dysphagia.
    • Severe cases: Hemodynamic or respiratory compromise due to extensive air spread.
  • Investigation:
    • X-ray: Shows radiolucent streaks, “ginkgo leaf sign” on chest radiograph.
    • CT scan: Detects deeper air pockets and the source of air leakage.
    • Ultrasound: May reveal hyperechoic scattered densities.
  • Management:
    • Mild cases: Observation, as resolution usually occurs within 10 days if the underlying cause is controlled.
    • Oxygen therapy: Helps nitrogen washout and promotes reabsorption of gas, especially in pneumothorax/pneumomediastinum.
    • Ventilated patients: Reduce tidal volume, PEEP, and avoid bronchospasm to minimize progression.
    • Surgical intervention (for severe cases):
      • Bilateral infraclavicular incisions (2 cm) to release air.
      • Subcutaneous drains in extreme cases.
    • Airway management: Consider tracheostomy if there is a tracheal tear with worsening subcutaneous emphysema.
    • Antibiotics: If mucosal injury is suspected to prevent mediastinitis.

Gas gangrene (Option B) is caused by Clostridium species and involves severe tissue destruction and infection, often in the context of deep wounds or surgical procedures. It typically leads to more systemic signs such as fever, shock, and tissue necrosis, which are not seen in this case. It is not directly related to chest trauma or the presence of crepitus, making it an incorrect option.

Acute tubular necrosis (Option C) refers to kidney damage due to ischemia, toxins, or infection, leading to renal dysfunction. It does not present with crepitus or air trapped in the subcutaneous tissue, and is unrelated to chest trauma. Therefore, it is not relevant to this clinical scenario.

SVC syndrome (Option D): Superior vena cava syndrome results from partial or complete obstruction of the SVC, usually due to thrombus formation or tumor infiltration. It presents with symptoms such as face/neck swelling, distended neck veins, cough, dyspnea, orthopnea, and upper extremity swelling. However, SVC syndrome does not involve crepitus, which is the hallmark of subcutaneous emphysema.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • CT pulmonary angiogram is the gold standard for diagnosing pulmonary embolism, as it allows direct visualization of the pulmonary arteries and identification of any occlusions.

Investigations for Pulmonary Embolism (PE)

Clinical Evaluation

PE symptoms are nonspecific, often leading to excessive use of CT pulmonary angiograms. Age-adjusted d-dimer testing is recommended for patients over 50 years with low-to-moderate PE probability.

D-Dimer

A sensitive but nonspecific test for PE. Elevated levels indicate possible PE but can also occur with conditions like MI, pneumonia, or sepsis. Normal d-dimer helps rule out PE.

Electrocardiogram (ECG)

Common findings include sinus tachycardia(most common) and the S1Q3T3 sign (most specific) (S wave in lead I, Q wave in lead III, inverted T wave in lead III). T-wave inversion in V1 to V4 suggests RV strain or ischemia.

[[figure-1]]

Venous Ultrasonography

Uses loss of vein compressibility as a key indicator for diagnosing DVT, which is associated with PE. Doppler imaging can assess blood flow dynamics.

Chest X-ray

Often normal but may show specific signs like Westermark’s sign (focal oligemia), Hampton’s hump (wedge-shaped pleural density), or Palla’s sign (enlarged pulmonary artery).

[[figure-2]]

Chest radiograph demonstrating focal oligemia (Westermark’s sign) in the right lung (area between white arrowheads) and a prominent right descending pulmonary artery (Palla’s sign) (black arrow).

[[figure-3]]

The chest radiograph demonstrates a wedge-shaped opacity (arrow) in the right middle lobe consistent with Hampton hump.

Chest CT with Contrast

The primary imaging test. It offers high-resolution visualisation of pulmonary vasculature. RV enlargement on CT indicates a higher risk of mortality.

Lung Scanning

A second-line test, mostly for patients who can’t tolerate contrast. High-probability perfusion scans (two or more segmental perfusion defects) strongly suggest PE.

Magnetic Resonance (MR) Imaging

MR venography with gadolinium can diagnose DVT when ultrasound is inconclusive, though MR pulmonary angiography (Option D) is less reliable for smaller PEs.

Echocardiography

It is not reliable (Option A) for directly diagnosing PE but useful for detecting mimicking conditions. McConnell’s sign (RV-free wall hypokinesis) is an indirect sign of PE.

[[figure-4]]

CT Pulmonary Angiography

Identifies intraluminal filling defects or abrupt vessel occlusion.

Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan (Option C) can suggest the likelihood of PE by showing mismatched perfusion defects, but it is not as definitive as other imaging modalities.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st edition, Page 2094-2097

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Thus, the most consistent diagnosis based on presentation and investigations is methotrexate-induced pneumonitis.

  • The patient has been on methotrexate therapy for 4 months and presents with subacute symptoms of cough, dyspnea, and bilateral ground-glass opacities on HRCT, which are characteristic of methotrexate pneumonitis.
  • It is an immune-mediated reaction, often occurring within the first year of treatment, with symptoms including dry cough, dyspnea, fever, and nonspecific radiologic findings like ground-glass opacities.
  • The hallmark of diagnosis includes clinical features, exclusion of infections, and improvement after discontinuation of methotrexate and corticosteroid therapy.

Bacterial pneumonia (Option B): Usually presents acutely with fever, productive cough, and localized consolidation.

Congestive heart failure (Option C): Features dyspnea, basal crepitations, cardiomegaly, pleural effusion, and often systemic edema.

Sarcoidosis (Option D): Characterized by bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and non-caseating granulomas, not acute basal ground-glass opacities.



Reference:

Methotrexate-induced pneumonitis in a patient of rheumatoid arthritis - PMC

explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - Pleural effusion:

  • Pleural effusion involves the accumulation of fluid in the pleural space, leading to compression of the lung. Diminished breath sounds over the affected area are a characteristic finding. It is a common complication in lung cancer patients.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Constrictive pericarditis:

  • Constrictive pericarditis is characterized by the thickening and fibrosis of the pericardium, leading to impaired diastolic filling of the heart. It typically presents with symptoms such as dyspnea and fatigue, but it is not associated with diminished breath sounds over a specific lung region.

Option C - Cardiac tamponade:

  • Cardiac tamponade results from the accumulation of fluid in the pericardial sac, leading to impaired cardiac filling. This condition can cause symptoms such as dyspnea and dizziness, but it is not associated with diminished breath sounds in a specific lung region.

Option D - Pneumothorax:

  • Pneumothorax reduces breath sounds, but typically over the upper/anterior chest, not the lower posterior lung fields, which instead suggests fluid.

question: A male patient with infertility presents a disorder comprising the triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. Which of the following is the correct diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Definition

  • Primary decrease in HCO3⁻ or increase in H⁺ ions
  • Characterized by ↓ pH and ↓ HCO3⁻
  • Compensatory mechanism: ↓ PaCO2 through hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing)

Types

High anion gap (AG > 12 mEq/L)

Normal anion gap (AG 6-12 mEq/L)

Causes

(Mnemonic: MUDPILES)

  • M: Methanol
  • U: Uremia (Renal failure)
  • D: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
  • P: Paraldehyde, Phenformin, Propylene glycol
  • I: Iron tablets, Isoniazid
  • L: Lactic acidosis
  • E: Ethylene glycol
  • S: Salicylates (late phase)

(Mnemonic: HARD UP)

  • H: Hyperalimentation (TPN)
  • A: Acetazolamide
  • R: Renal Tubular Acidosis (Option C)
  • D: Diarrhea
  • U: Ureteral diversion
  • P: Pancreatic fistula
  • GIT fistulas

Clinical Features

General Features:

  • Lethargy
  • Confusion
  • Fatigue
  • Nausea/vomiting
  • Deep, rapid breathing (Kussmaul)

Specific Features:

  • DKA: Fruity breath, polyuria, polydipsia
  • Uremia: Itching, volume overload
  • Lactic acidosis: Shock, hypotension
  • Toxic ingestion: Visual disturbances (methanol), oxalate crystals (ethylene glycol)

Metabolic alkalosis (Option B): Would have elevated pH and high HCO₃⁻, not low values.

Respiratory acidosis (Option C): Would show high pCO₂ and low pH, not low pCO₂.

Respiratory alkalosis (Option D): Would have high pH and low pCO₂, but here pH is low.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Fat embolism is the most likely diagnosis, given the recent trauma, respiratory distress, altered mental status, and petechial rash, which are characteristic signs of Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES). Symptoms often develop within 24-72 hours following fat emboli entering circulation.

Fat Embolism Causes

Blunt trauma: Accounts for 90% of cases, especially involving extremity fractures.

Associated conditions:

  • Acute pancreatitis
  • Diabetes mellitus
  • Burns
  • Joint reconstruction surgeries
  • Liposuction
  • Cardiopulmonary bypass
  • Decompression sickness
  • Parenteral lipid infusion
  • Sickle cell crisis
  • Pathologic fractures

Increased risk factors (in trauma patients):

  • Age 30 years or younger
  • Closed femur fracture
  • Multiple long-bone fractures

Pathophysiology of Fat Embolism Syndrome (FES):

  • Mechanism: Not fully understood but involves fat emboli entering circulation, usually after major trauma or surgical procedures (intramedullary nailing).
  • Pulmonary effects:
    • Fat emboli occlude microvasculature, leading to inflammatory responses and endothelial injury.
    • Pulmonary consequences mimic acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), presenting within 24 hours with symptoms of respiratory failure.
    • Fatty acids released from emboli increase vascular permeability, causing alveolar haemorrhage and oedema.
  • Systemic effects:
    • Involvement of the brain and kidneys, especially in patients with patent foramen ovale
    • Neurologic symptoms include encephalopathy and cerebral oedema due to cerebral vasculature occlusion.
    • Histopathological image

[[figure-1]]

Pulmonary Embolism (PE) (Options A) can present with sudden dyspnea and hypoxia.

question: A patient was admitted to the ICU 48 hours after an accident in which he sustained a fracture of the femur. The oxygen saturation in the rebreathing unit was 100% but his SpO2 remained at 60%. The patient is in a state of confusion. Diffuse petechiae are noted on examination. Chest radiograph showed lung fields to be clear. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's presentation with fever, breathlessness, cough with expectoration, and the CT scan findings of consolidation with an air bronchogram strongly suggest a pneumonic consolidation due to lobar pneumonia

Clinical manifestations of Lobar pneumonia:

  • Common Symptoms:
    • Fever
    • Cough
    • Sputum production (often mucopurulent)
    • Pleuritic chest pain (Localized pleuritic pain is common, especially in lobar pneumonia)
  • Constitutional Symptoms: Fatigue, headache, myalgia, and arthralgias may occur.
  • Severe pneumonia can lead to:
    • Dyspnea.
    • Confusion, sepsis, and multi-organ failure.
  • Clinical Signs:
    • Tachypnea (increased respiratory rate)
    • Increased vocal fremitus
    • Egophony (E to A changes)
    • Dullness to percussion
  • Auscultation Findings: Presence of crackles or rales, and bronchial breath sounds (tubular type breathing).

Investigation

Findings

Initial Evaluation
  • Clinical suspicion based on patient history and physical examination.

Chest Radiography
  • The most important initial test for pneumonia diagnosis.
  • Shows pulmonary infiltrate; indicates type (lobar, interstitial, unilateral, or bilateral).
  • Cannot reliably differentiate between bacterial and non-bacterial causes.

[[figure-1]]

CT Scan
  • More accurate than a chest X-ray.
  • Focal dense opacification of an entire lobe occurs, with relative sparing of the large airways. Associated findings may include ground-glass opacities in a lobar or segmental pattern, indicating areas of partial involvement or atelectasis.

[[figure-2]]

  • Image shows left upper lung lobe consolidation of heterogenous density, with multiple air bronchograms, and small left pleural effusion

Laboratory Tests
  • Complete Blood Count (CBC):
    • Look for leukocytosis (leftward shift) as a sign of infection.
    • Leukopenia may indicate a poor prognosis.
  • Inflammatory Biomarkers: ESR and acute phase reactants to assess severity.

Sputum Analysis
  • Sputum Gram stain and culture critical for suspected lobar pneumonia.
  • Sputum culture is the most specific diagnostic test for identifying the causative organism.

Influenza Testing
  • Recommended during winter months due to the risk of co-infection with pneumonia.

Patient Stratification
  • Use CURB-65 and the pneumonia severity index to determine hospitalization needs.

Additional Testing
  • Hospitalized patients: sputum culture, blood culture, and/or urine antigen testing before antibiotics.

Invasive Procedures
  • Thoracocentesis, bronchoscopy, pleural biopsy, and pleural fluid culture are rarely performed.
  • Open lung biopsy is the ultimate specific diagnostic test.

Mediastinal mass (Option B):

  • A mediastinal mass typically presents with symptoms like chest pain, dyspnea, and cough but not with classic symptoms of pneumonia like fever and cough with expectoration.
  • On CT, a mediastinal mass appears as a localized area of mass effect in one of the mediastinal compartments.

[[figure-3]]

Pleural effusion (Option C):

  • Pleural effusion would appear on CT as a fluid-filled space in the pleural cavity and does not cause consolidation with air bronchograms.
  • Breathlessness is common in pleural effusion, but the characteristic CT finding would be a homogenous opacity in the pleural space.

[[figure-4]]

Diaphragmatic hernia (Option D): A diaphragmatic hernia would show up on CT as an abnormal position of abdominal organs (such as the stomach or bowel) in the thoracic cavity.

[[figure-5]]



Reference:
  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page: 1011, 1012, 2200.
  • Typical Bacterial Pneumonia - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
  • Lobar pneumonia | Radiology Reference Article | Radiopaedia.org
question: A 35-year-old female patient presents with fever, breathlessness, and cough with expectoration. A CT scan was done, which is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of fever, night sweats, ptosis, and bilateral facial nerve palsy, along with leukocytosis and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, strongly points to sarcoidosis.

Sarcoidosis:

Sarcoidosis is a chronic multisystem inflammatory disorder of unknown cause, characterized by the accumulation of T lymphocytes and mononuclear phagocytes, leading to the formation of non-caseating granulomas in various tissues of the body.

Clinical Presentation

Lungs (90%)

  • Interstitial lung disease
  • Pulmonary fibrosis
  • Cavitation (Rare)
  • Pleural involvement (1-5% cases) with occasional pleural effusion

Pulmonary Symptoms: Dry cough, dyspnea, chest pain

Lymph Nodes (75-90%)

  • Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy (hallmark)
  • Parotid enlargement

Extrapulmonary Symptoms:

  • Skin
    • Erythema nodosum (tender red nodules, often on shins)

[[figure-1]]

    • Lupus pernio (purple-blue shiny lesions on nose, cheeks, lips, and ears)

[[figure-2]]

  • Eyes: Anterior Uveitis
  • Kidneys: Hypercalcemia with or without hypercalciuria
  • Nervous System: Facial nerve palsy, Peripheral neuropathy
  • Heart: Cor pulmonale (secondary to pulmonary fibrosis)

Constitutional Symptoms: Fever, fatigue, night sweats, weight loss

Syndromes Associated
  • Lofgren's syndrome: Features include erythema nodosum (painful red nodules on the shins), hilar lymphadenopathy, and periarticular arthritis.
  • Mikulicz syndrome: Involves bilateral enlargement of the parotid, submaxillary, and sublingual glands.

Histopathological Features
  • Presence of non-caseating granulomas in affected organs
  • Granulomas are often composed of epithelioid histiocytes and giant cells (Langerhans or foreign body type)

Inclusion Bodies in Giant Cells:

  • Schaumann bodies (calcium-protein inclusions)

[[figure-3]]

  • Asteroid bodies (stellate-shaped inclusions)

[[figure-4]]

Initial Diagnostic Workup

History and Physical Examination

  • Assess for respiratory symptoms and extrapulmonary signs
  • Check for bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy and skin lesions

Chest Imaging

  • Chest X-ray (Stage 1: bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is a hallmark finding)

Laboratory Investigations

Serum Angiotensin-Converting Enzyme (ACE)

  • Elevated in 60% of cases (non-specific but supportive)

Calcium Levels

  • Hypercalcemia due to increased 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D production by macrophages in granulomas

Bronchoalveolar Lavage (BAL)

  • CD4/CD8 ratio > 3.5 supports sarcoidosis (not diagnostic alone)

Pulmonary Function Tests (PFTs)
  • Restrictive Pattern
  • Decreased FVC and TLC
  • Normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio
  • Decreased DLCO (diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide)

Imaging Studies

Chest X-Ray: Staging based on lung involvement

Stage 0

Normal

Stage 1

Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy

Stage 2

Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy with pulmonary infiltrates

Stage 3

Pulmonary infiltrates only

Stage 4

Pulmonary fibrosis

High-Resolution CT (HRCT):

  • Ground-glass opacities
  • Perilymphatic nodules
  • Fibrotic changes

Histopathology

Tissue Biopsy (Gold Standard)

[[figure-5]]

  • Non-caseating granulomas in lung, lymph nodes, or skin
  • Exclusion of other granulomatous diseases such as tuberculosis (caseating granulomas) and fungal infections

Other Diagnostic Tests

Gallium-67 Scintigraphy

  • Panda Sign: Uptake in lacrimal and parotid glands

[[figure-6]]

  • Lambda Sign: Uptake in bilateral hilar and right paratracheal lymph nodes

[[figure-7]]

Positron Emission Tomography (PET)

  • Identifies active inflammation and organ involvement

Differential Diagnosis
  • Infections: Tuberculosis, fungal infections
  • Autoimmune Disorders: Lupus, rheumatoid arthritis
  • Malignancies: Lymphoma, metastatic carcinoma

Diagnostic Criteria
  • Compatible clinical and radiographic presentation
  • Non-caseating granulomas on histopathology
  • Exclusion of other granulomatous diseases

Tuberculosis (TB) (Option B): TB can cause fever, night sweats, and hilar lymphadenopathy but typically presents with cough and hemoptysis, which are not mentioned in this case. Facial nerve palsy is rare in TB unless there is extensive dissemination, which is unusual in early stages.

Lymphoma (Option C): Lymphoma can present with fever, night sweats, and hilar lymphadenopathy. However, it is less likely to cause bilateral facial nerve palsy and ptosis as part of its presentation. Lymphoma would typically involve lymph node enlargement and may present with systemic symptoms, but it is usually not associated with granulomatous inflammation seen in sarcoidosis.

Hypersensitive pneumonitis (Option D): Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (also known as extrinsic allergic alveolitis) is caused by an immune response to inhaled antigens and primarily affects the lungs, leading to symptoms like dyspnea, cough, and fever. However, it does not typically cause bilateral facial nerve palsy or hilar lymphadenopathy, as seen in this patient.



Reference:
  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page: 461, 841, 844, 846, 852, 853, 1362, 1364, 1366, 1367, 2160, 2161, 2829-2835.
  • Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page: 608-610.
  • Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page: 214, 368, 371, 372, 696, 697.
question: A patient presents with fever, night sweats, ptosis, and bilateral facial nerve palsy. Investigations show leukocytosis and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation indicates asbestosis, a form of pneumoconiosis caused by prolonged asbestos exposure. The key diagnostic features in this case include the patient's 20-year occupational exposure in a factory setting, presenting symptom of breathlessness, and most importantly, the HRCT findings of pleural thickening and fibrosis.

Pleural involvement is a characteristic feature of asbestos-related lung disease, distinguishing it from other occupational lung diseases.

Workers in the shipbuilding and construction trades, including pipe fitters and boilermakers, are occupationally exposed to asbestos.

  • Asbestosis is a diffuse interstitial fibrosing disease of the lung.
  • Past exposure to asbestos is specifically indicated by pleural plaques on chest radiographs, which are characterized by either thickening or calcification along the parietal pleura, particularly along the lower lung fields.
  • Pulmonary function testing in asbestosis reveals a restrictive pattern with a decrease in both lung volumes and diffusing capacity.
  • Complications include carcinoma of lung and mesothelioma.

Coal worker pneumoconiosis (Option B) is characterized by small nodules diffusely distributed throughout the lungs, with upper lobe predominance and eggshell calcification of hilar lymph nodes. The presence of pleural thickening rather than nodular opacities makes this diagnosis less likely.

Silicosis (Option C) typically presents with multiple small nodules in the upper lung zones with a characteristic "ground-glass" appearance. The absence of these findings and the presence of pleural thickening make silicosis an unlikely diagnosis.

Berylliosis (Option D) presents with early-stage parenchymal nodules and later develops lymphadenopathy and interstitial fibrosis. The prominent pleural involvement seen in this case is not typical of berylliosis, and the exposure history doesn't suggest beryllium exposure.



Reference:
  • Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2168
  • Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 615
question: A 45-year patient working in a factory for the past 20 years presents with breathlessness. HRCT chest shows pleural thickening and fibrosis. Diagnosis is?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The given flow-volume loop is suggestive of COPD, as it demonstrates an obstructive pattern characterized by a concave ("scooped-out" or "coved") expiratory limb and increased residual volume (RV) due to chronic air trapping.

  • COPD is characterized by persistent airflow obstruction resulting from a combination of small airway disease (airway narrowing due to inflammation, mucus, and fibrosis) and emphysema (destruction of alveoli with loss of elastic recoil).
  • Spirometry is the investigation of choice and shows:
    • ↓ FEV₁/FVC (<70%)
    • ↓ FEV₁
    • Normal or mildly ↓ FVC
    • ↑ RV (air trapping)
    • ↑ TLC (hyperinflation)
  • The concave expiratory limb reflects dynamic expiratory airflow limitation, caused by premature collapse of small airways during forced expiration due to reduced elastic recoil and increased airway resistance.
  • Progressive airflow obstruction leads to incomplete exhalation, resulting in air trapping and dynamic hyperinflation, which increases the operating lung volume and is a major cause of exertional dyspnea.
  • Typical clinical features include:
    • Chronic cough
    • Sputum production
    • Progressive exertional dyspnea
    • Prolonged expiration with wheeze
    • Hyperinflation (barrel chest) in advanced disease
  • Chest X-ray shows hyperinflated lungs with flattened diaphragms
  • CT chest is the most sensitive imaging modality for detecting emphysema and small airway disease.

Asbestosis (Option A): Produces a restrictive ventilatory defect with reduced lung volumes, not an obstructive flow-volume loop.

Myasthenia gravis (Option C): Causes respiratory muscle weakness resulting in a restrictive pattern without expiratory flow limitation.

Vocal cord paralysis (Option D): Produces an upper airway obstruction pattern with flattening of the inspiratory and/or expiratory limb, rather than the characteristic scooped expiratory curve seen in COPD.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 2202-2204, 2249.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient’s risk factor (chronic alcoholism) and clinical presentation suggests pneumonia caused by Klebsiella pneumoniae.
  • Alcoholism predisposes to aspiration of oropharyngeal secretions containing Klebsiella, leading to necrotizing pneumonia.

[[figure-1]]

Specific aetiology of pneumonia:

  • Alcoholic patient with Pneumonia: Pneumococcus pneumonia.
  • Alcoholic with Red currant jelly sputum: Klebsiella pneumonia/Friedlander pneumonia.
  • COPD & smokers end up with Hemophilus influenzae. (Option D)
  • Structural lung disease Eg. Cystic fibrosis where mucus plugs thickened present - Pseudomonas aeruginosa (Option C) /Burkholderia cepacia
  • Contact with Birds: Chlamydia psittaci
  • Contact with Bats: Histoplasmosis
  • Contact with Rabbits: Francisella tularensis (Tularemia)
  • Contact with Goat/sheep: Coxiella burnetii can cause Q fever.
  • Hotel/cruise: Legionella pneumophila

Streptococcus pneumoniae (Option A)Most common cause of community-acquired pneumonia, but typically presents with rust-colored sputum and less necrotizing disease.

question: Identify the condition in the following X-ray.

correctAnswer: A. Hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hyponatremia
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Chronic vomiting leads to hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis with hyponatremia.

Development of metabolic Alkalosis due to vomiting

  • Occurs due to a net gain of bicarbonate (HCO3−) or loss of nonvolatile acid (usually HCl) from the extracellular fluid, commonly caused by vomiting.

Generation Stage:

  • Vomiting leads to the loss of HCl from the stomach, preventing HCO3− secretion in the small intestine.
  • As a result, HCO3− gets retained in the extracellular fluid, leading to the development of metabolic alkalosis.

Maintenance Stage:

  • After vomiting ceases, the kidneys fail to appropriately excrete the excess HCO3−, maintaining the alkalosis.
  • This failure is influenced by factors such as volume deficiency, chloride deficiency, and potassium deficiency, combined with a reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

Saline-Responsive Metabolic Alkalosis:

  • In cases of volume, chloride, and potassium deficiency, the alkalosis can be corrected by restoring extracellular fluid volume through intravenous administration of NaCl and KCl.

Saline-Unresponsive Metabolic Alkalosis:

  • In cases of hypokalemia due to hyperaldosteronism, the alkalosis may require pharmacologic or surgical treatment, rather than saline correction.

Metabolic Alkalosis:

  • Metabolic alkalosis is characterized by an increase in arterial pH, elevated serum bicarbonate [HCO3−], and increased PaCO2 due to compensatory hypoventilation.
  • Often presents with hypochloremia and hypokalemia.
  • Occurs as a mixed disorder with respiratory or metabolic acidosis or alkalosis.

Clinical Features

  • Neurological: Mental confusion, obtundation, potential seizures
  • Peripheral Nervous System: Paresthesias, muscle cramps, tetany (similar to hypocalcemia effects)
  • Cardiovascular: Aggravation of arrhythmias, particularly in COPD patients

Electrolyte Imbalances

  • Potassium (K⁺): Hypokalemia, especially in cases involving secondary hyperaldosteronism or diuretic use.
  • Chloride (Cl⁻): Hypochloremia, frequently accompanying alkalosis, especially in cases of vomiting or diuretic use.
  • Calcium (Ca²⁺): Symptoms may mimic hypocalcemia despite normal levels.


Options B, C, and D are incorrect.



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 365-367
  2. Arterial Blood Gases - Physiopedia

question: A 55-year-old patient presented with chronic projectile vomiting and weight loss. What is the expected metabolic abnormality to be seen here?

explanationHtml:
• The patient has primary metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation.

Stepwise Acid-Base Diagnosis:

Step 1: The patient's pH is 7.2 (normal: 7.35-7.45), indicating acidosis.

Step 2: The bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) level is 10 mmol/L, lower than the normal range (22-30 mmol/L), suggesting metabolic acidosis.

Step 3: Use Winter's formula to calculate the expected pCO₂ compensation for metabolic acidosis:
Expected pCO₂ = (1.5 × HCO₃⁻) + 8 ± 2
For HCO₃⁻ = 10,
Expected pCO₂ = (1.5 × 10) + 8 ± 2 = 21-25 mmHg.

Step 5: The patient’s actual pCO₂ is 30 mmHg. This is higher than the expected range (21-25 mmHg), indicating partially respiratory compensation.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principle of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 360
question: A 55-year-old male presented with tachypnea and mental confusion. His blood sugar is 350mg/dl, pH-7.2, HCO3-10, pCO2-30. What is the metabolic abnormality?

correctAnswer: B. Needle decompression into the 5 th intercostal space anterior to the midaxillary line
explanationHtml:
Pathophysiology

  • D/t ‘one-way valve’ air leaks from the lung or chest wall.
  • Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any escape, collapsing and compressing the affected lung.
  • The mediastinum shifts to the opposite side, reducing venous return and compressing the opposite lung, leading to decreased cardiac output and function. This can result in sudden death.

Causes

  • Penetrating Chest Trauma.
  • Blunt Chest Trauma with parenchymal lung injury and persistent air leak.
  • Iatrogenic Lung Injury (e.g., central venepuncture)
  • Mechanical Positive-Pressure Ventilation.

Clinical Features

  • Tachypnea and Tachycardia
  • Hyper-resonance and Decreased/Absent Breath Sounds
  • Resonant Percussion with severe mediastinal/tracheal shift
  • Cyanosis and Hypotension
  • Chest Pain
  • Distended Neck Veins
  • Subcutaneous emphysema

Emergency Management

  • Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confirmation.
  • Immediate Thoracocentesis (needle): Wide bore needle (typically a 20- or 22-gauge) in the 5th intercostal space in the safety triangle.
  • Decompression should be performed in the "safe triangle."
    • Safe Triangle Boundaries:
      • Posterior: Latissimus dorsi
      • Anterior: Lateral border of the pectoralis major
      • Inferior: A line drawn perpendicularly from the nipple to the back, just anterior to the mid-axillary line.

[[figure-1]]

  • In critical situations, a finger thoracostomy can be done in the same location.
  • Nasal Oxygen for support.
  • Intercostal Tube Placement (ICT) once stable and confirmed by chest X-ray.

Additional Care

  • Antibiotics and analgesics for treatment.
  • Ventilator Support with IPPV in severe cases.

Start IV fluids with a large bore cannula (Option A): While IV fluids are important in managing hypotension, they do not address the underlying problem of tension pneumothorax, which is the primary cause of the patient's instability.

Take the patient to the ICU and intubate him (Option C): Intubation and ICU care may be necessary later, but delaying decompression can lead to rapid deterioration. Positive pressure ventilation without prior decompression could worsen the tension pneumothorax.

Start positive pressure ventilation (Option D): This is contraindicated in tension pneumothorax because it can further increase intrathoracic pressure and exacerbate the condition, leading to cardiovascular collapse



Reference:
  • Bailey & Love’s Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page 374
  • Sabiston Textbook of Surgery, 21st Edition, Page 404, 405,1632
  • Tension Pneumothorax - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf.

question: A 53-year-old woman underwent hip replacement surgery. A week after the surgery, the patient developed swelling of the legs associated with pain on palpation. Her heart rate is 70 beats per min. There is no history of hemoptysis or significant weight loss. There is no previous history of pulmonary embolism. What is the risk of developing pulmonary embolism in the patient based on Well’s score?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Kartagener syndrome:

  • Kartagener syndrome is characterized by a triad of symptoms: situs inversus (dextrocardia seen on CXR), chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis. The recurrent lung infections in this case are consistent with the chronic respiratory issues seen in Kartagener syndrome. The dextrocardia noted in the CXR supports this diagnosis.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Cystic fibrosis: Cystic fibrosis primarily presents with thick, sticky mucus leading to lung infections, pancreatic insufficiency, and other issues. While it causes recurrent lung infections, it is not associated with dextrocardia. The diagnosis is typically supported by sweat chloride tests and genetic testing.

Option C - DiGeorge syndrome: DiGeorge syndrome includes a range of congenital defects, including heart defects, thymic hypoplasia, and hypoparathyroidism. It does not typically present with dextrocardia or recurrent lung infections as a primary feature.

Option D - Down syndrome: Down syndrome is associated with a variety of congenital heart defects and may include respiratory issues. However, it is not specifically associated with dextrocardia or a particular pattern of recurrent lung infections that would align with Kartagener syndrome.
