explanationHtml:
• Cystic fibrosis is identified as the primary diagnosis based on the classical triad of symptoms presented. The diagnosis is supported by the presence of recurrent respiratory infections with thickened sputum (indicating pulmonary involvement), bronchial wall thickening on chest X-ray, and steatorrhea since birth (indicating pancreatic insufficiency).
  • The condition is characterized by a genetic defect in the CFTR gene affecting chloride channels, resulting in thick secretions in multiple organ systems.

Pathological features of Cystic Fibrosis

Organ System

Pathological Features

Clinical Manifestations

Diagnostic Findings

Respiratory
  • Thick mucus plugging
  • Bronchiectasis
  • Chronic inflammation
  • Submucosal gland hypertrophy
  • Chronic productive cough
  • Recurrent infections
  • Progressive dyspnea
  • Digital clubbing
  • Obstructive pattern on PFTs
  • Bronchiectasis on CT

Pancreatic
  • Duct obstruction
  • Acinar cell destruction
  • Fibrosis
  • Fat replacement
  • Malabsorption
  • Steatorrhea
  • Failure to thrive
  • Fat-soluble vitamin deficiency
  • Low fecal elastase
  • Elevated fecal fat
  • Low vitamins A, D, E, K

Sweat Glands
  • Abnormal chloride transport
  • Normal gland structure
  • Salty-tasting skin
  • Heat intolerance
  • Salt depletion
  • Elevated sweat chloride
  • >60 mEq/L diagnostic

Hepatobiliary
  • Bile duct plugging
  • Focal biliary cirrhosis
  • Multilobular cirrhosis
  • Neonatal cholestasis
  • Portal hypertension
  • Gallstones
  • Elevated liver enzymes
  • Ultrasound changes

Hyaline membrane disease (Option A) primarily affects premature infants and presents immediately after birth with respiratory distress. This condition does not manifest with chronic respiratory infections or steatorrhea seen in this 5-year-old child.

Alpha 1 anti-trypsin deficiency (Option C) typically presents with progressive emphysema and liver disease but does not cause pancreatic insufficiency leading to steatorrhea.

Malabsorption syndrome (Option D) typically presents with steatorrhea, diarrhea, weight loss & various nutrient deficiencies but does not account for the specific respiratory manifestations present in this case. The combination of respiratory and gastrointestinal symptoms points more specifically to cystic fibrosis.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Volume I, Page. 2176, 2177
question: A 5-year-old child presented with recurrent respiratory infections with thickened sputum. Chest X-ray showed bronchial wall thickening. He has been suffering from steatorrhea since birth. Which of the following is the first differential diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
• The clinical manifestations indicate a suspicious lung mass requiring tissue diagnosis. CT-guided biopsy is the most appropriate next step given the peripheral location of the mass near the apex of the lung.
  • It is a minimally invasive procedure where a radiologist uses CT imaging to guide the insertion of a needle into the lung mass to obtain a tissue sample for analysis. The procedure provides accurate histopathological information about the nature of the mass, including whether it is cancerous or benign, which is crucial in a patient with significant smoking history and hemoptysis.

Evaluation for Suspected Lung Mass

Non-Invasive Diagnostic Methods

Sputum Cytology
  • Non-invasive initial diagnostic test
  • Most useful for central lesions (Option C Ruled Out)
  • Higher yield in large, proximal tumors
  • Low sensitivity due to high tissue variability

CT Chest
  • Contrast-enhanced
  • Extension to upper abdomen (adrenal level)
  • Sensitivity: 55%, Specificity: 81%
  • Identifies tumor location, extent, and lymph node involvement
  • Lymph node ≥1cm in short axis considered suspicious

PET/PET-CT
  • Higher accuracy than CT (Sensitivity: 80%, Specificity: 88%)
  • Identifies metabolic activity and potential metastases
  • Reduces futile thoracotomies
  • Helpful in identifying recurrence post-therapy

Invasive Staging & Biopsy Methods

CT-Guided Transthoracic Biopsy
  • Preferred for peripheral lesions (Option A)
  • High diagnostic accuracy
  • Minimally Invasive
  • Risk of pneumothorax (especially in emphysematous patients)
  • Contraindicated if high bleeding risk or severe emphysema

EBUS-TBNA
  • CP-EBUS: Real-time sampling of mediastinal/hilar nodes
  • RP-EBUS: For smaller/peripheral lesions
  • Navigation bronchoscopy for mapped approach

Endoscopic-TBNA
  • Samples through esophageal wall
  • Accesses stations 2, 4, 7, 8, 9
  • Sensitivity: 89%, Specificity: 100%

Mediastinoscopy
  • Used after negative needle technique
  • Samples para-tracheal nodes
  • Sensitivity: 78%, Specificity: 100%
  • Mortality risk: 0.08%

VATS/RATS
  • For mediastinal lymph node sampling
  • Full dissection during lung resection
  • Minimally invasive approach

Cancer Type

Location

Primary Investigations

Additional Investigations

Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) - Adenocarcinoma

Peripheral/Outer regions of lung
  • CT-guided needle biopsy
  • PET-CT scan
  • Blood tests for tumor markers (CEA)
  • Molecular testing (EGFR, ALK, ROS1)
  • MRI brain (for staging)
  • Pulmonary function tests

NSCLC - Squamous Cell

Central/Main bronchi
  • Bronchoscopy with biopsy
  • Chest CT with contrast
  • Sputum cytology
  • Mediastinoscopy
  • Bone scan (if symptoms)
  • PD-L1 testing

Small Cell Lung Cancer (SCLC)

Central regions, rapid spread
  • CT chest/abdomen/pelvis
  • Bronchoscopy
  • Blood tests (ProGRP, NSE)
  • MRI brain (mandatory)
  • Bone marrow biopsy
  • Nuclear medicine scans

Large Cell Carcinoma

Any location
  • PET-CT scan
  • Core needle biopsy
  • Immunohistochemistry
  • Molecular profiling
  • EBUS-TBNA
  • Liquid biopsy

Carcinoid Tumors

Usually central airways
  • Octreotide scan
  • Bronchoscopy with biopsy
  • 24-hour urine 5-HIAA
  • Chromogranin A levels
  • MIBG scan
  • Endoscopic ultrasound

Bronchoscopy (Option A): While bronchoscopy can be useful in evaluating central lesions or endobronchial tumors, it may not be effective for evaluating peripheral lung masses, especially those located near the apex.

Sputum cytology (Option C): Sputum cytology is inexpensive and noninvasive but has a lesser sensitivity than biopsy, especially when there is a clear indication of a suspected lung mass on radiography. The yield for sputum cytology is highest for larger and centrally located tumors such as squamous cell carcinoma and small-cell carcinoma.

Sputum for AFB (Option D): While TB can cause hemoptysis, the appearance of a 3cm upper lobe mass near the apex on chest X-ray is inconsistent with the typical presentation of TB and indicates a suspected malignancy for which a tissue diagnosis is more urgently needed.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 595-601
question: A 45-year-old patient with a history of smoking a pack of cigarettes for the past 15 years presents with hemoptysis. Chest X-ray shows a 3cm upper lobe mass near the apex of the lung. What is the next best step for managing this patient?

explanationHtml:
• Dressler syndrome is a post–myocardial infarction autoimmune pericarditis that can be associated with exudative pleural effusion.
  • The effusion results from inflammation of the pleura, leading to increased capillary permeability and high protein content.
  • Exudative effusions typically satisfy Light’s criteria.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Heart failure: Pleural effusion in heart failure is usually transudative, caused by increased hydrostatic pressure. It typically has low protein and LDH levels.

Option B - Rheumatic arthritis: Rheumatoid arthritis can cause pleural effusion, but it is relatively uncommon and usually seen in long-standing disease. It is not the best answer in this context compared to Dressler syndrome.

Option D - Nephrotic syndrome: Nephrotic syndrome causes transudative pleural effusion due to hypoalbuminemia and reduced plasma oncotic pressure.



Reference:
  • Harrison’s Principles of internal medicine 21st edition Page 2199
  • Pleural effusion
question: Which of the following is a cause of exudative pleural effusion?

explanationHtml:
• Silicosis, a progressive occupational interstitial lung disease caused by inhalation of crystalline silica dust. On HRCT, silicosis characteristically shows ground-glass opacities, particularly in early stages.
  • The ground-glass appearance on HRCT refers to an imaging pattern in which the lung parenchyma appears hazy due to partial filling of the air spaces with fluid, inflammatory cells, or fibrosis.
  • They appear as hazy areas of increased attenuation in the lung parenchyma without obscuring the underlying bronchial and vascular margins. As the disease progresses, nodular opacities called silicotic nodules develop, typically with an upper lung zone predominance, and may calcify over time, resulting in eggshell calcifications.

Silicosis:

  • The leading cause of Interstitial lung disease (ILD) in India, frequently resulting from occupational exposure in the glassware, mining, quarrying, and construction industries.
  • Manifests after 10-20 years of continuous exposure.
  • Radiological features:
    • The chest radiograph may show profuse military infiltration or consolidation, and there is a characteristic HRCT pattern of ground glass opacities known as “crazy paving”- A feature of acute silicosis
    • Multiple well-circumscribed 3–5 mm nodular opacities predominantly in the mid-and upper zones.
    • Enlargement of the hilar glands with an “egg-shell” pattern of calcification (seen in 20% of cases).
    • As the disease progresses, progressive massive fibrosis (PMF) may develop.

Asbestosis (Option A): Asbestosis is a chronic lung disease caused by the inhalation of asbestos fibers. The characteristic findings on HRCT include linear opacities that typically have a subpleural and lower lung zone predominance, with fine reticular lines, thick bands, or honeycombing. Ground-glass appearance is not a typical feature of asbestosis.

Anthracosis (Option C): Anthracosis, or coal workers' pneumoconiosis, is caused by the inhalation and deposition of coal dust particles. The primary HRCT finding is the presence of small, rounded opacities, often referred to as coal macules or coal nodules found in the upper lung zones. Ground-glass opacities are not a characteristic feature.

Bagassosis (Option D): Bagassosis is an acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis caused by the inhalation of moldy bagasse. While HRCT findings in bagassosis can vary, they typically include centrilobular nodules and air-trapping. While ground-glass opacities may be seen, they are not the predominant or characteristic feature.



Reference:
  • Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 2169, 2191
  • Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 615
question: In which medical condition is a ground-glass appearance observed on high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT)?

explanationHtml:
• This patient's clinical presentation, combined with the findings from the chest X-ray, points towards the Pancoast tumor, a form of lung cancer that occurs in the apex (upper part) of the lung.

Pancoast Tumor: A Pancoast tumor, also known as a superior sulcus tumor, is a type of lung cancer that arises in the apex of the lung, often extending to involve nearby structures, including the chest wall, nerves, and blood vessels. These tumors are typically non-small cell lung cancers (NSCLC), most commonly squamous cell carcinoma or adenocarcinoma, strongly associated with smoking, which is a major risk factor.

Clinical Presentation

The symptoms of a Pancoast tumor are primarily due to the tumor's location rather than systemic effects of lung cancer.

Pain: Severe shoulder, arm, or chest wall pain is common due to invasion of the brachial plexus (C8-T2 nerve roots).

Horner's Syndrome: Results from sympathetic chain involvement, characterized by:

  • Ptosis (drooping eyelid)
  • Miosis (pupil constriction)
  • Anhidrosis (loss of sweating on the affected side)

Weakness and Atrophy: Weakness of the hand muscles and atrophy, due to compression of the lower brachial plexus.

Other Symptoms: Cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss may be present if the disease is more advanced.

Diagnosis

Imaging:

  • Chest X-ray: May show an apical mass.

[[figure-1]]

  • MRI (IOC): Provides detailed information about local invasion into nearby structures.

Biopsy: Confirms histological diagnosis.

PET Scan: Assesses metastasis.

Management

  • Radiotherapy: Preoperatively to shrink the tumor.
  • Surgery: For resectable tumors, such as lobectomy or chest wall resection.
  • Chemotherapy: For advanced or unresectable tumors.

Superior vena cava obstruction (Option B): This condition can occur due to a tumor compressing the superior vena cava, causing swelling of the face, neck, and upper limbs, but it would not explain the combination of ptosis and pain radiating to the arm. It is usually associated with anterior mediastinal tumors, not typically with Pancoast tumors.

Upper lobe pneumonia (Option C): Pneumonia could cause chest discomfort and radiographic findings, but it would not explain the drooping eyelid (ptosis) or neurological symptoms in the arm. Pneumonia would also show consolidation on a chest X-ray, not a mass.

[[figure-2]]

Aspergilloma (Option D): Aspergilloma is a fungal infection that typically occurs in pre-existing lung cavities (e.g., after tuberculosis). It could cause chest pain and cough, but it would not explain the ptosis or brachial plexus symptoms. The chest X-ray would typically show a fungal ball within a pre-existing cavity.

[[figure-3]]



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page: 565, 566, 598, 1011, 1679.

Schwartz's Principles of Surgery - 11th Edition, Page: 680, 699.

question: Comment on the lung disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • pH 7.28 is decreased, suggestive of acidosis, the pCO2 = 60mmHg which is elevated, hence the acidosis is likely respiratory.
  • The bicarbonate is 28 meq/L implying that compensation is partial (partial compensation/inadequate compensation)

This is a case of inadequately compensated respiratory acidosis because:

  • In acute respiratory acidosis, HCO3- will ↑ by 1 mEq/L for every 10 mmHg ↑ in pCO2
  • In chronic respiratory acidosis, HCO3- will ↑ by 4 mEq/L for every 10 mmHg ↑ in pCO2
    • In this patient, ABG shows:
  • pH: 7.28
  • PaCO2: 60 mmHg
  • HCO3-: 28 mEq/L
  • Normal PaCO2: 38-42 mm Hg

Thus, the difference in PaCO2 = 60 - 42 = 18 mm Hg

As this patient has COPD which is the most likely cause of respiratory acidosis in this patient, it is chronic respiratory acidosis

  • We know for every 10 mmHg ↑ in PCO2, HCO3- should ↑ by 4 mEq/L
    • For 1 mmHg ↑ in PCO2, HCO3- should ↑ by 4/10 mEq/L
    • Thus for 18 mm Hg ↑ in PCO2 , HCO3- should ↑ by 7.2 mEq/L
  • In this patient HCO3- should be approx 33 mEq/L, but it is only 28 mEq/L, hence it is only partially compensated respiratory acidosis

Incorrect Options:

Fully compensated respiratory acidosis (Option B): If this was the condition, the HCO3- should have been approximately 33.

Fully compensated respiratory alkalosis (Option C) is incorrect since the ABG in the given scenario is respiratory acidosis.

Inadequately compensated metabolic alkalosis (Option D) is incorrect since the ABG in the given scenario is respiratory acidosis.

question: A 70-year-old diabetic man presents after a fall. He is having a high fever, cough and breathing difficulty and appears confused. CXR shows lobar consolidation. Labs show elevated BUN and creatinine. Which is the most appropriate management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The scenario here is severe pneumonia signified by admission to the ICU; hence, the best treatment modality is beta-lactam + macrolide, i.e., Ceftriaxone + Azithromycin.

Treatment for Lobar Pneumonia

  • Treatment depends on severity; assess if inpatient or outpatient management is needed.
  • CURB-65 Score: Used to stratify patients with the following factors:

CURB-65

Symptom

Score

(C) Confusion

1

(U) Urea: BUN >19mg/dL (>7 mmol/L)

1

(R) Respiratory rate ≥30/min

1

(B) Blood Pressure - Systolic BP ≤90 mmHg or diastolic BP ≤60 mmHg

1

(65) Age ≥65 years

1
  • Hospitalisation Criteria:
    • CURB-65 score 0: Outpatient treatment
    • Score 1 or 2: Indicates hospitalization
    • Score ≥3: Indicates ICU admission and more intensive therapy.
  • Empiric Therapy:
    • Outpatient:
      • No comorbidities: Monotherapy with macrolides (Azithromycin, Clarithromycin).
      • With comorbidities (chronic lung/heart disease, diabetes, smoking, HIV): Newer fluoroquinolones (Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin, Gemifloxacin) or a combination of beta-lactam (e.g., amoxicillin) and a macrolide.
    • Inpatient Non-ICU:
      • Newer fluoroquinolones (Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin) alone or a combination of beta-lactam (e.g., Ampicillin, Ceftriaxone) and a macrolide.
    • Inpatient ICU:
      • Combination of macrolide (Azithromycin) with beta-lactam (e.g., Ampicillin-sulbactam, Ertapenem, Cephalosporins) or a newer fluoroquinolone (Levofloxacin).
      • If risk of aspiration, consider Ampicillin-sulbactam or Ertapenem; for Pseudomonas infection, use anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (e.g., Piperacillin-Tazobactam) with anti-pseudomonal fluoroquinolone (e.g., Ciprofloxacin).
      • For MRSA, add Vancomycin or Linezolid.
  • Duration of Therapy: Typically 5 to 7 days, extended if clinical response is delayed.
  • Influenza Treatment: All hospitalized patients testing positive for influenza should receive Oseltamivir, regardless of illness onset.

Incorrect Options:

Amoxicillin with clavulinic acid (Option A): Inadequate for this patient due to the severity of his illness and the risk of resistant organisms. Monotherapy with amoxicillin does not provide sufficient coverage for his condition, especially considering the possibility of Pseudomonas and MRSA.

Azithromycin (Option B): Not appropriate for this patient due to the severity of his condition, indicating he requires more intensive treatment. Azithromycin is preferred for outpatient therapy, suitable for lower-risk patients without significant comorbidities.

Piptaz + Ciprofloxacin (Option D): Piptaz (Piperacillin/Tazobactam) is a combination which is a beta lactam antibiotic. Ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic. However, as mentioned above this is not suitable for the condition of the patient here as a macrolide is necessary along with a Fluoroquinolone or a beta-lactam to treat severe pneumonia.



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page: 1012.
  2. Typical Bacterial Pneumonia - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

Explanation:

Kartagener syndrome is a subtype of Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia (PCD), a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by defective motility of cilia.

  • The underlying defect most commonly involves the dynein arms of the ciliary axoneme, resulting in impaired mucociliary clearance and recurrent respiratory infections.

Classic Triad of Kartagener Syndrome

  • Bronchiectasis
  • Chronic sinusitis
  • Situs inversus (dextrocardia)

Clinical Features

  • Respiratory:
    • Chronic productive cough
    • Recurrent sinusitis
    • Bronchiectasis
  • Reproductive:
    • Male infertility due to impaired sperm motility
    • Reduced female fertility due to abnormal fallopian tube ciliary function

Microvilli (Option A): Actin-based projections that increase absorptive surface area. Not involved in Kartagener syndrome.

Microtubules (Option B): Form the structural framework of cilia and contain dynein arms. Although the ultrastructural abnormality often involves dynein arms attached to microtubules, Kartagener syndrome is classified as a disorder of motile cilia.

Microfilaments (Option D): Composed of actin and involved in cell shape and movement. Not implicated in Kartagener syndrome.

  • Metabolic alkalosis occurs in Pyloric stenosis because the persistent vomiting of gastric contents leads to a significant loss of hydrochloric acid and a subsequent increase in plasma bicarbonate.
  • Respiratory acidosis is caused by alveolar hypoventilation, as seen in severe bronchopneumonia, where gas exchange is impaired.

The diagnosis is Tubercular Meningitis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

  • The presentation of subacute headache, cranial nerve palsies due to thick basal exudates, and the development of hydrocephalus are classic clinical hallmarks.
  • The CSF profile in TBM typically shows a cobweb appearance with lymphocytic pleocytosis (usually 10–500 cells/µL), significantly elevated protein levels, and characteristically low glucose.
  • The presence of basal enhancement on contrast MRI further supports this diagnosis over other types of chronic meningitis.

Viral meningitis (Option A) typically presents with a lymphocytic pleocytosis in the CSF, but the glucose level remains normal, and the protein is only mildly elevated.

Fungal meningitis (Option B) can mimic the CSF findings of TBM, but the acute development of hydrocephalus and cranial nerve palsies in a young patient in a TB-endemic area strongly favors a tubercular etiology.

Bacterial meningitis (Option D) is characterized by an acute onset, a predominantly neutrophilic pleocytosis in the CSF, and very low glucose levels, often with a positive Gram stain.

Chest tightness (Option A) is due to increased airway resistance and bronchoconstriction (asthma/COPD).

Inability to take a deep breath (Option C) is seen in COPD or restrictive lung disease due to hyperinflation or reduced compliance.

question: A patient presents with respiratory difficulty due to heart failure. Which of the following features is most useful in differentiating this condition from obstructive lung disease?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The CSF findings are characteristic of tubercular meningitis:
    • Lymphocytic pleocytosis (90% lymphocytes)
    • Raised protein (typically 1–5 g/L; may be markedly elevated)
    • Low CSF glucose (20–40 mg/dL; CSF:Plasma glucose ratio <0.5)
  • In this case:
    • CSF glucose = 40 mg/dL, plasma glucose = 100 mg/dL → ratio 0.4
    • CSF protein = 1 g/dL, indicating significant elevation
  • TB meningitis usually presents with a subacute course with headache, neck stiffness, fatigue, fever, and night sweats.
  • CSF may form a delicate “cobweb-like clot/pellicle” on standing due to increased protein and fibrinogen, from which AFB can be detected.

Viral meningitis (Option A): Viral meningitis usually shows lymphocytic predominance with normal CSF glucose and only mild protein elevation, unlike the low glucose and high protein seen in this case.

Bacterial meningitis (Option B): Bacterial meningitis typically has neutrophilic pleocytosis, markedly reduced glucose, and an acute presentation, making it less likely.

Fungal meningitis (Option C): Fungal meningitis can show lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose, and raised protein, but it is usually associated with immunocompromised patients and requires organism identification by tests such as India ink, antigen testing, or culture.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1127.
question: A 35-year-old man presents with headache and neck stiffness for 5 days. Lumbar puncture reveals the following CSF findings: 90% lymphocytes and 10% neutrophils with CSF glucose = 40 mg/dL (Plasma glucose = 100 mg/dL), protein = 1 g/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: B. Smoking cessation with chest physiotherapy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The most effective intervention to reduce postoperative pulmonary complications in a chronic smoker with COPD is smoking cessation combined with chest physiotherapy.
  • Smoking cessation improves mucociliary clearance, reduces airway inflammation, improves oxygenation, and decreases postoperative atelectasis, pneumonia, and respiratory failure.
    • Smoking cessation ideally ≥ 4 weeks preoperatively significantly reduces complications
  • Chest physiotherapy → improves ventilation, secretion clearance, and lung compliance
  • This combined approach has the strongest evidence for reducing perioperative pulmonary morbidity.

Prophylactic antibiotics (Option A): Not recommended routinely; they do not reduce postoperative pulmonary complications in stable COPD.

LAMA and LABA (Option C): Useful for chronic COPD symptom control, but not the most effective intervention for reducing postoperative complications compared to smoking cessation and physiotherapy.

Long-term methylxanthines (Option D): Limited role in COPD, narrow therapeutic index, and no proven benefit in reducing surgical pulmonary complications.



Reference:

Pre-operative optimisation of lung function - PMC
question: A chronic smoker with COPD is planned for elective abdominal surgery. What intervention best reduces pulmonary complications?

correctAnswer: A. Metabolic acidosis with compensated respiratory alkalosis
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This patient has metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation.
  • pH = 7.3 → acidemia
  • HCO₃⁻ = 10 mEq/L → primary metabolic acidosis
  • Expected compensatory pCO₂ (Winter’s formula) = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2 = 23 ± 2 mmHg
  • Measured pCO₂ = 25 mmHg, which is close to expected → appropriate respiratory compensation (respiratory alkalosis)
  • Therefore, this represents metabolic acidosis with compensated respiratory alkalosis, not a mixed disorder.

Metabolic alkalosis with compensated respiratory acidosis (Option B): HCO₃⁻ is low, not high.

Respiratory alkalosis with compensated metabolic acidosis (Option C): The primary disorder is metabolic (low HCO₃⁻), not respiratory.

Mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis (Option D): pCO₂ matches expected compensation, so this is not a mixed disorder.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 367, 368, 372

question: A patient is brought to the ER in circulatory failure. Labs shows pH = 7.3, HCO₃⁻ = 10 mEq/L, and pCO₂ = 25 mmHg. Which of the following best describes this patient's acid-base status?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient has emphysema, a COPD phenotype characterized by alveolar destruction and enlargement of air spaces.

  • COPD is defined by persistent respiratory symptoms with airflow obstruction, confirmed by spirometry (post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.7).
  • The patient has:
    • 30 pack-year smoking history → major risk factor for COPD.
    • Progressive breathlessness and chronic cough → persistent respiratory symptoms.
    • Minimal bronchodilator reversibility → favors COPD over asthma.
  • Chest X-ray findings suggest emphysema:
    • Hyperinflated lungs
    • Hyperlucent lung fields
    • Flattened hemidiaphragms
    • Elongated/narrow cardiac silhouette

These findings occur due to air trapping and increased lung volumes caused by alveolar destruction. Hyperlucency and reduced parenchymal markings are particularly suggestive of emphysema.

Asthma-COPD overlap syndrome (A): Requires evidence of asthma (history of childhood asthma, atopy, or significant bronchodilator reversibility), which is absent.

Interstitial lung disease (C): Produces a restrictive pattern with reduced lung volumes and interstitial infiltrates, unlike the hyperinflation seen here.

Asthma (D): Causes variable, reversible airflow obstruction rather than fixed obstruction with emphysematous changes.

question: A 60-year-old male with a 30-pack-year smoking history presents with progressive breathlessness and chronic cough. PFT shows persistent airflow limitation (post-bronchodilator FEV₁/FVC <0.7) with minimal reversibility. Chest X-ray is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation: 0.9% NS contains a high chloride concentration (154 mEq/L) compared to plasma (~100 mEq/L). Large-volume infusion causes dilutional decrease in bicarbonate and a rise in plasma chloride, leading to non–anion gap metabolic acidosis (hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis).

Ringer’s lactate (Option A): Contains lower chloride and lactate (metabolized to bicarbonate), which helps buffer acid; less likely to cause hyperchloremia.

Dextrose normal saline (DNS) (Option C): Has the same chloride load as NS but is typically given in smaller volumes for maintenance, so less likely to cause significant hyperchloremia unless large volumes are infused.

5% dextrose (Option D): Has no significant electrolytes and will not cause hyperchloremic acidosis.

explanationHtml:
The clinical manifestations indicate Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. This autoimmune condition typically presents with symmetric ascending paralysis and areflexia. The hallmark features include progressive muscle weakness that begins in the lower extremities and ascends upward, accompanied by diminished or absent deep tendon reflexes, which explains the patient's presentation of lower symmetric flaccidity and absent cord reflex.

Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS)

Category

Symptoms

Motor Symptoms
  • Progressive ascending paralysis (distal to proximal)
  • Areflexia
  • Weakness in legs causing rubbery legs and instability to stand
  • Truncal paralysis, quadriplegia, neck floppiness
  • Bilateral 7th nerve palsy
  • Bulbar palsy
    • Difficulty in handling secretions leading to aspiration pneumonia
    • A leading cause of death due to pulmonary involvement.
  • Diaphragmatic paralysis
    • Ventilatory support is required in 30% of cases.
    • Increased carbon dioxide levels.

Sensory Symptoms
  • Glove-and-stocking distribution paresthesias
  • Proprioception loss
    • Difficulty in climbing stairs
    • Pain in the neck/arm/shoulder is similar to over-exercised muscle
  • Sensory manifestations can occur before or along with motor manifestations.

Autonomic Symptoms
  • Autonomic dysregulation (e.g., orthostatic hypotension, bladder/bowel sparing/transient involvement)
  • Wide fluctuations of blood pressure, arrhythmias, postural hypotension
  • Reduced heart rate and blood pressure, neurogenic shock.

Multiple sclerosis (Option B): Multiple sclerosis typically presents with asymmetric symptoms and upper motor neuron signs, including hyperreflexia and spasticity, rather than the symmetric flaccid paralysis seen in this case.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Option C): ALS characteristically presents with both upper and lower motor neuron signs, including hyperreflexia, spasticity, and fasciculations, rather than pure flaccid paralysis with areflexia. The presence of both upper and lower motor neuron signs in the same body region is a hallmark of ALS.


Spinal cord injury (Option D): Spinal cord injury typically presents with a distinct sensory level and upper motor neuron signs below the level of injury, including hyperreflexia and spasticity, not the symmetric flaccid paralysis described. The injury pattern is usually asymmetric and depends on the mechanism and level of injury.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principle of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 3501
question: A patient presents with lower symmetric flaccidity and no cord reflex, suggesting which condition?

correctAnswer: B. High anion gap metabolic acidosis
explanationHtml:
Correct Option B - High anion gap metabolic acidosis

  • Calculation of Anion Gap:

    • The anion gap (AG) is calculated using the formula: AG=(Na+−(Cl−+HCO3−)

    • Substituting the values: AG=136−(110+6) = 20

    • The normal range for the anion gap is typically 8-12 mEq/L. An anion gap of 20 indicates a high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis: The calculated anion gap is 20, which is elevated. Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis would have a normal AG (8-12 mEq/L) and would be associated with a compensatory increase in chloride.

Option C - Respiratory acidosis with metabolic alkalosis: The pCO2 is low (13 mmHg), which indicates that the patient is not retaining CO2. This rules out respiratory acidosis. Additionally, the HCO3- is very low, not high, so metabolic alkalosis is not present.

Option D - Respiratory alkalosis with metabolic acidosis: Although the low pCO2 suggests a respiratory alkalosis, the primary disturbance is a metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap. The low HCO3- is indicative of metabolic acidosis rather than a primary respiratory alkalosis.
question: A patient presents with the following laboratory values: pH 7.2, pCO2 13 mmHg, HCO3- 6 mEq/L, Na+ 136 mEq/L, Cl- 110 mEq/L. Which of the following is correct about this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Diarrhea is associated with normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (NAGMA) due to excessive loss of bicarbonate through the gastrointestinal tract.
  • DKA (Diabetic Ketoacidosis), AKI (Acute Kidney Injury), and inborn errors of metabolism are examples of HAGMA, as they involve the accumulation of unmeasured acids in the blood, leading to an increased anion gap.

Common Causes

  • DKA

Normal Anion Gap:

  • Diarrhea

Anion Gap Formula:

Anion Gap = [(Na⁺) - (Cl⁻ + HCO₃⁻)]

  • Na⁺ = Sodium concentration (mEq/L)
  • Cl⁻ = Chloride concentration (mEq/L)
  • HCO₃⁻ = Bicarbonate concentration (mEq/L)

Normal AG: 8–12 mEq/L. AG > 12 indicates high anion gap metabolic acidosis.

  • A high anion gap may indicate metabolic acidosis due to conditions like diabetic ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, or renal failure.
  • A low anion gap can be seen in hypoalbuminemia or the presence of abnormal proteins.

Winter's formula

It is used to estimate the expected compensatory bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) level in metabolic acidosis with a high anion gap (HAGMA).

(Expected bicarbonate (HCO₃⁻) = 24 + (1.5 × anion gap) - 8]

question: All of the following are examples of HAGMA (High Anion Gap Metabolic Acidosis) except

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The laboratory values demonstrate a metabolic acidosis characterized by a low pH with compensatory respiratory changes.

  • The pH of 7.17 is significantly below the normal range (7.35-7.45), indicating acidemia.
  • The decreased HCO3 of 17.4 mEq/L (normal 22-26 mEq/L) suggests a primary metabolic acidosis.
  • The pCO2 of 25.7 mmHg is lower than the normal range (35-45 mmHg), representing appropriate respiratory compensation.
  • The negative base excess of -8.6 further confirms the metabolic acidosis.
  • Additionally, the elevated blood glucose of 334 mg/dL suggests possible diabetic ketoacidosis as the underlying cause.

Metabolic acidosis

Definition
  • Primary decrease in HCO3⁻ or increase in H⁺ ions
  • Characterized by ↓ pH and ↓ HCO3⁻
  • Compensatory mechanism: ↓ PaCO2 through hyperventilation (Kussmaul breathing)

Types

High anion gap (AG > 12 mEq/L)

Normal anion gap (AG 6-12 mEq/L)

Causes

(Mnemonic: MUDPILES)

  • M: Methanol
  • U: Uremia (Renal failure)
  • D: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
  • P: Paraldehyde, Phenformin, Propylene glycol
  • I: Iron tablets, Isoniazid
  • L: Lactic acidosis
  • E: Ethylene glycol
  • S: Salicylates (late phase)

(Mnemonic: HARD UP)

  • H: Hyperalimentation (TPN)
  • A: Acetazolamide
  • R: Renal Tubular Acidosis
  • D: Diarrhea
  • U: Ureteral diversion
  • P: Pancreatic fistula
  • GIT fistulas

Clinical Features

General Features:

  • Lethargy
  • Confusion
  • Fatigue
  • Nausea/vomiting
  • Deep, rapid breathing (Kussmaul)

Specific Features:

  • DKA: Fruity breath, polyuria, polydipsia
  • Uremia: Itching, volume overload
  • Lactic acidosis: Shock, hypotension
  • Toxic ingestion: Visual disturbances (methanol), oxalate crystals (ethylene glycol)

Approach to diagnose Metabolic pH abnormalities

[[figure-1]]

Respiratory Acidosis (Option A) is characterized by elevated pCO2 with normal or elevated HCO3 levels. In this case, the pCO2 is low at 25.7 mmHg, and HCO3 is decreased. Respiratory acidosis typically occurs in conditions like COPD or severe respiratory depression.

Respiratory Alkalosis (Option B) presents with low pCO2 and normal to low HCO3, but the pH would be elevated, not decreased as seen in this case. This condition is often seen in hyperventilation or high altitude exposure.

Metabolic Alkalosis (Option D) shows elevated pH and increased HCO3 levels, which is opposite to the findings in this case where both pH and HCO3 are decreased. Metabolic alkalosis commonly occurs with prolonged vomiting or diuretic use.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles Of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Volume I, Page. 361, 362, 364
question:
What is the diagnosis for the patient with the given ABG analysis report:

pH 7.17

Na= 139.7mEq.L

pCO2 25.7mmHg

K= 5.1mEq.L,

pO2 97mm Hg

Blood glucose 334mg/dL

SatO2 99%

HCO3 at 17.4mEq.L,

BE of -8.6

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Bicarbonate concentration is a calculated value in arterial blood gas analysis, derived using the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation based on measured PCO₂ and pH values.

The equation demonstrates how bicarbonate is formed when carbon dioxide dissolves in water to form carbonic acid, which then dissociates into hydrogen ions and bicarbonate:

PCO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ ⇌ H⁺ + HCO₃⁻

Understanding bicarbonate levels is crucial for assessing acid-base disorders:

  • Elevated HCO₃⁻ occurs in metabolic alkalosis or as compensation in respiratory acidosis
  • Decreased HCO₃⁻ occurs in metabolic acidosis or as compensation in respiratory alkalosis

ABG components include the following:

  • pH = measured acid-base balance of the blood
  • PaO2 = measured the partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood
  • PaCO2 = measured the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in arterial blood
  • HCO3 = calculated concentration of bicarbonate in arterial blood
  • Base excess/deficit = calculated relative excess or deficit of base in arterial blood
  • SaO2 = calculated arterial oxygen saturation (unless a co-oximetry is obtained, in which case it is measured)

pH (Option A) is directly measured in blood gas analysis using ion-selective electrodes that determine hydrogen ion concentration. It is not a calculated value but rather a primary measurement.

PO₂ (Option B) is directly measured using electrodes that detect oxygen partial pressure in the blood sample.

PCO₂ (Option C) is also directly measured, typically using a PCO₂ electrode that measures carbon dioxide partial pressure. Like pH and PO₂, it is a measured rather than calculated value.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles Of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Volume I, Page. 361, 362, 364
question: Which of the following is a derived / calculated value in Arterial Blood Gas analysis?

correctAnswer: A. Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation
explanationHtml:
The correct answer is:

a. Respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation:

  • As pH is 7.12 - Indicating acidosis
  • pCO2 is 50 - indicating Respiratory acidosis
  • HCO3 28 - indication increased renal [HCO3 – ] reabsorption (delayed)

The other options are not correct for the following reasons:

b.Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation - is incorrect

c. Respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation: This would involve a primary respiratory problem (decreased pCO2) with metabolic compensation (decreased HCO3) to partially correct the pH. However, the given ABG values show elevated pCO2 and HCO3, which is not consistent with respiratory alkalosis.

d. Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation: This would involve a primary metabolic problem (elevated HCO3) with respiratory compensation (elevated pCO2) to partially correct the pH. The given ABG values, however, indicate metabolic acidosis rather than metabolic alkalosis.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Relative bradycardia is where a person's pulse rate is lower than expected for their body temperature.
  • Causes include
    • Exotoxin mediated vagal stimulation
    • Cytokines liberated like in COVID 19 that may reset the hypothalamic thermoregulatory center and affect autonomic balance, leading to blunted tachycardic response
    • Subclinical myocarditis

Causes of Relative Bradycardia in Infectious Diseases : mnemonic: BE CAREFUL -These Little Cold Epidemics

  1. Brucellosis
    • Infection with Brucella melitensis leads to relative bradycardia due to inflammatory cytokines and increased vagal tone, despite high fever.
  2. COVID-19
    • Patients may exhibit relative bradycardia associated with myocardial injury and systemic inflammation, showing insufficient heart rate increase despite high fever and hypoxemia.
  3. Typhoid Fever
  4. Legionnaire's Diseasse
  5. Chlamydial Pneumonia
  6. Ebola Hemorrhagic Fever

question: Relative bradycardia is seen in which of the following infections?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Sustained fever is characterized by a continuous elevated temperature that does not fluctuate significantly.
  • It is commonly seen in typhoid fever, where the fever progressively rises in a stepwise manner in intial phase and then shows sustained fever

Features of Sustained or continuous fever

1. Temperature remains above normal throughout the day

2. Fluctuations do not exceed 1°C (or 1.5°F)

3. No return to baseline at any point during the day


Intermittent fever (Option A) is seen in malaria where it returns to normal between the spikes.


Remittent fever (Option B) is where it fluctuates > 1 C but never comes back to normal like in infective endocarditis.


Saddle back (Option C) fever is seen in Dengue fever.

Chest X-ray (Option A): Limited to evaluating respiratory causes and may miss abdominal pathologies.

Blood cultures (Option B) are important for detecting infections but may not identify structural causes of the patient's symptoms.

HIV test (Option D): Relevant for considering infectious etiologies but does not provide immediate insights into potential underlying structural abnormalities.

question: A 55-year-old male presents with a fever of 38.5°C (101.3°F) that has persisted for three weeks. He reports significant weight loss, night sweats, and fatigue. His medical history is unremarkable. On physical examination, he has splenomegaly and cervical lymphadenopathy. Which investigation would be the most appropriate next step in this patient's management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Fever of unknown origin (FUO) is defined as fever ≥38.3°C on multiple occasions lasting >3 weeks without an identified cause despite appropriate evaluation. This patient has prolonged fever with a negative diagnostic workup, fulfilling the criteria for FUO.

  • Common causes of FUO include:
    • Infections: Tuberculosis, infective endocarditis, deep abscesses, HIV.
    • Malignancies: Lymphoma, renal cell carcinoma.
    • Autoimmune/inflammatory disorders: SLE, vasculitis, Still disease, giant cell arteritis.
  • Evaluation of FUO:
    • Baseline tests: CBC, ESR/CRP, LFT/RFT, blood cultures, HIV test, chest X-ray, abdominal ultrasound, urinalysis.
    • Second-line tests: Targeted microbiology, CT/PET imaging, and biopsies.
    • Avoid indiscriminate testing; interpret abnormal findings in clinical context.

[[figure-1]]

Acute bacterial infection (Option B): Acute bacterial infections usually have an identifiable source, positive cultures, or clinical features suggesting a specific infection; persistent fever without an identified cause is more consistent with FUO.

Neutropenic fever (Option C): Neutropenic fever occurs in patients with significant neutropenia, commonly after chemotherapy or immunosuppression; this patient is not immunocompromised.

Drug-induced fever (Option D): Drug fever occurs after exposure to a causative medication and typically resolves after discontinuation; no drug history is provided.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 152.

question: A 30-year-old female presents with a fever of 39°C that has persisted for the past five days. She reports severe muscle pain, nausea, and retroorbital pain. On examination, she has mild dehydration and a negative tourniquet test. Which of the following investigations would be most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Encephalopathy is the most common neurological complication during course of dengue fever.
  • It can be due to brain underperfusion due to shock or bleeeding or multi organ dysfunction.

Dengue complications

Neurological
  • Dengue encephalopathy is most commonly encountered neurological complication of dengue virus
    • linked primarily to dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome
    • EEG may show abnormalities such as burst suppression and seizures
    • CSF profiles typically remain normal.
    • Neuroimaging can be normal or reveal diffuse cerebral edema.

Cardiomyopathy

Dengue virus-induced dilated cardiomyopathy should always be considered if a dengue fever patient has refractory shock and signs and symptoms of congestive heart failure.

Hepatic injury
  • Liver involvement in dengue is a crucial feature
  • The effect ranges from an asymptomatic rise in liver enzymes to the development of ALF
  • The most common atypical manifestation reported was hepatitis

Pneumonia
  • Staphylococcus pneumonia is an important accompanying problem seen in dengue patient
  • co-infection between dengue and influenza can result in exacerbation of pneumonia

Orchitis
  • Orchitis usually occurs together with epididymitis
  • Commonly seen in men between 14 and 35 years of age.




Reference:

Harrison's Principles of internal medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1665.

question: What is the most common neurological complication during the course of dengue fever illness?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Leptospirosis is classically associated with fever + retro-orbital pain + intense myalgia, especially in the calves and lower back.
  • Often occurs after exposure to contaminated water or animals (e.g., farmers, sewage workers).

Dengue (Option A) also presents with retro-orbital pain and fever, but calf pain is not as prominent. Myalgia is generalized and accompanied by rash, thrombocytopenia, and hemoconcentration.

Zika virus (Option C) presents with mild fever, rash, conjunctivitis, and joint pain — retro-orbital pain is rare, and severe calf pain is not a feature.

Typhoid fever (Option D) causes step-ladder fever, abdominal symptoms, and relative bradycardia, but no retro-orbital pain or focal calf tenderness.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of internal medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1442.

On examination, he has flaccid paralysis and absent deep tendon reflexes in the affected limbs. CSF analysis shows cytoalbuminological dissociation. NCV test confirms a demyelinating pattern. Which diagnostic criteria are used to diagnose this presentation?

correctAnswer: B. Airborne transmission from an infected individual
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This patient with HIV and a low CD4+ count (150 cells/mm³), fever, dry cough, and bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest X-ray likely has Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia .
  • PJP is a common opportunistic infection in immunocompromised individuals and iit s primarily transmitted via airborne spread from person to person.
  • The organism is inhaled, leading to infection in the lungs, especially when immune defenses are weakened.

Primary infection acquired from a contaminated water source (Option A): Pneumocystis jirovecii is not transmitted through water sources.


Ingestion of fungal spores from environmental reservoirs (Option C): There is no evidence suggesting transmission through ingestion of spores.


Reactivation of a previously dormant infection acquired during childhood (Option D): Partially correct but not the best answer. Although reactivation can occur, the question hints at new infection rather than reactivation.

question: A 40-year-old HIV-positive patient presents with fever, dry cough, and progressive shortness of breath. His CD4+ count is 150 cells/mm³. Chest X-ray shows bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of infection in this patient?

correctAnswer: D. Cultured on Sabaroud dextrose agar
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Pneumocystis jirovecii cannot be cultured using conventional laboratory culture methods.
  • Hence Beta 1,3 D glucan, BAL staining with Gomori-methamine stain where the cyst wall is stained black.
  • Due to intersttial pneumonia, Alveolar gradient is increased.
  • During treatment cotrimoaxazole is used.
  • But during treatment the release of inflammatory cytokines can lead to ARDS. Hence steroids are co-administered if PaO₂ < 70 mmHg or A–a gradient > 35 mmHg.

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1731, 1732.

question: A 35 year old truck driver with AIDS is having CD4 count of 150 cells/ cu.mm. He has sulfa drug allergy. Which of the following drugs can be used in this patient by nebulization route for prevention of this opportunisticinfection?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • This patient has a history of disseminated MAC, so he requires secondary prophylaxis (maintenance therapy).
  • Standard regimen = macrolide (clarithromycin/azithromycin) + ethambutol.
  • Prevents relapse of MAC and is continued until CD4 >100 for ≥3 months on ART.

Azithromycin monotherapy (Option A):

  • Used for primary prophylaxis when CD4 <50 without prior MAC.
  • Not adequate after previous infection → risk of relapse

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (Option B):

  • Used for PCP and toxoplasmosis prophylaxis, not MAC

Isoniazid + pyridoxine (Option D):

  • Used for latent tuberculosis prophylaxis, no role in MAC prevention.

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1597.

He is compliant with antiretroviral therapy (ART) and has a CD4+ count of 46 cells/μL. Which prophylactic therapy is recommended in this patient to prevent Mycobacterium avium complex?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option C - Oral candidiasis:

  • Oral Candidiasis is the likely diagnosis in these patients. In patients with HIV, there is decrease in the number of T cells making them more susceptible to infections with such agents.

Incorrect Options:

The patient has significant hypoxia with SpO₂ 92% and underlying cardiac disease (triple vessel disease). A non-rebreathing mask can deliver high-concentration oxygen (up to ~90% FiO₂) and is preferred in this setting to rapidly correct hypoxemia.


Nasal cannula and flow rate of 6L/min (Option B) provides low-flow oxygen, which may be insufficient for this patient.

question: A 55-year-old man with triple vessel disease presents with a persistent cough, fever, and shortness of breath. On admission he has respiratory rate 26 /minute and an sp02 92% on room air. His RT-PCR for SARS-COV2 is positive. What is the preferred oxygen delivery device for this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation and positive RT-PCR result confirm the diagnosis of COVID-19, characterised by an elevated neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR).


Laboratory findings of COVID-19:

Elevated Parameters

  • Inflammatory markers (interleukin 6, tumour necrosis factor α, ferritin, C-reactive protein) (Option B)
  • NLR (neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio) >6 (Option D)

  • D-dimer assay (Option A)

  • Liver enzymes and lactate dehydrogenase
  • Creatine phosphokinase

Reduced parameters

question: A 60-year-old woman with obesity and hypertension presents with a cough, fever and shortness of breath for the past four days. Her SpO2 is 90% on room air and her respiratory rate is 34/min. Her RT-PCR for SARS COV2 is positive. Which of the following is correct about laboratory findings seen in this case?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The patient's symptoms of persistent cough, fever, shortness of breath, and recent exposure to a family gathering raise suspicion of a viral respiratory infection, particularly COVID-19.
  • The above x-ray shows bilateral, peripheral, non-lobar ground glass opacities (hazy, grey areas)
  • RT-PCR (Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction) is the standard method for confirming the diagnosis of COVID-19 due to its high sensitivity and specificity.

HRCT chest (Option A) can show lung involvement but is not diagnostic.

C-reactive protein (Option B) is a non-specific inflammatory marker and cannot confirm infection.

Rapid antigen test (Option D) is less sensitive than RT-PCR, especially in early or mild disease.

question: A 55-year-old man with a history of asthma presents with a persistent cough, fever, and shortness of breath that started three days ago after attending a family gathering. His examination shows a SpO2 of 92% on room air and a respiratory rate of 26 breaths per minute, with the accompanying X-ray. What is the investigation of choice for this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Cystoisospora belli is a coccidian parasite that causes prolonged, watery diarrhea in immunocompromised individuals, especially AIDS patients with CD4 < 100.
  • Oocysts are large (20–30 microns), oval, and demonstrate acid-fast positivity (pink to red) on modified Kinyoun stain.
  • TMP-SMX is the first-line treatment and also used for secondary prophylaxis.

Metronidazole (Option A) is not effective against coccidia.

Nitazoxanide (Option B) is used in Cryptosporidiosis, not preferred here.

Albendazole (Option D) has no role against Cystoisospora.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1806.
question: A 35-year-old HIV-positive man with a CD4 count of 80 cells/mm³ presents with chronic watery diarrhea and significant weight loss. Stool examination reveals oval-shaped oocysts measuring 20–30 microns, which appear pink to red on modified Kinyoun stain, showing a characteristic sporoblast. Which of the following is the best treatment?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) esophagitis in immunocompromised patients presents with acute odynophagia, retrosternal pain, and well-circumscribed “volcano-like” ulcers, typically in the mid-to-distal esophagus.

Cytomegalovirus esophagitis (Option A) usually causes linear or longitudinal ulcers, not discrete “volcano-like” lesions.

Candida esophagitis (Option C) presents with white plaques and pseudomembranes, not well-circumscribed ulcers.

ART-induced esophagitis (Option D) is rare and usually manifests as mild irritation or inflammation, not characteristic ulcers.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1500.
question: A 36-year-old man with AIDS with CD4 count of 74 cells/μL presents with acute onset of odynophagia and retrosternal chest pain. Upper GI endoscopy reveals well-circumscribed, "volcano-like" ulcers in the mid-esophagus. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV should be started as early as possible preferably within 2 hours. It is not effective after 72 hours.
  • Drugs used are tenofovir, lamivudine and dolutregavir for 4 weeks.
  • Waiting for test results or seroconversion is incorrect and delays treatment.

Within 24 hours (Option B): Acceptable if <72 hrs, but not ideal; efficacy decreases as time passes.

Within 48 hours (Option C): Still allowed, but significantly less effective than initiation within 2 hrs.

After 72 hours (Option D): Not recommended; PEP is ineffective beyond this window.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1625.

question: A medical intern sustains a needle-stick injury from a known HIV-positive patient. What is the ideal time frame to initiate post-exposure prophylaxis for maximum efficacy?

correctAnswer: A. Continue till CD4 count &gt; 100 cells for one year and HIV RNA suppressed for &gt;3 months
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Fluconazole maintenance (secondary prophylaxis) in cryptococcal meningitis is continued until immune reconstitution with ART occurs.
  • It can be safely stopped when CD4 count rises >100 cells/µL and remains so for ≥1 year, along with sustained viral suppression for ≥3 months.
  • This indicates that the patient’s immunity is strong enough to prevent relapse.
  • Higher CD4 thresholds (like 200) are not required for cryptococcal infection.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1706, 1607.

question: You have started fluconazole for secondary prevention of cryptococcus neoformans meningitis. Which of the following is correct statement about it?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Tenofovir (in both its formulations, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate [TDF] or tenofovir alafenamide [TAF]) is effective against both HIV and HBV.
  • HIV uses reverse transcriptase to convert its RNA into proviral DNA.
  • Tenofovir inhibits this enzyme ➜ prevents integration into host genome ➜ stops replication.

Efavirenz (Option A), Abacavir (Option C), Ritonavir (Option D) is active against HIV only.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1616.
question: Which of the following drugs is effective against both HIV and hepatitis B?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Dolutegravir is a recommended first-line regimen for the treatment of HIV.
  • Drug classes:
    • Tenofovir & Lamivudine → NRTIs
    • Dolutegravir → INSTI
  • Advantages: Fixed-dose combination simplifies therapy, reduces cost, and improves adherence
  • Effective and well-tolerated in adults, adolescents, and HIV/TB co-infected patients

Zidovudine + Lamivudine + Raltegravir (Option A) is the first line regimen for HIV-positive neonates as this combination has shown effectiveness in rapidly suppressing viral load in infants and neonates.

Abacavir + Lamivudine + Lopinavir (Option B) is generally not used as the first-line therapy for HIV infection. Moreover, Abacavir requires HLA-B*5701 testing due to the risk of hypersensitivity reactions, which can be severe and potentially life-threatening.

Tenofovir + Lamivudine + Efavirenz (Option C) was previously recommended as the first-line therapy for HIV. However, according to the 2018 recommendations, efavirenz was replaced by Dolutegravir.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1616.
question: A 38 -year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV. He is asymptomatic with a CD4 count of 650 cells/mm³. Based on WHO recommendations, which of the following combinations would be best suited for treatment of this case?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • HRCT chest in an immunocompromised patient shows an air crescent sign (right lung) and Halo sign (posterior segment of the left lower lobe, abutting the vertebral body) seen in Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.
  • Galactomannan antigen test on BAL is a sensitive and specific biomarker for diagnosing invasive aspergillosis.
  • It detects a polysaccharide component of the Aspergillus cell wall that is released during active infection.

Histopathology (Option A): Shows septate hyphae branching at 45°, but biopsy yield is low (10–30%) and often difficult in unstable patients.

[[figure-1]]


BACTEC MGIT 960 (Option B): Designed for mycobacterial culture, not fungal infections.

Beta-1,3-D-glucan (Option D): Positive in many fungal infections (Candida, Pneumocystis, Fusarium), so it lacks specificity for Aspergillus.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1716.

question: A 55-year-old immunocompromised patient presents with fever, cough, and respiratory distress. CT chest is perfomed. Which of the following investigations would be most specific to confirm the diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In AIDS patients with CD4 counts >200 cells/mm³, community-acquired bacterial pneumonia—most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae—is the typical opportunistic infection, presenting with fever, productive cough, and lobar consolidation with air bronchograms on CXR.

Mycobacterium avium intracellulare (Option B) usually occurs at CD4 <50 cells/mm³ and presents with disseminated disease rather than lobar pneumonia.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Option C) can occur at any CD4 count but typically shows upper-lobe infiltrates and cavitation.

Pneumocystis jirovecii (Option D) generally occurs at CD4 <200 cells/mm³ and presents with diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates, not lobar consolidation.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1995, 1996.
question: AIDS Patient is having a CD4 count of 200 cells/cu.mm. He has had fever, cough and shortness of breath for the past week. Auscultation reveals scattered bronchial breathing in the left infra-axillary and infrascapular areas. CXR reveals air bronchograms in the left lower lobe. Which opportunistic infection is present in this patient?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Cryptococcal meningitis in AIDS patients can be rapidly confirmed with the CSF lateral flow assay, which detects cryptococcal antigen with high sensitivity and specificity.

  • Sensitivity and Specificity: It has a sensitivity and specificity approaching 100%, even in cases with a low fungal load.

  • Early Detection: It can detect the capsular polysaccharide antigen much earlier and more reliably than microscopy.

  • Speed: It provides results in about 10 minutes.


Gram staining (Option B): Gram staining is generally poor for diagnosing fungal infections. While Cryptococcus is a "Gram-positive" budding yeast, it is often missed or misinterpreted on a standard Gram stain.

  • It is much better suited for bacterial meningitis (e.g., Streptococcus pneumoniae).


India ink preparation (Option C): This is the classic for identifying the thick polysaccharide capsule. However:

  • Sensitivity is low: It only identifies the fungus in about 60–80% of HIV-positive patients and is even less sensitive in HIV-negative patients.

  • User-dependent: It requires a skilled microscopist to distinguish the yeast from white blood cells or artifacts.


Staining with mucicarmine (Option D): Mucicarmine stain is used to highlight the thick polysaccharide capsule of Cryptococcus in bright red. However, this is primarily a histopathology stain used on tissue biopsies (like the "soap bubble" brain lesions or lung tissue).

  • It is not the standard or most accurate way to confirm a diagnosis from a CSF sample compared to antigen testing.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1606, 1705.
question: A truck driver with AIDS is brought in with fever and altered mental status. His family reports a week-long history of worsening headache, fever, projectile vomiting, and confusion. Neuroimaging shows a soapy bubble appearance, and CSF shows 50 lymphocytes/cu.mm with low sugar and a mild increase in protein. Which of the following is the most accurate test for confirmation of the diagnosis of this condition?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • PCR HIV DNA is the most appropriate test for diagnosing HIV in infants <18 months because it detects proviral DNA directly in infected cells.
  • It is reliable even in the neonatal period and unaffected by maternal antibodies.
  • This makes it the preferred early infant diagnostic tool.

PCR HIV RNA (Option A) can detect viral RNA but is less commonly used as the first-line test in neonates.

Serum ELISA for HIV (Option C) is unreliable in infants <18 months due to maternal antibody interference.

p24 antigen (Option D) may be detectable, but sensitivity is lower compared to HIV DNA PCR in neonates.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1589.
question: A 3-week-old infant born to an HIV-positive mother is brought to OPD. The baby was delivered vaginally and was not breastfed. The mother has been on antiretroviral therapy throughout pregnancy. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to diagnose HIV infection in this neonate?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

HIV RNA PCR can detect viral RNA within 10–12 days post-exposure, allowing early detection of acute HIV infection.

Western Blot (Option B) is used to confirm HIV infection after antibodies have developed, usually 4–6 weeks post-exposure.

HIV PCR DNA (Option C) detects proviral DNA integrated into host cells and is less useful for very early detection.

ELISA for HIV-1 and HIV-2 (Option D) detects antibodies, which may not be present during the early “window period” after exposure.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1589, 1590.
question: A 28-year-old lab technician presents 10 days after sustaining a needle-stick injury while drawing blood from an HIV-positive patient. He did not receive post-exposure prophylaxis He is currently asymptomatic and anxious about possible seroconversion. Which of the following test will help in early detection of possible transmission of infection?

correctAnswer: A. ELISA positive for HIV plus any WHO clinical stage 4 condition that includes AIDS-defining illnesses
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

According to the World Health Organization (WHO):

AIDS is diagnosed in an HIV-positive individual when they have either:

  • A CD4+ T-cell count <200 cells/μL, OR
  • Any WHO clinical stage 4 condition, which includes AIDS-defining illnesses (e.g., Pneumocystis pneumonia, cryptococcal meningitis, Kaposi sarcoma, esophageal candidiasis, etc.)



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1557.

question: Which is correct about definiton of AIDS?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • HIV attaches to CD4⁺ T-cells using its gp120 envelope glycoprotein, which binds to the CD4 receptor.
  • After gp120 binds CD4, it undergoes a conformational change that allows interaction with a co-receptor (CCR5 or CXCR4) and then triggers membrane fusion mediated by gp41.
  • This patient’s CD4 count of 150, recurrent infections, and candidiasis strongly suggest advanced HIV infection.



CCR5 (Option A) acts as a co-receptor that allows fusion and viral entry after gp120 binds to CD4.




gp41 (Option B) mediates fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane after gp120-CD4 interaction.


p17 (Option C) is a matrix protein that helps maintain the structure of the virion but is not involved in attachment.

[[figure-1]]

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1557, 1560.
question: A 53-year-old man visits the clinic with recurring respiratory infections and oral candidiasis. Lab tests show a CD4 count of 150 cells/mm³, raising suspicion for HIV. Which structure allows the HIV virus to attach to CD4 cells initially?

correctAnswer: D. Viral transmission does not occur in the first trimester.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Vertical transmission of HIV can occur during any stage of pregnancy, including the first trimester, at delivery, or through breastfeeding.

ART has greatly reduced the risk of transmission (Option A) in recent times, combined with cesarean delivery, which has made mother-to-child transmission of HIV extremely low.

Transmission can occur through breast milk (Option B): HIV transmission can happen from the affected mother to the child from the first trimester of pregnancy, during delivery and breastfeeding.

Prolonged membrane rupture increases transmission risk (Option C): Amniotic sac is no longer intact, and the baby is directly exposed to maternal vaginal and cervical secretions, which may contain high levels of HIV.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1565.

Explanation:

The most appropriate initial treatment strategy for an asthmatic patient diagnosed with ABPA is Itraconazole combined with low-dose corticosteroids. Steroids are given as this disease is a hypersensitivity reaction to colonization of the airways with Aspergillus fumigatus. In contrast, invasive pulmonary aspergilloma is treated with voriconazole.


Invasive Pulmonary Aspergilloma occurs in immunocompromised hosts (e.g. neutropenic, transplant, prolonged steroids). It is a tissue-invasive infection and not a hypersensitivity.


Voriconazole (Option A): Voriconazole is the gold standard for Invasive Aspergillosis.

  • However, for ABPA (which is an allergic/hypersensitivity condition, not an invasive one), it is generally reserved as a second-line or salvage therapy if the patient cannot tolerate Itraconazole or if the disease is refractory. It is not the "initial" strategy.

Fluconazole with corticosteroids (Option C) is ineffective against Aspergillus species as it primarily targets yeasts like Candida by inhibiting ergosterol synthesis.


Posaconazole (Option D: Posaconazole is a potent, broad-spectrum antifungal. Similar to Voriconazole, it is typically used for prophylaxis in severely immunocompromised patients or as a later-line treatment for ABPA when first-line therapies fail.



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1717.
question: A 30-year-old asthmatic patient presents with worsening respiratory symptoms and is diagnosed with Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis . Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment strategy?

correctAnswer: D. Halo sign on HRCT chest
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The halo sign is seen with invasive pulmonary aspergilloma and not in ABPA. Both are different diseases, with ABPA being hypersensitivity to Aspergillus fumigatus and characterized by central bronchiectasis.

Imaging findings of Allergic Bronchopulmonary Aspergillosis (ABPA)

  • Presence of hyper-attenuated mucus in airways is highly specific (Option C)
  • Proximal /Central Bronchiectasis
  • Tram track appearance in CT d/t bronchiectasis
  • X-ray:
    • Cylindrical & proximal bronchiectasis with thickening of the bronchial wall (Tree in bud appearance)
    • Mucous impaction in dilated bronchi (Finger-in-glove appearance)
    • HRCT: Central bronchiectasis (Option B) and bronchial wall thickening with atelectatic areas.

Elevated specific and total serum IgE levels (>1000 IU/mL) (Option A) is seen in ABPA



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1715, 1716.

question: Which of the following findings is not seen with allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • SARS-CoV-2 spike (S) protein binds to the ACE2 receptor
  • ACE2 is expressed in:
    • Type II pneumocytes (lungs)
    • Heart, kidneys, intestine

This interaction is facilitated by the host protease TMPRSS2, which primes the Spike protein to allow fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane.

Receptor Utilisation Pointers:

  • ACE2: The primary receptor for SARS-CoV, SARS-CoV-2, and NL63.
  • Tissue Expression: ACE2 is highly expressed in the lower respiratory tract (Type II pneumocytes), as well as in the heart, kidneys, and gastrointestinal tract.
  • Pathogenesis: Viral binding to ACE2 not only facilitates entry but also downregulates ACE2 activity, contributing to the pulmonary inflammation and vascular dysfunction characteristic of severe COVID-19.

[[figure-1]]


Aminopeptidase N (CD13) (Option A) serves as the receptor for certain other coronaviruses, notably HCoV-229E.

CD4 receptor (Option C) is the primary receptor for HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus).

Sialic acid receptors (Option D) are the primary receptors utilised by Influenza viruses for cellular attachment.



Reference:
  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3167.
  • Jawetz, Melnick, & Adelberg’s Medical Microbiology, 28th edition, Page 617.
question: A 65-year-old man with comorbidities develops fever, dry cough, and hypoxia. Imaging shows bilateral peripheral infiltrates suggestive of viral pneumonia due to SARS-CoV-2. Which host receptor is primarily utilised by this virus for cellular entry?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In the management of COVID-19, patients are triaged into Mild, Moderate, or Severe categories to determine the appropriate level of care. An elderly patient presenting to the casualty with chest pain requires immediate risk stratification.

According to clinical management protocols (such as those from the WHO and Ministry of Health):

  • Respiratory rate > 24/min (Statement 1): A normal adult respiratory rate is 12-20 breaths per minute. A rate above 24 indicates respiratory distress and categorises the patient as having Moderate disease.
  • SpO2 between 90% to 93% (Statement 2): A drop of saturation into the 90-93% range on room air is a hallmark of Moderate COVID-19 and necessitates admission for oxygen therapy and monitoring.
  • Chest Pain (Statement 3): In a 60-year-old COVID-positive patient, chest pain is a "red flag." It could indicate COVID-associated pneumonia, a pulmonary embolism (due to the pro-thrombotic nature of the virus), or an acute myocardial infarction. This necessitates an inpatient workup (ECG, Troponin, Imaging).

Hypertension (Statement 4): While hypertension is a comorbidity that increases the risk of severe disease, stable hypertension alone is not an admission criterion. If the blood pressure is controlled and there are no acute symptoms, the patient could technically be monitored at home if their COVID symptoms were mild.

Age (Statement 5): Similarly, being 60 years old is a risk factor for poor outcomes, but age alone does not dictate admission to a Health Centre. An asymptomatic 60-year-old can often be managed with home isolation.



Reference:
  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1542.
  • https://covid19dashboard.mohfw.gov.in/pdf/RevisedNationalClinicalManagementGuidelineforCOVID1931032020.pdf
question:
You are posted as an intern in casualty. An elderly 60-year-old man is brought to you with complaints of chest pain. He has tested positive for COVID-19. Which of the following clinical features will prompt you to get this patient admitted to a dedicated COVID Health Centre?

  1. Respiratory rate > 24/min
  2. SpO2 between 90% to 93% on room air
  3. Chest pain
  4. Hypertension
  5. Age

correctAnswer: C. Diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Severe COVID-19 pneumonia is characterised by a massive inflammatory response leading to severe respiratory failure. The pathognomonic histopathological finding in the lungs of fatal cases is Diffuse Alveolar Damage.

  • Acute Phase: The alveolar spaces are filled with oedema, fibrin, and inflammatory cells.
  • Hyaline Membranes: The formation of eosinophilic hyaline membranes along the alveolar walls, resulting from the injury to Type II pneumocytes and subsequent plasma protein leakage, is the hallmark of DAD (also seen in Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome - ARDS).
  • Chronic Phase: Progression to proliferative changes, including alveolar epithelial hyperplasia and organisation/fibrosis.

[[figure-1]]

Diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes & lymphocytic infiltrates.

Lobar consolidation (Option A) is typical of acute pyogenic bacterial pneumonia.

Interstitial fibrosis with granuloma formation (Option B) is a hallmark of granulomatous diseases like tuberculosis or sarcoidosis.

Cavitary necrosis (Option D) is indicative of necrotising processes such as advanced tuberculosis, lung abscesses, or fungal infections like mucormycosis.



Reference:
  • Robins Basic Pathology, 10th edition, Page 353.
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7758785/

options.text: Diffuse alveolar damage with hyaline membranes

question: Histopathological examination of lung tissue obtained from a fatal case of COVID-19 most frequently demonstrates which of the following findings?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of acute dyspnea combined with characteristic radiological findings is highly suggestive of COVID-19 pneumonia.
  • SARS-CoV-2 pneumonitis classically manifests on CT imaging as peripheral, bilateral, multi-lobar ground-glass opacities. While GGOs can be seen in other viral pneumonias, the peripheral, subpleural distribution is seen in COVID-19 infection.

[[figure-1]]

CT chest showing patches of GGO.

Pulmonary tuberculosis (Option A) presents with cavitary lesions, apical consolidations, or miliary patterns rather than peripheral GGOs.

Bacterial pneumonia (Option B) commonly manifests as lobar consolidation, air bronchograms, and localised, dense opacities.

Pulmonary mucormycosis (Option D) is an angioinvasive fungal infection that presents with nodular opacities, the reverse halo sign, and massive tissue necrosis, especially in immunocompromised hosts.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 1540, 1541.
question: A 40-year-old patient presents with acute-onset breathlessness and mild hemoptysis. A CT chest scan reveals localised ground-glass opacity in the peripheral regions of the lungs. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

correctAnswer: C. An adult with a past history of treated malaria
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • COVID-19 severity is strongly correlated with underlying comorbidities that compromise immune function or reserve physiological capacity.
  • Clinical triage prioritises patients with high-risk conditions, such as chronic kidney disease (hemodialysis), immunocompromised states (post-transplant, immunosuppressive therapy), and advanced age (≥65 years).
  • A remote, successfully treated history of malaria, in the absence of current health complications, does not confer a heightened risk for severe COVID-19.

Risk Factors for Severe Disease:

  • Comorbidities: Chronic kidney disease (hemodialysis), cardiovascular disease, obesity, diabetes, and cancer.
  • Immunocompromise: Post-transplant patients or those receiving long-term immunosuppressive therapy. (Options A & B ruled out)
  • Advanced Age: Age ≥65 is one of the strongest independent risk factors for severe outcomes and mortality. (Option D ruled out)


Reference:

https://covid19dashboard.mohfw.gov.in/pdf/RevisedNationalClinicalManagementGuidelineforCOVID1931032020.pdf

question: During the triage of patients presenting with SARS-CoV-2 infection, which of the following individuals would be considered at relatively lower risk for developing severe disease?

correctAnswer: D. Sharing the same general environment but without high-risk exposure
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Low-risk contact includes being in the same area but without close, prolonged, or direct exposure. No direct contact with respiratory secretions
  • Risk stratification for COVID-19 is determined by the nature of the contact, duration, and the presence of personal protective equipment (PPE). Public health protocols categorise these to guide testing and quarantine requirements.

Risk Stratification Table:

Risk Level

Exposure Criteria

High-Risk
  • Touched body fluids.
  • Direct contact during the exam without PPE. (Option B ruled out)
