question: Which of the following exposures would be considered a low-risk contact for acquiring COVID-19?

correctAnswer: D. An asymptomatic individual with a positive rapid antigen test
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Public health case definitions differentiate between probable and confirmed cases for surveillance purposes.

  • Probable case: Relies on clinical, radiological, or epidemiological evidence.
  • Confirmed case: Defined by definitive laboratory evidence.

Case Classification Criteria:

  • Probable Case:
    • A patient who meets clinical criteria and is a contact of a probable/confirmed case or linked to a COVID-19 cluster. (Option C ruled out)
    • A suspect case with chest imaging showing findings suggestive of COVID-19 disease. (Option B ruled out)
    • A person with a recent onset of anosmia or ageusia in the absence of any other identified cause. (Option A ruled out)
    • Death, not otherwise explained, in an adult with respiratory distress who was a contact of a probable/confirmed case or linked to a COVID-19 cluster.
  • Confirmed Case:
    • A person with a positive Nucleic Acid Amplification Test, including RT-PCR or similar approved tests.
    • A person with a positive COVID-19 rapid antigen test who meets either the probable case definition or suspect criteria.
    • An asymptomatic person with a positive COVID-19 rapid antigen test who is a contact of a probable or confirmed case.


Reference:
  • https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8714223/
  • https://covid19dashboard.mohfw.gov.in/pdf/RevisedNationalClinicalManagementGuidelineforCOVID1931032020.pdf

question: Based on standardised public health case definitions, which of the following individuals would not meet the criteria for a probable case of COVID-19?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Seizures are not a characteristic symptom of COVID-19 and are not included in standard screening protocols; their presence should trigger an evaluation for other neurological or metabolic pathologies.
  • COVID-19 screening criteria are designed to identify individuals with an acute viral syndrome. While SARS-CoV-2 has diverse clinical manifestations ranging from acute respiratory illness to chronic long COVID and neuropsychiatric sequelae, the screening criteria focus on symptoms most indicative of active, transmissible infection.

Clinical Features of COVID-19:

  • Acute Symptoms: Cough, fever, myalgia, headache, dyspnea, sore throat, and gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea). (Option A ruled out)
  • Sensory Changes: Sudden onset of dysgeusia and anosmia (loss of taste and smell) occurs in a substantial number of cases. (Option B ruled out)
  • Mental Health & Cognitive Status:
    • Older individuals may experience a general decline in health status, including the onset or worsening of dementia.
    • Mental health consequences, including fatigue, depression, social anxiety, sleep disturbances, and cognitive deficits, are common during the acute phase and throughout the Long COVID period. (Option C ruled out)
  • Long COVID: A chronic condition (at least 3 months post-infection) characterised by varied symptoms, including pain syndromes, neuropsychiatric disorders, and increased suicidal ideation.


Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1541.
question: In the clinical screening criteria used to identify suspected COVID-19 cases in a community or hospital setting, which of the following findings is not typically included

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The global spread pattern of COVID-19, characterised by ongoing person-to-person transmission across multiple generations of cases, is best classified as a propagated epidemic.

A propagated epidemic is characterised by:

  • Person-to-person transmission
  • Occurrence of cases in successive waves (generations)
  • Gradual rise and fall of cases over time

This pattern fits the global spread of COVID-19, where infection spreads through continuous human-to-human transmission.

Continuous common source epidemic (Option A): Exposure to a single continuous source (e.g., contaminated water supply). Not person-to-person spread.

Intermittent common source epidemic (Option B): Exposure occurs at irregular intervals from the same source

Explosive point-source (Option D): A type of common source epidemic where all exposures occur at the same time and place (e.g., a single foodborne outbreak), leading to a rapid, sharp peak in cases.



Reference:

Park’s Textbook of Preventive and Social Medicine, 27th edition, Page 73.
question: The global spread pattern of COVID-19, characterised by ongoing person-to-person transmission across multiple generations of cases, is best classified as which type of epidemic?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The incubation period of COVID-19 is the time elapsed between exposure to the virus and the development of symptoms. Epidemiological data confirm that the vast majority of individuals who become infected will manifest symptoms within a 14-day window.

  • Median incubation: Typically 4 to 5 days.
  • 14-day window: Used globally for public health surveillance and quarantine protocols, as the risk of symptom onset after 14 days is statistically negligible.


Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 1541.

explanationHtml:

  • SARS-CoV-2 is primarily a respiratory pathogen. Transmission occurs mainly through the inhalation of respiratory droplets and aerosols, or through direct contact with mucosal surfaces (fomites).
  • While viremia can occur during the systemic phase of COVID-19, there is no evidence that SARS-CoV-2 is transfusion-transmitted. Blood donation screening and the storage process further mitigate any theoretical risk. Unlike Hepatitis B or HIV, respiratory viruses have not demonstrated potential for transmission via transfusion of blood components.

Transmission of COVID:

  • Droplets/Aerosols: The primary mode; transmission is most efficient in crowded, poorly ventilated indoor settings. (Options A and C ruled out)

question: During a discussion on the transmission dynamics of SARS-CoV-2, which of the following exposure situations is least likely to result in a new infection?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Label 1 represents the Spike (S) glycoprotein. This surface protein is the critical determinant of viral tropism, host specificity, and entry efficiency. It mediates these functions by binding specifically to host cell surface receptors (such as ACE2 for SARS-CoV-2) and facilitating the fusion of the viral envelope with the host cell membrane.

Structural Pointers for Coronavirus: Coronaviruses are characterised by large, club-shaped projections on their surface, giving them a crown-like (corona) appearance.

  • Spike (S) protein (1): The primary mediator of viral attachment and entry into host cells. Variability in the S protein is the primary driver of host-range expansion and species jumping.
  • Envelope (E) protein (2): Involved in viral assembly and maturation.
  • Membrane (M) protein (3): The most abundant envelope protein, crucial for defining the shape of the viral envelope and for budding.
  • Nucleocapsid (N) protein (4): Binds to the viral RNA genome to form the helical nucleocapsid, playing a key role in viral RNA synthesis and replication.

[[figure-1]]

  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Page 3167.

question: Based on the structural biology of SARS-CoV-2, which numbered structure is responsible for determining viral host specificity and the efficiency of cell entry?

Explanation:

For a proper nasopharyngeal swab, the patient’s head should be tilted back about 70°.
Proper specimen collection is critical for the sensitivity of COVID-19 diagnostic tests. The goal is to obtain epithelial cells from the posterior nasopharynx or oropharynx while maintaining stringent infection control standards to protect the healthcare worker.

Guidelines for Respiratory Specimen Collection:

  • Optimal Positioning: For both oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal swabs, the patient’s head should be tilted back approximately 70 degrees. This angle aligns the nasal passage and pharyngeal anatomy to provide a clear, direct path to the posterior pharyngeal wall or nasopharynx.
  • Swab Requirements: Use only synthetic fibre swabs with plastic shafts. Do not use calcium alginate swabs or swabs with wooden shafts, as these can inhibit PCR testing or reduce viral recovery.
  • Technique:
    • Nasopharyngeal: Insert the swab through the nares parallel to the palate. Advance until resistance is met at the nasopharyngeal wall, rub/roll the swab, and leave in place for several seconds.

  • Transportation: Specimens must be placed immediately into sterile tubes containing 2-3 mL of Viral Transport Media (VTM) and transported on ice.

  • C-Reactive Protein (CRP) is a key inflammatory marker used in COVID-19 management. It is an acute-phase reactant produced by the liver in response to IL-6. Its levels rise significantly in proportion to the severity of the infection and the extent of pulmonary involvement.

Inflammatory markers associated with increased severity of COVID-19 are:

  • PCT (procalcitonin test)
  • ESR
  • WBC
  • LMR (lymphocyte/mean platelet volume ratio)
  • HsCRP (high-sensitivity C-reactive protein)
  • NLR (neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio)

Low-Density Lipoprotein (LDL) (Option B): LDL is a lipid profile parameter. While cholesterol levels may fluctuate during acute illness, LDL is not used as a primary marker to monitor the inflammatory status of a COVID-19 patient.

Serum Creatinine (Option C): Serum creatinine is a marker of renal function. While COVID-19 can cause acute kidney injury (AKI), creatinine is not a specific marker for the systemic inflammatory "cytokine storm."

Alanine Aminotransferase (ALT) (Option D): ALT is a marker of hepatocellular injury. Although elevated ALT is commonly seen in COVID-19, it specifically indicates liver involvement rather than being the primary marker for general systemic inflammation.

question: Among the inflammatory markers used to monitor the severity of COVID-19, which of the following is an acute-phase reactant that typically correlates with the degree of lung involvement and systemic inflammation?

correctAnswer: C. Elevated D-dimer and Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • In COVID-19, high levels of D-dimer and Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH) are strongly associated with severe disease and higher mortality. Elevated D-dimer indicates a hypercoagulable state and a high risk of thromboembolic complications, while high LDH levels reflect extensive tissue damage and systemic inflammation.

Increased levels of the following laboratory markers are associated with poorer outcomes:

  • D-dimer
  • C-reactive protein
  • Lactate dehydrogenase
  • Cardiac troponin
  • Ferritin
  • Creatinine phosphokinase

Elevated Absolute Lymphocyte Count (ALC) (Option A): In COVID-19, lymphopenia (decreased ALC) is the classic finding associated with poor prognosis. An elevated ALC (lymphocytosis) is rarely seen in this infection.

Decreased Serum Ferritin levels (Option B): Serum ferritin is an acute-phase reactant. In severe COVID-19, ferritin levels are typically significantly elevated (hyperferritinemia) as part of the cytokine storm, not decreased.

Shortened Prothrombin Time (PT) (Option D): Patients with severe COVID-19 usually demonstrate a prolonged Prothrombin Time (PT) and activated Partial Thromboplastin Time (aPTT), reflecting a state of coagulopathy.



Reference:
  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 1541, 1542.
  • https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33223833/
question: Which of the following laboratory parameters is considered a reliable marker of poor prognosis and severe disease progression in a patient with COVID-19?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

In COVID-19, lymphocytosis (an increase in lymphocyte count) is very rare. On the contrary, lymphopenia - a decrease in lymphocyte count is a hallmark of the disease (Option A ruled out), and its severity often correlates with a poorer prognosis.

Common laboratory abnormalities seen in COVID-19 are:

  • Lymphopenia.
  • Mild thrombocytopenia. (Option D ruled out)
  • Elevated aminotransferase levels.
  • Elevated lactate dehydrogenase levels.
  • Elevated inflammatory markers - Ferritin, C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
  • Markers of a hypercoagulable state - high fibrinogen, high D-dimer levels, increased fibrin degradation products, prolonged prothrombin time (PT) and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT).

Elevated D-dimer and Ferritin levels (Option B): COVID-19 causes a hypercoagulable state and a "cytokine storm," leading to significantly elevated inflammatory markers like Ferritin, C-Reactive Protein (CRP), and D-dimer.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 1540, 1541.

FELUDA uses CRISPR-Cas9 technology (CRISPR = Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats)

  • FELUDA (FNCAS9 Editor Linked Uniform Detection Assay) is a paper-based strip test inspired by the Satyajit Ray character.

Reverse Transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR) (Option A): RT-PCR is the gold standard molecular method that involves thermal cycling and fluorescence detection, whereas FELUDA is a strip-based test that uses gene-editing proteins for detection.

Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (ELISA) (Option C): ELISA is a biochemical technique used mainly to detect antibodies (IgG/IgM) or antigens in the blood, not the CRISPR-based genetic detection used in FELUDA.

Asymptomatic individuals who are contacts of confirmed cases and receive a negative Rapid Antigen Test (RAT) result do not require immediate re-testing. Repeat testing is not done immediately with another RAT (Option A ruled out); instead, no repeat is needed if asymptomatic. If symptoms develop later, RT-PCR is preferred, not another RAT.

Mandatory re-testing after 24 hours, regardless of symptoms, is not required (Option C ruled out) as testing is done once (day 5-10 after exposure) unless symptoms appear.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The standard recommended quarantine period for individuals exposed to COVID-19 is 14 days from the date of last exposure. This duration is based on the incubation period of the SARS-CoV-2 virus, which typically ranges from 2 to 14 days.

  • Isolation is the separation and restriction of movements or activities of persons who are sick, to prevent the transmission of disease.
  • Quarantine is the separation and restriction of movements or activities of persons who are not ill but are believed to have been exposed to infection, for the purpose of preventing transmission of diseases.

Home quarantine for 14 days is advised when a person comes in contact with a COVID-19 positive patient.

The home-quarantined person:

  • Should stay in a well-ventilated single room and stay away from high-risk individuals
  • Should not attend any religious or social gatherings
  • Must wash hands often
  • Must change mask every 6-8 hrs
  • Their surroundings must be disinfected with 1% sodium hypochlorite solution
  • In case the person being quarantined becomes symptomatic, all his contacts should be home quarantined for 14 days and followed up for another 14 days or till the report turns out negative on lab testing.

5 days (Option A): This duration is often associated with the minimum isolation period for asymptomatic positive cases in some updated protocols to facilitate return to work, but it is not the standard full incubation-based quarantine for exposure.

7 days (Option B): While some guidelines suggest "test-to-release" strategies at day 7 with a negative PCR, the gold standard for full clinical safety remains the 14-day window to account for the maximum incubation period.

21 days (Option D): This is longer than the known maximum incubation period for SARS-CoV-2. Such an extended period is generally not required for standard quarantine unless there are specific complicating factors or highly unusual viral shedding patterns

The diagnostic criteria for MIS-C require evidence of systemic inflammation:

Children and adolescents 0-18 years of age with fever ≥ 3 days and two of these:

  • Rash or bilateral non-purulent conjunctivitis or mucocutaneous inflammation signs (oral, hands, or feet), e.g., hyperemia, periorbital erythema and oedema, strawberry tongue, and malar erythema.
  • Hypotension or shock.
  • Features of myocardial dysfunction, pericarditis, valvulitis, or coronary abnormalities (including ECHO findings or elevated Troponin/NT-proBNP)
  • Evidence of coagulopathy (PT, PTT, elevated D-Dimers)
  • Acute gastrointestinal problems (diarrhoea, vomiting, or abdominal pain)

AND Elevated ESR (≥ 40 mm), C-reactive protein (≥ 15 mg/L), or procalcitonin.

AND No other obvious microbial cause of inflammation, including bacterial sepsis, staphylococcal or streptococcal shock syndromes.

AND Evidence of COVID-19 (RT-PCR, antigen test, or serology positive), or likely contact with patients with COVID-19.

Types of MIS-C:

  • Kawasaki phenotype
  • MIS-C without shock

Decreased Ferritin (Option C): MIS-C is a hyperinflammatory state; therefore, ferritin levels are usually elevated, not decreased.

Thrombocytosis (Option D): While some pediatric inflammatory conditions show high platelets, MIS-C is more often associated with lymphopenia or thrombocytopenia during the acute phase of the illness.

  • Immunocompromised states are important risk factors, including diabetes mellitus and glucocorticoid treatment, as well as patients on ventilation.
  • Other drugs that are approved for its management include isavuconazole and posaconazole. Surgical debridement is the last line of management.

Clinical presentation:

  • Cutaneous mucormycosis - usually results after trauma
  • Gastrointestinal mucormycosis - primarily occurs in premature neonates who have disseminated disease or necrotising enterocolitis
  • Disseminated mucormycosis

Itraconazole (Option A): While an antifungal, it is not the primary treatment for Mucormycosis; however, newer azoles like Isavuconazole or Posaconazole are approved for management.

Fluconazole (Option B): This drug is generally ineffective against Mucorales species and is primarily used for Candida or Cryptococcus infections.

question: During the doffing of Personal Protective Equipment, which of the following areas is considered "clean" and safe to touch with hands that have just been disinfected?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • According to the established doffing protocols for COVID-19, the process must be performed in a designated area. The first component to be removed is the shoe covers. This is done by sitting on a "dirty" chair and slowly pulling the outer surface from the top down to the toes before discarding them. Performing hand hygiene or disinfecting gloves between steps is mandatory to prevent cross-contamination.

Preparation for doffing the PPE:

  • To be performed only in the designated area
  • Check for any leaks or soiling
  • The doffing room should have two chairs, dirty and clean
  • All the PPE must be discarded in the red bin
  • Hand hygiene must be performed after every step

Steps of doffing the PPE:

  • Engage the observer and ask him to check the PPE - the observer should check for any leak, tear, or contamination of the PPE. If contaminated, then it should be disinfected with alcohol-based wipes.
  • Disinfect the gloves
  • Remove and discard shoe covers
  • Sit on the dirty chair with legs apart
  • Remove the shoe covers by slowly pulling the outer surface, starting from the top and then pulling from the toe end. Discard them
  • Disinfect and remove the outer pair of gloves
  • While removing the outer gloves, the inner gloves should not be torn or contaminated.
  • Pinch the first glove on the outer surface at the wrist and pull it inside out.
  • Hold this glove in the other hand like a ball.
  • Slide the thumb inside the other glove and remove the inside-out balling around the previous glove, making it into a single bag. Then discard it.
  • Disinfect inner gloves
  • Remove face shield/eye goggle (Option A)- loosen the screw and remove the face shield by holding it from the back handle. Discard it.
  • Disinfect inner gloves again
  • Remove the hood and coverall suit/gown (Option C)
  • Slide back the hood by holding it from the top
  • Separate the zip flap and unzip the coverall suit
  • Holding the suit at the arms, slide it off the shoulder slightly, then pull the suit from the side of the waist.
  • Roll the arms out one by one.
  • By touching the inner surface of the suit, carefully roll out each leg. Discard it
  • Disinfect and remove inner gloves as previously described
  • Perform hand hygiene and wear a new pair of gloves
  • Remove and discard the N95 mask (Option D), which is the very last item to be removed
  • Do not touch the exposed surface of the mask
  • Stoop forward and first remove the lower strap
  • Then pull out the upper strap and remove the mask
  • Disinfect gloves
  • Sit on the clean chair and disinfect your shoes using alcohol wipes
  • Disinfect and remove gloves
  • Perform hand hygiene
  • Wipe the shoes on a sodium hypochlorite-soaked doormat at the exit
  • Exit the doffing area and take a shower


Reference:
  • https://www.aiims.edu/images/pdf/notice/COVID_19_HIC_SUPPLEMENT_VERSION_1.2__26_3_20.pdf
question: Which of the following components of the PPE kit should be removed first during the doffing process to minimise self-contamination?

• The correct donning sequence is designed to ensure that the most "clean" items are placed first and the barrier is complete.
  • The sequence begins with the Gown (to cover the body), followed by the Mask or N95 Respirator, then the goggles or a Face Shield to protect the mucous membranes of the eyes, and finally the gloves, which should be pulled over the cuffs of the gown to ensure no skin is exposed.

The correct sequence of donning PPE is first pair of gloves → coverall → Shoe cover → N-95 mask.

Preparation for donning the PPE:

  • To be performed only in the designated area
  • The health care worker must be prepared for the shift duty by
    • Taking a meal
    • Using the washroom
  • Drinking water before entering the donning area
  • Remove all accessories, jewellery
  • Change into clean hospital scrubs and closed washable footwear
  • Perform hand hygiene with soap and water

Steps of donning/putting on the PPE:

  • Hand hygiene
  • Wear the first pair of gloves
  • Make sure the cuff of the gloves goes as far as possible
  • Examine and wear coveralls
  • Examine the coverall for any damage
  • Start by wearing the leg sleeves and then the arm sleeves
  • Zip up and cover the zip with the flap attached
  • Wear a shoe cover
  • Sit on the clean chair and wear a shoe cover
  • Pull them up till your calves
  • Wear an N95 mask and a hood
  • Hold the mask like a cup in the hand with both straps hanging out in the front.
  • Place the mask on the face, pull and wear the lower strap first, placing it below the ears.
  • Then pull and wear the upper strap, placing it above the ears
  • The air leakage should be minimal around the mask when forcibly exhaling
  • Wear the hood covering the forehead and the cheeks
  • Wear a face shield/eye goggles over the hood and ensure the fit
  • Wear the second pair of gloves - pull the gloves to cover the sleeve cuff and forearm as much as possible

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation described and shown in the image is characteristic of COVID toes, which are pernio-like (chilblain-like) lesions associated with SARS-CoV-2 infection.

  • Clinical Presentation: These are erythematous-violaceous or purpuric macules/papules on the acral surfaces (fingers and toes). They may be associated with oedema, itching, or pain.
  • Mechanism: Though the exact cause is debated, it is thought to be an inflammatory response or a microangiopathic process.
  • Timing: These lesions often appear late in the course of the disease (post-viral phase). Patients may have negative RT-PCR tests but positive antibodies (IgM/IgG) at this stage.
  • Distinction: Unlike classic chilblains, these occur without a history of significant cold exposure.

Chilblains (Option A): These are skin sores or bumps (also called pernio) that occur as an abnormal reaction to cold, damp air. While the appearance is nearly identical to COVID toes, the patient's history explicitly mentions "no exposure to cold," which makes idiopathic or classic chilblains less likely than a viral association in a recovering COVID patient.

Varicella (Option C): This is caused by the varicella-zoster virus and presents as a generalised "dewdrop on a rose petal" vesicular rash that starts on the trunk and spreads to the face and extremities. It is highly pruritic and involves different stages of lesions (macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts) simultaneously, which does not match the localised, purpuric acral lesions seen here.

Eczema (Option D): Also known as dermatitis, this typically presents as itchy, dry, inflamed skin. On the feet, it might appear as dyshidrotic eczema with small, deep-seated blisters (pompholyx) or chronic scaly patches. It does not typically present as the distinct violaceous, bruise-like macules on the tips of the toes seen in the provided image.



Reference:
  • https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34272741/

• When there is an absence of the CD40 ligand in the B lymphocytes, they cannot switch, leading to the production of only IgM and hence will have a normal or increased IgM level (hyper IgM syndrome).

Hyper IgM syndrome

  • A rare primary immunodeficiency disorder characterised by low or absent IgG, IgA, and IgE, with normal or increased IgM levels.

Causes: Results from various X-linked or autosomal mutations.

Clinical Manifestations:

  • Pulmonary complications (e.g., infections)
  • Gastrointestinal issues
  • Autoimmune diseases
  • Hematologic abnormalities
  • Lymphoproliferation
  • Increased risk of malignancies

Diagnosis: Based on immunoglobulin levels and genetic testing.

Management:

  • Treatment varies depending on the genetic mutation and clinical presentation.
  • Options may include immunoglobulin replacement therapy, antibiotics, and management of associated complications.

Prognosis:

  • Depends on the severity of symptoms and timely treatment, but early diagnosis and management can improve outcomes.

A total lack of NK cells (Option A) or natural killer deficiency is a rare genetic disorder that has a genetic mechanism causing it. This is not associated with hyper IgM syndrome.

Lack of CD8-mediated cytotoxicity (Option B) can be as a result of many chronic autoimmune diseases (like multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, etc). It can also be seen in healthy blood relatives of people with autoimmune disorders. However, it is not associated with increased IgM production.

The inability of neutrophils to act against infections (Option D) is not associated with the absence of CD40 ligand of B cells.

The patient presents with fever and chills, with malaria and dengue ruled out, but rK39 test positive, which strongly indicates visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-azar), which presents with fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, and pancytopenia.

The rK39 antigen test detects antibodies against Leishmania donovani, the causative agent of visceral leishmaniasis.

The treatment of choice for Kala-azar is Amphotericin B, particularly liposomal Amphotericin B, due to its high efficacy and safety profile.

Griseofulvin (Option B) is an antifungal medication that works by inhibiting microtubule function, thereby interfering with fungal mitosis. It is primarily used for treating superficial fungal infections like tinea capitis and onychomycosis.

Dapsone (Option C) is an antimicrobial drug that inhibits dihydropteroate synthase, disrupting folic acid metabolism. It is mainly used in leprosy (Hansen’s disease) as part of multi-drug therapy (MDT) and for Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) prophylaxis in immunocompromised patients.

Hydroxychloroquine (Option D) is an immunomodulatory drug that interferes with antigen presentation by lysosomes. It is widely used in autoimmune diseases like SLE and rheumatoid arthritis, as well as in malaria treatment and prophylaxis.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

Legionnaires' disease is an atypical pneumonia caused by Legionella pneumophila, a Gram-negative intracellular bacillus.

Because Legionella is an intracellular pathogen, treatment requires antibiotics with excellent intracellular penetration.

Current drug of choice:

  • Azithromycin (preferred, especially in hospitalized patients and children)
  • Respiratory fluoroquinolones (Levofloxacin, Moxifloxacin) are equally effective alternatives, particularly in severe disease.

Legionnaires' Disease

Causative Organism

  • Legionella pneumophila
  • Gram-negative, pleomorphic bacillus
  • Weakly acid-fast (silver stain)
  • Intracellular organism

Source of Infection

  • Air-conditioning systems
  • Cooling towers
  • Water tanks
  • Hot tubs
  • Hospital water supplies

Transmission: Inhalation of contaminated aerosols (no person-to-person spread).

Risk Factors

  • Elderly
  • Smokers
  • COPD
  • Diabetes
  • Immunocompromised
  • Transplant recipients

Clinical Features

  • High fever
  • Dry cough
  • Dyspnea
  • Diarrhea
  • Confusion
  • Hyponatremia
  • Elevated liver enzymes

Diagnosis

  • Urinary antigen test (detects L. pneumophila serogroup 1)
  • PCR
  • Culture on Buffered Charcoal Yeast Extract (BCYE) agar

Treatment

  • Azithromycin
  • Levofloxacin or Moxifloxacin (alternative/preferred in severe disease)
  • Doxycycline (alternative)

Vancomycin (Option A): Active against Gram-positive organisms (e.g., MRSA). No activity against intracellular Legionella.

Streptomycin (Option C): Aminoglycoside mainly used for: Plague, tularemia, brucellosis (with doxycycline) and poor intracellular activity against Legionella.

Erythromycin (Option D): Historically the treatment of choice. Azithromycin has largely replaced erythromycin because it has better efficacy, better tolerability, more convenient dosing and fewer gastrointestinal adverse effects



Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9124264/
question: What is the drug of choice for Legionnaire’s disease?

explanationHtml:
Co-trimoxazole treatment is recommended for patients with HIV who present with symptoms of a respiratory tract infection and a CD4 count of less than 200 cells/cu.mm. Co-trimoxazole, a combination of sulfamethoxazole and trimethoprim, is commonly used in AIDS patients with cough due to its effectiveness against Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP). PJP is an opportunistic infection that affects individuals with weakened immune systems, such as those with advanced HIV/AIDS.

Amoxicillin-clavulanic acid + Azithromycin (Option A): This combination is typically used for community-acquired pneumonia (CAP), which often shows lobar infiltrates on chest X-ray. However, the normal chest X-ray and the high CD4 threshold for bacterial pneumonia make this less likely. Also, CAP typically presents with chills and rigors, which are absent here.

Amphotericin B (Option B): This is the drug of choice for disseminated fungal infections such as cryptococcal meningitis or visceral leishmaniasis. However, there is no evidence of cryptococcal infection (e.g., no headache, altered sensorium, or nuchal rigidity), and the patient’s symptoms are respiratory, not systemic.

Antitubercular treatment (ATT) (Option D): Tuberculosis (TB) is common in HIV patients, but it usually presents with chronic symptoms like prolonged cough, weight loss, night sweats, and upper lobe infiltrates on chest X-ray. The acute nature of the illness (5 days of symptoms) and normal chest X-ray make TB less likely.

Arterial pH >7.2 (alkalosis) is not a complication associated with Plasmodium falciparum infection. Severe malaria caused by P. falciparum can trigger metabolic acidosis in which the arterial pH is less than 7.2.

Hypoglycemia (blood glucose <40 mg/dL) (Option A) can be a complication of severe malaria, particularly in cases of P. falciparum infection. The parasite's impact on the liver and the increased metabolic demands of the infection can lead to low blood sugar levels.

The presence of serum creatinine levels of -5.2 (Option C), indicating a significant decrease in renal clearance, suggests acute kidney injury (AKI). Malaria-associated AKI can result from various factors, such as decreased blood flow to the kidneys, direct parasite-mediated damage, or immune-mediated injury.

Cerebral malaria, characterized by impaired consciousness and unarousable coma (Option D) is a severe complication that can occur in P. falciparum infection.

correctAnswer: C. Start ATT and then ART after 2 weeks
explanationHtml:
• Increased Risk: People with HIV are 18-26 times more likely to develop active TB than those without HIV.
  • HIV weakens the immune system, reducing CD4 T-cell counts, which are essential for controlling TB infection. This allows TB to progress from latent to active disease.
  • The underlying mechanism of IRIS is due to an imbalance between anti-inflammatory cytokines and pro-inflammatory cytokines that occurs rapidly after the recovery of immune function in HIV patients initiated on HAART.
  • Screening and Diagnosis:
    • Testing for Both Conditions: Patients with TB should be tested for HIV, and vice versa, given the high co-infection rate.
    • Diagnostic Challenges: TB symptoms can overlap with other opportunistic infections in HIV patients. Tests like sputum culture, X-rays, and newer rapid molecular tests (GeneXpert) help in diagnosing TB in HIV-positive patients.
  • Treatment of Co-Infection:
    • Anti-TB Therapy: This involves the standard TB drug regimen, usually with a 6-month course. Treatment may extend for cases of drug-resistant TB.
    • Instead of Rifampicin, Rifabutin is preferred in patients receiving protease inhibitors due to its property of being a less potent inducer of CYP3A4.
    • Antiretroviral Therapy (ART): Initiating ART is crucial for improving immune function. ART is typically started 2-8 weeks after beginning TB treatment to prevent immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS), depending on CD4 count and clinical status.
    • Drug Interactions: TB drugs, like rifampicin, can interact with ART drugs, requiring careful selection of the ART regimen to minimize side effects and maintain effectiveness.

explanationHtml:
• Amoxiclav, which is a combination of amoxicillin and clavulanic acid, is not considered a first-line treatment for Mycoplasma pneumonia. The drug of choice for Mycoplasma pneumoniae is Azithromycin.

Atypical Pneumonia (Walking Pneumonia)

Definition

Atypical pneumonia is a milder form of pneumonia, often caused by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, certain viruses, or moulds.

Symptoms
  • Cough, fever, chest pain, headache, and chills, resembling a bad cold.
  • As it is generally mild, not requiring bed rest or hospitalization, allowing people to continue daily activities called"walking pneumonia."

Etiologic Agents
  • Atypical pneumonia is caused by organisms that don't grow on standard cultures or appear on Gram stain, such as:
    • Mycoplasma pneumonia (associated with closed living conditions like at school and military barracks)
    • Chlamydia pneumoniae
    • Legionella species (from stagnant water sources or from air conditioners)
    • Respiratory viruses: Influenza, adenoviruses, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), human metapneumoviruses, and coronaviruses (e.g., SARS-CoV-2)

Prevalence
  • Cases of atypical pneumonia are increasing, particularly among young adults.

Diagnosis
  • These pathogens cannot be cultured in the usual ways, making diagnosis more complex.
  • Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a unique bacterium that lacks a cell wall and requires a specialized cell-free medium for culture (Option D) as it cannot be grown on conventional culture media.
  • Detection of specific antibodies (Option B) (IgM and IgG) against Mycoplasma pneumoniae, can be helpful in confirming the diagnosis.
  • PCR and other molecular methods are often necessary for confirmation.

Radiology

  • Chest X-ray findings in Mycoplasma pneumonia can vary, but bilateral infiltrates (Option C) are commonly seen. Infiltrates may appear as patchy or diffuse opacities in both lungs. However, chest X-ray findings alone cannot definitively diagnose Mycoplasma pneumonia and should be correlated with clinical symptoms and other diagnostic tests.

Treatment
  • The absence of a cell wall makes these organisms resistant to certain antibiotics that target cell wall synthesis, such as penicillins and cephalosporins and require treatment with macrolides like azithromycin, and fluoroquinolones, or tetracyclines like doxycycline.

question: An HIV-positive patient presents with the following finding. What is the diagnosis & WHO clinical stage of HIV?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The classical rash and other symptoms point to the diagnosis of secondary syphilis.

Classic Manifestations of secondary syphilis:

  • Mucocutaneous or cutaneous lesions and generalized non-tender lymphadenopathy.
  • The primary chancre may still be present in ~15% of cases, more common in HIV-infected individuals.

Skin Rash:

  • Macular, papular, papulosquamous, and occasionally pustular syphilides.
  • Lesions may be subtle, and 25% of patients with a visible rash may not recognize it.
  • Lesions initially present as pale red or pink, non-pruritic macules on the trunk/extremities.
  • Progress to papular lesions, often affecting palms and soles.
  • Severe necrotic lesions (lues maligna) may occur in HIV patients.

Hair and Mucosal Involvement:

  • Patchy alopecia of the scalp, eyebrows, or beard in 5% of cases.
  • Condylomata lata (moist, infectious lesions) may form in intertriginous areas (e.g., perianal, vulva, scrotum) in 10% of cases.
  • Mucous patches (painless silver-grey erosions) occur in 10-15% of patients, commonly in the oral or genital mucosa.

Constitutional Symptoms:

  • Sore throat (15–30%), fever (5–8%), weight loss (2–20%), malaise (25%), anorexia (2–10%), headache (10%), and meningismus (5%).
  • Acute meningitis occurs in 1-2% of cases, with up to 40% of early syphilis cases showing CSF abnormalities.

Ocular and Otic Involvement:

  • Ocular symptoms: pupillary abnormalities, optic neuritis, iritis, or uveitis; may lead to permanent blindness if untreated.
  • Otic symptoms: sensorineural hearing loss, vertigo, or tinnitus.
  • Prompt diagnosis and treatment are crucial for preventing long-term damage.

Less Common Complications:

  • Hepatitis, nephropathy, gastrointestinal issues (e.g., hypertrophic gastritis, proctitis), arthritis, and periostitis.
  • Hepatic involvement is common but typically asymptomatic.
  • Renal involvement results from immune complex deposition, leading to proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome.

Resolution:

  • Most secondary syphilis manifestations resolve spontaneously within 1–6 months.

Primary Syphilis (Options A): Primary syphilis is the first stage of infection caused by Treponema pallidum. The characteristic lesion is a chancre which is a painless, firm, round ulcer that appears at the site where the bacteria entered the body, which develops 10-90 days (average ~3 weeks) after exposure along with enlarged and non-tender lymphadenopathy. These lesions typically heal spontaneously within 3-6 weeks, even without treatment. It is typically seen on genitals (penis, vulva, cervix), anus/rectum, and mouth or lips.

Pyoderma Gangrenosum (Option C): It is an uncommon, inflammatory, noninfectious neutrophilic dermatosis characterized by rapidly progressive, painful skin ulcers with undermined violaceous borders, seen in the lower legs (especially pretibial region), trunk and upper extremities. Pathergy phenomenon, minor trauma can triggering or worsening lesion, is seen. It is associated with inflammatory bowel disease (crohns disease and ulcerative colitis), rheumatoid arthitis and leukemia.

Steven- Johnson Syndrome (Option D): Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) is a severe, potentially life-threatening mucocutaneous hypersensitivity reaction characterized by extensive epidermal necrosis, skin detachment, and mucosal involvement. <10% BSA detachment is seen in SJS. It is mostly drug-related (Allopurinol, carbamazepine, phenytoin, lamotrigine) or due to infection (mycoplasma pneumoniae, other viruses). Oral and ocular involvement are characteristic. Positive Nikolsky sign seen.

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 1428-1436

Explanation:

  • Viral load (HIV RNA levels) is the most reliable parameter for monitoring the efficacy of Highly Active Antiretroviral Therapy (HAART).
  • It reflects the amount of active virus in the bloodstream and is the primary marker for assessing viral suppression.
  • A tenfold reduction in viral load is typically expected within 1-2 months of HAART initiation, and the goal is to achieve viral load levels of <50 copies/mL within 6 months.

CD4+ T Cell Count (Option A): Although an increase in CD4+ count reflects immune recovery, it is less sensitive than the viral load for assessing early response to HAART. p24 Antigen (Option C): The p24 antigen is a core protein of the HIV capsid, used primarily in early diagnosis before seroconversion. It is not a marker for ongoing treatment efficacy.

Viral Serotype (Option D): The viral serotype is irrelevant for treatment monitoring, as most cases of HIV are caused by HIV-1.

question: A patient diagnosed to be retro-positive was started on highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Which of the following can be used to monitor treatment efficacy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

A patient with fever for 4 days, stable vitals, and thrombocytopenia (platelet count = 20,000/mm³) without any bleeding manifestations most likely has viral fever (e.g., dengue) or another self-limiting viral illness causing transient bone marrow suppression.

Paracetamol is given for symptomatic relief of fever in the first hour of management. NSAIDs (like ibuprofen or aspirin) are avoided, as they can worsen bleeding risk in thrombocytopenia.

Platelet transfusion is not indicated unless there is active bleeding or a platelet count <10,000/mm³ (prophylactically).

Antibiotics are not indicated empirically unless there is evidence of bacterial infection (e.g., toxic appearance, hypotension, or localising signs).

There is no role of steroids in uncomplicated viral fever or thrombocytopenia.

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 784.

question: A patient presents with fever and altered sensorium. Peripheral smear shows multiple ring stages. Best treatment is?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Brucellosis (undulant fever) is caused by Brucella species, often from livestock exposure or unpasteurized dairy.

  • Doxycycline inhibits bacterial protein synthesis, while Rifampicin blocks RNA synthesis, acting synergistically.

  • Combination therapy reduces relapse rates compared to monotherapy.

  • Treatment is given for 6 weeks to eradicate both intracellular and extracellular bacteria.

  • It prevents chronic complications like spondylitis and endocarditis.

  • This usual alternative regimen favoured by the World Health Organization and many national guidelines, consisting of rifampin (600–900 mg/d) plus doxycycline (100 mg twice daily) for 6 weeks.

  • The gold standard for the treatment of brucellosis in adults is IM streptomycin (0.75–1 g daily for 14–21 days) together with doxycycline (100 mg twice daily for 6 weeks).

  • Patients who cannot tolerate or receive tetracyclines (children, pregnant women) can be given high-dose TMP-SMX instead (two or three standard-strength tablets twice daily for adults, depending on weight).

  • Focal neurologic disease due to Brucella species requires prolonged treatment (i.e., for 3–6 months), usually with ceftriaxone supplementation of a standard regimen (Option D).

  • Brucella endocarditis is treated with at least three drugs (an aminoglycoside, a tetracycline, and rifampin), and many experts add ceftriaxone and/or a fluoroquinolone to reduce the need for valve replacement.

  • Antimicrobial prophylaxis is given to reduce the risk of infection after:

    • Occupational or other exposure to Brucella organisms,

    • Inadvertent immunization with live vaccine intended for use in animals, or

    • Exposure to deliberately released brucellae

      • Rifampin plus doxycycline for 3 weeks is given as prophylaxis, or Doxycycline monotherapy for 3 weeks can be given as a better tolerated option (Option A).



Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 1331-1335

question: 30 year old man presents with severe headache, fever for one day with altered sensorium. Nuchal rigidity is absent. Guarded LP was done and CSF shows 50 cells with 20% neutrophils and 80% lymphocytes with CSF sugar of 70 mg and RBS 100 mg/dl with protein= 90 mg/dl. Diagnosis is?

correctAnswer: A. It helps in determining the duration of antibiotic therapy
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Procalcitonin (PCT) is widely used to guide the duration of antibiotic therapy, especially in ICU settings and conditions like ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP). Serial PCT measurements help determine when to discontinue antibiotics, usually when PCT falls below 0.25–0.5 ng/mL or decreases by 80–90% from the peak value.

Role of Procalcitonin:

  • Helps detect bacterial infections early and differentiate from non-bacterial causes.
  • Guides when to start or stop antibiotics based on specific cut-off values.
  • Decreases by ~50% every 24 hours after infection control, helping monitor treatment.
  • Differentiates between infectious and non-infectious conditions in various diseases.
  • Reduces unnecessary antibiotic use in respiratory, postoperative, and other conditions.
  • Correlates with severity in sepsis, offering prognostic information.
  • Used in ED and ICU algorithms to manage antibiotic timing and duration.
  • Levels <0.1 ng/mL have high negative predictive value to rule out bacterial infections.

Incorrect Options:

It helps in identifying which empirical antibiotics to be given (Option B): PCT does not identify specific pathogens or recommend particular antibiotics. It only indicates the likelihood of a bacterial infection, not which organisms are involved or their sensitivity patterns. Empirical antibiotic selection is based on clinical judgment, local antibiograms, and patient risk factors.

It can be used to confirm source of infection (Option C): PCT is a non-specific marker of systemic bacterial infection and cannot pinpoint the source (e.g., lungs, urinary tract, blood). Imaging and cultures are needed to confirm the anatomical site of infection.

It is used to differentiate bacterial from fungal cause (Option D): While PCT can help distinguish bacterial from viral infections, it is not reliable in differentiating bacterial from fungal infections. Invasive fungal infections may not always cause elevated PCT levels, limiting its utility in such cases.



Reference:

Procalcitonin - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

  • The association with increased mosquito breeding further supports this diagnosis.

Dengue complications

Neurological
  • Dengue encephalopathy is most commonly encountered neurological complication of dengue virus
    • linked primarily to dengue hemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome
    • EEG may show abnormalities such as burst suppression and seizures
    • CSF profiles typically remain normal.
    • Neuroimaging can be normal or reveal diffuse cerebral edema.

  • Dengue virus-induced dilated cardiomyopathy should always be considered if a dengue fever patient has refractory shock and signs and symptoms of congestive heart failure.

Hepatic injury
  • Liver involvement in dengue is a crucial feature
  • The effect ranges from an asymptomatic rise in liver enzymes to the development of ALF
  • The most common atypical manifestation reported was hepatitis

Pneumonia
  • Staphylococcus pneumonia is an important accompanying problem seen in dengue patient
  • co-infection between dengue and influenza can result in exacerbation of pneumonia

Orchitis
  • Orchitis usually occurs together with epididymitis
  • Commonly seen in men between 14 and 35 years of age.

Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever

All of the following:

  • Acute onset of fever
  • 2-7 days duration
  • Hemorrhagic manifestations
    • Positive tourniquet test/Petechiae
    • Ecchymosis
    • Purpura/Bleeding from mucosa, GIT, Injection sites, etc
  • Platelet count ≤ 100,000 cells/cu.mm.
  • Plasma leakage
    • Rising hematocrit
      • Hemoconcentration >20%
    • Pleural effusion, ascites/Hypoproteinemia)

Dengue Shock Syndrome
  • DHF criteria plus Signs of Shock
  • Tachycardia/Cool extremities/Weak pulse/Lethargy/Restlessness
  • Pulse pressure <20 mm Hg with increased Diastolic pressure (e.g. 100/80)
  • Hypotension (Systolic <80 mm Hg for age <5 years/80-90 mm Hg for older child and adults)

Skin examination reveals multiple purpura and petechiae on the left shoulder, trunk, and legs. Similar cases have been reported linked to increased incidence of mosquito breeding. What is the most common neurological complication associated with this condition?

explanationHtml:
Correct Option A - Tuberculosis (TB):

  • The pleural fluid analysis shows an LDH level greater than 0.6 times the serum LDH and protein greater than 0.5 times the serum protein, which are criteria for an exudative pleural effusion according to Light's criteria. Tuberculosis is a common cause of exudative pleural effusion, especially in areas where TB is prevalent. Exudative effusions occur due to increased capillary permeability or lymphatic obstruction, and they are often associated with infections, malignancies, and inflammatory conditions like TB.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Heart failure: Heart failure typically causes a transudative pleural effusion, which is characterized by lower protein and LDH levels in the pleural fluid relative to serum levels. This option is incorrect because the fluid described meets the criteria for an exudative effusion, not a transudative one.

Option C - Hepatic failure: Hepatic failure (such as in cirrhosis) usually causes a transudative pleural effusion due to low oncotic pressure from hypoalbuminemia, not an exudative effusion. Therefore, it is not the most likely diagnosis in this scenario.

Option D - Renal failure: Renal failure can cause pleural effusions, but they are typically transudative unless complicated by infections or other factors. The described pleural fluid characteristics are more consistent with an exudative process.

• The microorganism that exhibits intrinsic resistance to meropenem and aminoglycosides but sensitive to cotrimoxazole is Stenotrophomonas.
  • Stenotrophomonas maltophilia is a non-fermenting gram-negative rod, similar to Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Acinetobacter.

Risk factors:

  • Chronic respiratory diseases (e.g., cystic fibrosis)
  • Hematologic malignancies, chemotherapy-induced neutropenia
  • Organ transplants, HIV infection, hemodialysis, neonates
  • Hospital settings, ICU stays, mechanical ventilation, tracheostomies
  • Central venous catheters, severe burns, trauma, mucosal damage, and prolonged antibiotic use increase the risk.

Management:

  • First-line treatment: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) (co-trimoxazole) at high doses (15 mg/kg of trimethoprim component).
  • Alternative treatments:
    • Fluoroquinolones (e.g., levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) have good efficacy, particularly in lung infections.
    • Minocycline and tigecycline show high effectiveness (80-100% susceptibility).
    • Ticarcillin-clavulanic acid, ceftazidime, colistin, and chloramphenicol can be considered.
  • Emerging treatments:
    • New agents like Cefiderocol, Eravacycline, Omadacycline, and Delafloxacin show promising in-vitro activity.
    • Combination therapies (e.g., TMP-SMX/ciprofloxacin, ticarcillin-clavulanate/aztreonam) have demonstrated synergistic effects.
  • Challenges:
    • Resistance to many common antibiotics like meropenem, and aminoglycosides is rising, necessitating new treatments.
    • Studies on aerosolized antibiotics, bacteriophage therapy, and other innovative approaches are ongoing.
  • Duration of treatment:
    • Pneumonia: Typically 7 days, extended to 10-14 days in immunocompromised patients.
    • Bacteremia: Generally treated for 14 days.
  • Source control:
    • Surgical removal of infected devices (e.g., central venous catheters) and drainage of infected collections is critical for successful treatment.

Option A, B, and C: These organisms are susceptible to meropenem and aminoglycosides.

explanationHtml:
• The patient has signs and symptoms of meningitis, which, along with the positive India ink stain leads to the diagnosis of Cryptococcal meningitis, which is a CNS complication of HIV occurring due to opportunistic infection by Cryptococcus neoformans.

Fungal Meningitis in AIDS

  • The leading cause of meningitis in AIDS patients is primarily Cryptococcus neoformans (C. neoformans), with C. gattii accounting for up to 12% of cases.
  • Cryptococcal meningitis is common in patients with CD4+ T-cell counts <100/μL, especially in untreated AIDS patients.

Symptoms:

  • Subacute meningoencephalitis with fever, nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, headache, and meningeal signs
  • Seizures and focal neurologic deficits are rare
  • Elevated intracranial pressure (Option A)

CSF Findings:

  • Mild increase in WBCs and protein
  • Low glucose
  • Elevated opening pressure

Diagnosis:

  • CSF: Positive India ink examination
  • Cryptococcal antigen detection in CSF
  • Blood cultures may also be positive
  • A biopsy may be needed for CNS cryptococcoma or distinguishing from immune reconstitution syndrome
  • MRI: Soap bubble appearance is seen in less than 30% of cases (Option D)

Treatment:

  • Initial: IV Amphotericin B with Flucytosine for at least 2 weeks. (Option C)
  • Continued with Amphotericin until CSF culture is negative, followed by Fluconazole (400 mg/d) for 8 weeks and then 200 mg/d until CD4+ T-cell count >200/μL for 6 months.
  • Repeated lumbar punctures may be needed to manage elevated intracranial pressure.

Immune Reconstitution Syndrome:

  • Occurs after initiating effective ART, leading to worsening of pre-existing opportunistic infections or autoimmune conditions.
  • Types of IRIS:
    • Paradoxical IRIS: Exacerbation of known pre-existing infections or neoplasms.
    • Unmasking IRIS: Emergence of previously undiagnosed conditions.
    • Immune Reconstitution Disease (IRD): Refers to IRIS related to opportunistic infections or autoimmune diseases.
  • Symptoms:
    • Lymphadenitis
    • Prolonged fever
    • Pulmonary infiltrates
    • Hepatitis
    • Increased intracranial pressure
    • Uveitis
    • Sarcoidosis
    • Graves’ disease
  • Mechanism: Related to type IV hypersensitivity reactions due to immune recovery as HIV RNA levels drop and immune suppression is reversed.
  • Management:
    • Severe cases may require immunosuppressive drugs (e.g., glucocorticoids) alongside specific antimicrobial therapy.
    • Due to the risk of IRIS (immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome), ART should be deferred by 4-6 weeks after the initiation of antifungal treatment.

Other Causes:

  • Other fungi like C. immitis and H. capsulatum, as well as amoebas like Acanthamoeba and Naegleria, can cause meningitis in HIV-infected individuals.


Reference:

Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page: 1574, 1576, 1577.

question: A 30-year-old farmer from Tamil Nadu presented with fever, myalgia, headache and cough. On physical examination, a lesion is seen on the chest. Lung auscultation shows extensive bilateral rales. Blood investigation showed positive IgM for scrub typhus. What would be the appropriate treatment?

explanationHtml:
• The image describes a violaceous lesion located on the hard palate, which is highly suggestive of Kaposi sarcoma (KS), especially in the context of an HIV-positive patient.
  • Kaposi's Sarcoma (KS) is a vascular tumor caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8), often seen in HIV/AIDS patients and classified as an AIDS-defining condition. It affects the skin, oral cavity, and internal organs like the lungs and gastrointestinal tract.

Clinical Stages:

  1. Patch Stage: Flat, pink or red lesions.
  2. Plaque Stage: Raised, purple or brown lesions.
  3. Nodular Stage: Firm, raised nodules, may ulcerate.

Variants:

  • Classic KS: Affects elderly men of Mediterranean or Eastern European descent.
  • Endemic KS: Common in sub-Saharan Africa, affecting younger individuals.
  • Transplant-associated KS: Seen in organ transplant recipients on immunosuppressive therapy.
  • AIDS-associated KS: Seen in HIV-positive individuals, especially those with low CD4 counts.

Pathophysiology: Caused by HHV-8, which infects endothelial cells, leading to angiogenesis and tumor growth.

Diagnosis:

  • Confirmed by biopsy showing spindle-shaped cells, angiogenesis, and extravasated red blood cells.
  • PCR or serology for HHV-8 can be used for detection.

Management:

  • ART: Restores immune function in HIV/AIDS, reducing KS lesions.
  • Chemotherapy: Liposome-encapsulated doxorubicin or paclitaxel for advanced KS.
  • Radiotherapy: Effective for localized lesions.
  • Surgical Treatment: Cryotherapy or excision for small lesions.

Basal cell carcinoma (Option A): This skin cancer typically presents as a pearly, nodular lesion, usually on sun-exposed areas, and does not have the violaceous coloration seen in Kaposi sarcoma.

Malignant melanoma (Option C): Malignant melanoma often presents as dark, irregularly pigmented lesions with asymmetry, and is not characteristic of the violaceous macules seen in this case.

Squamous cell carcinoma (Option D): Squamous cell carcinoma can occur in the oral cavity but usually appears as an ulcerative lesion or growth with a hard, raised edge, not as violaceous macules or plaques.



Reference:

Robbins and Cotran Pathologic Basis of Disease, 10th Edition, Page: 520-522.

question: A 50-year-old HIV patient presented with a painful lesion, as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The clinical presentation of a HIV-positive patient with persistent cough, weight loss, skin lesions (umbilicated papules and nodules), and bilateral nodular infiltrates on chest x-ray, along with a low CD4 count, suggests a diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis.

Histoplasmosis

A systemic fungal infection caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus endemic in regions like the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, Central/South America, and Africa.

Pathophysiology:

  • Acquired by inhaling fungal microconidia from contaminated soil (bird/bat droppings).
  • Yeast forms multiply in macrophages, spreading through lymphatics and bloodstream.
  • Immunocompromised hosts (e.g., HIV/AIDS, CD4+ <200/μL) are at higher risk of dissemination.

Clinical Features:

  • Asymptomatic: Common in immunocompetent individuals.
  • Acute Pulmonary: Fever, cough, chest pain, flu-like symptoms.
  • Chronic Pulmonary: Associated with COPD, presenting with cough, weight loss, and cavitary lung lesions.

Progressive Disseminated Histoplasmosis (PDH):

  • Systemic: Fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, thrombocytopenia.
  • Lungs: Diffuse interstitial or reticulonodular infiltrates.
  • Skin: Papules, plaques, or ulcers (~10% cases).

HIV with disseminated cryptococcosis (Option B): Cryptococcosis is commonly associated with meningeal involvement in immunocompromised patients. This patient's symptoms (including the skin lesions and lung involvement) do not suggest cryptococcosis, especially as there are no signs of meningitis.

HIV with molluscum contagiosum (Option C): Molluscum contagiosum is a skin infection caused by a poxvirus, typically characterized by umbilicated papules on the skin. While this patient does have skin lesions, the lung involvement and the bilateral nodular infiltrates on the chest x-ray point to a systemic fungal infection rather than a localized skin condition.

HIV with tuberculosis (Option D): Tuberculosis would typically present with symptoms like cough, hemoptysis, and weight loss. However, the patient's negative sputum CBNAAT for tuberculosis and absence of granulomas on imaging make tuberculosis less likely.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page: 1658-1660.

question: A 45-year-old HIV-positive male came with complaints of persistent cough and weight loss. He has skin lesions that appear as umbilicated papules and nodules predominantly on the face, trunk, and upper extremities. Chest x-ray showed multiple bilateral nodular infiltrates. His sputum CBNAAT for tuberculosis was negative and he has a low CD4 count. What is the probable diagnosis?

explanationHtml:
• For the given HIV-positive patient with cryptococcal meningitis, Liposomal amphotericin B is the preferred initial therapy due to its higher efficacy and better penetration into the central nervous system. The treatment regimen consists of liposomal amphotericin B (L-AMB) combined with 5-flucytosine for 2 weeks as induction therapy, followed by fluconazole for 6 weeks as consolidation therapy.

Cryptococcal Meningitis

Common Cause
  • The leading infectious cause of meningitis in AIDS patients is primarily due to Cryptococcus neoformans (C. neoformans); C. gattii accounts for up to 12%.

Clinical Presentation
  • Symptoms include fever, nausea, vomiting, altered mental status, headache, and meningeal signs.
  • Low incidence of seizures and focal neurological deficits.
  • Kernig’s Sign- Positive when passive extension of the knee elicits pain; indicative of meningeal irritation.

CSF Profile
  • It may be normal or show modest elevations in WBC and protein levels.
  • Decreased glucose levels may be observed.
  • Elevated CSF opening pressure is typical.

Diagnosis
  • Identification of organisms via India ink examination of CSF.

[[figure-1]]

  • Detection of cryptococcal antigen in CSF or blood.
  • Blood cultures for fungi are often positive.
  • The biopsy may be necessary for diagnosing CNS cryptococcoma and to differentiate it from immune reconstitution syndrome.

Induction therapy
  • IV amphotericin B (0.7 mg/kg daily) or liposomal amphotericin (4–6 mg/kg daily) plus flucytosine (25 mg/kg qid) for at least 2 weeks.
  • Monitor renal function to avoid flucytosine toxicity.

Maintenance Therapy
  • Amphotericin should be continued until CSF culture is negative, followed by fluconazole (400 mg/d PO for 8 weeks, then 200 mg/d) until CD4+ T-cell count >200 cells/μL for 6 months.

Vancomycin (Option A): Vancomycin is primarily used to treat bacterial infections, particularly those caused by methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). It has no activity against Cryptococcus neoformans, and would be ineffective in treating cryptococcal meningitis.

High dose fluconazole with flucytosine (Option B): While these antifungal medications are used in cryptococcal meningitis treatment, they are not the optimal initial therapy for severe cases. High-dose fluconazole with flucytosine lacks the rapid fungicidal activity of liposomal amphotericin B and is reserved for maintenance therapy or cases where amphotericin B is contraindicated.

Voriconazole (Option C): Voriconazole is primarily used to treat invasive aspergillosis and other filamentous fungal infections. It is not the drug of choice for cryptococcal meningitis as it has limited evidence for efficacy against Cryptococcus neoformans compared to the standard regimen.



Reference:
  • Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 1109
  • Davidson’s Principles and Practice of Medicine, 24th Edition, Page 1118
  • Cryptococcal meningitis
question: An HIV-positive man presents with a high-grade fever. Examination reveals a positive Kernig's sign. CSF shows reduced glucose, increased protein, and increased leukocytes. A diagnosis of cryptococcal meningitis is made. What is the appropriate management for this patient?

explanationHtml:
• The clinical manifestations indicate a severe form of pneumonia known as Legionnaires' disease.The presentation includes high-grade fever, cough, confusion, along with hyponatremia and elevated liver enzymes. It is a strict aerobe that is poorly stained with gram stain, explaining the negative gram stain results despite active infection. The patient's immunocompromised status (HIV positive) and age further increase the risk for Legionella infection.

Legionnaires' Disease

General Features
  • Incubation period: 2-10 days
  • Non-specific flu-like symptoms initially
  • Often more severe than typical pneumonia

Clinical Features

Respiratory

  • Dry cough
  • Shortness of breath
  • Chest pain

Systemic

  • High fever (102-105°F)
  • Headache
  • Myalgias
  • Fatigue

Gastrointestinal

  • Diarrhea
  • Nausea/vomiting
  • Abdominal pain

Diagnosis

Laboratory Tests
  • Blood Analysis- Hyponatremia, Elevated Liver Enzymes
  • Urinary Antigen- Most common test, rapid results, detects L. pneumophila serogroup-1
  • Culture- Gold standard, requires special media, takes 3-5 days
  • PCR

Imaging Findings
  • Chest X-ray: Focal infiltrates/consolidation, predominantly lower lobes
  • CT: Ground-glass opacities, consolidation, pleural effusions possible
  • Can be multilobar in immunocompromised patients

Treatment

Mild-Moderate Disease:

  • Azithromycin 500mg PO daily
  • Levofloxacin 750mg PO daily
  • Clarithromycin 500mg PO BID

Severe Disease:

  • Levofloxacin 750mg IV daily
  • Azithromycin 500mg IV daily
  • Consider combination therapy for severe cases

Streptococcus (Option A): Streptococcus pneumoniae is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia, but it typically presents with a productive cough with rust-colored sputum. In this case, the sputum gram stain did not detect any organisms, making Streptococcus less likely. Additionally, the extrapulmonary symptoms are not typical for pneumococcal pneumonia.

Pneumocystis jiroveci (Option C): While the patient is HIV positive, the symptoms described and chest X-ray findings of bilateral infiltrates are not specific to Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia. PJP typically presents with a more gradual onset of dry cough and progressive dyspnea without the characteristic hyponatremia and liver enzyme elevation seen here. Also, chest X-ray shows pneumatoceles or thin-walled cysts and reticular opacities with septal thickening.

Klebsiella (Option D): Klebsiella causes pneumonia in individuals with a history of alcoholism or COPD. While the patient has a smoking history, the clinical presentation (including confusion and diarrhea) is inconsistent with Klebsiella pneumonia infection. Additionally, Klebsiella would typically be visible on gram stain.



Reference:

Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 1254-1257
question: A 70-year-old patient with a smoking history presents with high-grade fever, cough, confusion, and diarrhea. Chest X-ray shows bilateral infiltrates in bilateral lower lung fields. On sputum gram stain, no organisms were detected. Laboratory results reveal Na: 126mEq/L, AST:62, ALT:56, RBS:112 mg/dl, serum bilirubin of 0.8mg%, and a positive HIV test. Which of the following organisms is responsible?

correctAnswer: C. Negative skin tuberculin test and negative chest X-ray
explanationHtml:
• Cryptic tuberculosis is a rare and atypical presentation of tuberculosis where there is absence of both tuberculin skin test response (negative) and radiological findings on chest X-ray (negative), despite active Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection.
  • The standard diagnostic tools - tuberculin skin test (which measures delayed hypersensitivity response to M. tuberculosis antigens) and chest X-ray (which typically shows parenchymal infiltrates) - may not detect tuberculosis infection in its cryptic form.
  • In its severe form, known as cryptic miliary TB, the condition can lead to pancytopenia and massive hematogenous dissemination, with postmortem findings revealing multiple necrotic, nongranulomatous lesions.

Positive skin tuberculin test and negative chest X-ray (Option A) indicates a hypersensitivity response to M. tuberculosis without radiological evidence of active disease. This pattern typically suggests latent tuberculosis infection.

Positive skin tuberculin test and positive chest X-ray (Option B) represents the classical presentation of active pulmonary tuberculosis with both immunological response and radiological changes. In Cryptic tuberculosis, both these findings are absent.

Negative skin tuberculin test and positive chest X-ray (Option D) suggests active pulmonary disease without measurable immune response, commonly seen in immunocompromised states . While this can occur in some forms of TB, it does not represent cryptic tuberculosis where both tests are characteristically negative.



Reference:
  • Genotyping Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolates with few copies of IS6110: Value of additional genetic markers - ScienceDirect
  • IS6110-based restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) analysis of Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv and H37Ra - PubMed
  • TB lab investigations
  • Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Edition, Page 1367

Positive skin tuberculin test and positive chest X-ray
Negative skin tuberculin test and negative chest X-ray
Negative skin tuberculin test and positive chest X-ray

question: A 65-year-old male presented with unexplained fever and prolonged respiratory distress despite appropriate treatment. A diagnosis of cryptic tuberculosis was made. Which of the following is the correct statement related to this condition?

correctAnswer: B. Decreased FEV1, Decreased FVC, Normal or Increased FEV1/FVC ratio
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation and chest X-ray findings are suggestive of interstitial lung disease (ILD), a classic restrictive lung disease.

In restrictive lung disorders, lung expansion is limited due to fibrosis or stiff lung parenchyma, leading to reduced lung volumes and preserved or increased airflow relative to lung volume

Spirometry Pattern in Restrictive Lung Disease:

  • FEV1: ↓ Decreased (Due to reduced lung volumes)
  • FVC: ↓ Decreased (Primary abnormality)
  • FEV1/FVC ratio: Normal or Increased (Both FEV1 and FVC decrease proportionally, or FVC decreases more)

Decreased FEV1, Normal FVC, Decreased FEV1/FVC ratio (Option A): Suggests an obstructive pattern (e.g., asthma, COPD), where FEV1/FVC ratio is reduced.

Normal FEV1, Normal FVC, Normal FEV1/FVC ratio (Option C): Represents normal spirometry, inconsistent with symptomatic ILD and radiologic fibrosis.

Increased FEV1, Decreased FVC, Decreased FEV1/FVC ratio (Option D): Physiologically inconsistent and not seen in standard pulmonary pathologies.



Reference:

  1. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560880/
  2. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK560526/
  3. https://www.aafp.org/pubs/afp/issues/2014/0301/p359.html
