question: A 34-year-old South Asian man presents for a preventive health check-up. His LDL cholesterol is 168 mg/dL. He has no history of cardiovascular disease, but his father suffered a myocardial infarction at the age of 48 years. What is the most appropriate management?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • According to the changes in the 2026 AHA/ASA Acute Ischemic Stroke Guidelines, Tenecteplase has been upgraded to a Class I recommendation as the preferred first-line thrombolytic agent for eligible patients presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom onset.

  • The recommended dose is 0.25 mg/kg intravenously, with a maximum dose of 25 mg.

  • This replaces the previous preference for alteplase in many eligible patients.

  • Following intravenous thrombolysis, blood pressure should be maintained below 180/105 mmHg during the first 24 hours, while avoiding a systolic blood pressure below 140 mmHg to ensure adequate cerebral perfusion.

  • Early reperfusion remains the most effective strategy for salvaging ischemic but viable brain tissue.

AHA/ASA Acute Ischemic Stroke Guidelines (2026)

The 2026 AHA/ASA Guideline for the Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke replaces the 2018 guideline and the 2019 focused update.

The updated recommendations emphasise:

  • Faster reperfusion

  • Greater salvage of ischemic brain tissue

  • Expanded thrombolysis eligibility

  • Pediatric stroke management

New Stroke Classification

Disabling Stroke

Non-disabling Stroke

Deficits significantly affecting activities of daily living

Examples:

  • Complete hemianopia

  • Severe aphasia

Minor neurological deficits without significant functional impairment.

Treatment: Intravenous thrombolysis if eligible

Treatment

  • Dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) within 24 hours

  • Thrombolysis is not recommended

Extended Thrombolysis Window

Patients may undergo thrombolysis if presenting:

  • ≤9 hours from the midpoint of sleep, or

  • 4.5-9 hours from the last known well time

DWI-FLAIR mismatch and perfusion mismatch (new addition) are required in these patients

Thrombolytic Therapy

First-line Drug (Update): Tenecteplase

  • Class I recommendation

  • Preferred first-line thrombolytic

  • Dose: 0.25 mg/kg IV (Maximum 25 mg)

Blood Pressure After Reperfusion

During the first 24 hours after intravenous thrombolysis:

  • Maintain BP <180/105 mmHg

  • Do not allow systolic BP to fall below 140 mmHg

Blood Glucose Target: 140-180 mg/dL

  • The previous strategy targeting 80-130 mg/dL with intensive insulin therapy is no longer recommended.

Pediatric Acute Ischemic Stroke (New Section)

IV Thrombolysis

  • Alteplase

  • May be considered within 4.5 hours

  • Children 28 days to 18 years

  • Only for disabling neurological deficits

Mechanical Thrombectomy

Recommended for selected children:

  • ≥6 years

  • Large vessel occlusion

MRI: To exclude stroke mimics, which are more common in children.

Alteplase 0.9 mg/kg IV (Option B): Although alteplase remains an effective thrombolytic, the 2026 AHA/ASA guideline upgrades tenecteplase to a Class I recommendation as the preferred first-line thrombolytic for eligible adults presenting within 4.5 hours of symptom onset.

Dual antiplatelet therapy (Aspirin + Clopidogrel) (Option C): Dual antiplatelet therapy is recommended only for minor non-disabling ischemic strokes. This patient has right hemiparesis with global aphasia, representing a disabling stroke, for which intravenous thrombolysis is indicated.

Mechanical thrombectomy alone (Option D): Mechanical thrombectomy is reserved for selected patients with large vessel occlusion. In an eligible patient presenting within the thrombolysis window, intravenous tenecteplase should be administered first, with thrombectomy performed subsequently if indicated.



Reference:

https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/STR.0000000000000513
question: A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department 2 hours after the sudden onset of right-sided weakness and global aphasia. CT brain excludes intracranial hemorrhage. He has no contraindications to thrombolysis. Which of the following is the preferred initial thrombolytic therapy?

correctAnswer: B. Urgent clinical review with sepsis protocol activation
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient has a high NEWS2 score and clear clinical features of deterioration, including confusion, tachypnoea, hypotension, and hypoxia. A NEWS2 score of 7 or above requires emergency assessment, and suspected sepsis with deterioration should trigger immediate senior review and sepsis management.

Routine observation (Option A): This is inappropriate because NEWS2-9 indicates high risk of deterioration, not stable disease.

Discharge with oral antibiotics (Option C): Unsafe in a patient with possible sepsis and hemodynamic instability.

Repeat vitals after 24 hours (Option D): Delays urgent treatment and can miss rapid progression to shock.



Reference:

https://journals.lww.com/mjm/fulltext/2025/01000/recognizing_sepsis_early__a_proposed_national.

question: A 58-year-old man with fever, confusion, RR 26/min, BP 92/60 mmHg, HR 110/min, and SpO 93% on room air is triaged in the emergency department. His NEWS2 score is 9. What is the most appropriate next step?

explanationHtml:
• According to the GOLD 2026 guidelines, any patient with ≥1 moderate or severe exacerbation in the previous year is now classified as Group E, irrespective of symptom burden.

  • Previously, patients with a single moderate exacerbation could be classified under Groups A or B depending on symptoms.

  • Under the revised classification, Group E patients should receive initial dual bronchodilator therapy with a LABA (Long-Acting β₂-Agonist) plus a LAMA (Long-Acting Muscarinic Antagonist).

Triple therapy (LABA + LAMA + ICS) is not recommended routinely as initial therapy. It should be considered only in patients with blood eosinophil counts ≥300 cells/µL, as these patients are more likely to benefit from inhaled corticosteroids.

GOLD 2026 Guidelines for COPD

The Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) 2026 introduced significant changes in COPD classification and management.

The overall treatment goal is to achieve Low Disease Activity, defined as:

  • No exacerbations

  • No worsening of symptoms

  • No accelerated decline in lung function

The guideline also introduces:

  • AI-assisted diagnosis

  • Remote patient monitoring

to improve long-term outcomes.

COPD Severity (Spirometry)

Stage

Criteria

Stage I (Mild)

FEV₁/FVC <0.7 and FEV₁ ≥80% predicted

Stage II (Moderate)

FEV₁/FVC <0.7 and FEV₁ 50-79% predicted

Stage III (Severe)

FEV₁/FVC <0.7 and FEV₁ 30-49% predicted

Stage IV (Very Severe)

FEV₁/FVC <0.7 and FEV₁ <30% predicted

GOLD 2026 Guidelines for COPD:

Four Components Used for Treatment Modification (New)

Treatment should now be reassessed using:

  1. Symptoms

  2. Exacerbations

  3. Lung function

  4. Blood eosinophil count

GOLD Group

Criteria

Initial Pharmacological Treatment

Group A

• 0 exacerbations in previous year

• mMRC 0-1

• CAAT <10 (Chronic Airways Assessment Test)

Any bronchodilator

Group B

• 0 exacerbations in previous year

• mMRC ≥2 or CAAT ≥10

LABA + LAMA

Group E (Update)

≥1 moderate exacerbation or severe exacerbation in the previous year

LABA + LAMA

mMRC Dyspnoea Scale

Score

Description

0

Breathless only with strenuous exercise

1

Breathless when hurrying or walking uphill

2

Walks slower than peers or stops on level ground

3

Stops after walking about 100 m

4

Breathless at rest

Short-acting bronchodilator alone (Option A): Short-acting bronchodilators are used mainly for symptom relief (rescue therapy) and are not recommended as initial maintenance treatment for a patient classified as Group E.

LAMA (Option B): Single long-acting bronchodilator therapy is inadequate for Group E patients. The GOLD 2026 update recommends dual bronchodilator therapy (LABA + LAMA) for all patients with at least one moderate or severe exacerbation.

LABA + ICS (Option D): LABA + ICS is no longer the preferred initial regimen for COPD. Inhaled corticosteroids should generally be added only in combination with LABA + LAMA and primarily in patients with blood eosinophil counts ≥300 cells/µL or other appropriate indications.

https://goldcopd.org/2026-gold-report-and-pocket-guide/
question: A 67-year-old man with COPD presents for follow-up. Over the past year, he had one moderate exacerbation requiring treatment with oral corticosteroids and antibiotics but no hospitalization. Spirometry confirms persistent airflow obstruction. According to the GOLD 2026 guidelines, what is the most appropriate initial pharmacological therapy?

correctAnswer: B. Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This patient has a high-risk TIA (ABCD2 score of 4 or above) with DWI-positive imaging, meeting the criteria for dual antiplatelet therapy as per AHA/ASA 2026. DAPT with aspirin and clopidogrel is recommended for 21 days, after which single antiplatelet therapy is continued for secondary prevention.

  • This recommendation is supported by the POINT and CHANCE trials, which demonstrated that early DAPT significantly reduces the risk of recurrent stroke in the first 90 days after minor stroke or high-risk TIA compared with aspirin alone.
  • Aspirin should be initiated within 48 hours for all AIS patients; for high-risk TIA and minor stroke, DAPT is the preferred initial strategy.
  • The 21-day duration is deliberate, as longer DAPT durations increase bleeding risk without additional ischemic benefit in this population.

Aspirin monotherapy for 90 days (Option A): Aspirin alone is insufficient for high-risk TIA or minor stroke with an ABCD2 score of 4 or above. The 2026 guidelines explicitly recommend DAPT in this setting to maximise early secondary prevention.

Anticoagulation with heparin as first-line treatment(Option C): Heparin is not recommended as first-line therapy in non-cardioembolic TIA or minor stroke. Antiplatelet therapy is the evidence-based approach for non-cardioembolic events in the acute setting.

No antiplatelet therapy (Option D): Resolved symptoms do not diminish the risk of early recurrent stroke. A DWI-positive TIA carries the same urgent treatment implications as a completed minor stroke, and deferring antiplatelet therapy places the patient at significant risk.



Reference:

https://www.ahajournals.org/doi

options.text: Dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel
Anticoagulation with heparin as first-line treatment

question: A 61-year-old woman presents with a 30-minute episode of right-hand weakness and slurred speech that fully resolved. Her NIHSS on arrival is 0. ABCD2 score is 5. MRI DWI shows a small area of restricted diffusion consistent with an acute ischemic infarct. According to AHA/ASA 2026 guidelines, what is the most appropriate antiplatelet strategy?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • AHA/ASA 2026 recommends both tenecteplase and alteplase within the 4.5-hour window. The correct tenecteplase dose is 0.25 mg/kg (max 25 mg). This dose showed efficacy comparable to alteplase, with the added benefit of single-bolus administration.

Tenecteplase 0.4 mg/kg (Option A): This dose is not specifically recommended by the AHA/ASA 2026 guidelines. This higher dose was tested in trials but did not show improved outcomes and carries a higher risk of bleeding compared with 0.25 mg/kg.

Streptokinase (Option B): Streptokinase is not recommended in acute ischemic stroke. It showed significantly higher rates of hemorrhagic transformation and mortality in stroke trials and has been abandoned for this indication.

Urokinase (Option D): Urokinase is not a recommended agent for acute ischemic stroke in the AHA/ASA 2026 guidelines. It is not part of the current evidence base for stroke thrombolysis.



Reference:

https://www.ahajournals.org/doi.
question: A 58-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a sudden onset of facial droop and left arm weakness. Symptom onset was 3 hours ago. CT head rules out haemorrhage. Which thrombolytic agent and dose is recommended by AHA/ASA 2026?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

This 2-year-old boy presents with the classic clinical triad of Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (WAS):

  • Atopic dermatitis (eczema-like rash)

  • Recurrent infections (due to immunodeficiency)

  • Thrombocytopenia with small platelets (manifesting here as epistaxis, blood in stools, and a severely low platelet count of 25,000/uL).

Bruton's tyrosine kinase (Option A): A deficiency in BTK causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton's disease). Patients have severely reduced B-cells and immunoglobulins, leading to recurrent bacterial infections, but they do not have thrombocytopenia or eczema.

Fibrillin (Option C): A deficiency in fibrillin causes Marfan syndrome, a connective tissue disorder characterized by tall stature, long fingers, aortic aneurysms, and lens dislocation. It is not associated with immunodeficiency or low platelets.

Adenosine deaminase (Option D): A deficiency in ADA causes a form of Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) due to toxic purine buildup destroying lymphocytes. While patients have severe infections, they do not present with thrombocytopenia or the classic eczema seen in WAS.



Reference:

https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-gene-therapy-treatment-wiskott-aldrich-syndrome.
question: A 2 year old boy presented with atopic dermatitis like rash, recurrent infections, epistaxis and blood in stools. On investigations, his Hb was 11.1 g/dl, TLC was 9600/uL, and Platelet count was 25,000/uL. Which protein is deficient in this child?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Etuvetidigene autotemcel is indicated for pediatric patients aged ≥6 months and adults with WAS who have a confirmed mutation in the WAS gene and for whom HSCT is appropriate, but no suitable HLA-matched related stem cell donor is available. This patient meets all three criteria: a confirmed WAS gene mutation, severe clinical disease, and the absence of a matched related donor.

Splenectomy followed by lifelong prophylactic antibiotics (Option A): While splenectomy can transiently improve platelet counts, it does not correct the underlying genetic defect and carries a significant lifelong risk of overwhelming bacterial sepsis - particularly pneumococcal sepsis - making it a poor definitive option.

Initiation of long-term thrombopoietin receptor agonists (Option B): Thrombopoietin receptor agonists are used off-label to manage thrombocytopenia symptomatically but do not address the fundamental platelet dysfunction, immune deficiency, or the genetic cause of WAS - they are palliative, not curative.

Standard allogeneic HSCT from a mismatched unrelated donor (Option D): While allogeneic HSCT is a recognised curative option for WAS, outcomes are significantly better with matched sibling donors. In the absence of a matched related donor, etuvetidigene autotemcel provides a curative gene therapy alternative that additionally avoids the risk of graft-versus-host disease (GvHD).



Reference:

https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-approves-first-gene-therapy-treatment-wiskott-aldrich-syndrome.

A search for a suitable HLA-matched related stem cell donor is unsuccessful. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive therapeutic option for this patient?

correctAnswer: B. Immediately, ideally within 1 hour of recognition
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • For probable or definite septic shock, the SSC 2026 guidelines recommend administering antimicrobial therapy immediately, ideally within 1 hour of recognition. This is a strong recommendation because early antibiotic administration is one of the most important mortality-reducing interventions in septic shock.

Within 24 hours after cultures are reported (Option A): This is far too late in shock and is associated with worse outcomes.

Only after procalcitonin becomes elevated (Option C): Biomarkers should not delay treatment when septic shock is clinically likely.

Within 6 hours if blood pressure improves (Option D): Antibiotics should still be given urgently; improvement in BP does not justify delay in septic shock.



Reference:

https://journals.lww.com/ccmjournal/fulltext/2026/04000/surviving_sepsis_campaign__international.

question: A 54-year-old man is admitted with probable septic shock. The source is likely bacterial, and he is hypotensive with rising lactate. The treating team asks how quickly antimicrobials should be given. According to SSC 2026, what is the correct timing?

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The SSC 2026 guidelines make a new conditional recommendation that for adults aged 65 years or older with septic shock, an initial MAP range of 60 to 65 mmHg is preferable over higher targets.

65 mmHg or above (Option A): This is the general strong recommendation for septic shock in adults of all ages. However, for patients aged 65 years and above specifically, the 2026 guidelines issue a separate conditional recommendation for the lower range of 60 to 65 mmHg, reflecting evidence that higher MAP targets in this group increase vasopressor exposure and may increase mortality.

70 to 75 mmHg (Option C): Higher MAP targets have been associated with increased risk of atrial fibrillation and greater vasopressor requirements without a mortality benefit, and are not recommended by SSC 2026 as an initial target in either general adult or elderly septic shock populations.

80 to 85 mmHg (Option D): The SEPSISPAM trial comparing MAP targets of 65 to 70 mmHg versus 80 to 85 mmHg found no overall difference in mortality, but a higher risk of atrial fibrillation with higher targets. Targeting 80-85 mmHg is not recommended.



Reference:

https://journals.lww.com/ccmjournal/fulltext/2026/04000/surviving_sepsis_campaign__international.
question: A 71-year-old man with a history of hypertension is admitted to the ICU with septic shock secondary to pneumonia. He is on norepinephrine infusion at 0.18 mcg/kg/min. Despite adequate fluid resuscitation, his MAP remains at 72 mmHg, and the treating team is debating the target MAP. According to the Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 guidelines, what is the recommended initial MAP target for this patient?

correctAnswer: B. Consider senior review because a single score of 3 is important
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • A score of 3 in any single parameter warrants clinical review and should raise concern, even if the total NEWS2 is not very high. This reflects the fact that a single markedly abnormal vital sign can indicate early deterioration.

Ignore it unless total NEWS2 reaches 10 (Option A): This is unsafe and delays recognition of deterioration.

Discharge if all other values are normal (Option C): A single severe abnormality still requires review.

Repeat the score only after 24 hours (Option D): This is too long to wait for a patient with possible deterioration.



Reference:

https://journals.lww.com/mjm/fulltext/2025/01000/recognizing_sepsis_early__a_proposed_national

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • The Lumipulse G pTau217/β-Amyloid 1-42 Plasma Ratio is interpreted as positive when the ratio is ≥0.00738.

  • A value of 0.0081 therefore indicates the presence of amyloid pathology, making Alzheimer’s disease much more likely in a patient with compatible cognitive symptoms.

This blood test supports the diagnosis and should always be interpreted along with the patient’s clinical presentation rather than being used as a standalone diagnostic tool.

Alzheimer’s Disease

  • Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common cause of dementia, accounting for approximately 60-80% of dementia cases.

  • It is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterised by impairment of memory followed by decline in other cognitive functions, ultimately interfering with activities of daily living.

Pathophysiology

The two hallmark pathological abnormalities are:

  • Extracellular β-amyloid plaques

  • Intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau (neurofibrillary tangles)

These changes lead to:

  • Synaptic dysfunction

  • Neuronal loss

  • Cortical atrophy (especially hippocampus and temporal lobe)

  • Progressive cognitive decline

Clinical Features

Early stage

Progressive stage

Late stage

  • Recent memory loss

  • Repetition of questions

  • Misplacing objects

  • Difficulty learning new information

  • Language impairment

  • Executive dysfunction

  • Visuospatial impairment

  • Behavioral disturbances

  • Personality changes

  • Severe dementia

  • Dependence for activities of daily living

  • Dysphagia

  • Immobility

  • Increased risk of infections

Diagnosis

Diagnosis is based on:

  • Clinical history

  • Cognitive assessment (MMSE, MoCA)

  • Functional assessment

  • Neuroimaging (MRI/CT to exclude other causes)

  • Biomarkers when indicated

Biomarkers

  • CSF β-amyloid 42

  • CSF phosphorylated tau

  • Amyloid PET scan

  • Tau PET scan

  • Blood biomarkers (latest FDA-approved test)

Blood Test for Alzheimer’s Disease

Lumipulse G pTau217/β-Amyloid 1-42 Plasma Ratio

This is the first FDA-approved blood test for the early detection of Alzheimer’s disease in:

  • Adults ≥50 years

  • Patients presenting with cognitive impairment

The test estimates the likelihood of underlying amyloid pathology, helping identify patients who may have Alzheimer’s disease.

Principle

The assay measures:

  • Plasma phosphorylated Tau-217 (pTau217)

  • Plasma β-Amyloid 1-42

Both analytes are measured using a two-step Chemiluminescent Enzyme Immunoassay (CLEIA) on the Lumipulse G system.

The measured concentrations are combined to generate a ratio ranging from:

0.00000–1.00000

Interpretation

Plasma Ratio

Interpretation

≤0.00370

Negative (Option B):

  • Amyloid pathology is unlikely.

  • Other causes of cognitive decline should be investigated.

0.00371–0.00737

Indeterminate (Option C):

  • Further evaluation is recommended.

  • Additional testing such as CSF biomarkers or amyloid PET may be required.

≥0.00738

Positive:

  • Suggests underlying cerebral amyloid pathology.

  • Supports the diagnosis of Alzheimer’s disease in the appropriate clinical setting.

  • Clinical correlation remains essential.

Advantages of the Blood Test

  • Less invasive than CSF examination

  • Significantly cheaper than amyloid PET

  • Easily accessible

  • Suitable for early evaluation of patients with cognitive impairment

  • May reduce unnecessary invasive investigations

The test confirms vascular dementia as the cause of cognitive impairment. (Option D): Lumipulse G assay detects biomarkers associated with Alzheimer’s disease (amyloid pathology and phosphorylated tau). It does not diagnose vascular dementia, frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body dementia, or other neurodegenerative disorders. Clinical assessment and appropriate imaging are required to diagnose these conditions.



Reference:
  1. Harrison’s Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd Edition, Pages 3475-4377.
  2. https://www.fda.gov/news-events/press-announcements/fda-clears-first-blood-test-used-diagnosing-alzheimers-disease

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Oral semaglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist approved for improving glycaemic control in adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus as an adjunct to diet and exercise.

  • It has also received FDA approval for reducing the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), including myocardial infarction and stroke, in patients at high cardiovascular risk.

  • In addition, it promotes clinically significant weight loss.

Oral Semaglutide

Class: GLP-1 receptor agonist

Mechanism of Action

  • Stimulates glucose-dependent insulin secretion from pancreatic β-cells.

  • Suppresses glucagon secretion from α-cells.

  • Delays gastric emptying.

  • Reduces appetite, promoting weight loss.

Latest FDA Update

  • Approved as an adjunct to diet and exercise for adults with type 2 diabetes mellitus.

  • Extended approval for reducing MACE in high-risk patients.

  • Benefits extend to both primary and secondary cardiovascular prevention.

Oral Formulation

The oral tablet contains an absorption enhancer that:

  • Increases gastric pH.

  • Protects semaglutide from proteolytic degradation.

  • Improves gastrointestinal absorption.

Administration:

  • 3mg orally, OD x 30 days

  • 7mg orally, OD (after 30 days)

  • If the glycemic control is inadequate after 30 days with 7mg OD → increase the dose to 14mg orally, OD.

  • Taken on an empty stomach

Contraindications

  • Personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC).

  • MEN 2 syndrome.

Adverse Effects

  • Pancreatitis.

  • Diabetic retinopathy and its complications.

  • Acute kidney injury.

  • Hypoglycaemia (especially with insulin or sulfonylureas).

  • Hypersensitivity reactions.

  • Thyroid C-cell tumours in rodents (no definitive link in humans)090

Stimulates glucagon secretion from α-cells (Option B): Semaglutide suppresses, rather than stimulates, glucagon secretion from pancreatic α-cells. This contributes to lower hepatic glucose output and improved glycaemic control.

Is approved for type 1 diabetes mellitus (Option C): Oral semaglutide is approved only for type 2 diabetes mellitus. It is not indicated for patients with type 1 diabetes.

Is safe in patients with MEN 2 syndrome (Option D): Semaglutide is contraindicated in patients with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN 2, owing to concerns about thyroid C-cell tumours observed in animal studies.



Reference:

correctAnswer: A. It inhibits PDE4, thereby reducing inflammation and fibrosis.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Nerandomilast is a newly FDA-approved drug for the treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) in adults.

  • It acts by inhibiting phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4), thereby reducing inflammation and fibrosis within the lung parenchyma.

  • This slows the progressive decline in lung function, which is the major therapeutic goal in patients with IPF.

Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF)

  • Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the most common interstitial lung disease (ILD) occurring due to an unknown cause.

  • It is a chronic, progressive, and fatal fibrosing lung disease characterised by fibrosis and scarring of the lung parenchyma, leading to worsening pulmonary function and, ultimately, respiratory failure.

  • As fibrosis progresses, there is a decline in lung function with reduced TLC, FEV₁, and FVC, reflecting a restrictive ventilatory defect.

The FDA has recently approved Nerandomilast for the treatment of idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) in adults.

The drug helps slow the decline in lung function, thereby delaying disease progression.

Mechanism of Action

Phosphodiesterase-4 (PDE4) plays an important role in the pathogenesis of IPF by increasing inflammation and fibrosis.

Nerandomilast:

  • Inhibits PDE4.

  • Reduces inflammation.

  • Decreases fibrosis and scarring of lung tissue.

  • Significantly slows the decline in lung function.

Dosage and Administration

Recommendation

Dose

Recommended dose

18 mg orally twice daily, approximately 12 hours apart, with or without food

Alternative dose

9 mg orally twice daily for patients unable to tolerate the recommended dose

Adverse Effects

  • Diarrhoea

  • COVID-19

  • Upper respiratory tract infection

  • Depression

  • Decreased weight

  • Decreased appetite

  • Nausea

  • Fatigue

  • Headache

  • Vomiting

  • Back pain

  • Dizziness

It increases lung fibrosis by stimulating fibroblast activity (Option B): Nerandomilast reduces fibrosis by inhibiting PDE4. It slows the progression of lung scarring rather than promoting fibroblast-mediated fibrosis

It inhibits fibrosis by increasing PDE4 activity (Option C): Nerandomilast inhibits, rather than increases, PDE4 activity.


It reverses established pulmonary fibrosis and restores normal lung function (Option D): Nerandomilast does not reverse existing fibrosis or restore normal lung architecture. Its primary benefit is to slow the progression of fibrosis and the decline in lung function, thereby delaying disease progression rather than curing IPF.

Explanation:

  • According to the 2024 ATS/ERS classification of Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD), Alveolar Filling Disorders constitute a separate primary category.

  • This category includes

    • Acute Eosinophilic Pneumonia (AEP)

    • Chronic Eosinophilic Pneumonia (CEP)

    • Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (both idiopathic/unclassifiable and secondary forms)

    • Exogenous and endogenous lipoid pneumonia.

Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis (IPF) is not an alveolar filling disorder; it is classified under Primary (Idiopathic) Interstitial Pneumonia.

Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD)

Interstitial lung disease (ILD) comprises a heterogeneous group of diffuse parenchymal lung disorders characterised by varying degrees of inflammation and fibrosis affecting the lung interstitium.

The 2024 ATS/ERS update has revised the classification to improve diagnostic accuracy and better reflect the underlying disease process.

The American Thoracic Society (ATS) and the European Respiratory Society (ERS) updated the classification of Interstitial Lung Disease (ILD) in 2024.

  • Interstitial Disorders and Alveolar Filling Disorders are now recognised as the two primary categories of ILD.

  • Each category is further subdivided into Primary (Idiopathic) and Secondary diseases where applicable.

  • The updated classification also recognises diseases with combined patterns.

  • New disease terminologies and disease types are based on multidisciplinary criteria, rather than relying only on pathological and radiological patterns as in the previous classification.

  • This multidisciplinary approach allows greater diagnostic accuracy and enables reassessment of the diagnosis over time as new clinical, radiological, or pathological information becomes available.

2024 ATS/ERS Classification of ILD

Secondary Interstitial Pneumonia

Explanation:

  • Lenacapavir is the first FDA-approved injectable drug for HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP).

  • It is also the first and only PrEP drug that provides 6 months of protection against HIV with twice-yearly administration.

  • Clinical trials demonstrated excellent efficacy, with more than 99% of participants remaining HIV-negative, making it a major advance in HIV prevention.

HIV Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP)

Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) involves the use of antiretroviral drugs in HIV-negative individuals who are at substantial risk of acquiring HIV infection. It significantly reduces the risk of HIV acquisition when taken appropriately.

The FDA has approved injectable lenacapavir for pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) of HIV.

  • First FDA-approved injectable PrEP drug providing 6 months of protection.

  • First and only PrEP drug administered twice yearly.

  • In clinical trials, more than 99% of participants remained HIV-negative.

Mechanism of Action

  • Lenacapavir is a long-acting HIV-1 capsid inhibitor.

  • It binds directly to the HIV capsid and interferes with multiple stages of the viral life cycle, including:

    • Nuclear transport

    • Capsid assembly

    • Virus assembly

    • Viral release

Dosage and Administration

HIV Screening

  • All individuals must be screened for HIV-1 infection before every dose of lenacapavir.

  • Unknown or positive HIV-1 status is a contraindication to its use.

Initiation

Day

Dose

Day 1

927 mg by subcutaneous injection into the abdomen or thigh + 600 mg orally

Day 2

600 mg orally

Continuation: 927 mg by subcutaneous injection every 6 months, calculated from the date of the last injection.

Adverse Effects

  • Injection-site reactions

  • Headache

  • Nausea

Cabotegravir (Option B): Cabotegravir is also a long-acting injectable drug used for HIV PrEP, but it does not provide 6 months of protection. The recent FDA approval described in the question specifically refers to lenacapavir, the first and only PrEP agent administered twice yearly.

Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (Option C): Tenofovir disoproxil fumarate, usually combined with emtricitabine, is an established oral PrEP regimen. It requires regular oral dosing and is not a long-acting injectable agent providing 6 months of protection.

Emtricitabine (Option D): Emtricitabine is used in combination with tenofovir as part of oral PrEP regimens. It is not used alone for HIV PrEP and is not a long-acting injectable drug. The drug described in the question is lenacapavir, which has a unique mechanism as an HIV-1 capsid inhibitor and requires administration only twice a year.

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

MASH (Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis) is the newly adopted term for non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH).

Metabolic Dysfunction-Associated Steatohepatitis (MASH)

  • MASH is the new name for Non-Alcoholic Steatohepatitis (NASH).

  • It represents the inflammatory form of fatty liver disease associated with metabolic dysfunction and has the potential to progress to fibrosis, cirrhosis, and liver failure if left untreated.

  • The new terminology shifts the focus from the absence of alcohol intake to the presence of metabolic risk factors, which are central to disease pathogenesis.

Metabolic Dysfunction

MASH is associated with one or more of the following:

  • Type 2 diabetes mellitus

  • Pre-diabetes (insulin resistance)

  • High BMI or obesity

  • Hyperlipidaemia

  • Hypertension

The term MASH was adopted because it:

  • Highlights the underlying metabolic dysfunction.

  • Reduces the stigma associated with the term “non-alcoholic.”

  • Enhances diagnostic clarity.

  • Better aligns with the evolving understanding of fatty liver disease.

Screening

Patients at risk, such as those with:

  • Type 2 diabetes mellitus

  • Hypertension

  • Hyperlipidaemia

  • Other metabolic risk factors

should undergo liver function tests (LFTs) once every year.

Patients with elevated LFTs should undergo an imaging study, such as ultrasonography (USG), to evaluate for fatty liver.

Confirmatory Test

  • Liver biopsy remains the confirmatory investigation.

  • It distinguishes simple steatosis from MASH, which is important because MASH can progress to liver scarring (fibrosis).

Treatment

Management primarily focuses on correcting the underlying metabolic abnormalities.

1. Lifestyle Modification

  • Healthy diet

  • Regular exercise

2. Weight Reduction

  • Loss of approximately 10% of body weight may:

    • Reduce hepatic fat.

    • Decrease liver inflammation.

    • Potentially regress hepatic scar tissue (fibrosis).

3. Control of Associated Diseases: Adequate treatment of:

  • Diabetes mellitus

  • Hypertension

  • Hyperlipidaemia

is essential to slow disease progression.

MASLD (Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease) (Option A): MASLD refers to the broader spectrum of metabolic dysfunction-associated fatty liver disease. MASLD is the umbrella term replacing NAFLD, whereas MASH specifically replaces NASH.

AFLD (Alcohol-associated fatty liver disease) (Option C): Alcohol-associated fatty liver disease is a separate entity caused by excessive alcohol consumption. The condition described in the question is associated with metabolic dysfunction, not alcohol.

Autoimmune hepatitis (Option D): Autoimmune hepatitis is an immune-mediated inflammatory liver disease characterised by autoantibodies and elevated immunoglobulin levels. It is unrelated to the recent nomenclature change from NASH to MASH and is not primarily driven by metabolic risk factors.



Reference:

https://gi.org/topics/steatotic-liver-disease-masld/

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Nipocalimab is a newly FDA-approved monoclonal antibody for the treatment of generalised myasthenia gravis (gMG) in adults and children >12 years of age.

  • It acts by blocking the neonatal fragment crystallisable receptor (FcRn), resulting in a marked reduction in circulating IgG antibodies, which are the pathogenic antibodies responsible for myasthenia gravis.

Generalised Myasthenia Gravis (gMG)

  • Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction characterised by fatigable skeletal muscle weakness.

  • The disease is most commonly caused by IgG autoantibodies directed against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) or other neuromuscular junction proteins.

The FDA has approved Nipocalimab for the treatment of:

  • Generalised myasthenia gravis (gMG)

  • Adults

  • Children >12 years of age

A major therapeutic benefit of Nipocalimab is its ability to produce up to a 75% reduction in circulating IgG levels, which are the pathognomonic antibodies in myasthenia gravis.

Mechanism of Action

Nipocalimab is a monoclonal antibody.

  • Neonatal fragment crystallisable receptor (FcRn) is responsible for:

    • Transport of IgG.

    • Prolongation of the half-life of IgG.

  • Nipocalimab:

    • Binds to FcRn.

    • Blocks FcRn-mediated IgG recycling.

    • Reduces circulating IgG antibody levels.

Dosage

Stage

Dose

Initial dose

30 mg/kg IV infusion

Maintenance dose

15 mg/kg IV infusion every 2 weeks thereafter

Adverse Effects

  • Respiratory tract infections

  • Urinary tract infections

  • Peripheral oedema

  • Muscle spasms

  • Herpes zoster

  • Herpes simplex

  • Oral infections

Rituximab (Option B): Rituximab is an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody that depletes B lymphocytes. Although it may be used off-label in selected patients with refractory myasthenia gravis, it does not act by blocking FcRn and is not the newly FDA-approved monoclonal antibody described in the question.

Eculizumab (Option C): Eculizumab is a complement (C5) inhibitor used in selected patients with AChR antibody-positive refractory generalised myasthenia gravis. It reduces complement-mediated damage at the neuromuscular junction but does not reduce IgG levels by blocking FcRn.

Ravulizumab (Option D): Ravulizumab is a long-acting C5 complement inhibitor used for generalised myasthenia gravis in selected patients. Its mechanism involves complement inhibition, not FcRn blockade, and it does not directly lower circulating IgG concentrations.



Reference:

https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2025/761430s000lbl.pdf

correctAnswer: C. Routine complete revascularisation should be avoided in NSTEMI.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

According to the 2025 AHA/ACC guidelines, complete revascularisation is recommended in both STEMI and NSTEMI whenever appropriate. Therefore, the statement that complete revascularisation should be avoided in NSTEMI is incorrect.

Patients with ACS should also receive evidence-based secondary prevention measures, including dual antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statin therapy, and referral to cardiac rehabilitation.

Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)

Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) is a spectrum of acute myocardial ischemia that includes:

  • Unstable angina (UA)

  • Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI)

  • ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI)

The 2025 AHA/ACC guidelines provide updated recommendations regarding antiplatelet therapy, lipid management, PCI strategy, revascularisation, and secondary prevention.

Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT)

  • DAPT is recommended for all patients admitted with ACS.

  • Prasugrel or ticagrelor are preferred in patients undergoing PCI.

  • In patients with NSTEMI planned for invasive procedures, clopidogrel or ticagrelor are recommended to reduce the risk of major cardiovascular adverse events.

DAPT in Secondary Prevention

  1. Aspirin plus an oral P2Y12 inhibitor is recommended for at least 12 months in patients without a high bleeding risk. (Option A ruled out)

  2. Patients requiring long-term anticoagulation

  • Aspirin should be discontinued 1-4 weeks after PCI.

  • Continue:

    • Clopidogrel (P2Y12 inhibitor)

    • Oral anticoagulant

This strategy reduces bleeding risk while maintaining antithrombotic protection.

Lipid-Lowering Therapy

  • High-intensity statin therapy is recommended for all patients with ACS. (Option B ruled out)

  • A non-statin lipid-lowering agent should be added in patients:

    • Already receiving the maximum tolerated statin dose, and

    • LDL-C ≥70 mg/dL.

Procedural Strategy During PCI

  • Radial artery access is preferred over femoral access because it reduces vascular complications and bleeding.

Revascularization

  • Complete revascularisation is recommended in both:

    • STEMI

    • NSTEMI

  • Prompt revascularisation is recommended in patients presenting with cardiogenic shock.

Secondary Prevention

Following initiation of lipid-lowering therapy:

  • Obtain a fasting lipid profile after 4–8 weeks.

  • Refer all eligible patients for cardiac rehabilitation as part of comprehensive secondary prevention. (Option D ruled out)



Reference:

  2. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0735109725002025

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

According to the 2025 ADA Standards of Care, patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) or chronic kidney disease (CKD) should preferably receive an SGLT2 inhibitor (or a GLP-1 receptor agonist, where appropriate) because these agents improve cardiovascular and renal outcomes in addition to glycaemic control.

ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes (2025)

The American Diabetes Association (ADA) has released the 2025 Standards of Care in Diabetes, providing updated recommendations on screening, diagnosis, lifestyle management, pharmacotherapy, and glucose monitoring.

Screening for Presymptomatic Type 1 Diabetes

Individuals with a positive family history of type 1 diabetes mellitus should be considered for screening with pancreatic islet autoantibodies.

The recommended autoantibodies are:

  • Insulin autoantibodies (IAA)

  • Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies

  • Islet antigen-2 (IA-2) antibodies

  • Zinc transporter-8 (ZnT8) antibodies

These tests help identify individuals at risk before the onset of symptomatic type 1 diabetes.

Pharmacotherapy

1. Type 2 Diabetes with HFpEF or CKD

Recommend:

  • SGLT2 inhibitors

  • GLP-1 receptor agonists

These drugs provide cardiovascular and renal protection in addition to improving glycaemic control.

2. Stage 2 Type 1 Diabetes

For selected individuals aged ≥8 years with Stage 2 type 1 diabetes, the ADA recommends:

  • Teplizumab infusion

This delays progression to symptomatic (Stage 3) type 1 diabetes.

3. Type 2 Diabetes with MASLD and Overweight/Obesity

Consider:

  • GLP-1 receptor agonists

  • Dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonists

These agents improve glycaemic control, promote weight loss, and may benefit patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD).

Glucose Monitoring

For patients receiving:

  • Insulin therapy, or

  • Oral hypoglycaemic agents (OHAs)

the ADA recommends early initiation of Continuous Glucose Monitoring (CGM).

Benefits include:

  • Improved glycaemic outcomes.

  • Early detection and prevention of hypoglycaemia.

  • Better day-to-day glucose management.

Sulfonylurea (Option A): 2025 ADA Standards of Care specifically recommend SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with type 2 diabetes and HFpEF or CKD because of their proven cardiovascular and renal benefits. Sulfonylureas do not provide these additional benefits.

α-Glucosidase inhibitor (Option C): α-glucosidase inhibitors primarily lower postprandial glucose and are not recommended preferentially for patients with HFpEF or CKD in the updated ADA guidelines.

Meglitinide (Option D): Meglitinides stimulate insulin secretion and may improve glycaemic control but do not confer the cardiovascular or renal benefits emphasised in the 2025 ADA recommendations for patients with HFpEF or CKD.



Reference:
  1. https://diabetes.org/newsroom/press-releases/american-diabetes-association-releases-standards-care-diabetes-2025
  2. https://diabetesjournals.org/care/issue/48/Supplement_1
  3. https://www.guidelinecentral.com/guideline/14119/#section-anchor-1226455

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

  • Mirikizumab is a newly FDA-approved humanised IgG4 monoclonal antibody for the treatment of moderate-to-severe Crohn’s disease.

  • Clinical trials demonstrated that it is effective and safe, particularly in patients who failed to respond to previous biologic therapy or lost response over time.

  • In addition, Mirikizumab is also approved for treating adults with moderate-to-severe active ulcerative colitis (UC).

Crohn’s Disease

  • Crohn’s disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) characterised by transmural inflammation that can affect any part of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the anus.

  • It commonly presents with abdominal pain, chronic diarrhoea, weight loss, and extraintestinal manifestations.

The FDA has approved Mirikizumab for the treatment of moderate-to-severe Crohn’s disease.

  • Approved for moderate-to-severe Crohn’s disease.

  • Demonstrated efficacy and safety in a double-blind, randomised controlled trial.

  • Particularly beneficial in patients who:

    • Did not respond adequately to previous biologic therapy, or

    • Lost response over time to biologic treatment.

  • Mirikizumab is also approved for adults with moderate-to-severe active ulcerative colitis (UC).

Mechanism of Action

  • Mirikizumab is a humanised IgG4 monoclonal antibody.

  • It acts against the p19 subunit of interleukin-23 (IL-23).

  • This results in:

    • Inhibition of IL-23 binding to its receptor.

    • Reduced production of pro-inflammatory cytokines.

    • Decreased intestinal inflammation.

Dosage:

  • Induction Therapy: 900 mg IV at weeks 0, 4 and 8

  • Maintenance Therapy: 300 mg subcutaneous injection every 4 weeks, beginning at Week 12.

Adverse Reactions

  • Infections:

    • Tuberculosis (TB) screening is recommended before initiating treatment.

    • Patients should be monitored for signs and symptoms of TB during treatment and after treatment.

  • Hepatotoxicity

  • Injection-site reactions

  • Headache

  • Joint pain

Vedolizumab (Option B): Vedolizumab is an anti-integrin (α4β7 integrin) monoclonal antibody used for Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis. However, the newly FDA-approved drug described in the question is Mirikizumab, an anti-IL-23 (p19) monoclonal antibody.

Ustekinumab (Option C): Ustekinumab inhibits the p40 subunit shared by IL-12 and IL-23. In contrast, Mirikizumab selectively targets the p19 subunit of IL-23, which is the distinguishing feature highlighted in the recent FDA approval.

Infliximab (Option D): Infliximab is a TNF-α inhibitor used in inflammatory bowel disease. It does not inhibit IL-23 and is not the recently FDA-approved monoclonal antibody described in the question.



Reference:
  1. https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39581202/

explanationHtml:
Explanation:

According to the 2024 ESC Hypertension Guidelines, patients with diabetes mellitus or CKD should be started on antihypertensive therapy if BP is ≥130/80 mmHg, provided blood pressure remains elevated after 3 months of lifestyle modification.

This is a major change from the 2018 ESC guidelines, which recommended initiating treatment only when BP exceeded 140/90 mmHg in these patients.

2024 ESC Hypertension Guidelines

  • The 2024 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines introduce important changes in the definition, classification, cardiovascular risk assessment, treatment thresholds, and blood pressure targets for hypertension.

  • The guidelines emphasise earlier recognition and treatment of elevated blood pressure to reduce long-term cardiovascular risk.

1. Definitions and Grading

Blood Pressure (2024)

Blood Pressure (2018)

  • Non-elevated BP: ≤120/70 mmHg

  • Elevated BP: SBP 120-139 mmHg or DBP 70-89 mmHg

  • Hypertension: ≥140/90 mmHg

  • Hypertensive emergency: ≥180/110 mmHg

  • Optimal BP: 120/80 mmHg

  • Normal BP: SBP 120-129 mmHg / DBP 80-84 mmHg

  • High Normal BP: SBP 130-139 mmHg / DBP 85-89 mmHg

  • Grade 1 HTN: SBP 140-159 mmHg / DBP 90-99 mmHg

  • Grade 2 HTN: SBP 160-179 mmHg / DBP 100-109 mmHg

  • Grade 3 HTN: SBP ≥180 mmHg / DBP ≥110 mmHg

Note: A new category of “Elevated Blood Pressure” has been introduced, highlighting individuals at increased cardiovascular risk even before they meet the definition of hypertension.

2. Ten-Year Cardiovascular Risk Assessment

The 2024 ESC guidelines recommend use of:

  • SCORE2 for individuals 40–69 years.

  • SCORE2-OP for individuals ≥70 years.

These tools estimate the 10-year cardiovascular risk and guide management decisions.

3. Target Blood Pressure: Recommended Target Systolic BP

  • 2024 ESC Guidelines:

    • Diabetes mellitus, CKD (eGFR >30 mL/min/1.73 m²), Previous stroke: 120-129 mmHg

    • Intracerebral Haemorrhage (ICH):

      • Immediate BP lowering within 6 hours of symptom onset.

      • Target SBP: 140-160 mmHg.

  • 2018 ESC Guidelines

  • Immediate BP lowering was not recommended if BP was <220 mmHg.

  • If BP was >220 mmHg, careful reduction to <180 mmHg was advised.

4. Management of Specific Disease Groups

Diabetes Mellitus and CKD

  • 2024 ESC Recommendation

    • Initiate antihypertensive therapy if BP ≥130/80 mmHg, after 3 months of lifestyle modification.

  • 2018 ESC Recommendation

    • Initiate therapy only if BP >140/90 mmHg.

This represents a major shift toward earlier intervention.

Heart Failure: For patients with symptomatic HFrEF or HFmrEF:

  • The 2024 guideline recommends:

    • SGLT2 inhibitors, in addition to

    • Drugs already recommended in the 2018 ESC guidelines.

  • The 2018 regimen included:

  • ACE inhibitors (ACEIs)

  • Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs)

  • Beta-blockers

  • ± Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs)

Continue lifestyle modification alone (Option A): Because the patient has already completed 3 months of lifestyle modification and continues to have a BP of 132/84 mmHg. According to the 2024 ESC guidelines, antihypertensive therapy should now be initiated in patients with diabetes or CKD when BP is ≥130/80 mmHg.

Wait until BP is ≥140/90 mmHg before starting treatment (Option C): This reflects the 2018 ESC recommendation for patients with diabetes and CKD. The 2024 guideline lowers the treatment threshold to ≥130/80 mmHg after an adequate trial of lifestyle modification.

Initiate antihypertensive therapy only if target-organ damage develops (Option D): 2024 ESC guidelines do not require the development of target-organ damage before initiating treatment in patients with diabetes or CKD. Persistent BP ≥130/80 mmHg after lifestyle modification is sufficient to recommend pharmacological therapy.



Reference:

https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/45/38/3912/7741010?login=false

question: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic kidney disease (eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m²) has a blood pressure of 132/84 mmHg despite three months of lifestyle modification. What is the most appropriate next step?

correctAnswer: A. Elevated FeNO and blood eosinophil counts can support the diagnosis when spirometry is inconclusive.
explanationHtml:
Explanation:

According to the GINA 2025 guidelines, Type 2 biomarkers, particularly Fractional exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO) and blood eosinophil counts, can be used as supportive diagnostic tools when spirometry is unavailable or inconclusive.

However, these biomarkers should always be interpreted in the clinical context, as their absence does not exclude asthma, and they may be altered by other conditions or corticosteroid therapy.

GINA Guidelines for Asthma (2025)

GINA 2025 defines asthma as a heterogeneous disease characterised by:

  • Chronic airway inflammation

  • Variable respiratory symptoms, including:

    • Wheezing

    • Cough

    • Chest tightness

    • Shortness of breath

  • Reversible airflow obstruction

This definition emphasises both the inflammatory nature of asthma and the variability of symptoms and airflow limitation.

Role of Type 2 Biomarkers

GINA 2025 highlights the role of Type 2 biomarkers as supportive evidence for the diagnosis of asthma.

Indications

Type 2 biomarkers are particularly useful when:

  • Spirometry is unavailable, or

  • Spirometry is inconclusive.

Recommended Biomarkers

  • Fractional exhaled Nitric Oxide (FeNO)

  • Blood eosinophil count

Note:

  • Elevated Type 2 biomarkers support the diagnosis of asthma but are not diagnostic by themselves.

  • Absence of Type 2 biomarkers does not rule out asthma.

  • Type 2 biomarkers may be elevated in conditions other than asthma, reducing their specificity.

  • Corticosteroid therapy may suppress FeNO and blood eosinophil counts, potentially leading to falsely low values.

A normal blood eosinophil count effectively rules out asthma (Option B): The absence of Type 2 biomarkers does not exclude asthma. Patients with asthma may have normal biomarker levels, particularly if they are receiving corticosteroid therapy.

Type 2 biomarkers are recommended only to monitor treatment response and have no role in diagnosis (Option C): GINA 2025 specifically recommends FeNO and blood eosinophil counts as supportive diagnostic tools when spirometry is unavailable or inconclusive.

Corticosteroid therapy increases FeNO levels, improving diagnostic accuracy (Option D): Corticosteroids suppress Type 2 inflammation, resulting in lower FeNO levels and reduced blood eosinophil counts, which may mask asthma rather than improve diagnostic accuracy.



Reference:

https://ginasthma.org/2026-gina-strategy-report/
